_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Welcome back comrades, this is MF Kraven & you are watching less than 10 mins reviews. The Youtube series where I take a look at games i think seem cool & give my thoughts on them in less than 10 mins.I review games simply by telling you if I think it's Buy it Now, Wait for Sale or Do Not Buy. This review is the Steam version & have been given a review key by Phoenix Labs.Fae Farm is a farming sim rpg for up to 4 players. Discover the magical island of Azoria plagued by whirlpools. Full of whimsy & wonder, help the island folk by exploring the island to discover it's secrets, all while farming, cooking, decorating & ranching at your homestead. But can Fae Farm help you escape your dull life to a magical place or is it just another farming sim? Let's find out! //Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//It's like chibis & Miis had a love session & created these lovable fae folk. The artstyle is charming, cutesy & cool all in one. Plus the soundtrack to this, while sometimes no appropiate give me heavy Vince Guaraldi Trio vibes, and once winter hits? I know I'm gonna have that soundtrack on repeat.//Gameplay//You arrive shipwrecked to the island of Azoria, all because of a pesky whirpool. You then meet the mayor where they give you a homestead & in typical farming sim fashion, you clear your unkempt property. As you explore the island you're given a net, fishing rod & staff, all accompanied by your everyday tools that mind you never break or take inventory space up as they magically appear when you need a specific one. The game really takes off a few days into it when you have to explore the mines, reach level 25 and learn what's causing the troubles of the island. //Price// 39.99 USD//How many hours estimated//I'm only about 7 hours into the game & have barely scratched the surface, //Is it Playable on Steamdeck?//Yes it is playable, and while i've played it mainly on my laptop. Post review I will definitely be playing it on my SteamDeck//Final Thoughts//If you played a farming sim, you've pretty much played them all. So how does Fae Farm stand against the greats?I like it, I don't love it, there's a lot of good but a lot of things that take me out of the immersion. For example, there are only 6 love interests, 3 guys, 2 girls & one Non-Binary. Just talking to townsfolk and the available in the first days love interests will get you to "flirtatious". How about you back off on the romance? I'm just talking to... ok Jack is mad thiccc. But the rest of the townsfolk are boring & add nothing to your experience even if you befriend them...Whenever trying to access the inventory shed, sometimes the almanac comes up instead and while you're in there- the sorting always resets to alphabetical. The farming on it, is just okay. only three crops to start you off with & to unlock more things you must level up your farming, how? by farming which i sort of like but spring is coming to an end and it's looking like i'm gonna have to wait till next year to plant the other spring crops.when in the mines, while i love that my pickax switches immediately to shovel if i need it, i don't appreciate my staff or wand turning into a pickax while I'm about to battle. which doesn't really matter in the grand scheme of things i suppose cause if you do end up going to 0 HP- there are no real repercussions. I experimented by being a sacrificial lamb & lost nothing, just kicked out of the mines... and if you don't get to bed by midnight, same thing no repercussions just wake up in your bed at 6am. But i suppose this is what will make it fall in the category of a cozy game, which can appeal to other crowds- I'm certain that I'm not the target demographic for Fae Farm but i digress.My last complaint is a simple one, time only ever stops if you have it paused. While making furniture or in any other menu, time just keeps going. This kinda made me avoid working on my house up to now...Now that you've heard/read my gripes, lets go for why I still think you should buy this game. It's fun, the cooking mechanics, opening up more options by cutting up ingredients not just roasting them over a fire is nice. Having to use more clothes or warmer/cooler food & drinks otherwise you're penalized by having some stamina taken away is a welcome challenge even if it is minor.I love how you can just aimlessly throw your character around, you wanna swim in that lake? Cool. You wanna jump on those cliffs? Cool! Plus tracking townsfolk in other farming sims is so tedious, and with Fae Farm you can literally just use magick to know where people are and the compass will lead you to them. It feels liberating to have more involvement with your movement in a game like this. It's easy to level up & improving your tools early on motivates you to get copper or iron ores to make the necessary improvementsThe world is beautiful & the portal system can be achieved relatively early on (by hour 5 of my gameplay i had all 4 portals). The progression, while stunted at times because of missions, it feels like a nice pace. Like I said, I'm not the target demographic but yet Fae Farm has won me over. I'm gonna buy a copy for my partner & perhaps even my son as he's shown interest in it & it's just a breeze to play. My only real concern is the price, for the Nintendo Switch it's $60! Luckily for Steam users it's 40$. But that still seems a bit steep, $25 seems perfectly reasonable I'd do maybe even $30 but those extra 10-15 could buy you a Stardew Valley... and Phoenix Labs have some work to be done to be at Stardew's level.I'd be happy to change my review to Buy it Now! if some of the bigger known bugs/concerns are squashed. But for now, it's a Wait for Sale!

_childDocuments_.review: I find this game to be fun to play but overall it has several flaws that effect my rating and enjoyment of it. The world is super cute to play in and explore. For me attending to and growing your farm is enjoyable and rewarding and the best part of the game. However I find that several other farming games have done that and even more much better than fae farm has, and for a better price point. The townsfolk have no depth to them beyond the one-line description you're provided upon meeting them. It makes romancing them tedious as you get very few dialogue responses. Some things aren't explained well and i've had to look up several things. Such as when summer starts and you get a letter from Holly saying she has new summer seeds in stock but when visiting her there's only spring seeds in stock still. It wasn't explained that you keep buying spring seeds and use magical fertiliser to get summer seeds. Overall, I would say that it's a fun game and with a few adjustments (and a lower price point) it could be an amazing game.

Not immediately, you have to play a bit, but WINGS!!! And if you play with friends you can join each other worlds and help them out or mess up their home. I highly recommend this game if adventure/farming sim games are your thing. Enjoy!

name: TEVI
detailed_description: OUR PREVIOUS WORK About the Game The protagonist Tevi is nimble and agile, wielding both her trusty dagger and an oversized wrench for dishing out melee damage in style. Alongside her, companions Celia and Sable manifest as two floating orbitars, ready to unleash a variety of ranged offensive and supportive magic in battle. Adapt your combat style to suit any situation and bring down foes with flashy, dazzling combos! Every boss fight is a unique challenge requiring different strategies to tackle, all while you dodge their attacks and look for openings to counter-attack. As bosses change phases, their attack and bullet patterns become increasingly challenging, and they can even unleash devastating special moves. Continual offense can put bosses into a vulnerable BREAK state, during which you can deal massive bursts of damage. Scattered across the expansive world, there are over 300 different items and pieces of equipment waiting to be discovered. These can enhance your abilities or introduce new ones, allowing you to find ever-more creative ways to navigate the world and find secrets. A cornucopia of equippable sigils can be freely configured to create builds tailored to your preferences and playstyle. Dive into the vibrant world of Az, in which you will discover various cities, regions, peoples, and civilizations, each with their own tale to tell. Meet a large cast of strange and colorful characters along the way. As their tales unfold and intertwine, you'll be drawn into a tale full of adventure, friendship, mysteries, and danger... Get ready to embark on an unforgettable adventure, writing your own epic journey alongside Tevi! The characters in TEVI are brought to life by some of the most well-known names in the Japanese voice acting industry. Their outstanding performances make for an even more vivid and immersive experience! Tevi（VA: Lynn） Celia（VA: Yoko Hikasa） Sable（VA: Natsumi Fujiwara） Zema（VA: Tomokazu Sugita） Vena（VA: Rie Kugimiya） And many more! Multiple difficulty modes for players of any skill level A vast and vibrant interconnected world with 40+ areas A sweeping OST featuring 70+ original tracks A colorful cast of 50+ characters with voice acting Over 300 pieces of equipment and abilities to collect More than 20 unique boss battles

short_description: Embark on an epic action-adventure as you slash, dash, and combo your way through a vast, vibrant world. Explore and uncover hidden secrets. Customize your build to triumph in spectacular boss battles. Experience a tale of mystery, magic, and mayhem in TEVI, a bullet hell metroidvania!

_childDocuments_.review: Most of the game is good, though there is one rather glaring problem. The story. Not because of the writing (though the writing is comically bad at times), but because this game is story driven. As a result, all important movement/progression abilities are gated behind story progression.What this means is that there despite the world being very large and interconnected, there is no real reason to go and explore it instead of just following the quest markers. If you try. you'll never find a special item, or stumble onto a boss. The most you'll ever find is a potion or sigil before running into dead ends you can't clear without critical items gated behind story progress. It is quite unfortunate considering that Rabi-Ribi had pretty much avoided this problem, I guess this is due to the difference in head designers.Other than that, combat is fluid, music is good, story... exists. Just a shame the exploration is rather weak. It's what's stopping the game from being 'great' rather than just 'good'.

_childDocuments_.review: You ever wanted to play Metroidvania with intricate, customizable combat mechanics where you could use findable upgrades to alter individual moves in your character's combos? Then TEVI is the game for you. This is a surprisingly large Metroidvania with some actual depth, as the combat and systems are fairly technical and very well considered. This is easily one of the best of its ilk I've seen this year, save for maybe Blasphemous 2. There IS a whole lot of dialogue, though, which might be a turnoff to some. Granted, the voice acting is fantastic, as it's delivered by some industry vets (Rie Kugimiya and Youko Hikasa, for instance.) If you care for it, there's also a ton of lore and a well-considered backstory.But the real meat is easily the gameplay itself. The story is fairly linear and the map is dotted with exclamation points telling you how to find the way forward, but there are places you can go early, even if it's just to hunt for collectibles. These are in the form of potions that grant permanent bonuses or little sigils you can equip that change up Tevi's moves. The bullet hell bosses are also showstoppers, so fans of Rabi-Ribi will feel at home here (as well as with the Rabi-Ribi-esque arcade machine you'll find.) This one's just very much worth it, even at launch price. Full review:

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to be honest: this game is not as good as its predecessor, Rabi-Ribi. Overall, I am still recommending this game because there is still a lot of fun to be had, and it is certainly a polished game; however, if you are looking for a new Metroidvania that can capture the charm of exploration, this game is not for you.So what's the issue with the game? Coming from a fantastic Metroidvania like Rabi-Ribi, I was expecting a similar experience going into this game, but it just fails to capture the charm of a Metroidvania. On your first playthrough, you are locked into following a linear story. There is an illusion of exploration, but it's not actually there:  This is incredibly aggravating from an exploratory perspective; there is no longer any excitement or drive to explore the world once you figure out this secret. And believe me, this is such an easy connection to make after the second movement upgrade  I think one of the biggest charms of a Metroidvania is the ability to diegetically find movement upgrades while exploring; they should reward you for exploring the world and reward you with cool stuff that unlocks even more of the world to explore. You should never feel like you need to explore a certain area, but you should feel like you stumble upon the correct path by chance. And the "correct" path need not be just one particular movement item either. Games like Hollow Knight where you can basically go anywhere after you get wall climb is a fantastic example. It's just not the case in TEVI. There is only 1 real path to progress your exploration.Now, I understand that the game wants to push a certain narrative that isn't conducive to Metroidvania-style exploration, and I think that's fine. But I think it's certainly possible to have story progression without locking out entire areas behind the game with "let's not go this way right now." Like why not just block off the boss room of an area that's story related instead of blocking off the entire area? There were a handful of times where I got an exploration upgrade, and I didn't even know it! For example, I obtained a poison resistance item that would allow me to navigate poisonous areas without taking damage, but I obtained this item before ever even going to such a place. It almost feels like a completely moot item. There was no "Aha! Now I can look around X location" because I had never encountered X location to begin with.And my final point regarding Metroidvania exploration is that the overall area exploration room to room was incredibly frustrating. While room layouts have a wide variety of enemy, puzzle, or platforming focuses, the overall map structure was horribly contrived. What I mean by this is that TEVI's areas are riddled with 1-way paths. And it's not just a handful here and there, it's constant and ubiquitous. Even upon obtaining every movement item in the game, I am constantly finding myself not being able to easily navigate to where I want to go in a map because of all the 1-way paths. Semi-solids will block you from going down while crumbling blocks will prevent you from going up. Even going left and right can be blocked by slide passages or bomb blocks that are only accessible from 1 side. It's absolutely maddening to explore and incredibly not fun. What does this mean? Basically because of all the 1-way paths, even the exploration is basically linear. There have been an egregious amount of times where I thought there was 2-3 ways into a room only to learn that there's actually only 1 way into a room. It's absolutely disappointing. Like for ♥♥♥♥'s sake, even if you want to force me into a linear story, at least let me have the freedom to explore an area however I like!Now, there is a "Free Roam" mode that allows you to freely explore the map without any story triggers blocking your way, and it even gives you a reverse wall jump technique to help you sequence break more, but this mode is locked behind story mode: you need to beat the game before you can access this mode. Now this mood does solve the issues I've outlined above much more, but the issue is that it's an extra mode you unlock after beating the game. If you've already beaten the game and experience the forced story that herds you into every movement upgrade item, what's the point? Is Free Roam going to be that much more fun when you already know where 90% of everything is? Yes, it does make a few changes to the movement item's locations, but they aren't really that different at all. It feels like a weird bandage added to the game because they knew it would not have the Metroidvania charm but honestly, this should have just been the game from the start. Find a different way to implement the story after that.There are additional modes that are a bit interesting too, like the "Random Sigils" mode, which randomizes the locations of Sigils. This is an interesting game mode in theory, but in practice, Sigils are just badges. They affect combat (damage, mana, health, etc.) but they have no impact on exploration at all. It's a neat attempt at a Randomizer at least, but it's certainly not good enough compared to real fan-made Randomizers.Metroidvanias come in all shapes and sizess, and TEVI (and its predecessor Rabi-Ribi) took a unique spin on the genre by adding bullet hell to its enemies. It's a unique Metroidvania X Touhou genre that honestly elevates the experience. I think the boss fights were the most fun aspect of this game. They were a good mix of challenging yet fair. I really felt like I needed to learn a lot of bullet patterns to beat some of the bosses (before I learned how to kinda cheese them with OP Sigil setups). And although a 2D platformer bullet hell is quite different from an aerial bullet hell, a lot of techniques can still be relevant like fine weaving, streaming, and so on. In fact, the skills learned from other 2D platformers (like its predecessor Rabi-Ribi) can also be applied to this game. It really tests your ability to feel comfortable controlling your character and understanding how you can move them.This game lacks the core fundamental exploration of Metroidvanias. The movement progression is ultimately linear, and even when you have every item, navigating areas can still be linear with constant 1-way paths. You are never rewarded for going out of your way to explore but instead are punished with the lack of ability to go very far without following the story. That said, the boss fights are memorable, fun, and unique, and the combat and movement overall feel very fluid. The game still has a lot of great content, and if you just want to play a more straightforward action adventure game with great bosses then it's still worth your time, but if you're looking for a good Metroidvania, then this is not the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100% completing the achievement list (yes all 100 achievements). I think I finally can say my opinion with solid ground. First of all, DO NOT expect this to be Rabi-Ribi 2, it's just not in many aspects. However, that'll come up later in the review. So let's get on with the goods: gameplay (excluding story)when you compare the controls and the things you can do as the character to Rabi-Ribi, this game wins by a lot. It takes a while to get used to creating your own full set of combos, but its pretty satisfying to pull off. Rabi-Ribi is simple, a bit too simple compared to this control scheme. Voice acting is pretty spot on (and funny at times with how much I've heard their voices during animes). It lets me enjoy the story like watching an anime sometimes, but I'll talk about the story a bit later on. Bosses/bullet hells are pretty nice, as long as you don't play on the actual hardest difficulty, you'll have a good time with them (that is, if you enjoy playing bullet hells in the first place). mechanics and the boss designs/ bullet designs are pretty fantastic, just don't expect a new kind of bullet in every boss fight. otherwise this game would be huge just to contain the assets for each boss's bullets. Music is as usual fantastic, nothing to say about it other than saying that it's good. Map and Background designs (the looks, not the layout) are pretty upfront with how they made Rabi-Ribi, it's better than Rabi's maps imo. The map layout is pretty standard for a metroidvania style game. Although sometimes I wanna punch the person who design some of the boxes... OK, now towards the rather "poor" factor of the gameExploration...? Movement items? Where are they, oh wait, it's locked behind the "S T O R Y". yeah... coming from the extremely free-paced Rabi-Ribi and expecting TEVI to be a similar was pretty disappointing. I found myself to be looking for the movement items when i first played the game and only realized they are ALL locked behind the story after a few hours. I'm not saying it's bad for them to lock them behind said story, but coming from Rabi, it just feels weird. Oh yeah, the " S  T  O  R  Y". It is L O O O O O O O N G as heck. I didn't calculate the time, but from my first play-through of 30 something hours, maybe a third or even half the playtime was sank into the story (i feel sorry for the VAs otherwise, i know, my problem). And not only it's long, it is a pretty generic story too. But then again, i think it being generic is just the problem of expecting something that's extremely new into the modern game realm. Perhaps the story would be praised if it is a few years back. Sigils... wait what? aren't they supposed to be fantastic? Well, here's the thing, they're TOO GOOD in some combinations.  Once you know those combinations, you won't go to experiment how fun it would be to try some other things. And this leads to the final problem i have with the game. Powercreep, hold on... this ain't a pvp game, the hell this is doing here? What i mean is that you can just melt the boss if you go out to get a few items and stat boosts. Then they can't do anything but perish (though technically you can't do the same with the final boss, but eh).Overall, I enjoyed the game on first play-through and going for the full list, although it was a bit dry with the hardest difficulty with the last problem. Kinda sad there's not anything to do after the game ends though.The problems when comparing to Rabi might be a bit unfair, since they never said TEVI is Rabi 2 kind of game. _childDocuments_.review: TEVI is, at the end of the day, an inferior Rabi-Ribi that's been meddled with by people who didn't understand what was so good about Rabi-Ribi itself. While it has a number of small improvements that iterate on RR's solid foundation (more moment-to-moment combat options, and more build variety), ultimately the vision has been watered down into something more forgettable, and if TEVI were the game released back in 2016 instead of Rabi-Ribi, it would not have stood the test of time, and we would have never gotten a sequel. Let's get into why.However, let's be fair and discuss what the game does well, because that list is both long and deserving of plenty of praise.TEVI, being a gameplay-first game, delivers on that front with a combo-heavy, stylish boss rush sandwiched by meaty segments of calm, engaging exploration with a truly satisfying number of secrets to find. Enemies all typically have gimmicks to learn and respect beyond simple contact damage, and there are a number of times where theorycrafting an advanced strategy (such as manipulating enemy position for an optimal dropkick-bounce) can earn you a stat upgrade before you're supposed to be able to acquire it. The world this all takes place in is diverse, colorful, delightful, and, at times, downright depressing. The tone is all over the place, but rarely in a way that feels jarring or thoughtless. The gradation between the aesthetic of each area is often sharper than I'd like, with few visual indicators as to what area you're about to head into when going through any particular area exit, but that's really a nitpick and hardly something Rabi-Ribi ever thought about, either.The boss fights are also appropriately difficult, though advanced players or Rabi-Ribi veterans will be displeased to learn that the game's highest difficulty is locked behind completion -- a fact that is couterbalanced by the ability to adjust the difficulty any time from the MC's bedroom -- a location that is accessible during the vast majority of the game. Nevertheless, the bosses have been... toned down, both in difficulty and otherwise, and it's such a shame because Rabi-Ribi's greatest strength WAS its boss fights. There's far fewer flashy bullet-hell attacks, and you can really sense that the one designing the boss attack patterns definitely cared too much about whether a given attack was visually or thematically fitting for a given boss instead of if that attack was fun to negotiate with or not. Granted, the fun is still there, to be had, but it's toned down.And "toned down" is a phrase that, unfortunately, applies to most of the game as well.The character design and tone of TEVI, in my opinion, is probably the single biggest downgrade from Rabi-Ribi, going from one to the other. TEVI is not really a happy game -- not like Rabi was, at any rate. TEVI has many depressing moments and somber locations, and the character designs are much more down-to-earth, less provocative, and -- key point here -- much less memorable. More western-looking, too, which is definitely a your-mileage-may-vary thing, but personally, I would take the Rabi-RIbi art style any day of the week. It was much cuter, and while there is certainly a decent amount of cuteness to find in TEVI (there are two... let's call them "secret" characters in a visitable in-game casino, who PERFECTLY demonstrate that this team can definitely make adorable designs!!! It is within their power!), I just have to ask:Why?I'd like you to see these quotes from one of the higher-ups involved with the production of this game:>"Tevi was developed by the team behind Rabi-Ribi and has made many attempts and improvements: enhancing the art style and combat experience, adding a more complete story, and adding voice acting.">"We analyze some factors that we believe are the obstacles to Rabi-Ribi’s marketing, such as a weak storyline or anime art style that might not be very appealing in the Western gaming community.">"In the early days of the studio, we tended to do whatever good ideas came up, regardless of what kind of genre or how well the market was performing."Do you see the problem? I'm not one to spin a tall tale narrative about the choices made by developers I have never met, but I cannot help see statements like that without getting the impression that Rabi-Ribi -- one of my favorite games of all time -- is seen as... embarrassing, to some of the people who helped make TEVI into what it is. Embarrassing, without realizing that "cute, happy, sexy, high-octane, super-difficult, exuberant metroidvania punctuated by thoughtful-yet-transitory moments of sorrow with a kick-ass, downright-DANCEABLE soundtrack" is exactly the one and only thing I ever wanted from Gema-Yue. There are just... so many depressing metroidvanias out there. So many dark ones. So many ones trying to inspire dread or fear or loneliness or just trying to be like Metroid. So many ones that tread the same damn ground, and it seems to me that a desire to go where others have gone before turned what was probably a much better in-dev concept for TEVI into something that, despite trying to be something special, ended up turning into something more run-of-the-mill. In trying to "improve," the foundation suffered for it.So, those quotes regarding the art style do anger me a bit. Rabi-Ribi's art style did not need to be "improved," and the tone did not need it, either. What Rabi-Ribi needed was, at the end of the day, just an editor and some more thoughtful moment-to-moment dialogue.Guess what? TEVI actually has that, and it IS a breath of fresh air. Having a three-person party is probably the singular biggest upgrade TEVI has over Rabi-Ribi. The characters play off of each other, and Tevi is a wonderful protagonist. I can't say enough good things about her. She's charming, she's funny, she's endearing. She goes through genuine grief and has some pretty damn soulful motivations for what she does. Even the sillier motivations you can still "feel," deep down. Celia and Sable are both welcome for playing off of her at pretty much every opportunity, too. Personally, I'd have preferred if Sable was a girl, but that's just a matter of personal preference. Either way, aside from some very small moments of contrivance, I really believed in their slow, meandering road to becoming friends throughout the journey.And what can I say about that journey? That it took place in a wide, sprawling world? Yes. That it was appropriately long and satisfying? Sure. That every twist made sense?NOT BY A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LONG-SHOT, LMAOI cannot begin to convey to you just how many useless, throwaway characters this has. I cannot begin to convey to you just how long you go throughout the game without realizing what the ultimate evil you're opposing even is. I cannot begin to convey to you what an absolute FETISH this game has for twists you could not possibly have foreseen walking up to you and clocking you straight in the face. I won't belittle the writer of the game. I know writing is hard, as someone who writes, myself. I don't know their circumstances, but I do know that the story of TEVI, for all the HERCULEAN efforts it goes through to "improve upon" Rabi-Ribi's story, ends up being about the same level of quality -- a little better in many places, but a lot worse in a few key ones, too.That's really the story of TEVI, as a game, too. Two half-steps forwards, one big-ass step back. Blunders mixed with a plethora of tiny improvements and tweaks. However, I'm running up against the character limit, so let's wrap this up.  NEVERMIND. RABI 2 IS ON THE WAY, BOYS.

_childDocuments_.review: Tevi is a game I was looking forward to a significant degree and even participated in the beta that launched just a few months prior to release. While initially rough around the edges in the Metroidvania department, it had a charm that was enjoyable and didn't truly detract too heavily from what I enjoyed from Rabi Ribi.Flash forward a few months later to release and I find myself... disappointed? I want to really like this game, the art is great, the presentation of the levels and the music is sometimes even a massive step up from Rabi Ribi. Yet, why do I feel so underwhelmed?I see many praising the combat but for the most part it feels like it's trying to be fast paced while forcing you to hold off from attacking despite there being no feasible reason to, since most bosses in this game have patterns where they're just standing still vulnerable in place for a solid minute. While I understand the intent of the 'dominant' and 'submissive' state, the former being a superarmor mechanic with high defense; it feels like a system that's just there to make boss design simpler to design while making the average enemy a lot more tedious to deal with since it applies to every single enemy in the game.The metroidvania aspect just feels somehow tacked on? One of the biggest charms of Rabi Ribi was the existence of hidden techniques like the wall jump and routing which allowed you to complete the game without one of the most crucial items to your damage output, such as your hammer and bombs! In fact, I think they even let you skip ribbon for a while if you really wanted to. But in Tevi, I've found myself feeling like I'm on rails until the game decides most of these areas are open. Which for most games? Fine, it works. But one of the core parts of what makes Metroidvania's so fun to me is the fact that you can approach the world in mostly your own way even with an obviously intended path placed in front of you.As for the levels? So many of them are laid out with enemies that do a large amount of damage in really thin corridors while having the fore-mentioned super armor state after you wail on them for a while. Often making it so you have to play it slow and safe to pass through levels carefully. Strangely enough, this game includes a mechanic where enemies do more damage before they're killed at least once in a stage, which just feels... like a strangely weird and artificial way to handle new areas being difficult? Maybe I'm just being nit-picky here.While the presentation of the levels are great, the actual layout is not as ideal as I'd like. Rabi Ribi made it clear that there were some objects in the area that you couldn't exactly reach in the present, but I haven't had too many experiences with the like in almost eight hours of playing this game, often forcing me to just plant bombs at random corners and pray for an upgrade. Not a huge gripe, but a tad annoying when the game this is a spiritual successor to, does it better.Food items also require you to farm out a resource instead of buying in a shop; at first glance, this seems like a system to prevent you from having to backtrack to a shop over and over... But on the other, it's really annoying to farm over just buying them when you truly need them to crutch out a boss encounter.The story is a bit incessant and in your face when it doesn't need to be; I don't mind a story and I think Tevi's has been pretty alright so far, but it often breaks the pace of the gameplay; especially when some of these conversations only amount to small banter between the characters. Honestly, I'd personally prefer if these scenes were optional so you could approach these at your own pace.I could be wrong about there being no hidden techniques or routing and I'd honestly hope I am! Tevi has the foundation to be a great metroidvania but it just lacks the polish that I previously found in Rabi-Ribi. (Granted, I'm not sure if Gema-Yue even had a huge role in the development of Tevi) Ultimately, I don't think TOO negatively of the game; I just feel like I'm a bit underwhelmed with the game we got. If you're on the fence about Tevi, I'd still personally recommend it in most cases; I just wouldn't go in with the expectation that this will be 'Rabi-Ribi', which the developers seem to be very aware of, considering Tevi is a .TLDR; Tevi is good but underwhelming despite all of the personal complaints in this review, pick it up if you want an alright metroidvania. Just don't expect it to be anything like Rabi-Ribi fundamentally.

In RR most of them you had to buy it from Miriam with the exception of golden carrot.> Combat is significantly improved where enemies have state that determines how easily you can interrupt/stagger them, which can occasionally send them to flying (same thing can happen to you!). This applies also to bosses, though only if you break their toughness which is very well thought!> More quests available and it doesn’t have to be done in chronological order always.> Puzzles are more challenging in general, especially the way how you have to use your bombs to break through obstacles. > As much as I was a fan of farming EN (currency in RR) from defeating enemies, in TEVI you have to go out of your rway to find Zennies (currency in TEVI) as resources from blocks, which encourage a player to pay more attention at secrets.> The amount of sigils (badge) that this game offers is, compared to RR, outstanding… it offers so much different playstyles you can play on TEVI!> Unlike RR, where it is sometimes not possible to change the difficulty in mid-game. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Rabi-Ribi and consider Tevi a solid improvement, albeit it's still lacking in a few areas. I would nonetheless recommend it as a meaty metroidvania with a huge amount of areas and collectibles. are extremely solid. I had no issues with visual clarity during combat, which can break a bullet hell. Despite the huge amount of areas and visual variety, no areas feel "too flat" like some did in Rabi-Ribi. The only thing that felt inconsistent were the non-chibi enemies in  features some clever platforming and a couple of puzzles that were way better than I was expecting. were a mechanical highlight and I always appreciate difficulty options that alter patterns instead of simply fudging numbers. Few games put as much effort into difficulty options and balancing as this.The  has some real bangers.In contrast to the area music, I found the  forgettable. That made me far less compelled to grind them despite enjoying their mechanics. I think bullet hell bosses work best when coupled with outstanding character music as seen in Touhou and Undertale.The exploration falls into a couple . Several times I returned to areas after getting what felt like a meaningful ability only to realize I still needed a later ability to do anything, which is partly due to the  being woefully inadequate. For some bizarre reason they are the same as uncollected item markers, making them blend together. The arrow markers are not nearly enough to remind yourself of what ability you might need.Another questionable choice is opened  closing once you leave an area, which combined with the amount of one-way passages, results in a frequent feeling of the map lying to you while you re-explore for collectibles.The , despite being more interesting than Rabi-Ribi's in terms of world/lore/characters, still suffers in the long run. Because the game wants to introduce so many characters for bossfights, we end up with a lot of loose threads that don't come together for the end. The main plot itself ends up being surprisingly generic despite the effort put into the world and lore.

_childDocuments_.review: TEVI's everything we were promised and more, as expected of the team behind Rabi-Ribi. I love the art, the game in general, and the rewarding exploration. I'm going to enjoy this thoroughly. Unfortunately there is something that bugs me, and perhaps it's not that big an issue for most if any, but knowing both Japanese and English makes the translation feel botched and distractingly misaligned from the voice acting. I'm deeply considering disabling the fantastic vocal work just to enjoy the story as its written without the nauseating disconnect between what the actors are actually *saying* in Japanese to what the English translation has effectively ad-libbed poorly. It's well written, don't get me wrong, but it's also so far off the mark half the time that the jokes just don't land or hit right and it feels like tons of information is just *cut* from the dialogue.- Another note, since this seems not to have been fixed from the demo. There seems to be a script error that crashes the game if you alt-tab any longer than 10 minutes. Perhaps some kind of audio overflow or the like.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished 100% map and 100% items, all bosses and most npc sidequests. 78/100 achievements. I played the entire game on "Hard" difficulty.This is an excellent game - if you liked Rabi-Ribi then this is a no-brainer. It's very polished.It's an action platformer metroidvania - much like regular metroid / castlevania games. The game has a deep skill system that allows you to customize your playstyle around a few different archetypes. I found it quite fun to turn on/off sigils that would alter my combos and see how they worked. The combat gimmick is that most bosses (and some enemies) turn the game into a bit of a bullet hell. Most bosses have a super move or three that basically requires you to dodge bullet hell patterns for a while.Story and NPCs are well-written and very well voice acted. Art is fantastic, as is the music. Level design is mostly fantastic, and there are some great puzzles for some items. Combat is pretty fluid and predictable.Traversing the world is pretty fluid as well - especially once you unlock some fast travel. Map exploration is generously rewarded in this game.There are some minor issues:- Some of the areas have one-way paths that are really quite long. I found it REALLY frustrating at the end when I was cleaning up items and map cells. One area in particular is really bad about this.- You can't open the map for a small period after a map transition. This was intensely frustrating for certain side content, and when quickly traversing the world.- Bosses tend to enter a "I'm going to super move for 2 minutes and basically be invicible" mode when their health gets low. I'm not good at bullet hells and I found this really annoying. Touhou players will probably enjoy this. I wanted to fight.- Map completion percentages are super confusing and almost useless. They DO track correctly, but it's not intuitive what they're tracking at all.Tl;dr: Game is excellent, well worth $30. Rabi-ribi is also excellent - play both of them. Strap in for some difficult bullet hell sections and lots of backtracking.

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest point of comparison when I jumped into TEVI was Hollow Knight. And TEVI, by probably a landslide victory, has the far superior boss fights and combat. I really can't think of any other games I've ever played in my life that has had boss fights as intense, enjoyable, and empowering as the ones in TEVI. The average boss in TEVI probably has 4 times as many abilities and attacks as the ones in Hollow Knight, with some of the later ones completely dwarfing the competition too, and it really blew my mind seeing just how far boss fights in video games could be taken. The combat in TEVI also blows Hollow Knight's out of the water, with a huge variety of attacks and combos and equippable badges that change parts of your kit that you can find all over the world. TEVI I also found to be significantly more replayable. With a host of New Game+ options right out of the gate on release, they let you strongly customize and tailor further playthroughs to your liking with many options, from keeping equipped badges, to making bosses harder, faster, and many more. I've only ever replayed Hollow Knight once, but I can see myself replaying TEVI again and again.After TEVI, I tried out Rabi-Ribi, the other game by the devs of TEVI, and it also has a massive host of tough boss battles that manages to go even further than TEVI, but RR has been out for a much longer time and has had post-launch DLCs that have added more and more to that game. I did also feel like TEVI is a lot smoother and responsive to play, RR felt a little laggy by comparison. Things like quick hops to jump-rope over many floor projectiles, has a short cooldown before you can hop again, so after immediately touching the ground you can't jump right away, things like that added to the laggy feeling. Have not gotten all too far into RR though as of writing this.The one thing that I believe Hollow Knight trumps TEVI in, is its world and atmosphere. It does a masterful job at setting the mood and engrossing the player in a world that is dying and decaying, whereas TEVI feels a bit more.. themeparky in a lot of areas. Both games have stellar soundtracks but I think TEVI's got a lot more catchy tunes, and HK is more focussed on using its background music to set the atmosphere and mood of the world.I won't touch much on it, you can probably read some other reviews to hear more about it, but I didn't think TEVI's story was good. The voice actors, however, are incredible at their work and are an absolute pleasure to listen to.Overall, a glowing recommendation from me, and on to my favorite games of all time. The devs are also absolutely committed to engaging with player feedback and changing the rough parts of the game for the better, which is phenomenal.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Rabi Ribi then this game is for you. It feels like the spiritual sequal to that game and improves upon all the mechanics of that game. So far the story has made me laugh, cry, and say out loud "That's what she said lol!" There's full on japanese voice acting too which is amazing. Been waiting forever patiently since its release date was announced and I am not disappointed. The dev team behind Tevi deserves all the love for giving us such a fantastic game.
_childDocuments_.name: TEVI

_childDocuments_.review: As a very big fan of Rabi Ribi, Tevi had a lot to prove, but in the end I ended up liking Tevi even more than Rabi Ribi.The soundtrack of Rabi Ribi was undoubtedly a master piece, so good that you even want to listen to it on youtube. Tevi's is at least on par with it. Each soundtrack emphasizes the beautiful visuals perfectly. I think the soundtrack doesn't betray it's roots while possessing it's own identityAs for the art, many seem to complain about the style. I understand where these people are coming from. Compared to Rabi Ribi, Tevi's art is inferior but in no means badThere is so much fan service for Rabi Ribi fans in the form of references. Even Ribbon and Erina appear and they even got voices! I was so surprised. I mean there are not many ways to make old fans happier than with this.  There is also a Rabi Ribi mini game and other easter eggs. Hearing old Rabi Ribi tracks being used in this game even made my eyes a little wet :')I don't have to say much about the gameplay, since it is as good and fluid as Rabi Ribi'sA bit refined with crafting but the core gameplay is essentially the same My only slight complain would be the difficulty. As a rather casual player, Rabi Ribi was pretty hard by default which was a nice challange. Tevi on the other hand was rather easy (on normal) I had to set it to hard+ to make it how I expected normal to be. Strangely, the difficulty in Tevi's demo was perfect, I don't know why they nerfed it. But well, since you can change the diffcutly anytime without consequences , this is hardly a complainWhere Tevi really shines is the story. The story is not just in the background like in Rabi Ribi, this time it is a proper story with twists and turns and lots of (voiced) dialog, many likable characters and an interesting world.Tevi as a main character is also very likable with her strong and independent personality. I can't imagine anyone to not like her.My playtime for a single run was around 52h + 6h to 100% the map100% recommendation (you should play Rabi Ribi before this, since it would be a shame to not get the references)

_childDocuments_.review: MASSIVE improvement over Rabi Ribi.Gameplay is basically more of the same, but even more fluid. You no longer need to manage a "hold button" charge along with another to mash for melee attacks, so that allows for melee combos to become more elaborate as you have less of a mental stack to manage the shots. Ranged combat itself is far better for it too, you can either dump tons of damage at once with multiple charged shots or pace them alongside with the combos (although the target always "unstaggers" after a while). Customization is also huge with sigils, to the point where it kinda becomes a con. Building Sigil loadouts is a double-edged sword where you get to customize a build to perfectly enhance the way you play or cover your shortcoming, but managing the Equip Points can be an boring task when you're juggling which 8* you're dropping to make space for 2 4* or vice-versa.Boss design is also an huge leap. Unpopular opinion I guess, but bosses in Rabi Ribi weren't that good. They were too much bullet hell and not enough metroidvania. For a genre blender, it was massively unbalanced. This time around though? Perfection. Bosses have (most of the times) reactable patters while also not constantly pissing bullets everywhere. The actual bullet hell segments are left for the fight's climax only, which makes for a much better pacing and challenge. You can also turn the hitbox for it to be always on in bosses which makes the fight far more manageable.The game isn't easier though. It's still borderline frustrating if you just beeline it to the story's boss and never explore. Hard+ and Inferno is still a gauntlet for the aficionados. Even regular enemies can be your downfall up until the very endgame when you're truly and well overpowered.And this time around, the story actually makes sense! Because the true ending of Rabi Ribi feels like the dog ending in Silent Hill 2, but instead of being an easter egg you unlock as a fun sideshow,  it's the climax to the whole game. In here, story makes sense throughout and the whole just just feels like a coherent story. Art style is also a massive improvement. Prettier HUDs, menus, user interface, backgrounds, character sprites, and more. Plus an amazing OST in boss fights.Really, Tevi is a hit on all sixes. I have some gripes with how the story doesn't actually come full circle and leaves some questions unanswered, there's a couple of stages where the level design REALLY pissed me off (Verdawn Forest fog map can go ♥♥♥♥ itself), some songs get annoying, but none of these issues drag the overall quality down. Tevi is just consistent all around, showing that even if nothing really "new" is done it can still be enjoyable if it's just polished enough. Lessons were learned, improvements were applied. Can't ask for more from a game that was already good really.

_childDocuments_.review: Suffering from it's own success, as a standalone metroidvania, Tevi is a fantastic game, but standing next to Rabi-Ribi the boss battles and soundtrack feel a bit dull and lacking in spectacle, and the more free objective system has been dialed back to a more linear experience to go with it's larger focus on story.Still having a blast, but I do miss the 1000 cherry blossom style boss fights of old
_childDocuments_.name: TEVI

_childDocuments_.review: Solid spiritual sequel to Rabi-Ribi. Interesting gameplay mechanic additions and the exploration aspect is more fleshed out. Difficulty seems a bit lower. Boss fights are excellent but unlike Rabi-Ribi this doesn't feel like a bossrush game, for better or worse. It's more of a balanced metroidvania game. Movement mechanics are more gated behind progress and basically all mechanics are tutorialized instead of being left to player discovery.TEVI still suffers from having to unlock higher difficulty modes over multiple playthroughs and repeat the same metroidvania collectathon between them. Personally annoying since I mainly want to see the boss fights on Infernal, not hunt through hundreds of rooms for items again.I prefer the more linear stage design introduced in the Rabi-Ribi DLC (TEVI has linear & boss rush sections near the endgame, these feel similar) and would be more keen to replay such a game across different modes.In TEVI even though the exploration & secret hunting are improved: if they're not the games strongest point is it really worth expanding to be a bigger part of the game? (eg. exploration taking up more hours between every combat & boss section). Same goes for the story being more of a focus, but I don't really mind.For presentation I found the music to be great much like Rabi-Ribi. In-combat visuals are nice and it's generally clear to see what's going on, combining well with the snappy controls. That is apart from a screen shake effect introduced during a couple specific boss attacks that just makes it hard to see what's happening.

_childDocuments_.review: the game doesn't really feel like a metrovania for the first play through since every traversal option is story gated, there is back tracking but you'll not find a secret boss or a major upgrade. You can backtrack to find stat boosters which is nice but there's no sequence breaks or finding encounters that you you shouldn't. Even if you do make it to places earlier than you should there's nothing to do, NPCs won't talk to you until you progress the story properly. I assume the developers wanted to focus on the story of the game, everything seemed to take a back seat to the story, but even then it feels rushed or lacking. Characters are introduced and killed or forgotten not even 100 words of dialog later. They supposedly have a deep backstory with our characters but I can barely feel any of that connection. I want to backtrack and talk to NPCs as story elements are found but aside from main story related events most characters go missing. Talking to previous NPCs just leads to dead end dialog from the last moment they were relevant to the story. There's barely any side stories or side quests to flesh out the characters either. There's a lot of unsettled story elements by the time you finish the game, I want to find out what happened to some NPCs but there's no way to find or contact them. You want to write a story with emotional moments, but you're not even invested in your  own characters to flesh them out. Loved the voice acting it was a nice touch and must have been expensive, but that alone can't carry the game's story. It's only upon clearing the game the first time do you get the "free roam" mode. I assume the developers did this to focus on the story for the first play through, but it is a let down that your first time exploring, isn't exploring. and by the second time you'd have already known everything the game has to offer. the sense of explorations would have already been lost. I found myself bombing every wall or attempting to slide into every corner possible and often being rewarded for it. The crafting system/ upgrade seemed lacking? by the end of the game I had a surplus of yellow gems over purple gemsand only a few food materials that you cared about crafting only required 1 element. upgrades don't even require elements and just general materials and the yellow/purple gems. If I needed to craft or upgrade something the bottleneck would almost always be purple gems. Except frost elements, but those were story gated and almost everything's final upgrade required frost element. When you do find it though you'lWhat really carried this game for me was the combat system, leveling, and sigil systems, but the amount of sigils you'll end up with at the end of the game can be overwhelming. combos felt nice and the boss fights trying to maintain combos while dodging bullet hells was what made the game for me. jump puzzles and traversal for the most part felt nice too. I do wish there was a dedicated dash/slide button though. wanting to dash but accidentally jumping instead is quite literally the opposite of what I wanted to do, the same goes with air dashing but ground slamming instead.Overall I still had fun with the game, I rarely got bored or frustrated with it for that i "can" recommend it but it's definitely lacking in a lot of aspects that could have been polished or fleshed out more. Too many things took a backseat to the story and that's unfortunate. But still a fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: Like other reviews say, it's not quite as open as Rabi-Ribi, on the contrary, it's very tied to it's story which can be a hit or miss, depending on the player. _childDocuments_.review: Up and down its content, Tevi is among the best metroidvania's in the genre, and I don't say that lightly with the sheer quality that's out there. Tevi takes the formula of Rabi-Ribi's metroidvania and bullet hell  concepts, and takes it to the next level with a combat system that's deep, engaging, and really rewarding with the sheer variety of options that it presents. Boss battles are the highlight, forcing you to dodge complex strings of bullets while setting up your own combos in the process. Exploration in the environment may be slow at first, but will turn into some fantastic platforming challenges that won't turn into frustration fuel. It helps that the content here is beefy: coming in at 30 hours with 50% of the items collected on a Hard Run, and that's not hitting some of the extra content and other various things you can do.The story while having links to anime tropes, does a great job of establishing the three main characters are a Trio that you want to see a lot more of in the future. They work off each other rather well, providing good humor and emotion while still being believable in the overall plot of the game. The game can get wordy at points, but you don't mind with some of the storytelling here, and the character portraits are fun to dissect while trying to determine what's really going on . The music is in the top 3 of the genre if not the best, almost every track does a superb job of capturing the area/feeling that its going for, and many of them will make their way to your daily playlist. The minimal negatives which I feel are nitpicks are overshadowed by a package that will satisfy even the most hardened of critics, and is something that you need to play. Like now. :
_childDocuments_.name: TEVI

_childDocuments_.review: Tevi is a game that places the focus of its content in two very distinct places.The first is that of a deep combat focused metroidvania. Stuffed full of movement options, combat options, and collectible power ups drip fed to you over the duration of the game. Everywhere you go you're being given more power in an addicting loop.  It rewards you for taking every path. It rewards you for experimenting with new gameplay options. It rewards you for carefully examining the 100 different paper mario style badges you've collected. And after weighting the options, equipping the 75 that best meet the task at hand. Or best meet the style of gameplay that tickles your fancy.The bosses are touhou style bouts of bullet hell, in which you're dip diving and dodging whilst you weave in your fanciest and most well thought out combos in between the onslaught of bullets. When you're not fighting bosses, you've blazing through the world dropping a bomb in every corner on the off chance that there's a hidden item there. Usually there is. Whilst you do this a small army of tiny cute critters try to slow you do. Half of them are functionally unable to harm you. The other half make you wish you were playing on an easier difficulty. At some point towards the end, unless otherwise required, I simply dashed my way past them to get to the next boss. Not cause I wasn't having a good time with the silly critters, but because I was having an absolute blast with the bosses.The second focus is on the characters, narrative, and world. Unlike some other metroidvania's out there, Tevi has a visual novel shoved into it's otherwise gameplay centric experience. I quite enjoyed seeing the world and story unravel, and enjoyed the contrast between the ridiculous characters, and the harsh realities of the bleak world they inhabit. I laughed at least once, and was sad at least once. I usually don't even bother with the story in a game, I'm a cut scene skipping kinda guy. Yet I didn't skip a single scene, highest praise I could give the story of a game. It's uniquely light and fluffy in how the characters are presented and interact with each other. While maintaining a sufficiently heavy cream of emotions on top. It won't blow your mind, or usher in a new literary era of games as an art form. But it might get you to care about a fake rabbit girl and her whacky friends for a few hours.That being said, in order to access most of the game, you have to progress the story. Once you've beaten the game, you can play through the game again without the limitations of having to progress the story to unlock more of the game. It does feel a little linear if you let the story carry you from point to point, and don't take the time to go back and explore other areas yourself. People not at all interested in the story may feel slighted here, but I say it's worth the feeling of slightedness for the juicy gameplay bits.I beat the game on hard+ in about 21 hours. I felt quite satisfied with the story, exploration, and gameplay bits. In summary:I loved the game. It rules. 4/4
_childDocuments_.name: TEVI

_childDocuments_.review: Tevi is no Rabi-Ribi 2. If you liked Rabi-Ribi there is no guarantee you'll like this one. You can tell that Tevi is a passion project. It's polished, visually stunning and controls great. There is an incredible game in there somewhere.But Tevi struggles with presenting its more heavy themes properly, characters are too busy explaining things than showing actual personality. If they aren't explaining they're making bland low brow, and oftentimes inappropriate jokes. Early on a long time friend of Tevi gets introduced and dies 15 minutes later. Right after that Tevi banters with her pervy Caretaker figure. Scenes like that give emotional whiplash. Tevi as a main character is also so full of herself and incredibly competent at literally anything she does, it's hard to connect to her.While the pixel art is endearing and the CGs beautiful, the actual character designs just don't quite hit the mark with me. They're busy, more edgy than they really need to be. And to me personally it seems like they're just not doing the leg work required for a good design in a serious story. Tevi seems to always settle with just "it looks cool".The game does get so frustratingly close to getting things right a lot of the time. Sable has some great moments and even Tevi does too, when she's showing some genuine vulnerability in a moment of emotional instability.Rabi-Ribi does actually have a lot of these same issues, but it's intentionally smaller scoped, more focused and decidedly less ‘serious’'. Simpler designs, world, story and characters but few well executed emotional hooks.I am still excited for more projects by this team. I just really wish they'll take a step back with their next game.
_childDocuments_.name: TEVI

_childDocuments_.review: -Cleared on Expert-Most of my opinion was likely influenced from playing Rabi-Ribi recently along with playing the playtest. Overall, TEVI is a very fun game: it's not quite as good as Rabi-Ribi, but acceptable nevertheless.Story: 2/5Coming out of Rabi-Ribi, the story started off a bit interesting since it didn't seem like a lighthearted throwaway plot (not to say Rabi-Ribi's story was bad). Going to the relicts first more or less created that vibe. However, around the time I got to the last 2-3 chapters: the plot just becomes pretty forced. Alot of times I just wished that were options for multiple endings  if I went to a certain region first or had a specific item in my inventory before continuing story (like a certain bell you get), but instead there seems to be no divergence in story progression. There was one point in the game that I thought a decision mattered, but I think it was just  By the time I reached the final area, some scenes pretty much had me thinking, "why in the world would you have any doubts at this point" or "the enemy isn't even trying to persuade you to give up." So, the story isn't outright offensive, but it definitely falls apart after a certain point from being too forced.Gameplay: 5/5Obviously this game was meant to be sold mostly because of gameplay and it's great. Playing the playtest made me assume that I had already gotten my hands on all the sigils I'd be using for the main game, but instead there were plenty more to try out. For someone who played Armored Core VI, coming out of trying out mech parts and swapping them out for different encounters: TEVI gave me the exact same feeling when picking between using a loadout for general exploration, grounded bosses, or aerial encounters. Just like Rabi-Ribi, there would be plenty of times that I'd find a boss I like or disliked and then I'd make self-imposed challenges based on how much effort I wanted to put on the boss. In Rabi-Ribi it would be like, whether I wanted to clear the fight damageless (for achievement), no bunny amulet, or simply no consumables used. In TEVI's case, self imposed challenges could range from: limiting sigils, no consumables, no core expansion, no soul burst, I'm not quite sure about golden dodge but I guess that's an option too. Now, while golden dodge and core expansion are very cool new mechanics added to the game, I kind of wished that bosses counter played against these systems a little more. Yes, some bosses disabled core expansion: I think that's relatively good as is. Golden dodge on the other hand, while it is an amazingly fun way to play the game and maintain as much uptime on the boss as possible: I personally wouldn't mind more forced downtime or even better; more risks during during mechanics to make uptime scarier to maintain. The catacombs had that doom mechanic and the moment I got it: I assumed I'd be seeing a boss with that mechanic added in.  In a sense, I guess I'm saying that due to all the system mechanics that let you bypass some mechanics of fights, while having no achievements to take no damage from bosses during the whole fight: it feels like you can just facetank some bosses pretty hard even on expert every once in awhile. Maybe that issue would be resolved when I play BBQ difficulty, but generally it just feels like a FFXIV raid situation where, "oh I got hit, I should've died or came super close to dying, instead I just got damage down debuffs." When I saw some achievements that were like, "witness X special attack," I was immediately thinking that some bosses would have instant kill mechanics if you got hit. Nevertheless, the bosses were mostly pretty entertaining all the way to the end. Moving away from battle, the game had a decent amount of exploration to do just like Rabi-Ribi. Due to the introduction of cross bomb and cluster bomb: it was entertaining to try to find all the items instead of expecting a 1:1 Rabi-Ribi exploration experience. I imagine plenty of Rabi-Ribi players were disappointed with the lack of hidden techniques to effectively explore everything in chapter 1 out the gate.  There's probably much more to be said about gameplay, but this is what comes to mind right now. There were an enjoyable amount of Rabi-Ribi easter eggs in the game, and I was actually thinking of the chance that Erina and Ribbon would show up as a hidden boss, Graphics: 4/5I mean, it's Rabi-Ribi 2. Not much else to be said here. Though, seeing the CG every now and then was really entertaining. Some attacks are way more prettier than others to see, like .Audio: 4/5The music in this game is VERY good, but what makes this better than Rabi-Ribi especially after playing the playtest (which didn't have it): is the mental whiplash of hearing voice acting. I used the Rabi-Ribi voice mod for when Erina gets hit and simply hearing Tevi voice lines when dodging, attacking, getting hit just felt so shocking after hearing nothing in the playtest. The voice acting despite the lackluster story is really good. The only problem with the audio preventing it from getting a 5/5 would be that some long scenes with dialogue have no music playing whatsoever. While it is very motivating to hear Replica start playing mid dialogue, there were way too many moments where I'd expect to hear a bgm of some sort during a cutscene and nothing is playing at all, making the scene feel kind of awkward.Game Time: 5/5The main story would've probably taken me about ~16-18 hours without excess exploration. Given how there's going to be free DLC and probably more DLC in the future; this is good amount of game time while not dragging on whatsoever. Side Comments:- I know they patched it once, but tornado spin has been accidentally inputted SO many times that it's potentially frustrating. I'd personally wish for an option to map it to a shortcut instead of being manually inputted. Ironically I use cross bomb so often with the manual input that I rather have tornado spin replace it as the shortcut instead. So I would actually just wish that some special commands were just mappable to shortcuts instead of an option toggling obscure input methods.- I expect a chance of triple jump being enabled in the future with DLC or more bosses with a multi-jump mechanic like Malphage, but in spite of this: I wish hover could be activated by triple jumping instead of needing to hold up then jumping. The option to hover is so forgettable in boss fights that I ended up beating the game without hovering during bosses despite some boss mechanics probably wanting you to hover.TEVI is 100% worth playing if you love metroidvania games. The freedom to move around may not be as good as Rabi-Ribi initially, but if you enjoy challenging boss fights with freedom on character builds: then the game will surely be worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Tevi is another great game from the same makers as Rabi Ribi. Excellent metroidvania bullethell game - maybe not as good as Rabi Ribi and the plot starts falling over a bit at the end, but the game is still really good. Also, the music is way better than most other AAA games, let alone indies. Seriously, the soundtrack is awesome, just play the demo for an example of some tracks.Just... fair warning, it is a much darker game than Rabi Ribi. _childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the biggest positive: The boss battles. The game has over 10 bosses, and almost all of them have more than 10 patterns, which then have harder variations when the boss is at lower health. Every single boss is carefully-crafted, bringing entirely unique experiences that challenges the player in various ways. I played on the Hard difficulty, and found it perfectly-balanced. There are healing items that you can craft, but as you can't craft mid-battle, and healing items are generally very weak, you are still forced to learn to dodge boss attacks (and not just use heals to tank damage). TEVI has mastered the craft of 2D platformer boss battles, and if you are a fan of the genre, you'd be doing yourself a disservice by not trying TEVI out. You will not be disappointed. Just the boss battles alone would be enough reasons to buy this game, in my opinion.The combat is also very well-designed. It has optional depth - you don't need to understand most of the systems to beat the game (even at Hard difficulty). The Sigil system, for example, can be manually optimized to find the optimal "build" for each boss, but for most players it is perfectly possible to just treat it as an upgrade system where you can undo upgrades.TEVI is categorized as a Metroidvania on the store page, but I would say that it is actually a JRPG packaged into a Metroidvania. If you're expecting something like Hollow Knight (dark atmosphere, hostile environment, loneliness, vague goals to work towards while exploring), you won't find anything like that here. This isn't a bad thing, just that if you're genre-savvy, you may want to adjust your expectations. TEVI has a JRPG-like plot, and the game is segmented into several chapters. Sequence-breaking is almost-impossible by design, and although with skillful platforming it is possible to get to some areas early, you are just not rewarded for it. You'll be following quest markers to advance the plot, and aside from a few exceptions you're not given the opportunity to do them out of order. All of this means that TEVI plays more like an RPG where you do platforming to travel around the world, instead of walking on a top-down map. It is kind of like Megaman ZX in that sense. As TEVI has the length of a JRPG (30+ hours), the map is also really, really big, filled with visually-unique areas each with unique ecosystems and enemies. A small nitpick would be that these areas rarely have any landmarks (not counting towns/cities), but it's clear that most of the art budget went to the bosses.The weakest part of TEVI is unfortunately, its story. Let's just say that most of the plot points are pretty obvious to anyone who's played a few JRPGs, and the writing is generally lacking in subtlety, often telling you what a character is thinking when you could've guessed correctly on your own. This is  if you've never played any JRPG, or if you're buying this game for your children, but otherwise it really isn't that impressive. It's a shame too, because usually the writing is where indie games excel. The silver lining is that the Japanese dub is solid (as always) and the story CGs are really pretty.Overall, TEVI is definitely worth your time and money. The boss battles, especially.

_childDocuments_.review: It has better art, comparable music, a much more ambitious and complex story, full voice acting, and on paper is an upgrade over the developer's previous title Rabi Ribi. That said, I flat out had more fun with Rabi Ribi and was disappointed that this game didn't captivate me the same way RR did. In RR, the controls were simpler, the story was stupid and self aware, the music was catchier, and the game didn't take itself too seriously. This team, despite putting significant effort into worldbuilding and setting in this title, aren't telling a world class story with multi-layered characters. They're telling a maybe above average story that's constantly undermined by anime tropes and characters in skimpy outfits. There wouldn't be anything wrong with this if Tevi didn't take itself so seriously. Rabi Ribi, on the other hand, leaned into the fact it was stupid and was the more fun game because of it. I can only recommend Tevi if you've played Rabi Ribi already and want more of this team's high quality gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: The bosses mixed extreme balance issues ruin this game. It's a bummer b/c the controls are very smooth and mostly feel good, although the button mash system is a tad repetitive.Already by the second boss; WAAY too hard, and can literally destroy your game. I mean it; your save file is screwed. In theory you can change difficulty, but there's a save point right before the boss, and you're for some reason not allowed to go back to town until after the fight if you need to modify the difficulty, or just to farm more.The second boss for some reason has THREE health bars. Why???? Each health bar also has WAY too much health. You literally just sit there mashing one button on the boss for a while, trying to play perfectly. I got to this point, tried for hours, couldn't lower the difficulty, and I'm absolutely not starting over due to failed balance issues.Now lets discuss the difficulty settings. It's always super cringe when a game has 6+ difficulty modes. Just make 1 or 2 and balance your game properly. Every game I've seen with a zillion difficulties has problems in all of them: some things are far too easy and some far too hard. A game SHOULD be reasonable to beat on the hardest difficulty for any trained life-long gamer. If that can't happen, for gods sakes have a way to pad the game in-game. But also note... people who really need more extreme difficulty will make the game harder themselves: that's NOT the job of the game developer. Perfect examples: 3-heart runs, speedruns, etc.P.S. The game has issues with input where sometimes it just stops accepting input and you have to task manager force close the game. This happened to me during boss fights multiple times. Can you imagine spending hours on an obnoxious fight, get to the end, and the game randomly fails?
