_childDocuments_.review: Tips for making homemade pizza:Here are the basics. I go into LOTS of detail in the post below, (and in my two sister posts, Pizza Sauce and Pizza Dough), so keep reading for more info.Use a homemade dough with lots of flavor. I will bore your brains out about how to achieve this in my Pizza Dough post.Use a decent Pizza Sauce (here’s my recipe)Preheat your oven at least 30 minutes. Yes, really, set a timer. I don’t care when your oven beeps to let you know it’s reached the right temperature. Wait 30 minutes.Par bake your pizza crust to make sure your pizza has a crisp bottom and a cooked centerUse a pizza stone for crisp edges. Sorry, this is kind of nonnegotiable. Your oven sucks at pizza making. You need a hack.How to make Homemade Pizza – Step by StepThe best part about pizza is that it is actually pretty quick if you have everything ready to go. I’m going to share my exact method for baking pizza that I have been using for about 10 years now. It’s tried and tested, and results in delicious, crispy-edged, perfectly cheesy pizza every time. The first thing you must do is preheat your oven up as high as it will go. It takes longer than you think to heat your oven up all the way! You want to give your oven at least 30 minutes to preheat. If you have a pizza stone, make sure it’s inside the preheating oven.What temperature do you cook homemade pizza?The answer is always going to be: as hot as your little oven can go. For nice ovens, this can be up to 550 degrees F. For kinda crappy ovens, they are not going above 475 F. Pizza is traditionally cooked in 900 or 1,000 degree ovens. We can’t get our ovens at home quite that hot, but we want to get as close as we can. Figure out what your oven can do and crank up the heat.How to roll out pizza doughStart out with about 12-16 ounces of dough. I worked really hard to perfect my Pizza Dough recipe and highly recommend it! But any pizza dough, homemade or store bought, will work for this recipe. Prepare your work surface. I know most people dust the counter with flour, but I find that you risk ending up with a tougher dough this way. Too much flour = tough crust. (If your dough is very sticky, using flour is going to be just fine). Instead, of flour, I usually drizzle some olive oil right onto my counter. Use your hands to rub it around. Place your ball of dough in the center of your work surface and use your hands to press it down, starting from the center. Keep gently patting out the dough, moving the dough outward from the center. I like to leave a pretty healthy crust on the edges of my dough. Continue patting and stretching the dough gently with your hands until it is about 12 inches across. Of course you can use a rolling pin if you want! (Use your hands to lift up the edges of the pizza when you are done to get more a lip for the crust.) At this point, transfer the dough to a square of parchment paper. I highly recommend using parchment paper because it’s SO much easier transferring your pizza into the oven.Stretch and arrange the dough on the parchment paper. The dough shrinks a bit when you pick it up to transfer, just gently stretch it out again. Drizzle a bit of olive oil over the top of your dough. Use your hands or a pastry brush to rub the oil all over the top of the dough, especially the edges of the crust. This layer of oil helps the toppings stay separate from the dough, helping it cook more evenly. It also tastes delicious, especially on your crust, hello. If you love a thicker crust pizza, let the rolled-out dough rest for 10 minutes at this point.Do you need a pizza peel?A pizza peel is that wooden board with a handle that you see restaurants using to transfer pizzas in and out of the oven. I don’t have one, because a flat baking sheet works just as well, and takes up less space in my kitchen. But I’m sure you will feel super fancy using a special peel?? You do you. You’re going to need something flat for this next step:How to par bake pizza crustOnce the oven is up to temperature, we are going to do a 1 to 2 minute par bake. This step is technically not necessary, but I never skip it. It guarantees a thoroughly cooked crust. Nobody wants a doughy pizza, yuck. Use your pizza peel or a flat baking sheet to transfer the pizza dough and the parchment paper onto your pizza stone, pizza pan, or baking sheet. (I always just pull on the paper to move it onto the stone). Transfer to your stone or pan, shut the oven door and bake for 1-2 minutes, until it is slightly puffed. Use your pizza peel or flat baking sheet to remove the pizza (still on the parchment paper) from the oven. Poke down any bubbles. Leave the crust on the peel while you add the toppings. Start out with pizza sauce, of course.What cheese is best for homemade pizza?Mozzarella, mozzarella!! It’s hardly even pizza if there is no mozzarella, right? You need Parmesan too. You can use pre-shredded regular (low moisture) mozzarella from the store. It’s what I use most of the time. Mozzarella that you shred yourself is going to melt better though. The shredded stuff has anti-caking agents added to it that inhibits melting. If you are feeling fancy, you can also try out fresh mozzarella. (all the final photos in this post actually show regular low-moisture mozzarella fyi) You can find fresh in the deli section of your grocery store. While you are there, pick up a block of parmesan so you can add a couple tablespoons over the toppings of your pizza. Parmesan adds that little umph, don’t skip it. My biggest tip for getting the best melty cheese situation on your pizza is to use slices of cheese AND shredded cheese. You can use regular mozzarella for this, it doesn’t have to be fancy fresh expensive mozz. (sometimes if I don’t have block mozzarella I’ll even use string cheese!) Add a few thin slices of cheese to your pizza, THEN top with more shredded cheese. Using slices makes for the BEST melty cheese situation!Bake the pizzaOnce you’ve got your toppings on the pizza, it’s time to bake. Slide the pizza directly onto the pizza stone. I used to leave the pizza on the parchment paper while it baked, because it’s really easy to move the pizza where you want just by pulling the edges of the paper. But you will get a much crispier crust if you remove the parchment paper for the final bake. (The stone is porous and absorbs moisture, so that moisture doesn’t end up in your crust.) Your crust is sturdy enough after the 1-2 minute par bake that it’s not too hard to move the pizza onto the stone without the paper.How long to cook Homemade PizzaOnce your pizza is in the oven, you need to cook it for about 8-12 minutes. This is of course going to depend on how hot your oven is, and how thick your pizza is. The crust should be golden brown, and the cheese should be bubbly and also starting to brown. If you don’t have a pizza stone, use a spatula to lift the edge of your pizza to make sure that it is browning all across the center on bottom. If the bottom is still white, you are looking at a doughy pizza. No thanks. Leave it in longer.Homemade Pizza for LifeOkay, is that everything?? Do you have any more pizza questions? Let me know in the comments what I missed! I hope you get to make pizza soon. It really just never gets old, right?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very manic platformer that rewards speed and precision, that while easy to beat encourages completionists to challenge themselves.This goofy little game is an absolute treat. The story is goofy but simple; Peppino is running a pizza shop (that's barely getting by), when a sentient floating pizza called "Pizza Face" shows up and threatens to blow up his shop. The already anxious Peppino refuses to let that happen and in a manic state chases the guy down.The gameplay is fun and fast, and when you do well you can just TELL you're doing things right. You got dashes, sprints, groundpounds, ways to cancel and start your momentum fast but also options to let your momentum carry you. The game has a combo system that rewards more points (and needs to be maintained for the coveted "PERFECT" rank) if you can keep grabbing point items or defeating enemies (and just getting hit isn't enough to break it; but you gotta recover fast. Minor slipups are allowed, if you're quick!), and the game naturally rewards you to try to get through levels fast, even if it's not TECHNICALLY necessary.Levels themselves follow a pretty routine loop; Enter level, scour it for secrets and "toppins", the collectables needed to progress, use the level-based powerup or gimmick to continue through it, reach the Pillar at the end and destroy it triggering an escape sequence where you must get back to the exit (usually through an alternate route) before time runs out, and the adventurous can even redo the escape sequence without extra time for bonus points (And the coveted S and P ranks). This leads each level to feel like a fresh experience, if their wacky environments weren't enough already.Music is hella good. All great for the environment, with a nudge for the funky. They often keep me bopping even as I keep replaying levels over and over again.The graphics look like they were drawn in MSPaint, but in such a loving way that they recognized and fully abused how weird it would look to the fullest extent. Animations are always insanely exaggerated, things always lean on the absurd and honestly, it helps drive the sheer insanity of the situation.So for difficulty; the game isn't that tough to beat. You need to get the majority of Toppins in levels but most of them are right in the middle of your path, or so close to it that basic exploration will find it. And you can't DIE per se; getting hit just loses points. The only loss condition is if time runs out on the escape sequences (and even THEN, that only spawns Pizzaface; to be sure it's tough to escape as he's fast and just beelines straight to you, but you CAN outrun him), but that time limit is VERY generous; the game intends for you to beat the sequence TWICE on it after all. For people who just want to get to the end you probably won't have too much issue.But this game SHINES for those who want completionism. Each level has 3 secrets, plus Gerome the Janitor PLUS a locked door you need him to access. On top of that, S Rank requires you get all of these in 1 run AND do Lap 2 (the second escape), all at once (and P Rank asks you do THAT while doing the whole level without dropping your combo once). For the completionists, you will be using his full moveset, you are going to be trying levels over and over trying to get used to every single minor dip, wall, climb, enemy, pit, etc. What results is a beautiful self-satisfaction when you finally manage to get that one perfect run!So if I have to name flaws; The movement is great but sometimes it's not as responsive as it FEELS like it should be; I often feel myself getting stuck to walls, or bonking into them more often than I'd like (Hi Bloodsauce Dungeon). To be sure you get used to it, but it does lead to more than a few awkard "LET GO OF THE WALL PEPPINO WE GOTTA RUN" moments.And that's about it. This is a goofy whacky game about an anxious as hell everyman pizzashop owner who just wants to save his shop, who will literally march through hell and back if he has to. I love it. I'm now trying to 101% it. I'm not sure if I'm gonna do the Noise stuff, but even so, I'm gonna be enjoying this for a good while!IT'S PIZZA TIME!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a rare thing for a game to be so exactly like another game, but without being a carbon copy to have its own wacky identity.  Once there was a game called Wario Land 4 which, much to the Wario formula, devised levels that you ran through to find secrets, then scurry back to the exit when the timer ticks down.  It was an ingenious idea to make you rethink the level while backtracking, and add some extra tension.Pizza Tower is that very spiritual successor of a marvellous game concept, but with its own fresh style, additional gimmicks, and manically-terrified protagonist.  The controls are shockingly simple for how much versatility you get, though mastering them is a test of reflexes.  That said, the game is perfectly manageable for those who don't speedrun for a hobby, allowing a brisker pace when needed before the dreaded Pizza Time comes calling.A few of the level gimmicks do become frustrating, but the game never stays on one mechanic for too long to be bored by it.  It's fun, it's bouncy, the music is maddeningly good and does a wonderful job giving each level its own unique identity, along with the Klasky-Csupoesque art style that truly reflects Peppino's desperation.  Order up this game, it may be a bit spicy, but the taste is well worth it.

It means the levels are designed very cleverly to be played both ways and there are various twists and turns as you go. The art style may be divisive, but it works remarkably well in my view, especially in just how expressive it is. The game may appear garish and ugly on first view, but it's genuinely beautiful when you actually play it for yourself.The soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. It strikes all the right moods and helps keep the game entertaining and vibrant.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest. I have some mixed feelings about this game. I enjoyed a lot of my time playing it, but I don't have a lot of people I would recommend it to. It's probably because I'm getting older, but my friend group and I just don't have the wherewithal to spend hours upon hours getting every achievement. And this game is just BEGGING for you to replay every level, multiple times.It gives good reason for that replayability, too. Every level is unique and well designed, and it gets a lot of mileage out of it's platformer mechanics. The art direction is incredible, and feels at home with something like Earthworm Jim, and Ren & Stimpy. The off-the-wall style really matches the frenetic pace at which you'll be moving a lot of the time.However, that frenetic pace is also part of what is turning me off from replaying it over and over again. You can disagree, but a big part of me wishes that this game was a bit more chill. Granted, that's just me not meeting the game on it's own terms.In short, if you're looking for an interesting platformer reminiscent of Warioland and Donkey Kong, then this is an easy recommendation. _childDocuments_.review: Pizza Tower feels like a Wario Land parody thought up by Tim Buckley. It's fine, but it radiates with such a pretentious ego, like it thinks everything it's doing has never been done before and it's better than everything that came before and everything that will come after. And to it's credit, it's not bad.Pizza Tower is a solidly designed platformer. The mechanics are solidly designed, as are the few levels that I was able to play, the game is fast-paced and rewards boldness, and the combo system feeds into this encouragement of speed. Despite much of the game's base being derivative of Wario Land, the building blocks for a brilliant game are all present. All these mechanics all come together to form a fun 2D platformer, in theory. However, Pizza Tower manages to falter on its very nature.I'm not sure how much sense this makes, but Pizza Tower is addicted to its own hype. When playing this game, I get the sense that the developers believed everything they were doing was brilliant and hilarious. Everything looks like it was drawn in Microsoft Paint. Things are poorly drawn on purpose. There's a rat named Brick. Much of the art feels like it was drawn for the sole purpose of trying to get the game memed into oblivion. I want to love this game, but its pompous egotism makes it hard to love. It's trying too hard to be funny, weird and attention grabbing, which makes it boring.I would not say Pizza Tower is a bad game. It's a good game trying to be something it's not, and it's not a game I could recommend happily.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a term called "flow" in game design, and it's pretty much what it says on the tin: a state players achieve when they are so absorbed in what's happening that there is not a single other thought in their mind. Never have I encountered a game designed from the ground up to help you perpetually achieve this state. As soon as I'm done beating Pizza Tower, I'm going to immediately start a fresh save and beat it again, but better this time. I want to play every level until I know every jump, obstacle, and enemy placement by heart. I am driven to complete every single level and accomplish every task. I want to climb every mountain it puts before me and complete my love for it, because there certainly was a lot of love and effort poured into its creation. That's evident in every insanely smooth animation, every banger of a music track, and every little detail sprinkled about every corner of every single screen.Pizza Tower is something special. Forget the "indie" prefix; GAMES like this only come around once in a good, long while.

_childDocuments_.review: Pizza Tower is a game that wares its inspirations on its sleeve. On this very store page, the developers say that they are inspired by the Wario Land series and it shows in the main character's moveset and level design. One of the places where I appreciate it most though is the music. There's also a fair amount of Sonic in this game's design philosophy. There's a lot of rewarding of maintaining momentum and memorizing the layout of levels. Pizza Tower is able to manage whatever tone it wants for any given moment: humor, panicked rushing, thoughtful puzzling, horror, are just some of the moods individual levels excel at. One other thing that I feel should be touched on is how referential the game is while also having a strong identity. While other Italians who can run and jump quite well, pizza restaurants, pizza mascots, and a few memes are all referenced alongside a crossover with an obscure PlayStation platformer, Pizza Tower remains its own world with its own lore and characters. I highly recommend for anyone even remotely interested in 2D platformers.

_childDocuments_.review: The term "masterpiece" has a fascinating history. For millennia, artists were craftsmen who belonged to guilds. They frequently entered them when they were very young. Andrea del Sarto began at the age of 7, and Michelangelo began at the age of 13 in Ghirlandaio's workshop. They went through a learning process that could last as little as twenty months (in Venice) or as long as 13 years. You were a "journeyman" in the end. Art has the power to shake us up from the ground up, like an earthquake. It has the ability to deeply affect us on a soul level. When it does this, I believe we can legitimately bestow the title "masterpiece" on the works of art that do so. After all, that is why they are there.

_childDocuments_.review: First, I love the style. I grew up watching Ed Edd N Eddy, and to me this makes a great way to help people understand why I did. This game encapsulates the artistic nuance of the '00s perfectly.Gameplay-wise, I love it. There's a lot to see and explore and do. Despite being the kinda guy who really enjoys perfecting things, I didn't feel like staying around to study and perfect the levels myself. I know I could totally do it with time, and maybe that's why I don't wanna.When you're trying to get the most out of it, this game very much tells you what to do. Maintaining a "combo" comes down to reading the game's instructions effectively. It's perhaps the most forthcoming about it compared to lots of similar games. Mastering a stage isn't exactly simple-- you have to be comfortable getting into a flow state to do things as fast as you need to without panicking. But there's so little flexibility outside of researching the stage and then applying what you know that I'm just not curious about applying the effort.Katamari Damacy is similar, but the actual execution it tests you on is a little "gameplay awareness" about how to roll the ball most effectively and where items are on the map. Sekiro does something similar on an enemy-by-enemy basis. Punch-Out is basically also the same.But, I dunno, I appreciate Katamari allowing you to take a fuzzy approach to mastering stages. Sekiro and ULTRAKILL also let you take fairly fuzzy approaches to mastering fights as long as you don't make too many mistakes in sequence. The moment I P-ranked a few stages, I took a step back and said, "Yeah, I get it. I totally get it. It's fun. I just don't want to 100% it. I have lots of games to play which does exactly what it does while also letting you try to get a little creative about it."I tend to enjoy when "perfection" in a game is a checklist that makes for an excuse to keep playing, so long as I find the base gameplay fun. It just feels like, to me, the base game is so plain that the entire show ends up being about perfecting stages, and I don't really feel satisfied with doing it just because the game asked. Sekiro just asks, but half of it is about the experience, the story, the themes, and also there's many ways to interact with many different enemy attacks that it's not just nearly exclusively call-and-response like this game.With how basic the core game is, however, I can't imagine any way to get more replay value out of it than P-ranks, so I can't really fault it. It's fun, but it's just not something I'm going to spend like 50-100 hours playing.This is a markedly better speed game than Sonic, and is basically everything I think Sonic should be at a baseline. Peppino feels fast without being too fast for the screen. The speed gives him power, and the "flow state" of rapidly performing the expected inputs for various challenges is nice.I feel like speed isn't that cool without an element of freedom, though. There really isn't much to Pizza Tower if you're not going fast. Most diehard fans would even agree. I think one thing Sonic was attempting that was stronger in concept was the ability for Sonic to be a precise platforming character and also blindingly fast. I feel like fast and slow should be distinctly different styles with different gameplay emphasis on each rather than one being "better" than the other.Even though Pizza Tower encourages you to go slow at first to explore and research stages, I'm just not excited to do so in order to set up P-ranks, and the base gameplay is still so basic that I'm not doing it because I enjoy the options which slow-Peppino has. So why am I doing it? To say I've beaten enough of the game? To be able to leave a review like, "50 hours in Pizza Tower, yep, still boring. Did all this just to say it was still boring." As a note: I'm even more resentful to the idea of doing this because I have friends who play the game who think I'm just opposed to the idea of trying to do that. It's really not a matter of "giving it a try." I've P-ranked a few stages. I've beaten boss rushes in Sekiro. I beat Punch-Out Wii. I'm capable of learning. I just think there's a line I draw where I actively refuse to get satisfaction from something THIS simple. I've spent more time justifying not playing Pizza Tower while than playing Pizza Tower, which to me has been a more interesting puzzle than actually P-ranking more stages.Pizza Tower, to me, doesn't feel rewarding because there's very few decisions I can make other than choosing to do what the game tells me to do. ULTRAKILL lets you use many different guns to answer the threats of enemies. Sekiro's mechanics involve lots of physics and variables for you to play with in your efforts to master bosses, sometimes allowing you to find very unique solutions rewarding of your insight, while still requiring you to be very confident with certain tight challenges.Even within that box, Sekiro's inputs such as guarding give an extreme level of visual and audio feedback to accent the fact you did something, and to make amends for the fact it may have been a simple process such as "we asked you to guard this attack and then you did that, good job."However, I do want to one day come back and grab some P-ranks for the experience of just savoring the environment that some levels have to offer. I'm pretty sure that's basically the point. It's just a small way to create more meaning from the gameplay without being too obtrusive.Highly recommended, worth trying and beating, but most of the outstanding length for most people is from coming back for P-ranks. P-ranking stages is basically the final form of the game. If that sounds unappealing, the standard playtime is probably enough. This is about as simple as a game gets without being a story-driven role-playing game, and is one of the few that makes notice of its skill progression whatsoever.

_childDocuments_.review: I've 101%'d the game and gotten both speedrun related endings for both characters.I say this with zero exaggeration. Pizza Tower is the best 2D platformer that you will ever play and it's not even close. The controls are super tight, the speed is visceral, and the content is plentiful. Not once in this game will you ever feel like the controls or movement are limiting your ability to play, unless of course you're unaware of said movement, or you're old and your reaction time isn't what it used to be. Pizza Tower managed to enthrall me, a guy who rages at platformers, and keep me captivated. Not once have I ever gotten mad at this game, only my own inadequacy. The levels are wonderful, built to be rushed through, yet designed deliberately to always keep you on edge. Of course though, there are a couple levels that don't live up to the absurd standard that is set, but even those outliers are still superior to almost any outside experience.Additionally, I thought there was no way they could add another character with a whole new moveset and have it be as fluid, intuitive, and controllable as Peppino's. Boy was I ever proven wrong. Noise mixes it up like nobody's business and looks absolutely ridiculous while doing it. This is the type of content other lesser games might lock behind DLC, except that if it was it would actually be worth the price. It's just that good. Ultimately, it should be said that this game is not perfect. But boy does it do a great job at making itself out to be. Worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game if you like speedrunning or score attacks, playing the same stages over and over to make improvements. But for normal play, Pizza Tower isn't great. The game wants you to move quickly—a lot of moves require you to run uninterrupted for a while. The level design, though, stops you constantly. If you're supposed to move quickly, why are the levels labyrinthine? The first time you encounter most rooms, there's so much to process in them that you have to stop and look around. Every level also has several secrets hidden in walls that are indistinguishable from the surrounding area, so make sure to bash your head into every wall, ceiling, and floor too. Am I going fast and ignoring the scenery, or taking my time and exploring? The mix is awkward and annoying.If you want to play each level only once, then you're in for a boring experience, because the game poses no challenge. Getting hit only affects your score; you can't die. Falling in a death pit just respawns you right outside the pit. Winning isn't satisfying when you can't lose.On the other hand, if you want to use the game's many movement tools to clear stages in record time, you're in for a rough ride, because the time requirement for each stage's speedrun achievement is really tight. The game had demos for years before release, and people played some of the levels to death. The devs probably adjusted the speedrun times to be way too tight, catering to a rabid audience that had a lot of time and very few levels to play.If you want the opposite experience, and you want to slowly explore and appreciate each stage, say goodbye to most of the mechanics in the game. The game's scoring principles (defeating enemies in succession to build your combo meter, etc.) and momentum-based gameplay vanish as you laboriously ground pound, uppercut, and shoulder tackle every surface.The level design is full of nondescript rectangles, and the enemies don't do anything interesting or do much to impede you. The gimmicks unique to certain stages actually detract from the normal function of your character, making you wish you could just move normally.Pizza Tower can be a forgettable, challenge-free 6 hour game, or it can be a frustrating 60 hour time attack / score attack game. It looks and sounds cool, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so:This review used to be a lot shorter, but now that I've 100% the entire game, lemme say this right now--Don't believe me? I'll tell you here.In this game, you play as Peppino Spaghetti, an italian chef who's running behind on debt, and has to also climb a tower to stop Pizzaface from destroying your restaraunt. Sounds simple, right?Yeah well that's there the simple part ends, because this game has about 20 levels of pure platforming perfection, all the way down to Peppino's moveset.And sometimes Gustavo.The levels have their secrets placed deliberately in the spots they are in, and it feels like the level was MADE for them all. Requires EVERYTHING for an S-Rank, with the addition of keeping a combo from the very first room of the level all the way to you getting out of said level. Anyway yeah go buy this game and play it, it's worth your time.Total time to truly 100%: About 45-ish hours of playtime over the course of two runs through the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I never felt compelled to write a review for a Steam game until now. I've been vaguely aware of Pizza Tower while it was being developed, but my excitement for it waned after I saw the focus shift to speed as opposed to platforming - Wario Land 4 was definitely the main inspiration to the game's developer, but while that game leaned towards casually exploring your surroundings, revving up things in a stage only after you press the switch, Pizza Tower decided to wear the other side of WL4's coin on its sleeve. Seeing as that's not what made me fall in love with WL4 (it was the interesting locales paired up with creative and varied level design), it's no surprise that I stopped paying any attention to the game. Come the end of January this year, the game comes out and pretty soon receives a cult following. I start seeing it get mentioned and praised. "Maybe I should give the game a chance?" quickly turns into a "Nah" after a cursory glance, where I see the main character running around at insane speeds, with the focus obviously being on navigating the surrounding as fast as possible as opposed to jumping around and collecting stuff at your own pace (you actually can play the game like this, but I'll mention later why this would be a mistake). Still, my curiosity got the best of me after around three months and I sat down to play the game. After around nine hours I've beaten Pizza Tower. Despite not liking how the main character controls I ended up being mildly amused, primarily by the variety of environments, occasional segments focusing on platforming and the lovely art style (which could best be described as "Ren & Stimpy on acid"). The story could have ended right there, with me none the wiser. I'd walk away thinking that Pizza Tower is a mid-tier game with a unique art style, but lacklustre level design. I wouldn't understand what all the fuss was about. Luckily for me, I decided to try to achieve one of those P ranks I heard about, figuring out that the very first stage of the game is the best candidate for it. To P rank a stage, you basically need to know all about it - the complete level layout, the location of enemies and collectables and so on. It's no wonder, as that elusive mark of mastery requires you to keep a combo throughout the entire stage, collect all 5 of the toppings and the secret treasure (which is locked behind a door that only a janitor can open, him counting as yet another collectible), clear all three secret rooms and do a second run of the stage to boot. I don't know why someone like me, who not only ignores those "play almost perfectly" challenges but very rarely replays games he's already beaten, made the decision he did, but boy, what a lucky turn of events. After almost two painful hours (a part of them spent on mastering the controls as I didn't even know some of the moves that existed e.g. the dive cancel), I had my first P rank and was hooked. P ranks force you to be fast and you can realize how genius the level design of Pizza Tower is only when you're in that high-speed mode. That's why playing this game as you would Wario Land 4 would be a massive mistake. Only when you're blazing at high speeds and calculating multiple variables in your head (from where exactly that one collectable you need to collect to stop your combo from being uninterrupted is to precisely when you have to press the left arrow key so that you can make a turn while conserving your speed) does the magic of Pizza Tower become apparent. On the surface, the levels are perfectly functional but nothing special. It's when you try to P rank a stage that you start seeing the implications of their layout. That one enemy is placed there for a reason, it's on purpose that the ledge in that one area is just high enough for you to reach it with a tap of the jump button... it all makes sense now, it all clicks. I was basically hooked to the game after that first P rank, so it's no surprise that I P ranked the rest of the stages as well. One important thing to note is that I extremely rarely complete a game 100%, yet I did that with Pizza Tower. I actually did a bit more than that, as my save file sits at 101%. Replaying the stages for the purpose of P ranking them (some of them a lot of times as it goes without saying that certain P ranks are harder than others) made me fall in love with the game. I ended up not liking certain stages as much as I did, while some of the stages that I hated became some of my favorites. After around 27 additional hours of playing, I can say that Pizza Tower is not only one of the best modern games ever, but also one of the best games ever made. It's also an example of a game that surpassed its inspiration - I love WL4 a lot, but for all its good qualities it still doesn't give me as much joy or induce as much awe as Pizza Tower's exuberancy does. We're talking about a painstakingly crafted masterpiece that's filled with heart, that's bursting at the seams with character, that's radiating charm... you get the idea. McPig (the game's developer) understands game design on a deeper level, which is obvious not only from the way that he designed stages but certain other things as well, like the fact that he implemented the Shinespark from the Metroid series so gracefully to his game.I haven't talked in detail about many things here, from the boss stages (that have a P rank as well, the single requirement being that you can't get hit even once) to the fantastic soundtrack, but that's not the purpose of this review. This wall of text which barely anyone will read is there for those who are on the fence, not knowing if they should play the game or not. I say that Pizza Tower should be played. Still, you can fully appreciate it only if you put in a lot of effort. In simple terms, "P rank or bust".

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, you'd think that this game is just a knock off of Wario Land, and you'd be only 1 % right. This game manages to be more than just that by making emphasis on reaction timing, mobility, and even clever thinking on the fly. On top of that, Pizza Tower is genuinely a labor of love that I don't think can be topped. 2023 had some bangers this year, and this one is well done.Pizza Story lacks a narrative in the sense that it doesn't really have much to its story outside of "Peppino finds a tower and climbs it because he's in debt and needs cash." Peppino, the main character of this game, is a brutish pizza chef who grabs, punches, and bites his way through each stage like I bite my way through pizza. There's no real world building, nor any concrete story outside of assumptions.The art style is impossible to explain. It's a zany mix of so much that I can only describe as "school notes come to life." Everything, and I mean, EVERYTHING is expressive. Everything makes a reaction, everything has a face, everything will cry and laugh and get angry. It's all done by hand, pixel by pixel, managing to stand out amongst other pixel based indie games by looking more like a bunch of MS Paint doodles telling a story (or you know, lack thereof , you get what I mean.) And don't even get me started on the music. I'd be here all day, but I'm sure you've heard the titular theme of the game "It's Pizza Time." That's about all you need to know going in with this soundtrackThis game is well worth the price you pay and offers much replayability. It was one I highly anticipated for so long and now that it's here, it manages to go above and beyond what I expected. Thank you, Tour de Pizza, for making one of the greatest games I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Pizza Tower

_childDocuments_.review: It's not often I fall instantly in love with a game like I did with this one.  From the very start I knew that this game was special, hitting you with that zany, messy, unapologetic style that works so well for the character and world. This is a fast paced, exploration heavy platformer with so much speed and momentum that even Sonic would be jealous.  Unlike Sonic though Peppino controls like a dream.  It is rare for a character to be equipped with such fluid animations and movement tech, his entire kit can be strung together to keep that manic momentum going as you blast through the levels at mach speed.Going right along with it is a frantic soundtrack that keeps the player moving forward at all costs, paired with a large television screen that expresses Peppino's emotions at the time.  I can't express to you how much I love that television, seeing how Peppino is feeling based on what you're doing will never not be entertaining.  Whether it is running at full speed, having a wacky transformation, or the evil grin when you start building a combo, you can really feel the expressions through the beautifully animated sequences on the TV.  I know it is presumptuous to say, but even at this point I can't see how I won't be voting this for a contender for game of the year.  Thank you Tour De Pizza for giving this gift.  Edit: It is still my contender for Game of the Year

_childDocuments_.review: A fun platformer made to be fun. The game has a ton of silly animations and sprites, there's no padding, and content is generally polished and concentrated. You can beat the game in a reasonable amount of time, but part of the appeal to the game is speedrunning/replaying levels to get a high score. You can either play the game as a sonic-like, or a wario land-like, but because the gameplay fuses the two genres so elegantly, it turns into something more than simply a clone of a pre-existing game. Peppino has a decent amount of moves, and they've all been carefully considered mechanically to fill certain niches without any redundancy in the pursuit of absurd speed. Even the seemingly superficial silly taunt move can be used to freeze for 1/3 a second without killing momentum, while also functioning as a parry. Generally it's very difficult to die, but getting hit by an enemy makes you lose points, and slow down for a bit, meaning that rather than arbitrarily adding a fail-state with no artistic intent other than to embrace tradition, the game allows you to constantly decide how invested you want to be in avoiding enemies without feeling too easy. None of that getting hit by a random jumpscare enemy and going back to the start of a level BS that plagued classic sonic. The levels are designed to be highly replayable, further aiding the game's speedrunning aspect. A first run-through of a level generally goes in one of 2 directions. either you go "i wanna run really fast, even if it means avoiding point pick-ups" with you running into a wall occasionally or something, but allowing you to buildup your combo meter a lot easier, giving you bonus points. The alternative is you go "i wanna try to get all the pick-ups and secrets" generally resulting in missing a couple secret rooms, messing up the combo mechanic resulting in less points, or slowing down a bit too much. Additional run-throughs of a level allow the two playstyles to fuse together, as you get better and better at different sequences in the level and keeping your combo meter high. You can eventually try to go for an S ranking on that stage, giving you a rewarding feeling of accomplishment if you succeed. _childDocuments_.review: If you are even remotely a fan of platformers, this game is a must play. And if you’re a fan of the Wario Land games, this is a game you’re sure to fall in love with. Everything about this game is easily a 10 from me, and in fact, if I could go past that number, I certainly would! This is the only Steam game I’ve ever actually reviewed, and I believe this one absolutely deserves it. This game is like if Wario Land (specifically 4), Sonic, Rayman Legends, and Super Metroid were mixed into one slimy yet satisfying being. With an art style and aesthetic reminiscent of Earthworm Jim, Courage the Cowardly Dog, Rocko’s Modern Life, Ren and Stimpy, of course, paired with bombastic music that reeks positively of the 90’s and 00’s. I’ll be getting into what makes this game so awesome, and just why everyone should play it at least once! Firstly, the visuals. Even from the very get go, with the Tour de Pizza logo, you can immediately tell that this game is goofy in the best way. Not only that, but it’s also rich with coolness, energy, and strong passion, the intro showing that in glorious detail. The music is upbeat and determined, setting the mood for the game perfectly, not to mention showing the admittedly small story in a simple, quick way. It shows how kickass of a game this is gonna be, and it instantly puts you in Peppino’s shoes, giving you a fair reason as to why you should care about what happens to him and his pizzeria. It’s easily one of my favorite intros in a game ever, and it’s always pretty fun to watch! And I’d say it never runs out of charm throughout the entire game. Every enemy looks silly, fitting right at home with an old 90’s cartoon, and being so creatively designed! Everything in this game looks very wonky and crooked, which I absolutely adore! Plus, this game can really make itself frightening when it wants to, the scenery in several levels being rather unsettling, to say the least. But personally, I quite enjoy that as well, though maybe that’s just because I’m a horror fan. Every frame of this game is animated wonderfully, if the trailer wasn’t enough proof of that. I’ve always been a really big fan of pixel art, and this game certainly doesn’t disappoint. Color schemes are vibrant and unique, backgrounds are always incredibly detailed and full of so many gags and jokes, so many faces in this game are hilarious, there’s a lot to appreciate from a visual stance! And a highlight, it’s pretty often that they make Peppino look realistic for laffs. That's my favorite.Nextly, the controls, and very much what makes this game work so strongly. The way speed works in this game is pretty fun, what with how quickly Peppino’s able to move in general. The way movement in this game worked changed so much during development. The best way to prove this is by watching gameplay/playing Demo 0, 1, or 2, the contrast is like night and day. This game became MUCH faster, what with the new moves being added in and how momentum was changed. Peppino definitely picks up the pace a lot quicker now, which makes this into a fantastic speedrun game. I’ve never really been into speedrunning games myself, but with how movement works in this game, I’d be more than happy to take a crack at it for this one. I feel like even just watching someone play this game is exciting in itself, the speedy and punchy nature always being shown off. The improvisation in movement benefits strongly to how the game works itself, what with how levels work. Instead of reaching a “level clear” gate or something, you need to hit a pillar, named Pillar John, at the end of the level, then backtrack as quickly as you can, going back to the beginning of the level to leave. It’s a timed escape sequence, known as Pizza Time,  and if you don’t make it in time, Pizzaface will awake from his slumber and cause you to die in a sense, losing the level, along with everything you had picked up along the way. Of course, this only becomes more difficult throughout the game, more time being given to you for longer escape sequences. The kind of speed you can build up can make these the most exciting yet stressful parts of these levels, the possibility to succeed becoming more likely, as long as you keep your speed high and maneuver back efficiently. And better yet, once you complete the level, a new challenge will await you if you play it again. At the beginning of the level, either behind the entrance, be it nearby or in the same room, a translucent Pizza Portal will be present. It’s only activated during Pizza Time, and when you’re able to enter it, you’re sent back to the room where Pillar John was hit, being put to go through the escape sequence again, but with less time. Essentially, you’re going through a second lap, which the game makes clear. Doing this gives you an extra 3000 points right off the bat, and you’re able to rack up more points when blowing through enemies, but all at the risk of being hunted down by Pizzaface. I find it’s an amazing sense of replayability, being offered the chance to get a higher score and, in a sense, practice movement. In an incredibly aggressive way.I say that as a transition into the totally amazing soundtrack for this game. From what I understand, there were three musicians (Mr. Sauceman, ClascyJitto, and POST ELVIS) for this game, and they all did a killer job. Each track perfectly fits the mood for the stage and situation. And while there are a few songs I don’t exactly have strong feelings on, practically all of them are stunning. A few specific examples I have in mind are the escape theme and lLap 2's theme. Literally go buy the soundtrack if you like music, it’s available on here and Bandcamp! Soon going to Spotify! The escape theme, aptly titled, “It’s Pizza Time!”, composed by Mr. Sauceman, is probably the best way to demonstrate the kind of energy this game gives off. Which makes sense why it’s in the trailer! It’s frantic, energetic, funky, chaotic, and honestly kind of frightening! It is a song that has changed many times throughout development, and throughout, I’d say it’s maintained its level of craziness. It pulls no punches, starting off rather unnervingly with the echoey voices in the beginning, plus the electric guitars rattling menacingly, a premonition for what’s to come later in the song. The main leitmotif of the song is heard, which is pretty much just the main theme for this game, and it quickly builds up, soon jumping into the main madness you’ll be hearing throughout the rest of the song. It’s incredibly catchy, while also loudly reminding you that you’ve got to get the hell out there before it’s too late! It’s a song that keeps changing, going through different ways of audibly motivating you to hurry up! It’s an amazing way to demonstrate the kind of game this is, even with just listening to the song and seeing no gameplay. The song for Lap 2, “The Death That I Deservioli”, composed by Mr. Sauceman, contains a similar kind of energy, but much more forceful and aggressive, making the challenge of going for Lap 2 seem so much more epic (which it is). It starts off rather slowly, a rather repetitive beginning that’s just a looping “video-gamey” tune accompanied by drum beats, but it then soon picks up, speeding up and launching into a blood-pumping, desperate, nait-biting frenzy of a song. It’s an intimidating song, reminding you that if you ♥♥♥♥ up once too many, it’s over, and that Pizzaface will win. It will be the death you deservioli if you aren't careful.  As I’ve said, this is the first time I’ve ever really written a review for a game, and, well, this game compelled me enough to write about it, which I believe goes to show just how damn hard it slaps. This game really means a ton to me, and so I figured saying things that I appreciate about it could be fun, and also a good way to convince people to get this game. Hopefully it gets onto other consoles, I’m hoping it’ll be later this year! tldr: epic pizza game :D

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing aesthetics, amazing sound track, amazing momentum building and speed-run based platform game play. Honestly every second of playing this game was treat and brought a smile to my pizza face.Pizza tower does not attempt to go for the most polished and professional looking Visuals, but in doing so creates more charm and style than 2D games trying to look amazingly beautiful. It's art is nostalgic, abstract and surreal with lots of the enemies, bosses and environments looking like they were drawn in one evening by a school kid. I have not seen such random enemies since days of NES Platformers. But there in itself comes the fun and enjoyment, a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, where the Devs obviously had fun making the characters as comedic and absurd as possible. Pure visual comedy from facial expressions, simular to Ren and Stimpy. With less labour needed to create the MS paint style art, you can tell the Devs put a hell of lot of effort into the core game play, proving that high end visuals aren't everything. The animations is smooth and quirky, parts of the game almost remind you of watching old rubber hose style animation from the 30's, which I'm sure was an inspiration. The momentum building and speed-run style game play feeling satisfying to play and improve at. You can move so fast and chain moves together that at points you can feel unstoppable and almost like you're free-styling your own move-sets into the game. At it's best the game flows so well that you're not really even conscious of controlling Peppino, you're just a speed demon. Climbing the tower also gives you a good conceptual feeling of progression that you want to reach the top, and earning money to unlock new gates adds a bit more complexity and replayabilty, than simply playing the levels in a linear fashion.All in all best 2D platformer I have played since Super Meat Boy and best cartoonish visuals i've seen since games on the PS1. Had me coming back to play more everyday and hope it gets a sequel. Great, a Must Play.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute relic of a better time, released well over two decades of the games it took inspiration from.Pizza Tower is honestly one of the best games I've played in recent times, even from sheer happiness of seeing a game that is just fun to play. The gameplay, artstyle, music, audio cues, the little moments all just come together to make a game that is more like what was made in the times of the GBA. If you played Wario Land 4 you'll be right at home with this game, and if you can still remember some of the funny bits throughout that game you might also smile with this one.There's quite a lot that can be said about this game but most of it are things that are best seen by yourself. I went in mostly blind and had a really good time. But here's what you should know about this game: it is a fast paced platformer intended for 100% collectible speedruns, although you can certainly play without focusing on getting a perfect run or anything like that, the game doesn't punish you for it, all you need is the important items kind of like picking up the crystals throughout a Crash Bandicoot stage.The best part about this game is looking at the small details like the backgrounds and the subtle audio or animations from some characters. I loved looking through each level at a leisurely pace before later coming back to get anything I missed and when I finished the game I went attempting to get every pickup and secret.You should really try this game if you're really just looking for something that's just a nice change of pace.Overall my score for this game is a very genuine 10/10. It's really fun from the start to the end, and it actually made me happy throughout my playtime.That's not something you can say for most games nowadays.Personal nomination for the Steam 2023 "Game of the Year", "Best Visual Style", "Best Soundtrack" and "Best on Steam Deck" awards.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a crazy game: It's a fast-paced 2d platformer á la Sonic, with breakable blocks and menu design from Jazz the Jackrabbit, an invulnerable dash like in Wario and multi-use B-button from Mario franchise.However, it's not just a mix of the most groundbreaking platformer ideas in gaming, each idea is well implemented into a single game: You begin each level by slowly going through to pick up all secrets and items, taking note of the unreachable secrets. Then you destroy a pillar at the end of the level. The level turns on it's head as now you must backtrack with a timer. This is a great dynamic, especially because all rooms flow well in both directions, and support both the methodical snooping around and the mad dash for the exit. Shift makes you pick up speed until you're an invulnerable, unstoppable maniac.X is a dash-grab button, more gimmicky, like a Mario B button. If you grab an opponent, you pick them up. If you press down after the grab, you start sliding across the screen. If you press up, you do a double jump.These two dash buttons combine into a complicated yet easy to use system for both max speed and tight movement. The visuals are on another level. The MS paint style pixel-bound hand drawn animation juxtaposed with great sense of animation fundamentals. All characters are expressive and everything is always in motion. Each movement has their own wacky animation sets, even when an animation could've been reused.These visuals are used for cartoony visual gags. A funny face or two in a single action animation isn't an exception, it's a rule. Movement, speed, exploration. All placed in a single polished package. A combination of the greatest mechanical breakthroughs in the history of 2D platformers.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a rare game where I've gotten every achievement and cosmetic, not because of some completionist obsession, but because I wanted to milk out every last bit of gameplay I could.This is easily the best 2D platformer I've ever played. Although generally compared to its direct inspiration in the Wario Land series, what it actually delivers is a better execution of the Sonic games' mission statement: pulse-pounding speed performed with skill and style.Your first playthrough will likely be a short one - at face value, the game is not very difficult - but hidden behind a simple, charming game is an entire system of chained combos, secret collectables and narrow timing windows that will make you feel like a god when you finally achieve a level's best possible score through both careful planning and twitch reflex.I'm done with Pizza Tower now. There's a handful of moves I haven't fully gotten a hang of, but those are for the speedrunners (who, as you can imagine, *love* this game). As a private single-player experience, I have gotten everything I can out of it: felt every triumph, as well as the screaming rage of messing up a combo-chain near the finish line, which happened more times than I can count. But it's done now.If you want to know how good this game is: this entire review has been my vain attempt to keep the experience going for one more minute.So now, with a heavy heart, I say "Goodbye."And thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: The game mechanics are simple but using them in a more complex manner and understanding them makes you feel amazing. Also all of the the games aesthetics, music, and level design are so insane, chaotic, fun, and just amazing overall. The music always knows how to fit the style of a level, when to slow down, and when to speed up. Each level has such a unique design and mechanic, that it just makes you always wonder what in the world the next level could have. There could be a ghost mechanic, or literally driving a sausage around like it's a horse. The aesthetic and graphics of the game compliment the simple. yet complex, fleshed out, and incredibly chaotic gameplay. Peppino is insane and the graphics show that, from him going incredibly quick to the point of his face distorting. You should be able to get through the tutorial relatively quickly, hop in the levels, and have a blast. If you have a lot of free time and wanna get all the achievements, this game can go from a really short indie platformer experience , to a large game with tons of effort into it, reaching up to over 50 hours.This game can be incredibly frustrating at points, so persevering and patience is key. However, understanding the game mechanics, which isn't too hard to do, is key. It's challenging because levels are always surprising you to continue using the gameplay mechanics to their best ability. Many of the achievements are hard and many levels and boss fights may be hard too. However, the game uses this as perseverance to continue using the mechanics to the best of your ability to get better and use them in levels and boss fights. Even more frustrating may be the achievements, doing specific tasks on levels, not getting hit once in the boss fights, having to get better ranks of levels, but pushing through makes you feel very accomplished, and the game is overall incredibly fun.I heavily recommend this game to anyone, as it's price at $20 is incredibly worth it. However, I would definitely recommend it to people who understand a little about platformers. Along with this, it's definitely for more patience players, as getting better ranks and becoming better at the game in general takes time and patience. If you want to 100% this game and get every achievement, you need patience and to understand how trial and error works. It's recommended for people who can keep playing and keep enjoying it even when they mess up. _childDocuments_.review: Let me get one thing out of the way: I never actually played any of the Wario Land games before, so whether or not this game succeeds in being a spiritual successor to that series, I can't say. What I CAN say is that Pizza Tower may be one of, if not the best platformers I've played in such a very long time. I don't think I've ever experienced a game so tightly woven together like this one.You play as Peppino, a very angry and anxiety-induced pizza man, on a journey to keep his pizza business from falling into debt by running through a tower filled with dangerous and quirky stages. Or at least, that's the interpretation I got from the opening intro. Really, the narrative isn't a super strong point here, but that doesn't really matter. All you need to know is this game's aesthetics harkens back to the old school, squigly-style cartoons of the 90's/early 2000's, like Ren and Stimpy, Ed, Edd and Eddy and Cow & Chicken, and the humor is a definite match of those cartoons as well. But don't let that fool you: the gameplay and controls for this game are NO JOKE. Peppino's movement is phenomenal. Super tight with a lot of cool techniques to give yourself a plethora of ways of maneuvering around the stages. You got the basics, like dashing forward, jumping, wallrunning. You got some advanced movements like sliding, shinesparking, diving. And then you got the straight up advanced techs like dive cancel stomps, grab cancels, slide boosting. All of these can be strung together in order to keep control of Peppino as you make a mad dash for the goal. It all lends itself to a true speedrunner's dream, because if you string it all perfectly together, the speed becomes hella exhilarating. Ludicrous even (sadly there is no plaid costume for your character).Unlike most typical platformers, stages aren't designed with the typical "Point A to Point B" layout. Instead, each stage has you running through a huge, maze-like arena, figuring out the best path to get to the goal. Once you reach your goal, you are then tasked to make it back to the starting point as fast as you can, as you are given a time limit to do so. Run out of time and you'll start to be chased by the evil Pizza Face. Get caught before you reach the beginning and it's game over. BUT THAT'S NOT ALL. If you're feeling daring, you can partake in a lap 2 just as you reach the starting point, in which case you're tasked with running through the map AGAIN with the remaining time left. If you're able to keep your combo meter going by picking up items and attacking enemies with very little breather in-between as you make your way all across lap, you might just get the ever elusive "P" rank, to showcase your amazing Pizza skills.None of the stages in this game were ever bad. They were all so perfectly designed, I felt compelled to P rank every single one of them before even getting to the end game. Some stages had gimmicks, like picking up a shotgun in order to shoot down indestructable walls, grabbing a rocket in order to boost across the air, turning into a pizza box in order to flap across areas in a single bound. These gimmicks never felt tacked on; they all felt like a good mix up to the overall flow of the game. If I could make one complaint here, it's the fact that there is SO MUCH cut content for this game. I followed this game's development from the day it had its SAGE demo uploaded all the way to now. It's quite sad to see a lot of cool stuff get dummied out, but I guess that's also what helped make the game feel so tight so I can understand the choices the devs made in having to remove a lot of stuff, so if nothing else, it just means there's potential for DLC stuff. If that doesn't happen, it's not the end of the world, because this game is pretty much Pizza Perfect.Also, special shout outs to the music. It's super stylish. It's kinda hard to explain, but the best way I can do so is imagine if the OST of Sonic CD, Earthworm Jim and Jet Set Radio were all thrown into a blender spinning atop a turntable. The music just oozes style, from the sick hip hop beats of the pause music making you wanna break it down, to the frenetic electronic jam as you're dashing through lap 2 which further adds to the adrenaline rush of the experience. I'm telling you, if you put on a pair of headphones and play "The Death That I Deservioli" while going out for a jog, expect to find yourself a million miles away from home. It's THAT wild.This game is really good. If you love high speed platformers or just enjoy speedrunning, this is the perfect entry on the menu. So make sure to order it with extra cheese, and don't you dare save room for dessert.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you miss Warioland? Do you miss those really ugly cartoons from the 90s like Cow and Chicken and Kablam!, along with those weird mspaint 4chan comics from the internets early days?Don't you wish they all came together in some disgusting orgy and produced a baby? In Italy?Look no further, Pizza Tower is here. Part Heroin, Part Pepperoni, All parts Wario. This game is a fast, kinetic and fluid platformer that has you controlling a Chef running up and around a tower that plans on destroying his Pizzeria. You gotta run through each level saving your little topping friends from their cages, all the while smushing and punching and slamming anything that dares to stand in your way. You'll be running at enemies who scream in terror when they see the green white and red glory that is your forehead careening toward them at blazing hot speeds. Run up walls, dive down, and let no brick wall nor tomato goblin stand in your way.The game's distinct look achieves something most triple AAAA games do not, and that's cohesion. It's ugly, it's revolting, yet you can tell what is always going and where anything is, even at high speeds. Once you beat a level, you need to make a mad dash out by playing the level in reverse while rave chiptune music is blaring before the Pizza Monster wakes up to eat your soul. It's easy to remember where everything was, you have arrows and your chef buddy pointing the way, all easy to see no matter where they are or what their doing. It all fits together perfectly and really feels like it was made by a person and not some committee that's worried you might get lost or not see something.Since this is a modern day indie, it has the pleasure of taking the best things from previous games while putting it's own spin on it. Imagine if Super Meat Boy met Warioland, with very fluid controls and animations that all connect to each other seamlessly, while having unique levels that require memorization to truly master them. Nothing feels mean, nothing feels out of place, nothing feels out of reach. This leads to the game having a high skill ceiling, as its score system will award you letter ranks depending on how often you got hit, how fast you beat the level and how much you collected. I was at 2 hours in when I wrote this review and I got a few A ranks on a couple of levels, so the game isn't shy to hand you highish grades to show you "wow, you did pretty good there, but can you master it?". Most games would have awarded me a C or lower because I'm new, because I don't have all the powers yet, because I haven't seen all the mechanics yet. The game shows and teaches you everything right off the bat, it's up to you to figure these levels out, which paths to take, how many toppings to get on your pie, and whether you're feeling meat lovers tonight. Flying at mach speeds through levels with the music blaring without bumping into a wall is an incredibly rewarding feeling and you have no one to thank but yourself. No meters to manage, no powerups to abuse, just your two feet and your forehead, and maybe a handful of anchovies for those baddies that don't step aside. Jack in some of those pot needles of yours and let the Chef do the talking. Wario may have retired, but his deranged cousin in the asylum is still causing trouble, and it's up to you to direct his anger toward this Pizza Tower. 5 out of 5 pies.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic game. Having now played for 70 hours, unlocking every achievement, getting 101%, beating the game in under 2 hours, and getting >95% completion in under 4 hours, I think I can confidently say that this is one of the most charming and captivating games I have ever played. The movement is downright addictive once you start getting really good, and the feeling of getting a P-Rank for the first time is something I doubt I'll ever experience again. Once you beat the game for the first time you'll most likely be tempted to go back through and get an S-Rank, even more so once you find out about Lap 2 portals. You're encouraged to go faster and faster, getting smoother with every run. Once you get an S-Rank, you may be tempted to go even further, and get a P-Rank. Then you want to P-Rank EVERY level. Then, just to round out the collection, you might as well beat every boss without getting hit. And hey, what the hell, you've come this far, might as well round out those achievements. This game compelled me (and many others I'm sure), to go as far as possible, until there was literally NOTHING left to do. I'm currently trying to complete The Noise's save files, in the same way that I have Peppino's, and just when I thought I was running out of things to do in this game, Tour de Pizza shoves a big slice of Noise down my throat and suddenly I'm re-addicted to this game. Still not far through my first playthrough, and far from good enough to do what I have with Peppino, but I don't think I'll EVER tire of this game, and by the time I'm done, I'm sure the number of hours I'll have will be in triple digits. Thank you for this amazing game Tour de Pizza, and thank you for getting me through some of the most stressful exams I've lived through yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Pizza Tower is a special game. Wario Land inspired 2D platformer with very complex movement, brilliant level design, awesome art and soundtrack. Every level is unique aesthetic, song and gimmics like power ups and stage hazards.The cheezy core of the game is combo system and level ranks. To get a perfect score you have to start a combo in the first room, collect all the secrets (4), do lap 2 and not drop the combo a single time. Sounds very hard, but the game is designed around this system. Its not exactly like speedrunning a level - once you kill an enemy you get a point and timer starts, get to the next interactable thing (topping, enemy, treasure) and combo meter goes up again. Your goal is to plan out the rout to get something every 6.5 seconds or less. You can go surprisingly slow at many sections of the level and not drop a combo. You also have super taunt to quickly get an enemy anywhere on screen, which you can save up for a hard section. The timer doesnt really matter at the end.I want to encourage everyone who will play Pizza Tower to try and go for P(izza) ranks when you replay a level. It is very rewarding and with instant restarts and short levels will not take much time to learn a level. 10/10 My personal GOTY

_childDocuments_.review: Like a very gross but bizarrely captivating fanfiction I once read, Pizza Tower is the freakish spawn of Wario and Sonic the Hedgehog, dialed up to eleven and polished to a mirror sheen.Pizza Tower is a platformer that never wants you to feel  comfortable, constantly throwing new mechanics at you at a pace that is always exciting but rarely overwhelming. It's extremely dense with collectibles and secrets, and trying to find them all is a challenge that will likely multiply your total playtime several times over. There is zero chance that Pizza Tower will not see an extremely healthy speedrunning scene, and I fully expect it to make an appearance at SGDQ this year.If you like platformers, get Pizza Tower. If you're nostalgic for that fun 90s aesthetic, get Pizza Tower. If you like games that aren't afraid to get just plain , get Pizza Tower. If you don't fit into any of the above categories, you should still get Pizza Tower, because that's how good it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game from a friend not really knowing much about it beforehand other than it was a quirky platformer. After playing it, however, I started to really fall in love with it. There is a bit of a learning curve and a few moves that aren't explicitly shown off in the tutorial (and some through dialogue with NPCs), but once you develop a nice repertoire of moves the game starts to feel incredibly good to play. The music doesn't hold the game back either, with music that fits the chaotic, fast-pace of the game as well. Don't let the rough art style put you off, because there is an insane amount of love put into this game and it's many cartoony animations. The only downside I can think of is that you'll have the soundtrack stuck in your head even days after finishing it, but is that really a downside?EDIT: Decided to nominate this for 2023 Game of the Year, because while it isn't the highest budget or the most AAA game of the year, it's the one I can't help but think about ever since I first played it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pizza Tower is a Fever Dream Fueled Work of Art.I've been watching the development of this game since 2019 and I'm so glad it's finally here!It feels like they took Wario Land and Sonic the Hedgehog and fused them together into a nightmarish action platformer that hits all the right notes. There is a brilliant mix of speeding through levels as fast as you can, as well as stopping to find all of the snacks and treasure hidden about. Each level is designed to encourage flow and exploration, making it a blast to go back and replay them. Sometimes I want to see how fast I can complete it, and other times I spend getting lost looking in every corner for the hidden secrets. The vibe of this game is immaculate. Twisted characters, disgusting monsters, all in this lovely 90s-esque art style. And this is all held together by our hero Peppino. Every single action he does just oozes with personality and charm, he's quickly becoming one of my favorite mascots. This game is also capped off with an incredible soundtrack that feels fresh, funky, and very Wario like.Please do yourself the favor and dig into Pizza Tower. The amount of passion and creativity in this game is worth every moment of it.

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautifully designed game! It has charm oozing everywhere, the platforming is thrilling, and while the controls take a while to get used to thanks to Peppino's sheer variety in his moveset, they make up for by being extremely tight and satisfying to speed through every stage.Special mention to the visual design, being hilariously over-the-top, making generous use of squash and stretch, and having some of the wackiest facial animations I've ever seen in a long time. If I'm not viciously practicing a run through a stage, I'm more than likely having a blast just watching Peppino move, in game or on the TV Screen.I honestly can't think of anything to complain about. This is probably the best you're gonna get if you're looking for a fast-pace platformer that heavily rewards you for mastering the mechanics and level design, the best time for pizza time is anytime.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is harder to put down than your fourth slice of pizza. Every aspect of this speed-centered 2D platformer is cooked to perfection. As Peppino, you’ll blast through unique levels at mach speed, punt and piledrive your foes into oblivion, and haul your hind end back out in the adrenaline-filled Pizza Time. The game is quite easy to learn and beat, but brutally tough to master and fully complete. No matter your skill level, there is tons of fast-paced fun to be had. _childDocuments_.review: Having finished Pizza Tower 101% last week, this game has left a pizza-shaped hole in my heart. Absolutely masterclass. I might even call it the best 2D platformer. I genuinely can't believe how great it turned out after years of watching & waiting.It's very easy to appreciate on the surface alone; fantastic animation, style, music, and super tight controls. The only death in this game is running up the timer and losing to the few boss fights, so it shouldn't be  difficult for most people, but for those that want a real challenge afterwards, this is where this game went from simply flashy up to the top shelf; P-rank is rank given for doing a full completion of a level in a single run while never letting your combo meter drop until finishing. It sounds impossible, but it becomes an entirely different game as you soon realize how each level is designed to be played this way. The level of speed, reflex, and memorization required is so intense that it ceased feeling like Wario Land 4, and felt more like F-Zero GX.It's just really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. I can't recommend it enough.

A lot of Hideki Naganuma samples (more so, samples he used in his work shows up here) appear in the music, which is really nice.
