_childDocuments_.review: The latest in the line of Contra titles takes things back to the tried and true glory days of the franchise with 2D run and gun action. It is essentially a reboot of the franchise rather than a straight remake of the first game.Simple yet clean title screen greets the player upon booting up with some nice artwork over a flaming background. When choosing a character you get character portraits in the same style as the title screen which look very nice. Graphic options are limited to resolution only which is a little disappointing. The  section is a basic menu of options that you can scroll through and have text descriptions of the different weapons and gameplay mechanics. Could have given the player something a little more interactive and let them try out the weapons or mechanics themselves but it does the job still. No option for online play is a headscratcher too considering the last 2D Contra spinoff had had it. Another issue is that they were clearly working with a limited budget as the story mode cutscenes are mostly just text boxes that appear below with character portraits and voiceovers playing. Don't expect to see many cinematic cutscenes playing throughout. The camera might zoom in or out at times during cutscenes and very rarely change perspective to make things look more dynamic. Shame as the game uses 3D models and could have made use of them here with cinematic camera angles. Graphics are adequate in my opinion. I would have preferred pixel art as I think it plays more to the strengths of Wayforward but the game is not ugly. I've heard some compare the graphics to PS2 games but anyone that thinks that obviously hasn't looked at PS2 graphics for a long time or has never played a PS2 game in their lives. It's still far from a great looking game but the graphics do an adequate job.Sound effects of the weapons sound great and makes firing them all the more satisfying. The voiceovers in the game give the characters some personality but you can turn them off in the options if they grate on you which is nice. Music has this orchestral-style to it which doesn't really suit the subject matter in my opinion. There is a  superior retro soundtrack that can be unlocked in the perk shop which sounds fantastic though. However you can only play that soundtrack in Arcade or Challenge modes. Story mode you are stuck with the original. When booting up the game I found that I had unlocked OSTs for Castlevania, Contra and Konami Arcade Classics for having those games in my collection which was nice. Similar to how Snake would read you memory card back in MGS and talk about the games you had saves of back in the day.The game features 2-player local co-op in Story mode and up to 4-player local co-op in Arcade mode. There are multiple characters to choose from other than Bill and Lance. Some you will have to purchase from the Perk Shop using credits earned from gameplay. For  fans that grew up with the early games there are unlockable  to play as so let the nostalgia run wild. You have all the same weapons that you have seen before:They can be levelled up again if you pick up a second weapon pickup of the same type. Some weapons may behave differently in the hands of certain characters so experiment with them. You can choose to have a life meter to allow you to take multiple hits before losing a life or you can opt for one-hit kills like in most of the old games. New to this game is the option to shoot 360 degrees instead of using the standard 8-way shooting the series is known for. You can choose between 360 degrees and 8-way although you will have to use the analogue stick when using a controller as the d-pad can only register 8 directions. The new option does make the game easier but still works.New to the game is the Overload mechanic which lets you sacrifice your weapon for a powerful attack. Different weapons have different Overload effects so experiment with each and different characters might have different overloads with the same weapon. You can also summon a weapon pod manually if you defeat enough enemies.The Story mode is the essentially the same game you are used to but with story segments scattered throughout. The issue with this isn't that the story is bad (it's not good mind), but that it does slow down the flow of things. You start the Story mode playing as Bill/Lance and other characters become available as you progress. Even after completion you can only play specific characters on specific stages. Some characters will have abilities specific to only them and weapons may behave differently in the hands of different characters.The Arcade mode is basically the same as Story mode but without the story segments that most Contra fans will be familiar with. Also all characters are available to play on any level (assuming you have unlocked them). This is the mode I expect most players will be playing the most. Also you can play this mode with alternate soundtracks if desired.The Perk Shop is where you will be able to unlock some new characters, abilities and more using Contra coins earned by playing the game. Each character can equip up to 2 perks which can make the game easier if desired. The Perk Shop is similar to the shop you would find in Uprising Mode in HCU.There is a Challenge mode similar to Contra 4 which lets you take on bite-sized challenges in various levels. It can be things like reach the goal without firing your weapon, speedrun the level, beat the boss without dying etc. It can be quite a fun mode to play around with if you don't feel like running through the main game whilst also sharpening your skills. There is no reward for completing them all. No online multiplayer  is extremely disappointing. Hard Corps Uprising came out years ago and had online play and at a lower price point so this is a step backwards. Wayforward have been asked in AMAs and in their Discord but always seem to skirt the question. A datamine shows that online was at the very least considered at one point but there has been no official mention of it so I wouldn't expect it in a patch down the line. Would be nice of them to address it though.Speaking of patches I did encounter some bugs like my characters legs being sunk partway through the floor and when I died on the last boss and continued my character was nowhere to be seen (but could be heard) and I was unable to move until they finally appeared after a few minutes. Hopefully these bugs will be addressed.Lastly the price is very high for a low-budget game like this. I think $25 would have been a fair price. Not that it isn't a fun game because it is but because you expect more from your games for $40 these days. For comparison Cuphead, an extremely successful modern run & gun launched at half the price of this game and even if you include the price of the DLC it is still cheaper than this and a more polished product. This is consistent with Konami's practices though as they did a similar thing with Bomberman.It's fun for veterans and accessible to newcomers so I hope it does well. The lack of online play is a slap in the face in 2024 so I'd say get it on sale unless you are a hardcore fan.

_childDocuments_.review: Contra: Operation Galuga is a glorious revival of everything that made the classic Contra games legendary, while delivering modern flair and polish that never feels out of place. Developed with a clear love for the series, this game reimagines the retro run-and-gun gameplay with tight controls, explosive action, and an updated visual style that stays true to its roots.Modernized Gameplay: The familiar fast-paced action is paired with new mechanics like weapon upgrades and special abilities, making the experience both nostalgic and fresh.Stunning Visuals: Vibrant, hand-crafted pixel art combined with modern effects makes every stage a feast for the eyes without losing the classic Contra vibe.Challenging but Fair: True to its legacy, Operation Galuga is tough as nails but always rewarding. Perfect for players who enjoy mastering patterns and pushing their reflexes.Co-Op Chaos: Playing with a friend is pure adrenaline-fueled fun, and the game offers seamless co-op integration.Epic Boss Battles: Each level concludes with unforgettable encounters that test your skill and strategy, all accompanied by heart-pumping music.Short Campaign: Like its predecessors, the game isn’t incredibly long, but the replay value and different difficulty modes make up for it.High Difficulty Curve: New players might find it daunting at first, but that’s part of Contra’s charm, and old school gamers, like myself, may actually throw this in the   section of this review.Final Thoughts:Contra: Operation Galuga is a love letter to fans of the series and an excellent starting point for newcomers. Whether you're chasing that nostalgic high or looking for a challenging, high-octane shooter, this game delivers on all fronts.

_childDocuments_.review: ok Konami, this is proof right here that if you ported "Hardcore: Uprising" to the PC, the contra fans will f'ing love it!For those that don't know, Hardcore:Uprising was a game released on the Xbox marketplace and Playstation network for the 360 and PS3. It was basically a Contra clone that took Contra and made it better and with a metal soundtrack that was just as hardcore as the gameplay. I know that game had SOME influence as this "Operation Galuga" has a lot of similar mechanics from Hardcore: Uprising, specifically the perk shop and character specific abilities and a "Campaign" and "Arcade" mode that allows you to experience the game's story or just jump straight into the action like to good ol' NES (or SNES) days.Much like in Hardcore: Uprising, as you play the game you earn points that you can then use in the perk shop to unlock power-ups, upgrade character abilities, etc. I find it to be a decent mechanic to increase replay-ability as you are rewarded more points based on how difficult you make the game for yourself. For example: anyone who's played Hardcore: Uprising will recognize the Health bar mechanic this game has adopted where instead of dying in one hit you loose health until you hit zero and die and respawn. Operation Galuga, however, offers the option right out the gate to play with the health bar mechanic or switch to 1-hit mode like the good ol' classics which is a great way to cater to both new-comers AND veterans of the classic Contra games.Other mechanics similar to Hardcore: Uprising how you level up your special weapons in-game. When you pick up a special weapon, i.e. the "Spread-Shot" you'll get the level 1 version where you shoot a cone of 3 shots at a time. finding and picking up a second Spread-Shot will unlock the level 2 version where you shoot an arc of 7 shots at a time. Personally I don't care for this mechanic, but you can purchase a perk in the perk shop that automatically unlocks level 2 special weapons when you first pick them up, so It doesn't bother me too much.My only complaint with this game is that they went with a more orchestral remake of the OG sound tracks, all of which are recognizable if you've got the ear for it. And while It's not terrible, I still would have loved to hear some of the good old Metal Covers that some of the previous games had, ESPECIALLY from Hardcore: Uprising. Seriously, if you are a fan of heavy metal, look up the OST for Hardcore: Uprising and match it to this game while you're playing. It goes SO hard...Anyway, I recommend this game to fans of side scrolling shooters and anyone who's ever been interested in contra but has never had the chance to play it. As a remake of the first game on the NES, it's a great jumping on point for newcomers and a great addition for newbs and veterans alike.

_childDocuments_.review: My main Contras growing up were The Alien Wars and NES Contra. This a satisfying new entry. I got it mainly to couch co-op, and we enjoyed our first play through. The gameplay is fun and the controls feel tight. Graphics are pretty good eye candy. Ran well on the big TV w/ Steam Deck. Dash ability and weapon overload are nice additions. Some references to Alien Wars (my favorite Contra) were appreciated. Still, Alien Wars was packed full of legendary audio tracks like the Neo Kobe Steel Factory, but sadly these new music tracks don't even come close to hitting as hard. Some of the sequences in Alien Wars were horrifying, with the music really matching the levels, whereas this felt like more like cheesy fun. The actual gameplay is *maybe* the best Contra has felt.Need more hours to write a more informed review but I do not regret the buy. Is it as good as Alien Wars? Probably not. But it's still satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: My impressions video: WayForward rarely misses and given the incredible job that did on Contra 4 for the Nintendo DS back when, I was excited about this as soon as I saw they were involved. Despite Konami pulling a Konami and Konami-ing the heck out of the price of this title, this is a fantastic effort and one Contra fans are sure to love.This is mostly a remake of the original Contra, but has a ton of refinements and changes that make it feel more modern. It's not a long game, but is designed to be replayed and offers several different difficulties, modes and a bunch of unlockable modifiers to mix things up. It does support up to 4 player co-op in the arcade mode as well and while it sadly doesn't have native online support, it works great over Steam Remote Play. WayForward knows the story of Contra is ridiculous leans into that with purposefully cheesy writing and voice acting that makes it feel almost satirical. This is the vibe you want when making a new Contra game. I won't spoil it, but there's also a clear indication this one the first of a new Contra series, assuming this sells well enough.WayForward has found a fantastic niche for themselves in the modern retro space and has nailed it once again here. Unfortunately, I think Konami's ridiculous pricing is going to keep this from being the success it should be. As much as I loved it, the price stung for me and I've recommended most people should probably wait for a sale. There is a demo so you can judge for yourself if you want to pay the price of entry, but I think Konami would be smart to drop the price of this by at least 30-40% as soon as possible. They'd probably see a huge spike in sales then. But this is Konami we're talking about so, you know.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Contra game since the original NES version. Yes, it's expensive if you're going to run through it in two hours and be done with it, not worth it. If you're going to unlock everything and possibly play with friends from time to time, it's absolutely worth it. There are perks and extra characters to unlock, story mode, arcade mode, and challenges to complete.What I don't understand is why it doesn't have online co-op, Contra is made for co-op.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the negative. - The game is a remake of the NES title, Contra. It's now the fifth remake, counting the Wii one, the mobile one with gatcha and the compilation. So don't expect it to re-invent the wheel here. Also, the asset have been lifted from their battle arena version on mobile (or the other way around, don't know which came first). - The gameplay is on part with the last titles. Beside removing bombs for a Special move at the cost of your power-up, there's nothing new. Lazy would fit what that game is.- The game is buggy. Solo play is fine but playing with a friend online is a nightmare. For one, it doesn't recognise any controller that isn't plug or connected prior starting the program. It can only be use during shareplay so, in order to play, the program need to be running. See the problem there? Wether you or your friend will have to play on a keyboard for a game where a controller is MANDATORY... unless Steam take pity of you and you manage to voodoo the shareplay before the game start. The positive- If you played any other 2D Contra game, you know how good those games are. The same apply here. - Couch-Coop. So little game has it these days that it warrent a point all by itself.- Different way to play: Each character got their own ability (if you pick it at the begining) and have different traversal. Some use the Grappling mechanic of Contra 4 (the DS title), while other hover or have a double jump. Each have different HP (cause you can choose HP or One hit kill) and can wield one of the two variant that exist for each weapons. Also for the Hard Corp lover, Sheena, Brad Fang and Browny are there, including some of their weapon from the game. RIP, Ray.- 4 Player Coop. it's essentially a good party game... that is if you're the kind of friend that enjoy Monopoly and ruining relationship. Remember, you can steal lives if you are game over like the original.Verdict: It's a pretty good game, but I would get it on sale or I would wish it on Instant Gaming for a rebate. If, on a scale of ten, one is really bad and five is mid, I'll give it a solid 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Others have commented on the steep price, but if you're a fan of these types of old school run-and-guns or there's a sale going on, I would recommend picking this one up. This is another great installment in the series from Wayforward. The story mode is an interesting enough idea, but in practice it comes off a little dull and is often just a barrier between you and the action. Luckily you can just jump right in to the arcade mode to bypass all of that if you want to.I would also recommend playing with 1-hit deaths and none of the various perks that you can purchase. This will provide the "NES hard" experience of old for those familiar that in my opinion is much more fulfilling than blazing through everything thanks to multiple hits and crazy passive upgrades.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I would give this a 7.5/10.  It would be an 8 or even an 8.5/10 if the gem stage (I believe 6) wasn't such a sudden spike in difficulty, and it's really just this level that seems cruel and unusual (though my experience so far is only in coop and screen sharing woes are really bad on this level).First of all, keep in mind that one playthrough of Story mode (so including cutscenes) on Normal difficulty takes about 1h30m.  The end game results screen shows how much time you spent in gameplay, and for me on first clear that was 1h6m.  So this is a short game.  I believe Hard Corps Uprising on PS3/360 was about the same length and maybe $20CAD.  So take this for what you will.  It was $37CAD on GMG for a short while and I split the price 50/50, then let the person I split with activate it on their Steam account and I have access to it through Family Sharing.Coop the game gets a bit funky at times, due to the shared screen. There is one level where if you drop down off the screen before other players have also dropped down, you will fall off the screen and lose a life, instead of landing on a platform with an offscreen indicator.  There is also a level where poison is rising, if you fall behind in coop you are basically screwed and will lose lives not only due to falling behind as the poison rises to where the further ahead player is, but also because the spawn logic is a bit screwy on this level (you can spawn under a ceiling you don't have time to get around and on top of before poison reaches you and kills you again).  So if playing in coop, expect some frustration from shared screen woes.The game is overall easy (though I haven't gone beyond Normal difficulty), largely due to how much mobility you have - you have a dash and a double jump right from the getgo.  Also dying in one hit like classic Contra is an option, otherwise you start with 3 hit points and can get as many as 5 - even though you can buy +1 HP and +2 HP, if you use both of these perks at the same time (you are limited to 2 at once) you only go from 3 to 5 HP, not to 6, so 5 is the max.  Most of the stages you can get through pretty easily, however the level with the gems (I believe stage 6) is a *huge* difficulty spike, after that the game gets a lot easier again until the last five minutes of the last level with the mentioned poison section (that is probably far less of a pain in single player - I've only played this coop so far).If you enter the Konami code (UUDDLRLRBA on Xbox controller) on the flaming C screen before you get to the main menu, you unlock a 30 lives perk that you can purchase for 7500 credits.  You do not just get 30 lives instantly like you did in classic Contra, you have to buy the perk and equip it as one of your 2 to have access to the 30 lives.  Also remember that in coop, if one player runs out of lives and another has some stock, the player with no lives can hit start to steal a life.  There is also an achievement for doing this.Perks can be used in both story and arcade mode.  Arcade mode bosses have extra moves, I don't know if there are any other changes, but basically this means Arcade mode is the "real" game and story is something you run through once for unlocks (you get characters from Story to use/purchase for use in Arcade after clearing Story) or maybe twice if you don't do Story on Hard the first time and want the achievement for clearing it on Hard.There are no graphic options aside from resolution, no DLSS/FSR so you can run it or you can't.  The game is 30fps cap (not lock) 1080p when docked on Switch so that should give you something to compare your system to, if it is low end you might still be able to do 30fps but games like this need to be 60fps imo.  My system is a 12600k 3070 32gb RAM everything on SSD so it smoked this game.No online coop, and I've only played it local coop, so not sure how it works in remote play together.  However last few times I've used RPT, there has been virtually no input lag playing coop as client with host being 300km away, so RPTing this game for coop should be quite doable.Story mode is max 2 players, Arcade is max of 4.  I don't know if you can start Arcade as 4 player on first launch however, as I believe only Bill and Lance are unlocked until you make some progress in Story mode.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are interested in checking out Contra: Operation Galuga, please consider taking the time to read my review!I'm an avid Contra player having played some of the previous Contra titles, but this is the first title in the series where I have actually learned the entire game to an extent.The absolute first thing to say off the top -- full-priced, this game is rather expensive for what it is. A first time Story Mode run will run you about 2 hours. If you plan on playing this game to one and done the game's story, it is not worth it at all. However, the game has a number of unlockables and secrets to grind for, and every stage has a bit of a learning curve if you are aiming to play on the harder modes. In detail:++1. This is a WayForward game, so as you would expect, controls are responsive and on point. A staple for a Contra game.2. Customizable experience. Knowing how difficult Contra can be, there is great selection of characters and Perks to fine-tune a player's experience for accessibility or added challenge.+1. Good replayability. The game has multiple ways of encouraging replay. Learn to play each stage, unlock stuff in the shop, play the challenges.2. OST is good with a nice mix of modern and classic Contra tunes. More tunes can be unlocked in the shop.3. Voice acting. Very notable throughout the game.+/-1. Visuals. The 3D model visuals look dated, but it does the job to provide enough clarity under tense moments. Visual effects and animations can be hit or miss in some instances.2. Some bugs/glitches currently exist that can hinder a playthrough along with performance drops with some weapons on some stages.-1. Expensive for what the game offers for most players.In conclusion, this game full-priced caters to folks who want to relive moments of nostalgia and are avid Contra players looking to test their skill in a great modern title. For most players who may be interested, definitely consider picking this up for a good sale if you looking to give an old school arcade game a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, a great overall game.Retains most of the original mechanics of the classic contra with a modern twist to it. The perk system can make the game easier but they're optional. If you want to make the game challenging, then you can play it without perks.Great that the game can be played with controllers on the PC version. Feels more natural this way than with the keyboard. Also, you can unlock content to further enhance the gaming experience - some include unlocking the soundtrack from the original Contra and Contra 4.To me, the game has great replayability - as it should be. You can also play it your own way like using the right perks in a given situation or go for a perkless run.Looking forward to future installments of this game in a similar format. A bit pricey, so it might turn off some buyers, but it's still a great game. Kudos to the devs, art, and marketing team.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend it for its top notch action and imagination, but.....1. The original was set up to where, if you paid attention, you could avoid getting hit and losing lives. That is, unfortunately, not possible in this title. Some enemies literally fill the entire screen with laser blasts, corrosive goo, or whatever, and you will definitely get hit. So, get the idea of passing the game without dying at least a few times out of your head.  2. At some points, your character is totally obscured, making you an easy target. 3. There's no way to regain health (but you can gain lives).4. Most of the bonus characters you can earn are straight up horrible. Other than the two original guys, Ariana and the Probotectors are the only other characters worth anything since their movement set and weapons selections are the same as Bill and Lance's. _childDocuments_.review: As a fan of many of Contra's highs and lows (Alien Wars, Hard Corps Uprising, Shattered Soldier, Neo Contra, etc). This game is a great return to form after that mobile game and the terrible....Rogue Corps.As an old soul I've enjoyed Contra all through my life and still have a blast playing fun and challenging games like this. If you're a fan of hardcore 2D shoot-em-up action you can't go wrong with this purchase. It's got a plethora of characters, various difficulties and modes to try out. However, some like myself may not be a big fan of some of the additions to the story. Some of the new story elements and characters are cliche and seem like they've been ripped out of an old-school Sword & Sorcery book or the Power Rangers. _childDocuments_.review:
When the Red Falcon terrorist group takes over the Galuga Islands off the coast of New Zealand, elite Contra commandos Bill Rizer and Lance Bean springs into action, initiating an all-out war in which the fate of mankind hangs in the balance!

Run, jump, and shoot your way through eight levels using a devastating arsenal - including the spread shot, laser, and homing missiles - now with stackable upgrades and awesome Overload abilities! The intense action is customizable with three difficulty settings plus a variety of additional challenge options.

Contra: Operation Galuga is a thorough reimagining of the classic run-'n'-gun action game from the '80s, featuring modern graphics and sound, new stages, new enemies and bosses, new play mechanics, an updated weapons system, and explosive co-op combat for up to two players in Story Mode or four players in Arcade Mode!

name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story
detailed_description: Gridrunner . Revenge of the Mutant Camels . Tempest 2000 . Llamatron . In the British gaming universe of the 80s and 90s, nobody made games like Jeff Minter. Now, in a new interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse, you can play the history of one of the weirdest, wildest game developers to ever exist – a man who loved shooters and sheep, lasers and llamas. LLAMASOFT Journey back in time to an era of cassette tapes, photocopied zines, and README.TXT. An era in which a kid with a Commodore VIC-20 and dreams of radioactive sheep could become one of Britain's best-known game makers. A virtual museum of design documents, playable games, and all-new video features tell the fascinating story of a true independent game designer. PLAY THE ACCLAIMED ORIGINALS Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story includes 42 classic games from 8 different platforms, from Jeff Minter's earliest work on the Sinclair ZX81 and Commodore VIC-20, to later work on the Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Atari 800, and deep into the 16-bit era with the Atari ST and Atari Jaguar. GRIDRUNNER: REMASTERED Jeff's signature shooter masterpiece Gridrunner gets an all-new look from Digital Eclipse, updated into thrilling modern graphics and sound – while still running the core of the Commodore 64 version for 100% gameplay accuracy. GAMES, GAMES, GAMES Sheep In Space . Andes Attack . Attack of the Mutant Camels . Matrix . Metagalactic Llamas Battle at the Edge of Time . Hellgate . Laser Zone . And many more. All the Minter classics you've heard of (and several you probably haven't), now with new quality-of-life features to make playing them more fun than ever before. Two of Jeff Minter's earliest 'light synthesizers,' Psychedelia and Colourspace , are also included, with all-new options and features optimized for controller-based play. Finally, Jeff's demo of Attack of the Mutant Camels for the unreleased Konix Multi-System console is also included. THE GOLD MASTER SERIES New from Digital Eclipse ( Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection , Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration , The Making of Karateka ), the Gold Master Series presents iconic games in an innovative 'interactive documentary' format, putting the shared history of games and their creators into one comprehensive package.
about_the_game: Gridrunner . Revenge of the Mutant Camels . Tempest 2000 . Llamatron . In the British gaming universe of the 80s and 90s, nobody made games like Jeff Minter. Now, in a new interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse, you can play the history of one of the weirdest, wildest game developers to ever exist – a man who loved shooters and sheep, lasers and llamas. LLAMASOFT Journey back in time to an era of cassette tapes, photocopied zines, and README.TXT. An era in which a kid with a Commodore VIC-20 and dreams of radioactive sheep could become one of Britain's best-known game makers. A virtual museum of design documents, playable games, and all-new video features tell the fascinating story of a true independent game designer. PLAY THE ACCLAIMED ORIGINALS Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story includes 42 classic games from 8 different platforms, from Jeff Minter's earliest work on the Sinclair ZX81 and Commodore VIC-20, to later work on the Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Atari 800, and deep into the 16-bit era with the Atari ST and Atari Jaguar. GRIDRUNNER: REMASTERED Jeff's signature shooter masterpiece Gridrunner gets an all-new look from Digital Eclipse, updated into thrilling modern graphics and sound – while still running the core of the Commodore 64 version for 100% gameplay accuracy. GAMES, GAMES, GAMES Sheep In Space . Andes Attack . Attack of the Mutant Camels . Matrix . Metagalactic Llamas Battle at the Edge of Time . Hellgate . Laser Zone . And many more. All the Minter classics you've heard of (and several you probably haven't), now with new quality-of-life features to make playing them more fun than ever before. Two of Jeff Minter's earliest 'light synthesizers,' Psychedelia and Colourspace , are also included, with all-new options and features optimized for controller-based play. Finally, Jeff's demo of Attack of the Mutant Camels for the unreleased Konix Multi-System console is also included. THE GOLD MASTER SERIES New from Digital Eclipse ( Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection , Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration , The Making of Karateka ), the Gold Master Series presents iconic games in an innovative 'interactive documentary' format, putting the shared history of games and their creators into one comprehensive package.
short_description: 42 of the weirdest, trippiest, sheepiest games ever created. Enter the mind of Jeff Minter, the legendary creator of Attack of the Mutant Camels, Gridrunner, and Tempest 2000, in this interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse.

_childDocuments_.review: Pinch me, I'm dreaming.Atari 50 was an amazing package and everything, but I had little emotional connection to the games featured. This, on the other hand...I'd had a Commodore 64 for a few months, and was still getting a feel for what it could and couldn't do. Seeing the huge camel sprites in Attack of the Mutant Camels for the first time - then already a pretty old game - completely blew me away. I read a feature in Commodore Format about Minter and Llamasoft. At school the next day I tried to explain to my friends that there was this crazy hippie guy on a farm making games about sheep and llamas in space. In a way, I'd never truly connect with my peers again. My eyes had been opened to new worlds.They're all here. Sheep in Space. Ancipital. My favourite, Hover Bovver.Hover Bovver, the original lawnmowing game, is such a design classic. So satisfying and fun to play. (If there's something Minter always seemed to nail, it's "satisfying". That's how I'd describe the handling of the ship in Attack of the Mutant Camels as well, and gradually turning them different colours as you blast them.) It's a slight pity they didn't provide an option to skip the "I'll borrow Tom's mower" screens, always a bit of a frustrating wait, but they do feel a bit faster here?The overall presentation is, as might be expected from previous Digital Eclipse releases, superb. You can dig into reading about Minter's early life in the shadow of a British nuclear facility, or start picking through his games at your leisure. There are scans of his school notebooks, even. A narrative starts to emerge of a pioneer game designer who started out imitating the trigger-happy gameplay of every arcade machine, and then perhaps shifted in a different direction of trippy, quietly satirical non-violence.I'm not sure I'm entirely keen on the fake CRT TV framing for the games - even though it can be toggled off, there's a screen glare effect that doesn't seem to go away. Full widescreen display is an option, as weird as it makes the older games look. A few games optionally have infinite lives and other options. (Not Hover Bovver though. Never could POKE that one either. How do you POKE for "Tom's mower"?)Everything I would have wanted is here, cover art and instruction manuals included. The digital coffee table book format is a very nice bonus to justify the price tag. I would be very happy to see Digital Eclipse give this treatment to every software house of the 8-bit era.Highest possible recommendation. Not every game is going to be to everyone's taste, but it's a definitive collection of an often overlooked part of gaming history, and a handful of these should be in every collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: This could have been a great interactive documentary, but it lacks on to many fronts. While the presentation is spot on (just as in ATARI50), the games are the problem.First of all the games advertised as Atari ST games are in fact very inferior Jaguar ports made by a fan. These versions have terrible sound and don't do the original justice in any kind. It is not understandable why this decision was made. Digital Eclipse could have used an open source Atari ST emulator (e.g. Hatari) to present these games in the proper way.Also there are some games that should be in the collection, e.g. at least a few of the excellent C16 versions of some games (Voidrunner, clearly the best version of the game) and Llamazap for the Atari Falcon, Minter's last game in the home computer era or Trip-A-Tron a game where DE included the 80 page manual but not the program itself. I get it, you need mouse and keyboard to use it, but then give us at least the option to do so. You can also connect mouse and keyboard to a console, not many people would do this, but now 0 users can experience Trip-A-Tron. But then it boils down to the non-Atari-ST games in the collection as Trip-A-Tron was also a ST exclusive.Overall I can not recommend this collection in this sorry state.The whole thing feels incomplete. The videos are great, but overall this is not what it could be,
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: All the included “Atari ST” games are crappy Jaguar ports instead. For example Super Gridrunner is missing the wonderful mouse/analog controls of the original game, which allowed fine control of the player ship, making it unplayable in my opinion. Llamatron is missing many of the iconic sound effects and so on.Why not include an Atari ST emulator to show the original versions of the games? For me, this is a fake collection because of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who didn't grow up with any of the Llamasoft games, I wasn't really aware of Jeff Minter until maybe around the time of Space Giraffe getting released on XBLA. I had heard of Tempest 2000, but it just wasn't something I had really grown up around. And then I finally played TxK, Minter's attempt to make a new Tempest game without Atari, and I fell in love. I've always loved the sort of Vectrek style of using lines against black bacgrounds, and the sounds and effects made it feel like a real "arcade" experience. Since TxK, I've tried to play as many of Minter's games as I can get my hands on, but that can be tricky with not all of them having been designed for modern controllers/hardware. This collection brings together a ton of those games and gives them an updated control interface so you can play them with a controller.But there's so much more. The team at Digital Eclipse has included footage of interviews with Jeff from the documentary Heart of Neon, a film about Llamasoft's history. It's not the complete film, mind you, but the stuff they've included is really interesting and gives a much clearer picture of Jeff as a person. As with the Atari 50 Anniversary Collection, there is also an absolute buttload of additional content that shows off the devices these games were created on, notebooks and photos of development information, fully 3D rendered box art, and a ton more. It's a package that's bursting at the seems for anyone who has interest in these legendary games.There is one somewhat small thing, however, that I wish there was an easier way to get around. When you look at the timeline of all the games included, you notice that there's basically nothing included from around the early/mid 90's until you get to the modern, re-imagined version of Gridrunner. Jeff was making games at this time (and still continues to), but there is a distinct lack of those games. It makes sense for some of them, as they're still being sold separately (the Minotaur Collection and Polybius come to mind) but then there are ones like Gridrunner++, the games he produced for the iOS, or even stuff like Tempest 3000 (a DVD player game) that aren't in this collection, but you do see some of them in documentary footage. It left me really wanting to check them out, but with them not being included here, it will be way more difficult.Even with that aside, this collection is still incredible. Whether you grew up with these games or are just getting to experience them for the first time, this whole package is packed with all kinds of arcade-style game goodness. Not needing to download weird emulators and program stuff to a controller is definitely a plus, but I'm mostly just glad to get all of this in one place. A fantastic collection and I hope Digital Eclipse gets to keep doing more and more stuff like this. They are so incredibly talented at this, and you really feel the love they want to share with these collections.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Keep up the good work, Digital Eclipse! As someone who's getting into college to learn how to make games, these documentaries are really inspiring. Tempest 2000 is one of my all-time favorites and I'm a huge fan of Jeff Minter's work, so this compilation was a day-one purchase for me. I do wish Tempest 3000 was included, though. Hopefully, we'll get it in an update.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I will always show up for the Digital Eclipse interactive docmentaries, regardless of the topic. The timeline format is a genius method for archiving and communicating history in a logical, entertaining, and informative way.I've played Tempest 2000 before, but otherwise I was not very familiar with Jeff Minter because I am not a 60 year old British man. I really only knew him by name and reputation. My experience with The Jeff Minter Story followed something of an upside down bell curve. The beginning was fascinating and promising. Some of the things Minter accomplished with such primitive equipment and limited programming knowledge are mind boggling (3d3d is particuarly impressive). As the story progressed though, I found myself surprised and disappointed. I had assumed, based on reputation, that Minter's games were more ground breaking than this. Nearly everything is derivative of better known games, and while he usually puts a twist on the gameplay, it is always to the game's detriment. Sometimes less is more. More alarmingly, he continues to port and iterate on the same games and concepts repeatedly. In particular I was shocked how many times he returned to the well of copying the 2600 Empire Strikes Back game (a game that is okay, but hardly an all-time great in its own right) to diminishing returns.As I approached the end though, I began reflecting on everything I had played, read, and watched, trying to suss out why he was so regarded. There are a couple of things that come into relief in the latter half of the timeline that, I think, ultimately complete the arc and offer an explanation. The first is direct engagement with fans. Many of the zines/newsletters Minter published are included, and were perhaps my favorite inclusion, reading for all the world like a blog 20 years before that became a thing. The second is Minter's work on interactive visualizers. Watching and playing how he evolved this format from it's earliest, crudest beginnings, to modern platforms, was an absolute delight, and in my mind was his greatest creative accomplishment. It's important to understand that documenting the history of gaming is a noble pursuit, whether a particular collection of games is enjoyable to me personally or not. Even though I didn't really enjoy the majority of the games included here, the experience was, as always for Digital Eclipse, worthwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so glad retro gaming preservation is so big now. Trying to explain to anyone why Ancipital was awesome in 2005 was tough, but now anyone smart enough to buy this will know first hand.I only have maybe three people I would say are my idols, and Jeff Minter's always been one of them. Having all these new primary sources to read through and watch has been a great pleasure.High score fiends will be in heaven, pay full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Jeff Minter was probably the first coding hero of mine - so a digital retrospective of his work seems like a dream come true.The compilation itself covers most of Jeff's games from the earliest ZX81 titles through to Tempest 2000 on the Jaguar.  Much like the Atari 50 compilation you can follow the timeline through and get an understanding of the history of Llamasoft and see the games in context along with videos and other digital memorabilia, or you can just play the games.To be honest if you aren't already a fan of Llamasoft then you'll probably find yourself wondering what the Hell is going on with a fair few of the games.  For those of us who were fans back in the 1980s though, this is a dream collection of games - some obscure, some amazing, a couple of genuine legendary games and a couple of early duds, Headbangers Heaven for example is a real stinker, but still worth including.Also some of the games aren't necessarily the best version - or at least aren't the version that I'd want. Llamatron is the Atari ST version ported to the Jaguar (!) rather than the much better Amiga version for example.  Also a lot of the Sinclair Spectrum games are missing - if they can include pretty much all the other versions of Gridrunner, Gridrunner 2 and Voidrunner then why not the Speccy one?With all that said is it worth getting?  For me, it's a resounding yes.  There are some games that I'm always happy to play, such as Tempest 2000, some that I'm enjoying after a 20-something year break like Llamatron, and others like Sheep in Space that I'd missed first time round and am enjoying immensely.If you're not of the 8bit generation though your enjoyment of this may be a bit more limited.  You probably had to be there...
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Another triumph from Digital Eclipse. These Gold Master Series titles (plus Atari 50, which was basically one) are essential. Having started my Llamasoft journey with Tempest 2000, it's a bit of a let down that it's the most recent game included. I had hoped it would at least include the flawed, but still interesting, Defender 2000. But really, the games themselves are secondary here. The experience is the history, and as with Making of Karateka and Atari 50, it's a joy to go through. And hey, virtually all of Minter's catalog is now available on Steam (and Deck compatible!), and that's pretty great.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: They say "context is key" and here's a LOT of context from the 1980s UK gaming scene with Jeff Minter at the centre of focus.Read the articles, newsletters and quotes, watch the videos from industry veterans or just play all the games - mostly Vic20 and Commodore C64 - which chart not only Yak's improvement at the craft but also all his experimentation, culminating in the All Time Classic Tempest 2000, or: The Reason Most People Bought an Atari Jaguar In The First Place.Then! Go and buy Space Giraffe and Tempest 4000, which may look similar but in true Minter style have quite different gameplay mechanisms.Me? I'm staggered I can buy & play Sheep in Space in 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: "He writes 'em to play 'em."is displayed in black as you open the game. A tagline from an old ad, but it slowly dawns on you that this is the thesis of Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story.The second of the Gold Master series from Digital Eclipse that are less retro game collection and more digital museum exhibit, Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story invites you into a comprehensive of the first twenty years of Jeff Minter's career and encourages you to treat as indeed the exhibit of an artist. Just like any other artist exhibit, you slowly see Jeff grow in technical proficiency and develop his personal style and motifs- whether that's visual elements like the light synthesizer or gameplay mechanics like the assist droid. In a landscape of further consolidation and commodification in the video game industry, this is a tribute to a true independent spirit and a testament to true artistry.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting documentary, and probably the best (and in many cases, only) way to experience the early Minter genius.  I assume rights issues were involved, but the absence of the 'best' (and in some cases, only) version of later games is disappointing to say the least, together with all the supposed 'Atari ST' games being inferior Jaguar ports.  Recommended, but only if you already know Minter is your thing.  And even then, you'll still be playing Llamatron on WinUAE.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: It doesn't get any more retro than this. Yes, you can outdo even that one guy on Rumble with the Intellivision gameplay videos and play something even more obscure and precious. Vic 20, Commodore 64, Atari, and all the weirdest games including grid shooting and ruminating animals. I enjoy trying the different versions of Grid Runner from all the different systems. Llamatron 2112 is cray. Hover Bovver is weird and hilarious. There is another game that starts with a B that is five other games inside and the shooter is wild. What kind of a freaking game is that! Yo, you gotta try them all including Jeff Minter's "Centipede-at-home" as I call it. You memers will know what I'm saying. Mom, can I play centipede? We have centipede at home. You have to get this compilation.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant, feel-good romp through roughly  the history of one of the great survivors of Indie Prehistory, packed to the brim with wonderfully weird takes on the arcade canon. Not all of it hits (Mama Llama will continue to provoke debate and ire for centuries to come), but when it hits, it's utterly sublime. It'll make you want to pick up a keyboard and make your own.Now, where's that All The Long-Delisted iPhone Games DLC...?
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: I got this out of loving Digital Eclipse's docu-games, but this is an incredible, and informative game.Following the 40+ year journey of Jeff Minter through not only through his growth as a game developer, but as a vertical slice of the entire industries history from his perspective. I really loved this, and found many of his games that are playable within to be really delightful, and the live action interviews are all both entertaining, and very enlightening as to what development was like. By the end, I was invested in Jeff's story, and felt inspired by it.I highly encourage this Game compilation / documentary for anyone who's interested in the history of gaming, classic games, or aspiring developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad jaunt through Llamasoft's history, albeit with a few games missing along the way.However if you're hoping to have a blast on Jeff's C64 magnum opus, Iridis Alpha, don't bother.Shocklingly bad emulation of the C64 and includes the same bonus stage crash bug that's been around for 38 years!Buy it to read about a national hero and potter about on some of the early games, but for IA, download Hokuto Force's amazing, bugfixed version and play it on Vice or some emulator that actually works!
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Big fan of Jeff Minter's game since I had a Commodore 64 and a cartridge version of Gridrunner 2: Attack Of The Mutant Camels.  I buy anything he puts out on Steam, and when I saw this documentary filled with all the old games I had to buy it immediately.To be able to play Gridrunner 2 again so easily just by booting this documentary up on Steam.  One of the best things I EVER bought on Steam, ever ever!
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Jeff Minter + Digital Eclipse is a match made in heaven. Taking the same "virtual museum" approach as the (similarly excellent) Atari50 package, this fabulous collection presents a fascinating history of Llamasoft, with a wealth of old photos, videos and interviews.Better still, it includes over 40 playable Llamasoft games (across a wide range of systems) all of which are emulated extremely well for the most part making it incredible value for money and the easiest way to play some great games without having to fiddle with emulation. Presentation-wise and emulation-wise you get exactly what you'd expect from Digital Eclipse, which is a lovingly curated set of archival material, games and freshly-shot footage alongside lots of extras.The main weakness is that it stops in the early 2000s and wraps up the last 20 years of Llamasoft very, very briefly, with no games playable from that era - presumably due to licensing issues. The number of playable items (and the variety of systems represented) also decreases as you get to the later history. That's a shame, as it leaves the package feeling incomplete.Overall though, this is an incredible package that tells you a lot about Llamasoft and the development of the broader games industry from its earliest days, as told through the experiences of Jeff Minter who has been there to see it all.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing package.  Great history on Llamasoft and a wonderful collection of games.  I wish some of these would not have been Atari Jaguar conversions of the original games but I supposed it saved on software development time.  The more colorful games really pop on the OLED screen of my Steam Deck.  No issues whatsoever player on Deck.  Wonderful collection overall, highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: This package is worth it just for Tempest 2000 plus the three ST games.But you also get the reimagined Gridrunner Remastered, which is (I think?) the C64 version with updated graphics, and you can switch between graphics on the fly.You get earlier games, which are a mixed bag, but some of them are great (I love Metagalactic Llamas, for some reason). These go back to the ZX81.And you get a fantastic archive of game development, plus interesting documentary videos about Jeff and his work. The value here is over 10/10, and is certainly a game I'd buy for my Steam friends if I had any Steam friends at my decrepit age who played micros back in the day.Request 1: if it could be possible for Llamatron to allow droid helper AND twin stick, that would be grand.Request 2: Jeff agrees that Iridis Alpha is too hard (one of the videos). Put in some kind of option to make it easier, please. E.g. toggles to tone down Licker ships, make it easier to gain energy, turn off blowing up at high energy, and frankly turn off entropy. I know that changes the game entirely but, yes, I think it's a good idea to have the option. Also, being able to hold up to turn back to flying mode without having to run for ages while being killed would be nice - it's too easy to turn into land mode without wanting to, sometimes. I've watched a guide on Iridis Alpha. I've watched someone longplaying the game and saying it's harder to fight Licker ships on emulation - they could clear a wave in 20 seconds just by bobbing up and down and firing, so I wonder if that's relevant here.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: This product is a combination of historical information, some video material, some art and snippets of development documentation. It'll give you Jeff Minter's story (partly at least) and a time line of the games he's made over the years. It allows you to play the games, regardless of which platform they came out on. So VIC20, C64, ZXSpectrum, AtariST, etc. Up to 1990 and then as an added bonus Grid Runner reimagined from 2023. All playable with controller or keyboard. A chance to experience many of Jeff's games, up to 1990 in one neat package.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: That is a wholesome journey through videogame history of Jeff Minter. Surely a banger to try out Tempest 2000 and some of his addicting lightsynths. Too bad some of his apps are not included like Trip-a-Tron. However, such virtual museum of 42 games (even if some are small and primitive by today's standards) and Jeff's gamedev background is definitely worth the price. Definitelly recommended for Minter's fans!
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: My impressions video: If you're into games that are mechanics focused, Jeff Minter is a name you need to know if you don't already. An OG British game developer who was a true indie in an era where that term hadn't even been invented yet, this collection showcases his awesome work, design ethos, and fierce independent spirit with the same slick presentation that Digital Eclipse brought with  and .Presented as a playable documentary, this features timelines of Minter's history with quotes, high-detail scanned photos and documents, and a number of videos as well. This was produced in collaboration with the upcoming Heart of Neon documentary and I believe is where most of that footage as from. It's not nearly as high quality or well shot as the first-party Digital Eclipse footage from the other two collections, but it still does the jobs well enough.Beyond that is a huge selection of Minter's catalogue throughout the decades, including different platform releases of many of his titles. Everything gets modem touches such as rewind, save states and various ways to change the video appearance to your liking, plus high-resolution scans of the manuals. Even if you only came to this for the games, there's a lot to play here. Minter's design style and ideas aren't for everyone and some of his most esoteric titles are included here, but they're very mechanically rewarding for those willing to put in the time.My biggest criticism of this package is a similar one to what I had with Atari 50. There's a big section of Jeff's modern history (from about the Xbox 360 era onward) that is just plain omitted. Many would argue this era comprises some of his best work. Many of the games not talked about here are for sale on this very platform today, but you'd never know about them if you got your information on him solely from this title. Maybe it's because those titles are still for sale or because some of them are on platforms that are not yet easy to emulate, but the lack of any mention of them does a disservice to those who came here looking for a full history of his work. I do wonder if that's because in this era, there was a lawsuit involving Atari, which is Digital Eclipse's parent company (though that acquisition happened when this would have been mostly finished). That was under different management that has nothing to do with "current Atari" though, so again, it doesn't seem a good reason to leave all this out. The collection is still well worth playing, but given that DE markets these under the auspices of preservation, I don't like how two out of three collections so far have major historical gaps in them.The collection as a whole is great, whether you're an existing Jeff Minter fan like me or want to learn something about a developer who has always marched to his own beat and never let the industry get him down or stop him from doing what he wanted. Minter embodies the indie spirit and more people should know about him.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: I'm all in on the Gold Master Series stuff from Digital Eclipse. After The Making of Karateka and now Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story, I'll grab any of these.There's something really fun and exciting about playing a developer's games from the very beginning - a crude Centipede knock off for the Spectrum to a psychedelic Tempest sequel for the Jaguar. You can see Minter's voice and vision clarify over a decade, and you get bits and pieces of who he is from documentary snippets from a forthcoming film, and photography, notes to himself, and fun quotables. Comparing this with the previous game in this series, where Jordan Mechner is a guy who worked extremely hard on a handful of games, Jeff Minter was in the practice of programming a game in a week and sending it out into the world. You couldn't have picked two more different guys to profile, other than that their initials are the same.Great, weird, fun and all the additional context and background they provide - and the work they do to make the emulated games play nice on a game pad - lets you enjoy the games for what they are instead of weird old puzzles you noodle with for 30 seconds.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan then this is quite fun, the games run pretty well but there are some issues, the biggest let down is not online score charts, that would make this worthy, sadly there are not and as all the games are freely available to play on emulators the £25 asking price is a bit steep.Could have been better, such a shame, the images and bits of history are good but generally a little light on content, most have already been held on the origional Llamasoft archive and YakYak.It's a little look down memory lane 3/10 from me.Overall it's a poor effort on behalf of the makers of the system, far more effort could have been made to justify the price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Another quality installment in Digital Eclipse's series and a neat historical look at the UK computer scene of the 80's through Jeff Minter's experiences, especially for me as an American who had little knowledge of it; but man just like with Karateka I just don't like the vast majority of Jeff Minter's games in this collection. A good chunk of them are obnoxious sensory overload that go way too fast and/or are overly complex to a trollish degree. Also didn't change my opinion that Commodore games just sucked. Tempest 2000 is cool though and I definitely can see why it was the only reason to get a Jaguar. Funny thing is I felt Jeff's visualizer programs were more of an interesting topic when it came to his games because even if I wasn't totally into them Jeff had a clear passion for them as well as an ambition that was ahead of his time with them. Just as with Karateka, Llamasoft is a great historical piece but I just wish they could cover games that are mostly fun to play. Regardless I'm completely locked into with this series and definitely will be Day 1 once again for the next installment.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: While the documentary is fun and interesting, this collection's a mess and is a massive disservice to Minter's legacy.30 dollars isn't worth a documentary (that you can already just look up instead) lumped in with a bunch of poorly-emulated deceptive ROMs, and it's a shame too since the Atari 50 Collection is pretty decent apart from the glorified "after-market sequels" which are just fan ROM hacks.I refunded this game for a reason.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Expertly and lovingly put together - (where is Jeff at the moment anyway??). I have the excellent Digital Eclipse Karateka too but that was one game. The way this goes right back to his teenage years is fantastic and you hear about those little interactions which shaped his life and career, first messing around with the PET and ZX80. Every first gen videogame fan, anyone who learned coding on an 8bit machine should have this. I never really liked his early games but from Iridis Alpha onwards I started to appreciate the genius. And is it just me or did Andrew Braybrook reuse a bunch of Minter's sound effects in Paradroid?? I haven't yet got to the 1990s on this so I don't know if the amazing and audacious Space Giraffe is emulated, but I can still play that on the xbox360 anyway. It deserves a bigger audience than it ever got on XBLA.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew nothing about Jeff Minter before seeing this collection's trailers. And honestly I'm not sure I'm fully taken by his Llamasoft games. That's why it's so magical I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story is a great way to experience the mind of Jeff Minter and his work. Hearing about his PSVR version of Polybius got me interested in learning about his other pieces of work, and I grew attached to all of them. I absolutely love his trippy and weird games and experiences. They truly feel psychedelic, unreal, and just don't feel like human creations. Jeff Minter's games truly feel like they came from another world with how weird they are.HOW I GOT THE GAME:When I heard about Digital Eclipse doing a giveaway of this game on their social medias along with other games to celebrate the solar eclipse, I had to get on board and try to win this. Every time they posted a new code for this game, someone else beat me to the punch, snatched the code and got it. The goal post would constantly keep getting pushed back for me, and after multiple failed attempts to win this game, I started to lose hope.But then, a new code for the game shows up on Threads. The hint for the missing letters of the code was the atomic symbol for radon, which was Rn. Getting the clue, I rushed to activate the code to get my hands on this game because I was such a big fan of Jeff's work and I wanted to know more about him and his company. I put in the code with the letters that were missing, and then... "Activation Successful: ALPACA for Beta Testing".I did it. I got the game from the code and I literally freaked out. I was determined to get this game from the giveaway, and despite multiple shortcomings in being not quick enough, I was able to get the game code from the giveaway and redeem the game. I literally was freaking out. It was one of the major games I wanted to win from the giveaway, alongside The Making of Karateka, which I also won as well. I literally was so happy.MY REVIEW:So, this game is like a true gift. And when I mean that, I mean not only as an early birthday present since my birthday is coming up, but a real gift as a big Jeff Minter fan. You get to go into every bit of Llamasoft's history, learn about them, and watch videos. There is so much content to keep you entertained, and it is truly the best way to preserve games inside a collection like this one, or Atari 50, another game published by Digital Eclipse.And speaking of "games", you don't just get to learn about the games Jeff Minter has created. You actually get to *play* them. Yes, that's right. In this massive documentary-like game, there is a total of 42 different Llamasoft games that are all entirely playable from start to finish, which includes a remastered version of Gridrunner. You can sink literal hours into playing all of these different games through Llamasoft's rich history, even going as far back to play 3D 3D, their first game which is an impressive 3D maze for what it was designed for.Documentaries are usually never worth my time, I really hardly care less about them because I can not sit through them. But this? This is a great way to get people interested in watching these documentaries. But this is truly the first (technically second) interactive one, since you can zoom in on photos and 3D models and play various games from Llamasoft. It's not just videos. It's literally an interactive time machine.It is truly the best way to experience Jeff Minter's weird and trippy games. You get to play and learn about them at the same time. It is truly the best combination, and if it weren't for The Making of Karateka, this game probably wouldn't have happened. You could watch the history of companies before, but now, you can literally *play* the history, too. It is a combination that goes together like peanut butter and jelly. The videos are still in there as well, and they are very entertaining to watch, too. It's like you get to know more about Jeff as a person.And as a big time Llamasoft fan, this is a literal gold mine. A golden ticket into learning about how a company rose from making unlicensed ports into making entire full-on games with weird and trippy visuals (music, too). And learning about his Polybius VR game was truly the moment that made me interested in learning about him and Llamasoft more. If you are a fan of Jeff Minter's work like I am, this is without a doubt worth a purchase for any Llamasoft fan.You will not regret it. You will learn so much more about Llamasoft and Jeff, trust me.
_childDocuments_.name: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story

_childDocuments_.review: Digital Eclipse makes some of the best documentary-styled compilations of games, and this is no exception. If you like the history of video games and learning about designers while also getting to try some of these pieces for yourself without having to resort to tracking down physical copies, you'll like Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story.That being said, his games are not for everyone's tastes. You'll enjoy them if you like light shows (do NOT buy this if you have Epilepsy), animals, and arcade-styled score chasing games. It has all those things in spades, the best of which being Tempest 2000, which I found very hard to put down. Jeff's games are one thing, but his relaxed (very British) personality is another. He really is someone who perseveres, found his audience and brought them along with him on his creative journey. I found the documentary clips inspiring, entertaining, and the overall presentation package very well-done.8.5/10, I think this Gold Master series is really fantastic!

name: Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip
detailed_description: MORE FROM US About the Game Step into Terry’s flip flops in this short and delightfully sweet adventure of self-discovery as he uncovers what it means to be an inhabitant of ✨Sprankelwater✨ . Key Features: Explore a densely packed, tiny open world town at any pace and in any way you like. Slow, fast, by foot, by car, by paraglider! It’s up to you. Uncover a wholesome story through hilarious interactions with weird Sprankelwaterians. Collect TURBO JUNK and upgrade the boost capacity of Terry’s very own car. Catch insects, dig holes, destroy cars, become rich, wear hats. Listen to a joyful and heart-warming soundtrack from the composer of Wuppo.

short_description: Terry wants to launch himself into space using his new car. Doing something this cool and reckless will surely make him the talk of the town. Run, drive and glide through this small journey of big discoveries as Terry works towards achieving this goal.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great example of the burgeoning "relaxing adventure game" genre. If you like games such as A Short Hike, Lil Gator Game, or even Sable then you'll like this too.Unlike those other games, however, this game is made by the creator of Wuppo, which is a very very good thing. The trademark charm, humor, and bizarre world are present in this game just like Wuppo. The first thing that happens is you applying for a taxi job just for the car, then proceeding to never actually do your job. Afterward you're free to wander around this small but dense city and collect junk by doing various things so you can use the junk to upgrade your taxi's turbo boost enough so you can drive into space. This is taken 100% seriously by everyone. It plays like a slapstick GTA mixed with Mario Odyssey, and its a treat.HIghly recommended for fans of relaxing open-world games, addicting collectathons, and/or games with a unique artstyle and oddball sense of humor.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip

_childDocuments_.review: its is a very silly, low stakes game that I crave. It reminds me a lot of a Short Hike or Button City. You just go around doing whatever you feel like, no crazy challenges, just little mini games, things to explore and junk to be found. The dialog is also very funny. To me this is what a cozy game is. No tasks or clock counting down (looking at you stardew) just do whatever you feel like when you feel like it.Life is hard. I've played EVERY From Software souls-like. I am tired and I just want to have fun and release dopamine in a stress-free environment.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip

_childDocuments_.review: This love letter to Simpsons Hit & Run is delightful, charming, silly, and a damn good way to spend a handful of hours.The highlight is Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip's densely populated city full of comedic scenarios that subvert and play into the best tropes of gameplay concepts from generations past. When we look back on this era of indie games inspired by A Short Hike, I hope this one becomes a staple in that conversation.

_childDocuments_.review: 10h 3/10 1 I wrote  No  I'm unsure if you can continue after finishing the game. Yes, collecting all the collectibles is a bit of a grind No No No No No difficulty setting NoTiny Terry's Turbo Trip is an awesome (small) open-world game in which you play as Terry. your parents are on holiday and you are left alone. You have just one wish and this is the right time to go for that.... A car to get to space! So you go to the Job Application Centre to apply for a job... kinda... which comes with a car. And after you get the car it is time to explore the city. Meet some people and help them with whatever they ask for. I love the world Terry lives in. It is a city without many rules. So many times I saw cars crashed, or waiting in a line for nothing.. but that also makes total sense because if you have one person that parks in the middle of the road (Terry would never do that, would he?  :P) then the rest is stuck there as well. I felt a bit lost at the beginning of the game... it wasn't totally clear what I should do next, but that is because you can do anything you want. There are no rights or wrongs, just go to question marks on the map to meet people and help them out.  I would highly recommend destroying boxes and garbage bags because they contain money, and you'll need a lot of money! To buy equipment ( a net, a helmet that will tell you where to find Turbo Trash, a paraglider (PS I would also buy them in that order)), to buy hats, and also for some quests (aka To-do list items). For me as a Dutch person, it was so funny to see some of the names of people but also places. They are not totally Dutch words but are made up with parts of Dutch words. You don't need to know any Dutch to play Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip but it feels like a little easter egg. I had so much fun playing TTTT and I love the humor the game has. There are so many jokes, some in plain sight, some a bit hidden but I laughed out loud a lot of times because of the twist something took that I didn't expect. About the achievements in Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip, I'm unsure if you can continue after finishing the game. The game warns you about going to the finish, so you will clearly know what to do to end the game. After doing that I came back into the world but without any to-do list items. However, I completed them all before going through the ending so maybe that is why the to-do list was clear? Or maybe because you can't continue, which would make sense story-wise. I would also guess that having 450 Turbo Trash on you is missable. However, if you missed that it is quite easy to get that in a new game, and gladly the game has 4 save slots. What I love about the achievements in TTTT is that they are there for just doing everything. Nothing hidden and you don't need a guide if you don't want to. The ending is so clear that you don't need to know beforehand when that will happen to make sure you did everything. However, it has an achievement for getting every single Turbo Trash ( aka collectible) in the game. There is a hat that will tell you with audio when there is turbo trash nearby and I highly highly recommend buying that very early on to already mop up most of them while playing through the game. This will be the most challenging achievement as there is just trash hidden everywhere. In the sky, underground.. in buildings, at the top of buildings.. as I said, everywhere. I'm so so glad the developer added the Ape Escape helmet (kinda, but it reminds me of that) to tell you when you're close to the trash. I give Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip 4,5 out of 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: The main reason me and my friends saw this was due to the WASD convention this year in London at the Truman Brewery. We were incredibly tempted to steal the only (at the time) Terry plush but we didn't wanna get arrested that night. Thank you snekflat for going to the convention and enlightening me on this beautiful game.Terry is now my best friend. I shall have many dreams alongside him collecting turbo junk and driving off into space. The game's actually pretty damn good, about 6 hours of gameplay but all really fun to experience. What might be a good thing to mention is this was all during one session of play as I just got addicted to Terry'ing around. The humour is on point and the overall substance of the game doesn't feel stale at any point. _childDocuments_.review: Can't believe I haven't reviewed Tiny Terry earlier.This game is so small and contained, but scratches a very specific itch.1. It's a mini open-world game where you can finish the main quest fairly quickly, but the fun part lies in the side quests and challenges. The main premise is so dumb and cartoony, and I love it.2. You interact with goofy townfolk, that often have quirky demands, and upon completion, you are rewarded with some of the most out-of-left-field resolutions you can't help but laugh at. 3. The controls are so smooth and the platforming is //4. The comedy is physical, verbal, and meta at times (when an achievement pops up, it often provides a punchline). 5. You can wear costumes, jump, hit, drive towards or off of, explore, do just about anything you want in this town.It's like a tiny sandbox full of funny, engaging characters and storyline, with tight controls and superb sound design. Probably the most fun I've had with a video game in a long while.Just pure, simple, fun.
