_childDocuments_.review: I don't believe I've played a game like this in a long time. The atmosphere, the humor, the intrinsic quirkiness of the world, everything was clearly made from a place of genuine care. The map itself is well designed, and really packs a lot in a small package. The game's campaign itself is also a sizable length, I haven't finished it yet, but its probably a day's journey or more with the side quests. the only criticism I have is that terry himself doesn't have much mobility compared to other platformers or collectathons, however the action when messing around in the car I think makes up for that. _childDocuments_.review: If you're after pure, unfiltered gaming joy, you really owe it to yourself to give Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip a look. This 3D adventure platformer is unabashedly weird in all the right ways, while backing it up with solid gameplay and a pleasingly wholesome story that doesn't spoil the fun.Terry's goal is to go to space. To do that, he'll need a souped-up car that can make it up the side of the city's unfathomably tall skyscraper. That's where you come in. You'll guide Terry as he collects Turbo Junk (traded for speed boosters), searches for cash in all the wrong places, and gets involved in a spot of yoga, or orange football. The delightfully offbeat humour complements the playdoh aesthetic perfectly, and I chortled more than once at Terry's deadpan monosyllabic answers. Aside from a camera that occasionally sidles into overly-intimate territory (thanks to a rather restrictive upper and lower range - Terry seems to struggle to look up), controlling Terry and his shoe-shaped taxi is smooth and responsive, making for enjoyable platforming, looting, and careening around the streets of Sprankelwater. The city itself is compact, which brings me to one of very few criticisms I had: it definitely felt like the world could have been a bit bigger and more varied. That said, despite its pint-sized proportions, there's plenty to do: minigames, digging up loot, smashing containers, and a few side quests for friends, rounding out to around 5-6 hours of playtime with most achievements. There are also secrets to find, and collectible hats/gummy pups to amass.Getting into TTTT might take a minute, as there's relatively little instruction to get you started and the multi-level road layouts take some getting used to...but once you're hooked, the hours will fly by. TTTT oozes character and heart, from its whimsical animation style to its peppy soundtrack and sweet, playful story. My only wish is that there was even more of it!

_childDocuments_.review: Tiny Terry’s Turbo Trip ReviewPlease check out our video review:  Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip Honest ReviewWe all have dreams that may seem unattainable, especially when we become fixated on them. Terry only has one dream: To drive a car into space. If it sounds bonkers, keep watching this honest review. I want to thank Deadgood Media for the Steam Deck review copy, and to you for stopping by. StoryTerry lives on the island of Spranklewater. He has been left there by his parents who are on summer holiday, and want him to attend summer school. He has other plans though, and applies for a job to get a car and drive into space. Terry will encounter some interesting characters along the way and learn valuable life lessons. The writing is superb with a lot of ridiculous satire which compliments the whole presentation. GameplayThis is a sandbox game that can be played in first or third-person. The aim is to carry out different quests to collect money and junk. Money can be used to buy equipment and cosmetic items to progress through the game. Junk is the second currency that will allow your car to be upgraded with a booster, enabling you to launch into space. Both can be obtained from the environment via digging and breaking props in the environment. Several NPCs will require your aid and offer money and junk as rewards. How you carry out your adventure is up to you. Terry can visit virtually the entire island at will and carry out many activities, such as playing football with a fruit, stealing cars or finding blueprints. If you get lost or don’t know what to do next, Terry can dial 1 on his phone and get hints, or check your progress in the pause menu. The game is short, but don’t let this put you off a great experience.  Think of cosy games like A Short Hike, which can be done in a few hours but has a lot of substance. Your mileage will depend on how much you explore, collect and carry out.Terry cannot die in the game, regardless of becoming involved in many traffic accidents and prone to getting run over by locals. He can hitch a ride and drive any he likes. The game's main appeal is the humour-infused shinanigans Terry gets involved in and the collectathon. Some moments break the 4th wall slightly and the game has copious amounts of charm. I spent a lot of my time chuckling to myself after facing Terry towards the camera and spamming the shoutout button. It is a very silly feature, but it’s one I’d like to see in other games. Many may feel like the game needed to be longer or offer more, but it is a testament to how good the game is. There is a good balance of exploration and enjoying the experience without deadlines. Visuals audio and presentationTiny Terry’s Turbo Trip employs a visually captivating style through its use of simple yet vivid cel animations. The landscape is adorned with an array of buildings and flora, set apart by their slightly desaturated colours. This provides a striking contrast to the lively and vibrant NPCs and props, resulting in a visually dynamic and engaging experience. There is slight popping here and there, but it never really affected the experience. I did not encounter any bugs or framerate issues during my playtime. The audio is made up of whimsical catchy songs, and background effects that bring the island to life. ConclusionAt the time of writing, I was unable to get pricing information on the game. But it will require 8gb of space to download. I hope to see this doing well enough so Super Rare Games can bring it out physically and on other platforms.Tiny Terry’s Turbo Trip is yet another indie gem that offers a wholesome experience in short bursts. It offers a lot of relaxing and funny moments, whilst touching on some deep subjects about growing up. Fans of short wholesome games should check this out. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip is a game created by the developer of Wuppo, and with the short amount of time I've had playing it so far, I can safely say that this game is great! _childDocuments_.review: Tiny Terry's Turbo Trip is a fun, engaging comedy adventure that you can't help but love. Or at least, really like. It's humor is spot on but it also has a great narrative that at times goes beyond comedy to find poignancy.  The world of Spranklewater is fun to explore and admire for its gorgeous art and watching the NPCs constantly get into car accidents is hilarious.The gameplay kind of left me wanting a little more variety though. Much of your time is spent wandering the island, looking for an object, and bringing it back to an NPC. There are a couple of mini-games that break this up, and the game is pretty short at around 3 hours per playthrough. It's not bad at all, and I do recommend the game, but I do wish there was a little more bit to the game.Full video review:

name: Sucker for Love: Date to Die For
detailed_description: While investigating the mysterious disappearances plaguing your rural hometown of Sacramen-Cho, you end up kidnapped yourself! Trapped in the dark heart of the labyrinthian woods, your only hope for escape rests within the pages of the cultists’ strange purple spellbook. Amidst the scrawlings of madmen and images of otherworldly abominations, a passage describes how to summon The Black Goat of the Woods— Rhok'zan. The rest of the town seems to be under the thrall of Rhok'zan’s all-consuming aura of love, but for some reason you feel… different? Can you escape, or will you meet your demise at the innumerable hands of The Thousand? A fun four-chapter visual-novel romp through Lovecraftian mythos, inspired by classics like 'The Dunwich Horror' and 'The Shadow over Innsmouth' Introducing Rhok'zan, The Black Goat of the Woods: a new dateable entity! Multiple endings determined by player choice All new 360-degree, hand-drawn 2D environments! Nostalgic art style reminiscent of old school anime and classic dating sims! No horror elements this time, we swear. Come on, trust us haha.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the game has forced me to give a negative recommendation. It's not like I didn't enjoy it -- I did -- but it's so different from the first one that it's like I was tricked into playing it.The first game was a parody of dating sims using Lovecraft mythos elements for the setting. The protagonist was a hornball cultist willing to destroy the world to get a kiss from a monster. The rituals you perform, the toll they take both on the world and on you, and the horror of it all, all take front and center.It's like the developer went out of his way to make this game as different as possible from the first one: there's basically no dating (even as a joke, in the first game your goal was to romance the abominations) aspect to speak of, and the eldritch monster gets pushed more and more to the sidelines as the game progresses, which is just incredible.The protagonist is an asexual who's not even interested in the Black Goat at all. Or is she? She's somewhat inconsistently written in that regard, going from saying she feels absolutely zero lust for the heroine and just wanting to banish her, to being excited about being her dream girl in the span of 10-20 minutes. She's so much the opposite of the first game's protagonist that in order to start interacting with the heroine you *have* to grab a spray bottle in case she flirts with you. You know, in case you're playing a quirky sort of dating sim and flirting is too much for you.Finally, the rituals are practically a vestigial feature, and again the more the game progresses the more they get pushed to the side. The cosmic and body horror just isn't really there, either. At one point you have to get in a cocoon that's supposed to liquefy your organs to make your body more malleable for further transformations, and I thought "okay, the game is gonna let me look in the mirror and see what a Brundlefly I must look like now". Nope. To drive the point home, at several points the protagonist gets hurt (deep cuts, broken bones) and the game makes it a point to say that the black woods will conceal the damage from you. "Don't worry, player. In this game about Lovecraftian abominations, there's no horror to be found whatsoever."In summary, I don't know who the game is for. It *feels* like it's made with a particular audience in mind. I don't who those people are, but I don't think it's for the people who played the first game and wanted more. If you come in expecting that, it'll feel like getting a slap to the face.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry, I like this dev, and I think it's important to support indie devs, but you should just play the first Sucker For Love. This game is not like the first one, and I think the trailers give a false impression of what this game is. This is not a dating sim with horror elements, this is a horror game with one, fake dating element that you don't interact with. There is only one "dateable" character, the goat, despite the trailers giving the impression otherwise. There are not endings for each girl you don't even get to pick one. You end up with the goat no matter what. The "dating" elements have been entirely replaced with horror in this game, to the point where I don't think this should even have the "dating sim" tag. The horror elements are not nearly as strong in this game. Eldritch horror is replaced with a slasher-esque horror and overdone time-loop gimmicks. Wandering the house is way too scripted to be scary. The challenges are also too easy. Most enemies you'll accidentally beat and not realize why. You never spend enough time facing one enemy to truly understand any of the patterns and complexities they might have.After thinking about it for a bit, I think the answer is clear. This game was delayed at one point to give the developer more time to finish working on it. I think they were forced to cut content, and reduce the scale of the game. They chose to focus on creating a purely horror experience and cut most of the dating aspects. The time loop makes much more sense when you think about it being designed for that kind of experience instead. The previous game had multiple routes that you had to load checkpoints to reach, and a time loop would make that aspect of the gameplay canon. Each girl once "saved" from the cult has a designated spot that they sit in the house. They have a custom sprite for it and everything. You can talk to them and get some flavor text, but they will disappear upon chapter end. It makes far more sense if they were supposed to be permanent. You could unlock different girls and progress different routes naturally as you played the game. Instead, the girls disappear at the end of their chapter, and never return. I think the setting also makes more sense when you think about it this way. Instead of facing a single enemy each chapter, threats stay present as you progress the time loop. So eventually you'd be facing every threat at once near the end of the game. I'm fairly confident in this theory, and it's sad because there's a genuinely brilliant game in here that I think the developer just didn't have the resources to see though. There's plenty more examples in favor of this theory too, like the 80's theme that was advertised in some of the games promo material only being present in the menus and two character designs. This game isn't bad, but I don't think the best way to experience this game is to play it. I think the best way to experience this is to wait for your favorite streamer to play it, and watch them instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Had I not played and enjoyed the first installment of this fine series, that front cover of Rhok’zan, the blasphemous goat milf of my dream, would have gored itself into my mind and lived there eternally, rent free.. Sucker for Love 2 expands on the great promise of courting eldritch horrors and weaves a great narrative around Stardust, a forlorn girl looking for her past in a town of pale reflections. This time however, we only ever get to court one god, but in addition the game introduces a whole cult of quirk side characters as well as some cameos from ages past, all with top notch voice acting as a cherry on the top! This time around the gameplay got more of a slasher horror wibe to it and the 90s aesthetics are spot on. Some of the segments felt a bit slow paced but overall the creepy ambience of the dilapidated house with its occult paraphernalia strewn about made for a joysome crawl.The game is fairly short (around 6 hours) and worked decently on a Steam Deck. I would argue it is well worth it if you are into light dating sims, quirky humor with excellent lewd dialogues broken up with wanton bloodshed. This is high quality smut for the modern cultists with a furry (or eldritch horror, pick your poison) edge to it! Time to write some wriggly fanfic! ^_^

_childDocuments_.review: Sucker for Love: Date to Die For is not like the first game. But it doesn't try to be. It is honestly refreshing to see a game dev willing to branch out and experiment rather than just make an updated version of the same thing as before. And in this experiment, AkaBaka succeeds with flying colors.I love the new character Stardust, and how her relationship with Rhok'zan develops. The way she clashes with the various villains and how she overcomes them is honestly touching, and the story ends in a very satisfying way, especially for fans of the original.In terms of game mechanics, while I do miss the dating sim mechanics from the first Sucker for Love, the much improved horror aspect of the sequel more than makes up for it. Traversing the house for the first time is genuinely spooky, and the way it ramps up in the next chapters is great! The idea of a home being violated and made unsafe by unknown, hostile enemies is a great horror trope. There are a handful of jumpscares, but the game doesn't rely on them as a crutch. You WILL get a lot of jumpscares if you're not good at navigating the house, but by the third chapter you will have definitely memorized the house layout.Mild spoilers, but one moment that really stands out to me is the first time I was trying to avoid Billie. I had opened a door about halfway just as I saw the Billie enter the room, closed it, backed up, and ran away. It was very tense, in the best of ways.On that note, the door opening mechanic is SUCH a good touch. It harkens back to classic Resident Evil, only instead of waiting for the cutscene to end, you have to open it yourself, and that little bit of extra player control makes it pretty scary in the early game. The first time I opened a door all the way at once without checking what was on the other side was the first time I got really scared, and damn that was good. From then on until the last chapter, I was very slowly opening doors, and spotting the instant death on the other side just before it got me.Lastly, I really appreciate that the power of love is still the main story element. For Darling, it was a lustful love that overcame the eldritch powers beyond the stars, and for Stardust, it was her platonic love for mankind, even the ones that were her enemies, that won the day.10/10, make Muu romanceable in Sucker for Love 3!

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I would wish steam had a middle option for reviews, but alas my final opinion is swaying in a different direction.Pros:-more characters compared to the last game-very nice old anime artstyle-nice soundtrack- very good final sequence that honestly could be a game of it's own.Cons:- When dying and going to the checkpoint flowchart you're forced to the beginning of it, and have to scroll back to the point where you died. Not a big deal but a bit irrating if you don't quite understand some stuff and keep dying like me.- It feels weird to have a visual novel with no backlog.- On that note, I'm not sure how it works but it feels weird when voicelines are cut-off completely if you click during the text display. A few times skipped some voicelines by accident.- Some stuff feels underused (like the mechanic of wearing stuff, and the candles in particular - there's so many colors for them, yet over the course of the whole game you use like 3. What's worse is that candles are pretty much overlapping the button to open the book so sometimes you accidentaly change color when you mean to open it. Annoying if you need to have a specific color for a ritual to work.)- the chanting element feels very wonky, but that might just be my mouse.- the plot has some good ideas going for it but imo it feels we kinda skipped a lot Overall I think the game should be a bit longer. I know it's comedic in nature, but I don't think it needed to be this short.

_childDocuments_.review: It had a ton of potential but ended up being kind of a disappointment.Performance is pretty bad even on good hardware. _childDocuments_.review: As much as I hate to say it, I can't really recommend this game as someone who was a massive fan of the first installmentI did enjoy this game quite a bit, but it just doesn't feel quite rightI absolutely loved the art and narrative of the story, I think story-wise it was more interesting than the first, but gameplay wise it just didn't hit the mark like it did with the first one.Playing the first one, I remember having a fun time doing different actions to see small easter eggs or in order to get a different ending; but this one is essentially completely linear with the only options really being to get a game over by becoming missing or successfully survive. As well as that, there was a weird amount of waiting in this game. Unlike the last game, there were multiple rituals where the main challenge was to just... wait, which felt like a waste of time since it felt like I shouldn't have really needed to wait even if it was for suspense, since there was essentially no suspense when I was waiting.I did enjoy the aspect of stealth this game added though, made some sections very tense. Only for the first go-around however. Since most of the npcs tend to stand at the same spots the whole time, all the suspense goes away because I become fully aware of where they are. With there only being 2 or 3 cases of randomness that I can recall, which I won't specify for spoiler reasons.Also, as a side tangent, I find it very weird that after episode 2, the mic quality of the voice acting tends to go all over the place with some characters, sounding more bassy or slightly distant for some reason. While I think the va's did an amazing job delivering their lines, it just kinda irked me hearing the mic quality suddenly change for what felt like no reason. I understand it was probably something behind the scenes, but it did still get to me a little(Hey those spoilers I just mentioned not too long ago, they're gonna be here in this big paragraph so be warned)Going back to the story though, I did thoroughly enjoy it. I love Rhok'zhan as a character as well as the while admittedly small, nice dynamic she has with Stardust where whenever Rhok'zhan tries flirting with Stardust,  Stardust shoots it down immediately to create some funny jokes (I also liked the jokes when you meet Muu in episode 1000). Stardust however, I enjoyed the obstacles she had to go through rather than her character. The fact that she had to go through different realities in order to slowly break down the thousand was an interesting premise along with Buck who would keep trying to get rid of Stardust. But again, that's just the conflict she has to fight against, her character is pretty much a goody-two shoes trope which I don't think is as interesting as the very immoral first protagonist who selfishly just wanted to smooch some eldritch beings no matter how badly the world was destroyed. The last thing I'll mention is that this actually being a prequel (I'm assuming but is heavily implied) is something I do like, specifically the small scene Rhok'zhan has where she tells Ln'eta and Estir about her dreams and humans, setting up the first game.Despite the fact I did just praise this game with that big paragraph about the story, I still don't believe you should play it. It is better to either watch a youtuber play it or explain the story, you will likely get a very similar experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the first one you more or less know what you're in for:- Great characters- Sexy lovecraftian gods- Strange rituals you must perform to kiss them- Multiple routes and endings- Good music- A damn good storyThe sequel takes the already good writing and gameplay of the first and I think does a good job of adding to and improving on the formula. Instead of the one room you now have a whole house to explore and run around avoiding death while you perform various cult rituals. Without spoiling any of the story elements I will say I loved the loop of this one and the overall vibe. Lowkey really wish there were 1000 chapters.Like the first game the final chapter is a doozy of memorizing all the possible things that could kill you and how to counter them. I got exceptionally lucky with the RNG, getting the same one a few times in a row resulting in a quick and easy zero death run; but even as I was nearing the end of the countdown to victory the tension was palpable and I was just waiting for something to go wrong in the last 30 seconds. It may be over in only a few short hours but every second is worth the price of admission. So have yourself a good time and kiss that goat milf!

_childDocuments_.review: A thoroughly enjoyable yuri romance visual novel with an older (cosmic horror goat mommy) woman. Funny, enjoyable dialog as befitting the genre of a yuri romance, with moments of pure cuteness and hilarity. As the game progresses it becomes far more darker in tone, while still meshing the lighthearted approach of the protagonist and the growing love of something truly unfathomable; all under an anime 90's OVA lenses.The gameplay shifts past regular visual novel to be a mix of light item collecting, puzzle solving, survival elements as you progress through the story.Enjoyable music and pleasant voice acting really sell this, I could actually see this as an OVA series on VHS during the 90s, a mix of the macabre horror and upbeat lightheartedness through the entire bit. I was enthralled with every moment and was sad to see it end. I graciously await for a third entry (if any).As far as LGBTQIA+ representation, this one feels organic. It doesn't feel like a token entry, preachy, or pure fetish fuel (although lets be real, goat mom will definitely awaken some "I'm not a furry, buuut" people). at all. We need more games with representation like this, an organic telling of it and not an overwhelming browbeat and telling the audience they're wrong if it's a concept they're unaccustomed to or mixed in feeling.In closing, I only have three things to say. I want the "Moooooood" t-shirt as merch, so badly, I'd wear that every day. Is it possible to remaster the first one or at least update and put achievements in with it? And... please, PLEASE, make a third one to the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Akabaka and DreadXP were kind enough to send me a copy of this game a week early for review purposes, I’ve linked the video below if you’d prefer a funnier version of this review, both are spoiler free. I did not play the first iteration of Sucker for Love, but the uh… main character caught my eye lets say, while I was scrolling. Its quite hard to miss her. The game itself is toted as an upgrade from previous versions with fully 3d environments and what that amounts to in game is a horror game in between visual novel sections, and its actually a fairly competent one at that. You have to slowly avoid the enemies in the house by scooting around them as they wander looking for you opening the doors slowly enough to notice them and closing them fast enough to run away if they spot you. There was a pretty impressive mechanical depth that grew as the game went on that frankly, I wasn’t expecting. It was actually very good and the mechanics never got old, same as the gameplay loop. The story, to be as spoiler free as possible, is pretty serviceable with very decent voice acting. I got all the achievements (a few bugged for me unlocking on Steam I have to fix, I’d chalk that up to pre-launch copies of games being weird on Steam moreso than the game itself) and saw all the endings and never felt bored or like I wanted to stop, but my playtime does tell a story in and of itself. The game is short, so judge accordingly if you think that 4-5ish hours is worth the price. There isn’t much bloat so thats 4-5 hours of straight gameplay and cutscenes for the most part but still. As far as issues go, I did encounter a few minor technical bugs that the devs were aware of and working on fixing for launch. The only one I’d be careful of is that the game freezes if you pause during chapter 3 for some reason, beyond that there was nothing I’d consider major and even that is avoidable if you know about it. On the technical side still I will say that the game ran fairly well, but sometimes on the audio side things were a bit much. If you listen during the video when I let the game just kinda play in a few sections to showcase the audio and voice acting, there is this ambience thats very aggressive and overtakes other noises sometimes, and the game doesn’t have individual volume sliders. Also the UI can be a bit obtrusive at times, thats kinda it though I didn’t have many issues with the game overall and I am usually quite critical. As far as getting all the endings, there is an easy checkpoint system the game uses so you can go right to important events and sort of play from that moment in a new save if you’d like so its not very difficult. Overall this was a pretty good game and most importantly, I had fun. I think thats the most you can really ask anymore. Linked below are both my steam curator page if you would like my reviews to show up on Steam for you as well as the youtube video I made on this game, which I would really appreciate support on, both for myself as well as for the game. If the video pops off theres a better chance the game does too. Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: My thoughts are slightly mixed, but definitely very positive overall. Firstly, Rhok’Zan and Stardust's relationship is INCREDIBLE. Every moment they spend together is great, with my only real issue being that there isn’t more of it! There's a pretty huge timeskip after the second chapter and I wish we’d spent more time with the two of them, watching their relationship flourish. One element of their relationship that is pretty impactful to me personally is that Stardust is asexual. Not only is the idea of an eldritch god of lust getting with an asexual goth just a fun dynamic, I’m really happy to see asexual representation in a dating sim. It’s pretty rare and it feels so good to see someone like myself represented so well.A lot of the other characters are great too! A few favourites from the first game are back and as entertaining as ever and a lot of the villains hit the perfect balance between threatening and fun. Again, my only real problem is that a few of them feel like they don’t get nearly enough screen time. The biggest example of this for me is a certain Shoggoth who I would have absolutely loved to have seen more of but only really gets one scene right at the end. She was so fun!My biggest problem with the game is that it kinda feels like it has a split focus. All of the dating sim and VN stuff is fantastic, but that isn’t actually the bulk of the gameplay. Most of the time it kinda plays like a point and click dungeon crawler? It’s pretty involved and a step up from the first game for sure, but I really wish less time was spent wandering around your gigantic house looking for ritual components and more was spent with the fun characters.In conclusion, this game is great! Much like the first game, and as I have said many times throughout this review, my biggest problem is that I want to spend more time with these characters and it leaves me hungry for more! I would also maybe have shrunk the size of the house a little, like 10 near-identical tatami rooms is a bit overkill and makes traversal a little bit of a slog. However, these issues don’t ruin the game at all and I’d highly recommend it if you want a good humorous dating sim with a surprising amount of substance!

_childDocuments_.review: As a monster ♥♥♥♥♥♥, the first Sucker for Love has always been a favourite. Estir had my heart in a chokehold. So when I heard of the sequel with an older eldritch being as the love interest, I knew I had to buy it and play it. And now that I’ve completed it, my thoughts are a bit… mixed. I will still recommend this since it’s a pretty good experience but I would highly encourage you to wait for a sale.+ I like the new gameplay of walking around and opening the doors. It adds a layer of tension that leans more into the horror elements of the game. Plus, a good opportunity to showcase some nice background art.+ The nods towards the first game with including  and  were pretty great. I was really excited to encounter them. Plus  is adorable. + The design for the new characters is pretty great. It has that same appeal as the first one while exploring more ‘tropes’. Wish we were able to romance Nanni or Billie (or even Kidd for those attracted to men) in the same way that Estir was an alternate route in the first game.+ I like the sound design. Being able to hear  adds so much to the spooky factor. I really appreciate the subtitles as well as an accessibility feature. I’m hoping they play further into this if they do another game, maybe add some binaural aspect into it to help you navigate around.= The writing is… okay. It had some funny beats like in the first game but Rhok’zan doesn’t feel as endearing as Ln'eta or Estir. I have my thoughts about the MC as well. It’s great to see a female lead this time around and it’s nice to explore asexuality and that it’s not the same as being aromantic. Still, she doesn’t feel quite as endearing as D. Maybe Star just doesn’t appeal to me personally but I was able to more easily relate to D than to her.= The art is pretty great but there are some instances of a sprite being low resolution. Nothing too jarring but it’s there.- The game feels super unoptimised. It lags quite a bit when moving from one room to another or finishing one section. It feels weird since you don’t really think a game like this would encounter those issues. Yes, this happens even with the Compatibility Mode toggle. Some odd bugs here and there as well with stuff not properly loading in and loading a different checkpoint than the one you clicked. Being unable to take screenshots also sucks, I don’t even know why some Steam games do this.- The enemies feel a bit lacklustre. The idea of them hiding behind doors and you being able to slowly peek and back away is great, but it doesn’t feel like they explored or played with this enough. I’m glad they don’t become annoying but I was hoping they would do more.- The final challenge against Buck is… surprisingly easy. Disappointingly so.

The rituals are much more simplified (bad), but now you need to actively move around places to do them.(good!)5. The game's as long as you'd expect, roughly 9 hrs if you sit down and take your time to enjoy it.6. The game is quite easy.7. There's very few alternate endings, which is a shame because the 1st game really allowed you to go wild with them. The good thing is that the final ending is REALLY satisfying.I did not experience any serious bugs or glitches during my playthrough.Also regarding Rhok'zan:All in all, SFL: Date To Die For is a good sequel, but there are a couple shortcomings that prevent it from being the best it can when compared to the 1st game.It would've been nicer to have more complex rituals (like using the chalkboard and candles more, or closing and opening windows too), or being able to do more casual chat with Rhok'zan or being able to unlock more alternate endings instead of just 1.

_childDocuments_.review: This turned out to be a fun story that challenged the player to think about what love is. The humor, the horror, and the romantic elements all play a role in the way the game explores different aspects of love. "A Date to Die For." It isn't really a dating-sim. The major purpose isn't to win affection so much as to get you think of the different types of affection(s) people have for one another and how they might experience it. The game does it really well.The actual game-play works just fine. It isn't amazing but you move through one house and pick up things in one location and take them to another (you have a map that spells everything out, and the checkpoint system is generous). It's a short game so it never gets tedious. There are some scary bits-- timed sections, smart use of sound effects, and jump scares. It mostly works.  There are some moments of genuine tension as you click through the rooms trying not to turn around, and there are moments of real paranoia as you slide a door open slowly to see if someone is lurking behind it. I was able to get the "true" ending and, I doubt I'd play it again for the other side-paths but, I'm happy I gave this a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really fun and charming game. The aesthetic, art, characters, humor, and voice acting were all fantastic, and though it felt like the gameplay loop overstayed its welcome at points I enjoyed the tension of sneaking through the house and avoiding enemies as well. I liked Stardust a lot as a protagonist, and I don't agree with the reviews and discussions calling her bland. She's meant to be this determined and saccharine character who feels like she could have been plucked from any kids anime about the power of friendship, and I personally felt that worked well as contrast to the oppressive atmosphere of the Black Woods. I also enjoyed the unique dynamics  brought to a game like this. I liked Rhok'zan a lot as a love interest, and it was very easy for me to get on board with  Final(?) ending spoilers: All that said, the game was too short and the gameplay loop often felt like it existed mostly to pad out the sparse interactions between the characters. In some ways it's a positive reflection of the game that my biggest criticism boils down to "I wanted more game!", but I also think comparisons to the first game are unavoidable, and this is where the game really fails compared to its predecessor. I don't feel like I got to know Rhok'zan or the other primary characters as well as I did Ln'eta and Estir. There also weren't alternate routes in the same way as the first game; differences between the normal and true endings for each chapter boiled down to single choices that didn't affect much beyond the endings themselves. There  a weird door that no one has figured out yet, but I somehow doubt it holds substantially more gameplay or character beats behind it. I'll update my review if I'm wrong.This is also more of a nitpick, but other than the way to get the true ending in chapter 1, it didn't feel like there were very many gameplay segments or puzzles that the game didn't stick a big blinking star on to direct you toward. This one comes down to personal preference, but I would have liked more segments that didn't hold my hand so much.Overall I would recommend this game and I would recommend it for full price, but I hope the devs take some of the criticisms this game is receiving to heart for their next project.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're coming here from the first Sucker for Love, like me, it's hard to wholeheartedly recommend this one, at least as far as the gameplay goes. They innovated a lot with the almost adventure-game-like map you move through, but I feel they just didn't execute on it enough. What they did do was interesting, but I felt there was more they could have done. The final rush is probably the strongest showing of their new elements, but it's entirely too easy, especially compared against the first game's. The elements that remained from the first game, meanwhile, feel a little stripped down as a result; rituals are less involved, have fewer steps, fewer ingredients, fewer variables to change. I think I only changed something on a blackboard one time, and never had to change fire to more than one color. However. To play either of these games for the gameplay is like saying you read playboy for the articles, as they used to say in my day. So how does the meat of the experience stack up? The art is, of course, beautiful. Character designs? Amazing. Music? Great as ever. Voice acting is just the right level of cheesy; it knows what it's shooting for and achieves it, imo. Writing, also, spot on. My one complaint in that regard is that things felt a little rushed to me; I would have liked a longer story with more minor villains and more opportunities to get to know our goat mommy--and more time to really get into our main villain's characterization. He wasn't quite the dark mirror to our mc that I might have liked from such a story. Would also have liked more splits in the routes, more varied bad ends. But our mc is a delight and I believe in her, I want her to have all the best things in this world.In all I really did enjoy my time with the game, and I'm looking forward to whatever this team puts out next. Numerically, I'd give it a solid 7/10. A little underbaked, perhaps, but delicious all the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Still pure nightmare fuel in a cutesy anime dating sim wrapper but with the emphasis less on the nightmare fuel and more on romance that withstands the test of space and time and the horrors beyond. Stardust takes All-Loving Hero to memetic levels and I absolutely love it. Nothing more heartwarming or hilarious than whipping out "The Power of Friendship" more casually than a shounen anime like its a life hack. Gonna say it straight: I love Stardust as a protagonist. She's a lovable, friendly airhead who lives life without the existential dread the rest of us deal with on a daily basis, which is ironically her greatest strength. She's the best friend we never knew we wished we had.There's a lot more focus on plot rather than "Kissy-Kissy Cthulhu," which I like, because it gives space for humor and for the characters to be characters, and I love that none of them are left hanging. The piece tying it to the first game wasn't what I expected, but what I got was even more adorable, so I still give it a thumbs up.The change from FNaF single-room setting to a more open space is daunting at first, but you gradually figure your way around. It allows each chapter to gradually add more layers to the difficulty without just throwing it in your face all at once. The spell-reading definitely feels less clunky and frustrating than the first one, so it's not as big of a hassle as it could've been. I also like that the final level has checkpoints. That's a big one. If I had to restart from the beginning every time, I might've given up after four or five tries....It kinda breaks my heart that the game can get a bit buggy and crashy though. My game client stopped responding during transitions - not ALL of the time, but sometimes. Enough to mention. There's definitely going to be some patches in the future, considering the amount of love and effort the developer put into the game. I forgive it partially because I feel it will be fixed and partially because it actually made me laugh once. When my game's script kept bugging out and crashing as I opened the door to the final true ending, I didn't even realize it was a crash. I thought it was part of the game. Like, "You got your happy ending, but this is as much as your puny human mind can comprehend. Alt+F4. GG no re noob," like the ending gag Doki Doki Literature Club tried to pull but done more effectively.Then I looked it up on YouTube and realized there was actually just a little more and my game just decided to drop a duke at the last second XDEDIT: They fixed it the day right after I posted this review. Damn they work fast! lol

_childDocuments_.review: Edited review after finishing the game.Let me start with the bad so as to get the original points I made out of the way. The game has issues. Mostly bugs starting in the later chapters, visual bugs and save state bugs. However, as of the time of writing this, there has already been a patch that fixes some of these, so perhaps some of the bugs I noted are already fixed/going to be fixed soon.Performance is still very hit or miss. I played through the game twice. The first playthrough was miserable. I had lag issues very frequently to the point where I had to restart the game around 10 times. Which for a game of this length, is not good at all. But in my subsequent playthrough, the game only slowed down to a crawl once, which made the experience so much better and more enjoyable to the point where I was able to look past my first run having so many issues, hence why I am now recommending this game.Also a bit of a shame that Rhok'zan is the only romanceable eldritch being in this game. Not even an Auntie Nyan Nyan head crush? She looks amazing in this game, damn it! Why waste it?!Now on to the good.The gameplay is fun. I enjoyed the survival and traversal elements added to this game compared to the last one that was fairly stationary as you only had 1 room and 2 'sub-rooms' for the entire game. The door opening is a bit clunky at times but I think it adds to the urgency of moving when you know something is nearby. So all in all, gameplay is fun.The rituals were cool. I liked the added variety to what you needed to do, now that you had more space to do it in. Wish there was a bit more of it but I understand why it was kept at the scale that it was, and it's pretty good anyways. The final boss was fun. Rhok'zan is a cutie. She is the main focal point of this story and she is really good to boot. Generally the characters in this game were good, while some less so than others, the ones that actually mattered were really good and elevated this game greatly.All in all, when this game works, it is great, and I am recommending it... When it works. I'm sure this will get fixed and the issues mentioned will not be a problem anymore, so I want to judge the game based on its actual content, and the content is great. Play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sucker for Love was an interesting concept buried beneath repetition and an overly saccharine story rammed with anime cliches. Date to Die For is an improvement on a lot of levels, but inherits many of the same core issues, chiefly, it's still weeb ♥♥♥♥.Let me qualify that statement: I like anime. Well, some anime. Like any other medium, it has its standout examples as well as its bad tropes. The same goes for visual novels, a lot of them are brilliant and a lot of them suck donkeys. The problem with a lot of indie, heavily anime-inspired VNs is that they're too focussed on delivering an experience that feels like their inspirations to find a truly original and interesting angle. Games like 2064, Murder By Numbers and Hatoful Boyfriend sand off their edges to such an extreme that they become incomparable to the greats that they were aping in the first place.Hatoful Boyfriend might be the most apt comparison to Sucker For Love, given that it is also lampooning dating sims specifically. It also had a great, or at least very funny concept and starts out strong, but soon gives in to overly sentimental fluff and incomprehensible twists. Don't get me wrong, I generally liked both Hatoful Boyfriend and SfL, but I eventually found that they both grew fairly tedious and eye-rolly. Date to Die For shares a lot of these same issues, but does improve on them in a few key areas.First, the gameplay is a lot better. Being able to freely explore a full house rather than a one-bedroom flat feels liberating and enables much more creative horror sequences. The visuals are better too, in fact the presentation all round is great. Stardust, your protagonist, is much better than the last game's PC, if only because she's far less singularly obsessed with the idea of seducing the Elder God, but that can leave her motivation muddled at times. Still, a boring character is usually better than a slightly creepy one, so definitely deserving of the "most improvement" award there. And overall, I found this game a fair bit creepier than its predecessor, but it still wasn't exactly scary.All of that is to say though that I just wish Date to Die For was more gratuitous. Normally shock-value and fanservice are black marks against a game, but here their absence is missed. For a game seemingly about trying to kiss a giant breasted goat Mommy, it's shockingly tame, with barely a swear word in sight and no nudity to speak of. The game almost seems to resent having to depict any violence or gore too, so while many of its creature and character designs are great, it just doesn't utilise them well enough.It's just that when you're going into a game about doing horrible rituals for an Eldritch God with huge boobs so you can kiss them, you expect something pretty full-on. I don't want the game to be porn, god there's plenty of hentai on steam now, we hardly need any more. But I did want it to utilise the potential juiciness of its concept more, rather than deliver something as tame as this. The new spray bottle mechanic is a fantastic example, this allows you to spritz a character any time they start to get flirty, usually to chuckle-worthy effect, but this only comes up a handful of times. At the end of the day, Sucker for Love is too afraid to take big risks, leaving you with a generally charming if slightly dull experience. It's better than the first game, or at least more fun, but there's so much unused potential here.

_childDocuments_.review: tall dominant four eyed goat mommy furry eldritch god gex sayI just finished completing this game and all I have to say is that I fell in love with this series even more.First learning about it from Markiplier, I fell in love with the absurdity of the game and the concept of it; along with the whole occult theme which I was a huge fan of.To my eyes, this was the perfect "goofy" game- something that I consider to be the very peak of that definition; that's what I said about the first game.I remember one day, I saw that the game was in development, and announced to be release, when I saw that, that was during the time I just had my computer, and this game was one of the very first, if not, the first game I've placed on my wishlist. Eagerly waiting every single day for its announce, months have passed and I've forgotten about it, it felt normal to me to see it as "TBA" until out of nowhere, with no announcement, it was on Introductory Sale, I had to swipe it at that very moment and alas, I have the game.This game had met my very expectation, while also surprising me with new elements, I have no way of describing how this game had the same exact feel and touch like the first game, yet feeling so vastly different that I struggle to compare the two and say they came from the same series: in a good way.So much so that I actually bought the first game just to fully compare them and I had NO intention before this, nor have I ever planned to buy the first game since I already know what's going to happen as it had been fresh in my mind even months after, that game has had that kind of an effect on me.I know this all may sound incredibly goofy and silly to many people reading this review, a game about trying to smooch a tall outer eldritch goat mommy but it's exactly why I love this game so much, or this series as a whole; it's absurdity that makes things feel new to me, the fact that I can look at this from a perspective purely from a humorous standpoint and enjoy how goofy it can get, the game can take serious and dark undertones and it may even have a bigger impact due to its contrast, but regardless, it still feels light for me that I feel that I have nothing to worry about and I can just fully expect myself to enjoy it, period.Sucker for Love is honestly one of my favourite games ever and I wish for more, I hope to see more of this series in the near future since I can't get enough of this specific concept that somehow tickles my funny bone, from the incredibly well-planted comedic timings in the game, to hilarious visualizations, to charismatic characters, and even breaking the rule of thumb when it comes to visual novels and acting satirical in that matter, it's all just so great to me and it makes me happy.Even completing the game and focusing purely on the story standpoint, it is SO different from the first game that at many points of the game, I wondered if it'll even be aligned to what we know of from the previous game, and at many points had it surprised me so much that it's actually jarring- so much so that I know this'll forever stuck with me, and fill me with many questions that will be unending, and will make me crave for more lore, more story, and more answers.The voice acting is GREAT, one of the best and most charismatic cast I've ever heard of compared to many other visual novel games I've played; game interface is friendly, game isn't too demanding, confusing, or punishing, easy to come back to different parts of the game, and especially, not OVERWHELMING one bit, game is easy to follow; while mostly being a visual novel, it has had so many different tidbits here and there that makes the game so incredibly fun with how interactive it can be, with little jokes and references here and there, and I will forever always love that FINAL TAPE in these games; gives me a major FNAF vibe.I could write a 52 page essay for this game but I know I'm overstaying my welcome for the review when I initially planned this to be a whole lot shorter.All I will say now is that this game is amazing, and I love it, so much so that I can't express enough how much I love it and will forever be restricted either from how many words I can type to the attention span of your average reader.AkaBaka and DreadXP, please do more!P.S., can we have more Estir?P.S.S, I also experienced a glitch that was TERRIFYING as all living heck.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this is not a dating sim. Even if you end up dating a character at the end. Dating sims are a clearly-defined genre of games. This is a horror game with Sucker for Love: Date to Die For is missing a lot of the aspects of the first game, Sucker for Love, that make the first game so great.While this game is a decent horror game in its own right, I expected many of the same aspects of the first game. Sucker for Love: Date to Die For's main focus is the overall narrative rather than the effect of each ritual and the dichotomy of horror and comedy in a human trying to date a god from the Cthulhu mythos. In this game, you can't lookin the mirror after every spell and see the horrifying disfiguration you have gone through in order to get one step closer to summoning the Cthulhu of your dreams or how your spells are effecting the world outside and how you've doomedthe rest of the world for your own dumb desire. Whatever happens as a consequence of the (female) protagonist, Stardust's rituals is contained to the small town of , which doesn't give you the same sense of dread about how you've doomed the entire world like in the first game.Another aspect I don't like about this game, which is more subjective, is how there is only one dateable character, the furry. The neat thing about the first game was how there were 3 dateable characters, each with their own good and bad endings. In this game, the story is split into chapters and you either get the "happy ending" or the "true ending" for the chapter. Not quite as fun as the endings in the first game.Ultimately, my negative review for this game is due to the hype it created around being like the first game, only to be very different. It gave me the wrong expectations and let me down. This game on its own might be fun to someone else, but it's not my cup of tea.The part where you have to survive all of the horrors in chapter 4 would be fun if the house wasn't such a large maze with so many similar looking rooms in all directions, so that it'd be a bit easier to focus on what is happening and what to do next rather than trying to re-orient yourself constantly.

_childDocuments_.review: I don’t usually play visual novels unless it does something unique and boy Sucker for Love: A Date to Die For, is as unique as they can get. The best thing about this is the voice acting, they did a great job and was the thing that made me jump the furry gun to try this. It’s one of the main reasons I don’t play visual novels, so voice acting is *chef’s kiss*The game has you sadly date just one character, the goat that you see with insanely giant melons. I know many people will like her instantly because the fanbase is 99% furries, which I am not. She is the goddess of lust and yet her rizz was more desperate than sexy, but that might have to do with it also being a comedy game. The main character is asexual which adds to the comedy. I do wish the main character was voice-acted, but I bet she isn’t because how else will the target audience self-insert if they hear someone else? I as a non-furry didn’t connect with her compared to Lae’zel from BG3, this game only had 8 hours to do this and there wasn’t enough there to make me like her besides her insanely large balloonsIf I were to give it a score, it would be a 6/10, the number gamers hate to see and instantly means it’s the worst game ever made because a 7/10 is the lowest a game can actually get. But it's also such an insanely niche game as well in that you already bought it when it came out, or will never touch this because you don't want to become a furry. Also for a game about dating, there sure felt like a lack of that.You spend most of your time, when not get talked to sexually by every character, backtracking through a house Groundhog Day-style. You don’t get any choices until the end, but for non-furries there is only one true ending. You can tell it had a small budget as the PNG has white stuff around the edges at times, and no, stop thinking dirty thoughts you creep. The art for the backgrounds are clearly low resolution but you do move around it in 3D space which to me felt novel and might explain why it’s low resolution. The characters are of course made to stand out and look good no matter the gender, race, or deity level. I hope they get more money to go bigger and I’m not talking about the goat's titties, I mean more characters to date, choices, and more engaging gameplay beyond walking around a house picking up items. Sucker for Love did make me realize that dating games are fun to goof around in, so this won’t be the last one, I mean there is the first game to try next and even has more dating.There is a death by snu snu-cat mommy that is written and voice acted so well, she needs more screen time and her own game and if that happens, well.... until then you could just watch the video where I question if I am a furry or not ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Please, may I have another?TL:DR vers.Goat Mom.Long version.Wow. Normally I'm not big on horror titles, and yes, this IS horror, but this hit that great balance of being filled with horror, humor and hope. I've played through both games and the first was good, but limited by the space used. This opened the game up to a whole house and introduced dangers that you had to avoid consciously and requires a bit more creativity and skill to get through.Some complain about the long waiting sections in a few places. I can sort of understand, but feel that those were used well actually. If you're playing blind like I was, not knowing how long some things would take and hoping you'd found the right solution added to the tension. That was one place where the timer in a few sections took away, but only if you were aware of how the timing of those sections worked. Not gonna spoil any of it though. One of my favorite parts of this game is the character designs, not just of Rhok'Zan, but of everyone really. It grabs that older anime aesthetic tight and just feels right for this story.  Added to really good voice work, everyone pops to life in the best ways.My only real complaint for this is that it would be nice to have a gallery mode, so you can check out unlocked illustrations or maybe even an artbook DLC. There is so much awesome, but it can be inconvenient to try and filter through the game just to find that one awesome or funny moment. Or a favorite creature design.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, its easy to dismiss this game as 'haha funny goat milf' and while yes Rhok'zan sure as ♥♥♥♥ is an excellent selling point, there's... more to it. I went in expecting a fun little horror slash dating-sim VN and came out with a gift. Sure, you get to [REDACTED] the [REDACTED], you have to [REDACTED] so you don't get [REDACTED], and yeah, you [REDACTED]; but... Along the way there's this subplot wherein you do your utmost to retain your humanity. You fight back against the easy route. You can choose to keep what makes you *you.* Some endings rely on you going out of your way to do that, most notably one of the endings in the third chapter. It's... difficult to put into words, that experience, but all I will tell you is that it is excellent. It pays to be human, it tells you. There's little out there that manages that. Oh, and if waxing poetic about reading too into a goat-milf-dating-horror-vn wasn't enough for you, the art is stellar, the music absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rocks, the gameplay loop is interesting without getting stale, the controls and UI are comfy to use, every chapter of the game (though short they may be for some) is fun to play and easy to replay to get the alternate paths, the characters are likable and lovable (Billie dating when??????), and not to mention all the achievements are fun to hunt for. Overall, most worthwhile ten bucks I've spent. ♥♥♥♥, if I had an inkling as to how good this would have been, I'd happily pay full price, and not to mention there's *another one.* Another game, probably just as good.

_childDocuments_.review: A short, fun, interactive horror visual novel. I personally loved the story presented here where you are very curious about the world and the cult surrounding this small town. The setting is just superb and works fantastic for the spooky vibes that the game aims to create. I found the writing to be fantastic. It just created such a believable and interesting world. I loved the ritual aspect intermingled with surviving and trying to figure out the story and gimmick surrounding each character. There were never any frustrating moments as you could figure out all the roadblocks with a bit of thinking. I never felt lost which helped keep the pacing at a good baseline. I think taking place in one location really made the house feel almost like it's own character where I felt very connected to moving through it and almost didn't want to leave by the end. Only real criticism I have coming away from the game is I wish there was more dialogue or emphasis on Rhok'zan herself. Outside of scripted dialogue you are only able to talk to her like 3 times but I wanted to spend so much more time with her. I wish you could ask her questions or give her a hug or just anything other than what's ultimately here. There are no dating elements here. More than anything, I just want so much more interaction with Rhok'zan than what is currently here. I feel like there is so much potential for more stories to be told in this world and it would be a shame to not explore it more. Overall great game. Rhok'zan is the GOAT

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't recommend this game more, this game was an amazing experience to play through, from the phenomenal voice acting, to the great comedy, with a dash of intriguing horror elements, and don't forget the amazing story as well, this game is possible the best way Sucker for Love could of had a sequel! _childDocuments_.review: Just to get this out of the way early, I would say there are only three caveats to this game1. It's very short. My 5ish hours at review time represents a 100% playthrough of the game, all achievements as well. While it's better bang for your buck than a movie, that might be enough value for you from a game.2. If you've played the first game (and you probably have, since this is the sequel), this one is much more horror-focused than romance focused. You may or may not be into that, but there is an accessibility option for jumpscare warnings which I appreciated immensely.3. This game is much more linear than the first game. While there are a couple endings for each chapter, there is only a single love interest. And she's great, don't get me wrong, but if you were hoping for a greater variety of romanceable characters you aren't going to find that here.Besides that, the game is delightful in terms of story, voice acting, and music. The main character is lovable and so is our Eldritch  romance interest. The other characters you meet along the way are similarly interesting and fleshed out, and the overarching plot is compelling.If you love monster girls, you'd be remiss not to pick up this game, even at full price. Even so, I'm hoping that further installments will be more similar to the first game in terms of the number of love interests and tone while still delivering on the heartfelt moments and character developments from this installments.

_childDocuments_.review: Sucker for Love: Date to Die for doesn't try to be the same game as it's predecessor. Where the first game had 3 romantic Lovecraftian monster girls to romance, this game only has one. It does however have a few humans trying to kill us that we can make fall in love with us as well. The main gameplay difference between the games is that now, we can move around the house. This mechanic however I believe proved to be more of a nuisance than a boon. Too much of the game is walking around in circles instead of romancing up our new Goat GF. One of the improvements that the new game has over the previous entry is the horror element. Whereas the first game only had one chapter of scary ambiance, all of Date to Die For's chapters are trying to scare you in some way.One final criticism I have for the new game is it's endings. The first game was packed full of unique and different endings depending on your actions and the success of your dates. In Date to Die For however, each chapter only has 2 endings, as well as a generic bad ending shared between all chapters. The 2 real endings in the chapters aren't even that different from one another, just being a normal and a true ending. With the final chapter having at least one unique ending in it as well. Overall I'd rate Date to Die for a 6/10. It's definitely not as good as it's predecessor, and it feels like it tried too hard to be a different game. Adding in new gameplay features took away from what everyone loved about the first game, dating Lovecraftian monster girls. These new gameplay elements took up so much time. I managed to beat the game in under 4 hours, which was faster than the first game, but I probably spent around half an hour getting to talk with Rox'anne.Going into the third installment I hope Akabaka really focuses on giving the people what they want, more Lovcraftian Beauties for us to date.If I could summarize my thoughts in a single sentence: the game needed less walking and more talking.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great game bogged down by technical issues.I'm not sure if it's the lighting or the many overlaying pngs, but this game runs at an absolutely horrendous rate. It crashed my pc twice in fullscreen mode, and still performed rather poorly when in windowed mode (I even had the game set to laptop/performance mode). It seemed to be using a significant portion of my gpu, which feels odd for a game like this. Of course, the last game was far from perfect, but it feels as if the technical issues were a bit more glaring in this one.That being said, the story and characters are wonderful. The cast was full of colorful, endearing characters, and I loved how the game tied itself in with its predecessor. Not to mention the fantastic art direction and voice acting. If you liked the first game, you'll definitely enjoy this one. I especially enjoyed the morbid truth ending, especially in contrast with the good ending. I would also like to commend the developer for listening to the feedback from the previous game. The final battle segment was much less infuriating, and much more forgiving than the previous entry. I also loved the inclusion of a jumpscare warning setting! It was a really nice qol feature for me, since I tend to get overwhelmed easily when jumpscares are concerned.All in all, I would say this game is definitely worth your time, if you can stomach a bit of performance issues. My advice is that if it runs poorly, do NOT play the game in fullscreen. This helped ease the strain on my computer a bit, and when the game crashed it wouldn't require a reboot of my pc.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, first of all, I'd like to thank the developers. You, guys and girls, did a great job. I loved the first game, and while I didn't buy it, I enjoyed watching playthroughs of it. But when I saw the demo of the second game, I decided to buy it when it would get the release. And so I did and played through it. And I liked it. Not as much as the first game, but it was fun to play nonetheless. So thumbs up.As for the game itself :First, I'd say I like the first one better, but that would be somewhat unfair. These are two different games. The first one is a comedic dating sim with the Lovable Sex Maniac trope of a protagonist pursuing the female eldritch gods to woo them, while the second one is actually a stealth horror (i.e. not actually presenting itself as one but being one once you stop and think about it), where the female eldritch entity is actually pursuing the protagonist, who is an asexual girl, in order to woo her, while the latter tries to survive the horrors thrusted upon her.Second, as mentioned above, different protagonists with different goals. The male one summons the eldritch gods to smooch them with no regards to his own or the world's safety, while the female one summons hers out of desperation, and only because the ritual book assures that the summoned eldritch god is "benign".Third, I view the male protagonist as purely comedic one, while actually liking the female one. She is brave, determined, cheerful, optimistic, kind and compassionate. She is a loyal friend, loving daugther and sibling. She plays a bass guitar and loves cute things to the point hyperventilating. Honestly, if I were to meet such a girl in real life, I'd try asking her out.Fourth, oh, the idea ^_^. How do you prevent a human brain from melting when laying eyes upon an eldritch god who multiplies your lust thousandfold? First, make her a woman, since women are normally not sexually attracted to one another. Second, make her asexual.Fifth, "Stardust" is also a synonym for an addictive drug that starts with "C". So no wonder Rhok'zan pursues her so much.Sixth, a different premise. The male protagonist pursued his gods while seeking their consent before smooching. The problems in the second game begin after a smooch was stolen without a consent. Thus three broken hearts right at the beginning and mending them begins with a platonic meaning of the word "partner".And seventh, I'd say the game has only two drawbacks: moving around the house gets a bit tedious after a while and I feel that there are not enough interactions with Rhok'zan.All in all, the game was worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: Sucker For Love: A Date To Die For is the second (or third, depending on how you look at it) game in the Sucker For Love series, and the second one you have to pay for (as the original that was part of Dread X Collection 2 is a free stand alone title at this point). I quite enjoyed the previous title, Sucker For Love: First Date, so I had some pretty high expectations for this one. Does it live up to the original? Was the wait worth it? Well, that's what I'm here to talk about.To start, if you're somehow unfamiliar with these games, Sucker For Love is a series that puts the cosmic horrors of Lovecraft through a waifu-ification filter, and slaps the result into point and click visual novel titles. The original DXC2 version, and the expanded First Date were dating sims that used a ritual book to conduct forbidden ceremonies in a pursuit of smooches with characters based on Cthulhu, Hastur, and in a way, Nyarlathotep. You'd collect the things you need, set the stage, and then chant an incantation from within a Eldritch tome by dragging your mouse slowly across the words. It was a unique system, but it works for the type of game these tend to be.A Date To Die For, unlike it's predecessor, isn't really a dating sim though. In fact, I'd say it leans a little more into the "horror" of dealing with Lovecraftian entities, even if the game is still as comedic and weeby as it's always been. You're still going to be chanting for rituals and collecting things to do them, but the process is actually both simpler and harder at the same time. How? Well, explaining that is going to take me a few minutes. In terms of conducting the rituals, there aren't nearly as many this time, despite the game being as long as the previous one, more or less. You no longer have to worry about swapping items around, as failing rituals isn't really a risk any more. Instead, it's the path to getting to the ritual site that may prove to be more challenging.A Date To Die For decides to up the ante, so to speak, by having you navigate an old Japanese style house that the protagonist, Stardust, is in because it once belonged to her family, but now is the base of operations for a cult who worships Rhok'zan, this game's waifu-ified cosmic being. She is based off of the Black Goat of a Thousand Young, Shub-Niggurath, and is basically a fertility goddess, as well as a goddess of lust. You basically work with her to put a stop to THE THOUSAND (the group name is spelled with all caps in game). whom are the aforementioned cult that have taken up residence in Stardust's old family home. The goal is to uproot the Black Forest, the domain of Rhok'zan, because it's been twisted by the wickedness of the cult's leader, whom has an admittedly petty desire to make Rhok'zan suffer.To help Rhok'zan be rid of the cult, the bulk of what you'll be doing is navigating the house to collect materials for the rituals, or to go to a new ritual site. You do this by moving your mouse to edge of the screen to turn in place, and you click on doors to begin to open them. You then have to manually drag the door open before clicking past the opening to move between rooms. This allows you to creak the door open, see if it's safe, and decide if you wish to proceed. Yes, you read that correctly, you have to make sure it's safe to move between rooms. Each "episode" of the game, rather than being a dating sim where your goal is to smooch Rhok'zan, is dealing with a member of THE THOUSAND and their unique challenge while trying to complete the same ritual. "The Uprooting," to foil the plans of the cult. This means that the house will have hostile entities to deal with, and that's why you can move doors the way you can. It builds some solid tension, due to the way it controls, but for the most part, it works.However, this is where I have to dock some points, because there are a few sections that push this control scheme to a point where I just don't think it's fun. Specifically, dealing with a trip from the main ritual room (Stardust's old bedroom) to a room with a Radio in it that you need to get to and chant in three times. This is made more annoying because while Chapter 2 has a single stalker type threat, the game needs you to get to this room, turn on the radio, and then chant the phrase 3 times without fail in order to properly conduct the ritual. When you have a stalker that can move through rooms fairly quickly, you feel pressured to move quickly, and may fumble a lot. I died to this more than anything else in the game up until this point. It was bloody infuriating, because the way you move between rooms is slow on purpose, but you have to haul ass to get to do the ritual before you get killed. This one section soured my mood immensely. Thankfully, it's the only time the game actively made me outright angry. Combined with the game keeping the checkpoint based save system from the previous title, and there's a fair bit more frustration this time around.Another area of complaint gameplay wise is the final episode. Much like First Date, the player has to survive a gauntlet of little challenges for a period of time. However, unlike First Date, where it was just completing small rituals to stop curses and the like, this has you navigating the house to deal with threats for 7 minutes. You still need to consult the book in order to know how to deal with stuff, but some of the things don't really explain aspects well. There's specifically a knocking one that is clearly just here to make getting the "G.O.A.T." Achievement harder for no real reason at all. It's mildly annoying.In terms of writing though, the game retains a lot of the charm of it's predecessor, but with more of serious edge than First Date by a large margin. It actually approaches the idea of stuff like the existential dread of eternity and immortality through it's plot, and it's interesting. I think the game's decision to have the protagonist be Asexual and having to deal with a very Thirsty fertility goddess goat lady is quite fun, especially because you get a spray bottle that let's you basically go "NO! BAD!" when Rhok'zan gets TOO thirsty for her own good. You also get to spray a few others, but this is a thing that only comes up at set points. Still, it's funny when it does. The humor is all still very on point, and is able to lean a little more into the Lovecraftian horror influence than before.The art and sound are still as solid as ever. I actually think this game's overall presentation is better than First Date by a fair bit. There's no visual glitches I noticed, and barring one or two missed voice lines, it's largely still as good as the first game in that department. Voices are all really solid, with the voice of Rhok'zan being a stand out because it really does sound like the voice of a fertility goddess to me, so special kudos to her voice actress. The art for the sprites is honestly a cut above the first game, and the sound design is better, if only because the variety is there. It also has an anime ending style song in there too, so that's cool.Overall, I will say that I do like the game, but I don't think it's quite as good as First Date. While I think the overall writing was really good, the general formula of things sort of loses it's charm the deeper I got. The only thing that kept the gameplay interesting, for the most part, was the new gimmicks for each chapter. While it is better in terms of overall presentation, and I do appreciate the attempt a more serious story, I think it ultimately doesn't quite live up to First Date's highs for me. I still think it's rock solid, but the price point for the amount of content on offer (about the same amount as First Date) really has me hesitating on saying it's worth it for everyone. I think if you liked First Date, you'll like Date To Die For just fine, but if you're like me, it'll leave you wanting a little more out of it. 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend playing this game. It's definitely a different game than the first one though, so keep that in mind if you plan on playing it. But if you're in it for the dating sim aspect alone, I'm not sure that you'll enjoy the experience.One plus side that this game has over Sucker for Love is it's horror. Having to open every door by hand, unsure if there is something lurking on the other side, is a great tension-builder. This mechanism never got old for me, and I think the short length of this game helped with that. It took me less than 6 hours to 100% the game (even after getting lost for a bit). I played this game with a friend who doesn't play horror games, and she was freaked out the whole way through. There is an option to have an alert before a jumpscare occurs, but, if you can handle a little bit of fear, I'd recommend leaving that setting off. I do need to point out that the old trailers are a bit misleading on what happens in the game. These changes are likely due to the game's direction not being fully figured out at the time, but it does end up meaning that you can't really rely too heavily on the trailers to know what direction the story goes. I'd view the trailers more-so as gameplay reveals and not as story or character reveals.If you're on the fence about this game, I'd recommend going ahead and getting it. I think its pretty fun overall!Edit:
