_childDocuments_.review: Humanity has been wiped out and now androids are working to restore it. The only problem? They don’t understand what humanity truly is.CRYMACHINA is another one of those visual novels disguised as an action JRPG. While there is gameplay, about 75% of your time is going to be spent reading or listening through character dialogues and cutscenes. I personally don’t have a problem with this as a big VN fan, but this should be made clear upfront for those expecting a full-blown action JRPG.The combat is real-time and mostly revolves around spamming the same few inputs as it’s effectively a two button hack and slash without any fancy combo strings. The entire game I found myself just using the same combo over and over. Light attack string, heavy attack to raise them into the air, light string, heavy attack to bring them to the ground, light string, and then a finishing move to end the combo.That’s literally all I did for the majority of the game’s bosses. There are some where I needed to dodge more often, but most I was able to simply stun lock and repeat this combo over and over until the fight was over. It is not a difficult game by any means and there is no “hard” difficulty to set it to.It’s weird though, because while I was able to do that to most of the bosses, when I did get hit it was usually for like half of my HP. And a lot of the bosses straight up can just one shot you. So it does hurt if any enemy actually lands a hit, it’s just that hardly ever happened in my case. The difficulty balance is just all sorts of weird here. The core to the combat is also a bit weird. There’s a decent enough amount of feedback when I actually hit an enemy, but when I am the one being hit, it is oftentimes hard to even notice. I’ll be fighting a boss and suddenly have half of my HP and I’m like, “when did I even get hit?”.The combat at least does good in some areas - mainly the different weapon types and the dodging and countering feels good too, it’s just brought down by how simple and monotonous it is.The level design is just outright terrible, lazy even. The entire game is literally hallways and platforms in a cyberspace-like environment. There is virtually no exploration outside of maybe an additional hallway to a chest, there’s no complex structures, just hallways, pillars, walls, emptiness really.It’s so bad that some levels are literally just a straight path to the boss room. You walk forward, kill a few random enemies that spawn, and keep walking forward and suddenly you’re at the boss room which is just a slightly wider hallway. It took maybe 1 minute to reach that boss room, so what exactly is the point of even having the stuff prior to it? It’s like the game is trying to maintain this illusion of substance when there really isn’t any.The entire experience is mission-based. You enter a level, run to the boss room, kill the boss, and are sent back to this hub area - all menu-based by the way - where you get a story cutscene, mandatory character dialogue scenes, the chance to edit your loadout, and then you need to head back in to the next mission. The loop is very defined. Nothing really breaks this formula and really, it’s kinda dull as a result.The story is really the only thing propping this game up. I’ve played other games from this developer and they can be very hit or miss, so I was a bit surprised here. We get a full-blown post-apocalyptic story that deals with the deeper meaning behind relationships and even broad topics like humanity without feeling like it was written by an edgy middle schooler like Monark was. I’m not going to make the case that it’s some super involved, multi-level story, but for JRPG standards, it’s fairly interesting.Maybe a lot of that is due to the setting - basically a futuristic world where humanity was wiped out by a world war and androids are attempting to restore humanity, but struggle to understand what exactly being a “real human” entails. I am a bit of a sci-fi nerd, so that setup definitely pulled me in.The real winner here though is the pacing. CRYMACHINA is faster-paced, but not too fast. There are slower moments of character building, but they come in bite-sized pieces and don’t overstay their welcome. The twists and turns of the main story are weaved in with these character building moments and it’s actually quite a good combo. The studio did a great job balancing the pacing there.The game also isn’t too drawn out. It can be completed in just 10 hours if you’re doing just the main content. There are side missions, but the game is so easy that I didn’t even touch those until the end, there was just no need to. There are some additional, optional dialogue sequences too. Overall, you can probably squeeze maybe 20 hours if you do all of that content, maybe even 30 if you want to go the completionist route and kill all of the optional bosses and such.That said, it’s not too replayable and I can’t see myself returning to the game in the future. Not that that matters to me personally, but I know others value that aspect so it’s important to note.I guess the character designs are cool and the music isn’t that bad either, but the graphics, the cutscenes, and really just the overall aesthetic are not really that good, barebones even. This is obviously a low budget JRPG and it shows in pretty much every area.I played through the entire thing at 4k max settings hovering around 144 fps on my RTX 3080 Ti. But again, I can’t say that was surprising given that this looks like something from two console generations ago. There’s a decent amount of settings to change too, so there is room to play around with if you’re on lower end hardware.CRYMACHINA is a decent story wrapped up in some truly boring gameplay and a cheap overall aesthetic. The combat is monotonous, the difficulty simply isn’t there, and the level design is just outright awful. This is saved a good bit by the story, with its cool setting and solid pacing, but unfortunately, that is coupled with the rest of the game and it’s honestly just not worth it, at least at full price. This is a budget JRPG with a premium price tag and I would 100% recommend waiting for a significant drop in that price before giving it a look.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game very optomistically. I thought this was going to be a fascinating game based on the  it had at the time (it still does, but in the event it changes...), but after these three hours of gameplay there are just too many things nagging at me.The game is undoubtedly beautiful from a music and visual standpoint. Some of the cinematics are pretty good though a lot of the in game cutscenes could be improved a bit as it appears a bit choppy. The story is a little generic and they bring up a lot of things like the . It's a bit jarring and would be more interesting if they more or less implied it, but the dialogue is very on the nose and the conversations feel a little forced and out of nowhere sometimes. The story doesn't flow very well and it's pacing feels off. When I first noticed my level when I got the chance, I was already Level 34. Why there at the very beginning?  I don't know how long the game is, but whatever its length, it feels like it should be much longer.And that reminds me of another thing. I mentioned starting at level 34, right? Okay, so why are you at first restricted to a maximum of level 40? No, seriously, why? And then after  does you're level max only goes up by 5? Why couldn't you have just started at level 0 or 1? Why limit level growth so much? Is it because the levels are short and there's only like 3 per 'area'. The decision making with this is so irritating. Yes, there's two other ways to increase your character's abilities, but one is equipment which is a roll of the dice at best, and the other is an alternate unit which you have to balance between your characters and a couple other things. So if it wanted you to prioritize between one or the other it's not doing a very good job at inferring that. And getting them is very feast or famine. Normally, you'll get a lot after every stage  but trying to grind for them outside of that is incredibly difficult. The environments, in their own way, are pretty in a cyber sci-fi kinda way, but it's not exactly something new and it all feels the same. Whenever you go into a 'new area' stuff may change but it doesn't feel you went all that far. They try to explain it away with worldbuilding saying things like , but it just feels lazy and unrealistic.The combat is alright from a basic standpoint, but there felt like no real build up in the skill set. While the tutorial stuff was fine. It gave you all the options in the first couple levels and seemed to expect you to be able to use them all effectively. This is especially egregious when the game will not let you kill some beginning enemies because it wants you to use a specific attack or feature as its the tutorial. Which I get as a tutorial mechanism but when they are actual enemies doing full damage to you it is frustrating seeing them forever at the 'one sliver of health' but it won't let you kill them because you didn't use this one specific type of attack which I never used again. This gets onto my next issue with the combat, it is so fast and unrelenting that you basically have no time to even react. This wouldn't be so bad if there was a slow build up and you had plenty of time and enemies to get used to all the different mechanics and use them effectively. This is not the case. The stages are very short, the most enemies I've seen by  is about 10. And the enemies attacks are flashy, can be very quick, and it often doesn't feel worth it enough to try these different mechanics.What prompted me to give this review, however, is . Now, while I like this boss's concept and have no issue with it in that sense, this boss's fight is so damn frustrating that it finally made me sit back and review all the things that'd been nagging at me up until that point that I'd been ignoring. This boss has areas that light up when they are about to be attacked. Standard procedure. But often time it feels like how much time you have before the attack lands is significantly shorter than what you expected. Attacks hit behind you and since the soundbite feels the same regardless of where it hits, you can't judge how far away the attack is. A thing that hasn't been an issue up until now is that you tend to flinch with hit. This boss throws several attacks one after another in very rapid succession that a minuscule to a quarter/half you hit points in damage. This game apparently has zero i-frames. All this couples to you going from near full hitpoints to a game over screen before you even can attempt to react. And when this boss's area of effect covers basically the entire area you're stand on with very minimal exceptions. Again, this would be so difficult if the game built you up to this in any way or allowed you to properly level up, but it doesn't. And it makes for such a frustrating experience when you are chain combo'd out of no where because attacks are happening behind you that you can't see and there's so many attacks happening at once that you have little time to react... within the first three hours of gameplay. It feels like this boss should be way later in the game.And I'm not ashamed to admit I was playing on the Casual Mode for this game, not the normal mode. I don't even want to consider how brutal this boss would be outside of that. I don't know, maybe I'm just bad and need to 'git gud', but quite frankly I can deal with hard games. This just seems unfair.Maybe I'll come back later and try again, potentially revising my thoughts on it then. But for right now, my overall opinion of this as a game is not very high. Outside of its game aspect, I enjoy it very much, however. But for a game, I recognize that's not exactly something positive for it.

_childDocuments_.review: First thing first, this game is too expensive given its content and launch price. I would consider it worth for maybe half of the full price. But I impulse-bought it so here we are.: 10/10. I'm sure most people who bought this game by this point can agree to this. I bought the game pretty much specifically for this.: 8/10. There are certainly a couple bangers, Enoa's CV is a beast. But I probably won't listen to them very often separately.: 9/10, your typical good post-apocalyptic setting with highly intelligent AIs, reminds me of Horizon Zero Dawn a lot. Side note: Even some of the plot twists are pretty similar. The story progression is a little Nier-like, it criticizes how cruel "real" human, and by extension our society, can be. And something less sentient like a machine can have higher capacity of empathy and love than a real human.: 7/10. There're these Tea Parties which basically is a place for the main cast to interact and talk to each other, and some of them are tied to the main story. There're hours upon hours of dialogue(all amazingly voice acted btw), but I couldn't help but feel like the main protagonists(besides Enoa) barely changes or gain more flavor throughout the conversations. I wanted to feel proud for the girls but I feel like I still barely knew some of them by the end of the game despite hearing them talking for like 20 hours. Some missed opportunity here.: Non-existent. Expect empty, straight hallways with enemies popping in.: 5/10. It is 120% needlessly complex. If you don't care about gear, you'll probably do fine. If you like to min-max, you're gonna have a hard time getting in to it. I never got an explanation of roughly 2/3 of the stats as to what they actually do. And there isn't a English wiki as of the writing of this review. I have probably spent around 15 hours on the Japanese wiki trying to teach myself on how this game actually works and where to actually get good gear(more rant on that in the next paragraph).: 1/10. There's this Subnetwork system similar to Labyrinths in Bloodborne where you enter some codes and get procedurally generated levels, but they suck at giving you good gears if you're just blindly going through them. I kept a piece of my gear that I picked up in the first 3 levels all the way until endgame to find a better replacement(there're only 3 gear slots btw this isn't like rings in Souls games.) The game also never tells you that you need to beat a named boss THREE times to get all the things on its loot table, and you can only get a weapon after the third time(besides main story bosses). And guess what, you can get the 3rd BEST weapon for a character you haven't even unlocked yet if you happened to enter the right code and beat the boss in there three times which nets you SIX TIMES the damage compared to her starting weapon. Also, the balancing between the 3 controllable characters are also pretty wild. With the same build, the better character can output 10 times the damage compared to the worst, and I'm not even exaggerating. Auxiliaries(the two floaty thingy) have a very complex system with countless build and moveset options which convinced me that this system will be the most innovative from this game when I first started. But their damage scaled horribly into mid-late game and the best combo is just to use one for buffing yourself and the other for debuffing enemies. Oh, and the best buffs and debuffs are consumed on equip. Yeah, you are actively punished for experimenting.: 3/10. They do look flashy, there's parry and perfect dodge. The philosophy is similar to FF7R where you are supposed to drain the enemies' generator gauge, push them into WEAK state and DOWN state, and unleash your big damage there. But bosses have 5 moves at best, and they mostly consist of one melee attack and several pew-pews. The hilariously broken balance also doesn't help with the experience. You either kill the boss in one attack loop or you suffer because for some god forsaken reason you can't chain perfect dodges and most of the moves bosses do are multi-hit.Overall I'm willing to give this game a 6.5/10. I made the mistake of trying to min-max this game. If you're just here for the narrative ride I think you'll have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: A fantastic story and the best soundtrack of the year but it is sadly held back by uninteresting level design, minimal enemy variety and shallow gameplay with unrealized potential. The main game is relatively short and you will be reading the best parts of the game instead of playing them. Pick it up on a sale.For a more detailed breakdown: The game is insanely easy and the way the level up system works can make overleveling yourself to the point of trivializing every encounter by accident a real concern, This hurts the game narratively a lot because fights that carry a heavy burden and threat to the characters end up having no momentum and are a walk in the park. even if you do play those stages at the same level as the enemies you will find the game is too easy. The bosses were supposed to be the highlight of the game to make up for the lack in level design but most of them end up falling flat because of this.That said the opposite end of the spectrum showcases a different problem with enemies being able to one shot you very easily if you are too underleveled and this game commits the highest sin an action RPG could ever commit by having an stat (Composure) that dictates your hit rate against higher level enemies, if your Composure is not high enough your attacks will straight up do nothing even if you land the hit, so trying to fine tune your experience by underleveling yourself can become a problem if your Composure is too low. This stat can be leveled up individually using EGO (A different upgrade currency than ExP) and also increased by using different gear so make sure to no neglect this too much if you do try to play the game under the recommended level.The game would benefit greatly from a higher difficulty setting that ramps up the aggression of the enemies and expands their movesets a bit more.At the end of the day looking past the issues with the gameplay you will find a pretty interesting story with many twists and turns, execellent voice acting and accompanied by a perfect soundtrack. The story had me smiling ear to ear when seemingly minor and unimportant details become extremely relevant and makes putting everything together very satisfying.11/10 peak kinography held back by 4/10 gameplay and weird difficulty balancing.Ecclesia is a chad.

And you can cope as much as you want and call it "art style" and stuff like that, but when I see a valve with 6 sides in the 2023 game for 80 euros I am just at a loss for words. And even though the levels are beautiful, they still look empty, they look boring. Same textures, same models, same everything on every level except different patches you can take. I mean, if you are making a linear structured game based on levels in 2023 you at least expect some details and effort put into them, right? But no, you copied and pasted the same 10 models all over 80 euros game, added different fog colors and that's it? Let me remind you, that god of war costs CHEAPER than your game. And you know that, you know that your level design is bad and boring and you still allow this game to be published in this state. This is just insulting...Let's talk about combat.I know it has been a big issue even from the Crystar times, and applause to you, it was a big step up! I mean it was a step up from the Crystar level, but combat in your game is like 100 steps down from all other games.Did you play genshin impact? Or dark souls maybe? From what time in history did you pull this button smashing piece of crap gameplay in your brain and call it a good decision? It's simply unbelievable that after all these comments your fans left you, all this crying, you allow yourself to publish a game with the combat system from prehistoric era and call it a fun gameplay. I can't even imagine what was you thinking...Oh! Almost forgot, animations!I am sorry to ask, but why.. Why is your game has so few animations? But what triggers me most, after doing such a bad and lazy job at animating characters you allow yourself to cut corners even more by doing BLACK SCREENS TO CHANGE POSES. WHAT? ITS UNREAL ENGINE THAT HAS ANIMATION BLENDING BUILD IN. IT'S LITERALLY 2 BLUEPRINT NODES, 3 MINUTES OF WORK MAX. HOW?Also, story.I mean it's alright. Considering how bad all other stuff in the game is, the story is just simply mid.Also, is it only me, but Popator is like a "dad" to all machines, right? And it's not like family type love, its full blown romantic relationship. Emmm?? Isn't it's just an *wrong thing to do*. Am I the only one who noticed that? How does it even work?Anyway, that's time for the Ami Pop Quiz! Finally!Was it too hard to add a few more checkpoints on the levels? No.Was it too hard to ask your friend to help you map keys the right way for the PC? No.Was it too hard to add a few more poses for the sitting characters? No.Was it too hard to model more stuff for the levels? No.All of this wasn’t hard at all. It doesn’t cost much money or time, there is no possible excuse why all of this wasn’t done by you. _childDocuments_.review: CRYMACHINA? A Mechanical Tale of Ambition and Mixed Execution! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)In the post-apocalyptic realm of CRYMACHINA, mechanical girls are on an unrelenting quest to become Real Humans. As an action RPG, the game invites players to navigate this world through the eyes of three main characters: Leben Distel, Mikoto Sengiku, and Ami Shido, as they engage in fast-paced action RPG combat, customize their weapons, and confront formidable adversaries.The game introduces players to a thought-provoking narrative, emphasizing the essence of humanity and the blurred line between artificial and organic life. It all starts with Leben, who awakens in a desolate, post-apocalyptic landscape and is greeted by Enoa, an android. Together, they embark on a journey to pursue the elusive status of a Real Human.CRYMACHINA weaves an emotionally charged storyline through synthetic beings, exploring themes of love, family, and destiny. The characters, brought to life by talented voice actors, create a compelling and immersive experience. The game's anime-style aesthetic is a visual treat, drawing players into the world of synthetic beings, with 4K resolution support ensuring stunning graphics.However, CRYMACHINA isn't without its drawbacks. While the premise and character designs are intriguing, the execution falls short in some areas. For instance, the combat system, though real-time, often feels monotonous, reducing encounters to a repetitive series of button inputs. The lack of complexity in the combat system and the absence of a challenging difficulty setting may leave some players wanting more.Furthermore, the level design leaves much to be desired, with a lack of exploration opportunities and uninspiring environments. The game primarily consists of linear hallways and platforms, making the exploration component feel superficial and the world less immersive.CRYMACHINA operates on a mission-based game loop, where players move from one level to another, slaying bosses and returning to a hub area for story cutscenes and character dialogues. The predictable nature of this loop can make the experience feel somewhat dull and repetitive.It's worth noting that the game's visuals and presentation are not on par with top-tier titles, reflecting its budget constraints. Despite offering 4K resolution support, CRYMACHINA may not impress those with high expectations for cutting-edge graphics.In conclusion, CRYMACHINA is a game of contrasts. It tells a captivating story with a unique premise, engaging characters, and solid pacing. However, it falls short in terms of combat complexity, level design, and overall aesthetics. With a premium price tag, some players may find it challenging to justify the investment in this budget RPG. Waiting for a significant price drop or discounts might be a wise choice for those interested in exploring the world of CRYMACHINA while managing their expectations.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: Recommended it or not?It really boils down to what is your focus of Crymachina?This game reminds me a lot of Nier: Automata: exquisite character design, unforgettable soundtracks, unique story. Gameplay in the other hand: clunky jump & dash actions, extremely repetitive levels, in one sentence: neither live up to the modern standard of a hack n slash genre nor ARPGs.Technically, I brought this game for its art and soundtracks, it’s like seeing a unique antique in an auction house, despite its bidding price is high, I could hardly reject the will of possess it. To me, it’s better buying it than 10 common artifacts equally the same value to my lab.I wrote this review solely on purpose, sending the message to developers: the studio you’ve cooperated for the game art did an amazing job that made me not only overcome the prejudice of the price, but also deciding to storm the game until a 100% completion. It’s my appreciation for bringing such a wonderful piece of state of art to my collection. Moreover, the CV behind Enoa is a legend. Not only did she portrait Enoa perfectly, but also left some soul-calling vocal songs that I added to my private playlist. I have only 8 all time favorite songs to be played over and over among one million songs I’ve listened to. Now, 1/8 is from this game.However, if I were gameplay focused, above wasn’t my true color.I wouldn’t recommend this game at all. As I’ve said before, the jump & dash in the middle air animation are wonky and quite uncomfortable to control. It’s easily misstepped and fell off an edge during an exploration. There are few enemies in the game, same looking, same attack pattern, different names( not important), level differences which matters to be precise. Levels are pretty repetitive. The real problem isn’t combat being simple or levels are repetitive, they’re too simple to be called ‘fun’. Here’s my own sample video of the levels as a prove of what I said.Well, if you can get over with the repetitive thing like I did and start enjoying it somehow, then I believe, you will like this game.But still, developers should’ve let players have chance to control rival characters, experiencing the story from different perspectives for example, like Fate Samurai Remnant has done. It would add diverse value to the game, better than it is now. Personally I think the pace of the game has some issue too. Part of the game is heavily presented as a VN. The game’s surprisingly talkative as hell, you often do long conversations, watch cut scenes, then suddenly rejoining a furious battle against sci-fi monsties. The contrast is a bit too extreme, no?Unfortunately gameplay wise, Crymachina doesn’t live up to the standards of modern ARPGs or  hack & slash genre should be. If this is your focus of a game, I wouldn’t recommend it. I won’t even advise buying it with a discount. Better skipping it, playing something else entirely for better hack n slash or ARPG experience like Fate Samurai Remanent or the incoming Tales of Arise new expansion: Beyond the Dawn.S.C’s Score: ∞/???  I cant rate it, don’t wanna drag my personal sentiment into it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Backtracking: The Game"A couple of changes and this game could be really good:- With the "search" option for searching "secret" levels to spice up the main story you are given a very interesting and addicting tool to sidetrack and play the game in your own pace. Unfortunately you face a lot of restrictions along the way which makes those tools completely useless. There is no archiving your own findings until you find the "hints" in the main story, making it bothersome to explore things for yourself. - Finding the secret bosses in the levels is also beeing "rewarded" by fighting an enemy with unknown level (who always outlevels you by the time you can solve the puzzle to find them for the first time), which is bothersome since there are no checkpoints until the very last room in each mission. Trial & error and solving puzzles is somehow rather punishing than rewarding. Leaving all the puzzles you encounter untouched because you know you can only benefit from solving them after hours of mainstory later is not a good game design.- There are level caps for each chapter. Clearing that one secret level you found, or killing that secret boss in your last story mission is not even possible until like 3 chapters later. A whole ecosystem to grind small advantages if you wanted, but restrictions on every corner will stop you every time. Very early in the game you already feel like this whole skillpoint/level system has no value at all.tldr: A good game design that is luring with almost infinte sidestracking potential and tools to do so, just to put you on rails and borders on each side to make sure you have to ignore that stuff for most of the time. The story on the other hand is fresh and exciting, unfortunately it gets burried under a well below average gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favourite games this year, if not my GOTY.God-like soundtrack (courtesy of Sakuzyo), exceptionally endearing characters, a sorrowful but ultimately optimistic story full of twists & turns that'll keep you guessing, beautiful artwork / environments and fun action RPG combat (despite some jank): these are all on offer here.If you are into Drakengard / NieR and are looking for something new but similar (that leans a bit more into visual novel territory): I would  suggest checking this game out, in addition to its precursor / thematic prequel: Crystar.Playing through them, you will, without a doubt, notice so many familiar elements that it should come as no surprise that the director of Crystar / Crymachina, Fuyuki Hayashi, is a huge fan of Yoko Taro's works and has had the opportunity to learn directly from him.In summary: don't let this (or Crystar) go under your radar.

_childDocuments_.review: Music and artwork are top notch. The story is really cool too. Gameplay could be "hit-or-miss" (lol).The combat is essentially a light attack / heavy attack masher with timed dodges. But it has committed the greatest action-rpg sin of preventing skilled players from fighting optional bosses (available from the first few levels) when underleveled. Large level gaps between the player and enemy will just cause all of your attacks to "miss" or do 0 damage, meaning you will be forced to remember which stages house the optional bosses, then return to them much later in the game. Which is a shame, because being appropriately leveled will make you steamroll most of the fights in this game.Gameplay consists of short action stages with (generally) low difficulty and many brief VN-style dialogues and lore to read between levels. After spending much more time reading than fighting, it was clear that the balance between combat and reading may not be for everyone. It's very Honkai Impact-esque in that regard.I like it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: tld;r, 7/10 game, not worth full price and arguably not even worth the $38.99 I paid for it. Despite this, I still finished the game and enjoyed the story, so I'll recommend it.Crymachina is another mediocre RPG from the makers of Crystar. Similar to Crystar, the art direction, voice acting, and character design are all excellent. The story here starts off slow but picks up around a third of the way through, and I found myself invested in the characters and the ending of the story. I also thought the ending of the story was good and provided a definitive conclusion to the game.The ARPG combat is serviceable but a little uninspired. Two of the three characters felt pretty similar to play, and there is not a lot of depth to chaining combos together. Auxiliary weapons were a cool idea but ultimately don't give you a lot of control over their exact usage, so it felt underwhelming, even with the possible customizations. Also, the game is never actually clear on how to open up the equipment screen, so I spent an embarrassing amount of time with starting gear (it's the select button btw).Still, if you're looking for a good story (and a lot of lesbians), you found the right game. My 14 hours of playtime represents a clear of the main story of the game. There seems to be a lot of post-game content if you want to grind and enjoy the combat, but personally I could take it or leave it, so I'm just going to call it here. Get it on a steep steep sale if you can.

_childDocuments_.review: CRYMACHINA is a special title for me because it reminds me of SENRAN KAGURA. It is a combination of a visual novel and an action game. The plot and everything else is presented in the form of dialogues. After completing the game I can say that it was a good title, I liked the characters and the plot in the game and the combat system. The game itself had no problems or bugs. Moreover, the game time was not that bad because in total it took me 54 hours, which is a pretty good result, I think. That is why I can recommend it to all SENRAN KAGURA fans.
_childDocuments_.name: CRYMACHINA

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game as a lot to offer certain people so I do recommend it, but ultimately I'm not sure it's a game for me. The visual novel elements were a lot stronger than I expected and the gameplay is a bit simplistic. The story is interesting enough and if you like AI girls sitting around talking with some sometimes cheeky conversations then it'll probably sit well with you. I didn't get as many hours into it as I thought I would though. Depending on how much you want to grind the game can be hard or easy and there's a lower difficulty you can pick which ultimately lets you make it incredibly easy so you can just chill out and do the story. The music is fantastic though, that's for sure. The art style is also not the most popular style but fits the setting well and is sure to find a crowd.
_childDocuments_.name: CRYMACHINA

_childDocuments_.review: A truly beautiful story, with a lot of the otaku influence and expressions I truly adore. It builds on what Crystar established in very satisfying ways, with a very unique worldview and a lovable cast full of personality.The action gameplay is, much like Crystar, the weakest element, but it mainly serves to put you in the shoes of the main character's struggles rather than standing for itself so I can forgive that. Compared to Crystar though, it solved a major issue that the previous game faced which is padding. In this game, levels are short and focused, with few enemies, and the controls are responsive - which is enough to make it fun enough to not hold back your enjoyment of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels similar to Blue Reflection, but with action combat. Characters were well written and the story is quite intriguing, but the gameplay is fairly mediocre. Combat starts fairly easy, but the difficulty curve grows faster than you can level or gain better equipment. The last chapter of the game demands that you perform perfect dodges and parries, but the timing is very inconsistent and it never felt good. Worth it for the story and characters, but I'd skip this one if you mostly care about the gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: First thing first, this game piqued my interest because of its art style, it looks really cool and fairly unique. I like the visuals of the game. I'm not saying it's groundbreaking or anything but art direction is good, character art and design are really good. And the music, amazing, so long one enjoys the "rhythm game vibe." Action and action-rpg are my go to genre so I'd say the battle gameplay is passable but definitely not what would carry the game. The story was enjoyable and I appreciate the banter between the characters and all their interactions generally speaking. Those tea parties (bonding) are enjoyable. Overall, while this game wasn't a master piece, I had a good time. The game is structured around missions in closed areas. No open world, a couple of branching with light puzzles for optional fights, but mostly linear paths. Also side note, the game is not hard but it's merciless. If for some reason a game over happens, there is no continue, only restart the whole mission, no check point, just something to keep in mind before trying those optional fights in main missions that may be much higher level when first came across.I highly recommended playing the game until reaching the true ending (credit roll) and I'd say getting all the achievements isn't hard, only a couple of them might be tricky but they're mostly naturally obtained though several will require grinding, other than that nothing too hard. While I do recommend this game, I think it's overpriced (I did receive it as a gift though), I believe 40 USD would be a fair price for this game. I don't mind that the game doesn't last for hundreds of hours, if anything it's refreshing to not have to put hundreds of hours to see everything the game has to offer.Pros:- Enoa (she's so adorable)- Character interactions- The art- The music (sakuzyo), I love BEAT BEAT BEAT- The story- The equipment system is interesting- Light yuri?Cons:- Gameplay passable, waste of potential brought by equipment system- Overpriced, it's an AA game with a price tag of an AAA basically- Light yuri? (It's not a mistake, I'm just indifferent but figured some people might want to know)

_childDocuments_.review: Now I usually don't do actual reviews for games, just leaving it at a joke or two and moving on. However, I think this is a game that warrants a proper review. As of writing this, I have just finished the main game.★★★★★  By far the highlight of the game. Without going into any spoilers, the story is what most compelled me to keep playing the game after the first two hours or so. Those first two hours are a little rough in my opinion, with a few jokes that didn't quite stick for me, but past that the writing is absolutely phenomenal, and has me already planning to replay this title at some point relatively soon. While many of the points following this may seem negative, I cannot stress enough how much the story is worth playing for, with one twist in particular being one of the most memorable and impactful I've seen in media, let alone a video game.★★☆☆☆  This is where most of my biggest issues with Crymachina stem from. While the combat itself is... fun, if a little heavy on the button mashing, many of the attacks and all but one of the character's dashes feel a little slow and clunky, and I found there were multiple times where I was being hit while stuck in an attack input even though I was trying to dodge.   Secondly, you're going to need to be prepared to grind. While most of the game can be played through with relative ease only doing the main story, near the end the "suggested" (suggested meaning required, in this case, due to the very high changes in stats between levels) level for your characters and required exp to level  up rises drastically. I'm fairly certain roughly 3 of my last 4 hours of the game were spent repetitively running the same missions to gather enough exp to progress.  There's also little to no tutorial, with most of the guides being hidden behind an in game manual that, admittedly, I skipped over reading. As such, it took me until I literally could not progress due to difficulty to figure out how to even level up my characters.  While it may seem like these issues would add up to an unplayable, un-enjoyable game, I think that is far from the case. While there are certainly problems with the gameplay I wish would be addressed, they aren't problematic enough to have made me want to stop playing, and I make it a point to not finish games that I'm not enjoying.★★★★☆  In general, the music and visuals of the game are phenomenal. The soundtrack by Sakuzyo is actually how I originally found out about this game, and I spent months listening to it on repeat before actually playing the game. Likewise, Rolua's work on the character portraits is stunning, bringing so much more life and emotion to the game beyond a "generic anime game". Likewise did the few animated sections of the game not fail to stun me; the artistic team behind them is clearly  talented and made it known.  The levels, while mostly similar in general aesthetics, are likewise wonderful to look at, and I never found myself growing tired of seeing the extensive mechanical interiors of Eden as I progressed through them. Each new area has enough variation as to feel distinct from the others, while still feeling like part of the same structure.  My one problem here is the character models. They feel a little off putting and rigid, even beyond what would make sense for a machine stylistically. They did grow on me somewhat, but certainly gave off an uncanny valley feeling that persisted through the entire game. ★★★★☆  I really,  wish I could give Crymachina five stars, with the story, art, visuals and general atmosphere deserving more than that on their own. However, the issues with the combat, while not particularly having enough of an effect to dissuade me from continuing, are too present for me to give the five star rating this game so deserves otherwise.  In a way, I wish this was an anime- there are clearly very talented writers and artists that worked on this game and I wish they had more time to shine through amidst the clunky combat and somewhat lacking character models. If you're looking for a combat focused ARPG, Crymachina isn't for you. Go play Scarlet Nexus if you haven't. But if you're ready to immerse yourself in a world and a story, and grow to care about a small, enjoyable cast of characters who play off of each other incredibly well, you'll love this game, and I wish you the best of times with it.Also the lesbian robots were cool

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, Crymachina may be overall a low budget game, but this doesnt mean theres no quality being offered.Music - One of those rare games that offer vocal tracks. It has a very good soundtrack and i even sometimes listen to it outside of the game. Artwork - Very unique character designs, which i didnt see anywhere else before with this style. I even showed some of the designs to someone, who didnt hear about this game before. Became instantly a fan of the character Zoe.Story - Those who like their anime games having dark themes will easily get invested thanks to the very good writing. There was no character i disliked.Storytelling - I feel the game did a very good job to convey everything that happens in a way, that its easy enough to understand to the player. This is no small feat in my opinion considering with everything that is going on in the story and it being mostly presented in VN style.Also another strong point of Crymachina is the pacing of the game - something that was really messed up in its spiritual predecessor Crystar (and tbh most modern games in general). Crymachina is kinda on the short end when it comes to playtime with 15-20h for the mainstory depending on the player. But in exchange, its completely free of filler and prolonged mindnumbing grinding with neverending dungeons that all look the same. I wouldnt really say it offers less story content in comparison to crystar at all. Its also refreshing playing a JRPG that does respect your time for once (this is why i actually was motivated enough and played a 2nd time from start to finish. Yes, in my opinion Crymachina has replayability). But be aware theres also a postgame with some extra bossfights and you can hunt down every single personality data (which is super repetitive) and the best equipment for those that want to sink more time into this.

_childDocuments_.review: There are two very annoying sects of queerbaiting RPGs and RPGs which act way more high-concept than they actually are.CRYMACHINA is the antithesis to BOTH of these categories, being unabashedly queer and having a clear thesis on humanity and how we relate to it. Lesbian love saves the day, and it feels 100% earned.There's no point really writing about the gameplay, even. It's good! There's some weird spots of difficulty pacing, but it never holds the game back. It's got a really intense style of combat zen that I don't see in many games. Doesn't even matter! It'd already be a 10/10 even if the gameplay weren't fun! I desperately need more games like CRYMACHINA to come out. No slop, no slog, just doing one thing and doing it perfectly.

_childDocuments_.review: Crymachina is a spiritual sucessor to Crystar, which was one of my favorite game stories with some of the worst gameplay ever. I'm happy to report that gameplay, this time around, while still far from ideal, is VERY VERY much improved, having much simpler level design, faster stages, boss fights that aren't HP sponges and WAY BETTER combat mechanics overall. Where it struggles is giving you proper feedback upon getting hit, a lot of times you will die in this game without even noticing you were at low HP, or you just straight-up get 1-hit-killed by a completely random attack that didn't look or feel that strong.Despite that, however, it is not as painful of a gameplay experience as Crystar, hence I don't need to recommend cheating to get through it. And the story.... maaaann, the story. It managed to surpass Crystar which had already quickly become one of my favorites. The character interactions are ON POINT here and I got very very attached to this cast extremely quickly. At first, it felt slightly weaker than Crystar, but the plot twists hit hard and the story goes in very interesting directions, it had me fully hooked past a certain point and I love it to bits.There are a few references to Crystar here and there, and some thematic parallels, but it is mostly unconnected. So if you're wondering whether or not you have to play Crystar first: You don't. I do, however, highly recommend that game (albeit, with cheats) as it also has an incredible story.Overall I'm extremely impressed with both Crystar and Crymachina and they both recently became some of my favorite games ever. The story is truly touching and I fell in love with the characters.Enoa is the best.

_childDocuments_.review: CRYMACHINA is a good game that is close, but not quite an excellent game.Its weakest point is the pacing of the gameplay, with the majority of it being in the postgame. During the story you will mostly be fighting very small groups of enemies and be constantly interrupted by cutscenes, making it difficult to fully enjoy the combat. This is in contrast to the postgame where you'll be fighting the same enemies in the same rooms with no dialogue, no cutscenes, no story at all to break it up. Averaging out the two would have made the game flow much more smoothly.Regardless, the narrative more than makes up for its shortcomings. It easily draws you in and makes you eager to find out what happens next, to see every interaction between the characters, to discover more about the setting.CRYMACHINA has an interesting story coupled with a distinct art style and beautiful soundtrack; making it a very memorable game.It isn't perfect, but it certainly deserves a gold star.

_childDocuments_.review: Global grade (final impression, not section average) : ★★★★★★★★★☆Crymachina is a visual novel with a side part of action RPG more than a action RPG itself. The gameplay is not terrible per se, but not good either. The price tag is hefty. But the story and characters are worth a gold star and are almost enough to justify playing Crymachina. And lastly, another gold star for the musics and general audio feeling.Would I recommend it to the average player ? Surely, under a sale.Would I recommend it to the yuri audience ? Most certainly.Merely the weak point of the game. Fortunately if you only desire to do the story you’ll bear with it roughly ~13h. But if you want to know ALL about the story you’ll spend more time for it. The gameplay is the very definition of the MEH grade. It works, but is utterly outdated. The RPG part felt shallow in the sense that your attributes consume an exponential amount of points, meaning you’ll be just fine raising a bit of everything and not give it a second thought. The good point of the gameplay is that overall, the progression is fairly smooth, you need few grind to go through main story ~12h content and the game feature difficulty spikes only through optional content. But if you do desire to do the extra content (which you might want because of how good is the story), then the gameplay will become a hidrance. I suggest you do the main story in normal mode, then switch to casual mode for extra content. The gameplay is mostly numbers and rest assured that the end game in casual has some challenge, especially the hardest boss, so doing it in normal mode is only for those willing to put a lot of hours.For a moderate budget game Crymachina is quite decent looking in my regard, and have an overall anime mood I like. But the nicely looking parts cohabits with a world design which feels a bit… empty. In the sense that everything is artificial, it is normal to see metal everywhere. But the buildings and platforms models lacks some refinement. But overall it’s enjoyable to the eye, it does the job. Solid boobs physic by the way, although the gameplay would have needed such attention.Music wise, Crymachina is marvelous. Most of the musics are not « gotta listen to them forever » grade, but all of them are absolutely appropriate to the writing style of the game and its setup. They perfectly participate to the immersion, especially in key moments usually driven by the story. As for sounds in a general manner, it’s pleasant, whichever it is combat or menus. The only missing star is that conversation audio may mix at the end of the mission with the subsequent cinematic. But since the game is subbed it’s not so much a problem.Crymachina goes suprisingly deep in character development and character elements of the story, although a fair part will require you to grind to unlock all the records. A lot of efforts has been made by the developers and it provide you with a wide diaspora of backstories. Even secondaries characters or character memoirs may have some crucial piece of information. And the best about it is that the more you dig, the more you want to know about all of them.Special mention to the main quatuor (Eona, Leben, Ami and Mikoto) which has been given special attention to make them consistent, heartwarming and … humane.Probably the main reason you want to consider giving Crymachina a try. The story is a bit hard to grasp on the first run, and just going through it will leave you with a LOT of missing information. But its first quality is to give just enough information through the main story missions and records so you ultimately understand at least the idea being its creation, the main events, and the general message behind it.The story has a lot of subtext, and require to seek for them if you desire to have the whole picture, as the main story alone leave a lot of open questions, especially toward the purpose and the backstory of each Deus Ex Machina and their creators. But once you assemble the whole puzzle it’s a remarquable and well thought piece. An harsh one, but nevertheless impressive. It’s good to a point I went for a 100% despite the lackluster gameplay, something I very rarely do since I’m not an achievement gamer. I just always wanted more of it, digging every single piece of personal data.What makes it feel special is how swiftly it swap being « manichean » mode and « scientific » mode. You’re constantly shaken between raw, brutal emotions and cold, down-to-earth explanations, a left brain <-> right brain permanent yoyo particularly appropriate in the physical and psychological strain happening to our « heroines » at the root of Crymachina. Breaking the fourth wall through immersion while never making contact with the player, a feat I very rarely saw. The story, even complete, has room for interpretation, especially since it is sometimes hard to draw a line between humanity and the machinas trying to save it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was 15 levels below the final boss. I brute forced it out of stubbornness. Don't do what I did. It took me 4 hours to succeed, with a lot of cursing and shouting. Unless you just like the challenge, level up your characters. That being said, I did it. Now, I might have missed something prior to getting to the end, but I'll have to double-check. EDIT: LOL I GOT ITCRYMACHINA. This game is pretty cool, man. Beautiful setting, lovely characters, interesting premise with some good themes, simple-but-fun combat system. I welcome this new IP. Difficulty-wise it's about as hard as you make it. As I said earlier, I was clearly underleveled. Despite that, I was able to make it work. I imagine staying at the recommended levels make things substantially easier. EDIT:  you can , but I haven't learned how to do that yet, lol.The story plays out primarily in dialogue between segments, which are largely slice-of-life conversations between characters. There are few cutscenes in the game, so if you dislike reading you can just skip through dialogue. Obviously, I wouldn't recommend that. Due to this, you can progress through the game at a pretty steady pace. There's no walking segments or hidden loading screens. It's nice, since it doesn't take long to get back to the action.Battles move quickly. Damage output is high, so there's a lot of "kill or be killed" scenarios during combat. Provided the enemy is in sight, attack animations, as well as other visual and audio cues make it possible to react to what the enemy does. It's not as dodge-heavy as, say, Bayonetta, but you will need to use your options to mitigate damage and counterattack. There's a good enough variety of enemies to keep things interesting. Even the "recolors" behave differently and gain new abilities. The bosses are all pretty fun, and they get damn near nutty in the lategame. They definitely force you to utilize your defensive options well. Of course, like with any RPG, leveling up enough will allow you to steamroll the game. Characters have their own fighting style, and I found it fun to get a good idea of where each excels. The auxiliary weapons are helpful in adopting new approaches to fighting. Hell, they pretty much made the final boss possible for me. You get a decent variety to choose from with some freedom to experiment. There's not much in terms of combos. You have light attacks and a heavy attack/launcher. That combined with your other weapons is your arsenal. You make it work from there. Enoa provides support as well.The levels are short and arcadey, which makes for pretty quick pacing in most cases. I enjoyed that, as it rarely felt like the game was dragged out longer than it should be. While you don't explore levels, you do at least get a chance to look around the environment. As I said, the setting looks nice. Increasing the camera distance and FOV will probably do you well. My only real issue within the mechanics is that the stat parameters are vaguely explained. While I don't expect whole formulas to be provided, I would appreciate, for example, being told the difference between Willpower and Strength. It's difficult to determine how you want to develop your characters when you have to reload the game to see the effects of stat changes.The game seems to get dunked on for being a budget title, but that's what you get with Furyu. It's a solid game, and there's little that I dislike about it(outside of that bug that I frequently ran into during the final boss that had me mysteriously getting stuck in corners of the stage, left to facetank the next attack). Am I getting a sequel? Probably not. Does it need one? I don't know, as I think there's still more left for me to discover. It was a great time, and never overstayed its welcome. The OST is very well-done as well. I'm probably going to buy the album whenever that becomes available for purchase. EDIT: It's actually available for purchase through Sakuzyo's(the composer) website as well as his bandcamp page.If paying full price for a new game is a problem for you, you can wait for a sale. If you're looking for a game to dump hundreds of hours into, this ain't it. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed CRYMACHINA, there are a lot of things the game has improved on compared to their previous game Crystar. The level design is a lot shorter, usually taking between 1-5 minutes to clear a level. I find this to be a great improvement over Crystar's levels that were mostly lengthy grinds, as the combat was not that great. The combat in CRYMACHINA is almost the same as that in Crystar, but with some improvements. The enemy AI has improved, they don't just mindless walk towards you as they did in Crystar and the enemies are a threat doing much more damage in CRYMACHINA. The story still has that focus on deeper meanings, in this case on what it is to be human, but is far shorter than Crystar. I like the characters in the game, but would have liked the story to be longer so I could take more time learning about them. I spent about 10 hours going through the main story + some side content, and another 6 hours for the post game content to get all achievements. The post game content is where this game falls a bit short, as it is mostly just grinding away to increase your character's level to actually do post game levels. At the end of the story my characters were around level 65, where post game is around level 90-120. The problem is the exp and EGO you need to empower your characters is given very sparingly, it becomes a tedious grind. 5 of the 6 hours I spent on post game was just trying to level my characters. Still while a lot shorter, I enjoyed this game as I enjoyed Crystar. I would recommend you wish list the game and purchase it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Liked:- Environments. Although the paths you take through the levels are extremely linear, I really enjoyed just looking around and taking in the places I was being railroaded through.- The art style, especially of the characters. The eyes, the portraits, the *eyes*… I like it.- The music. The XTrinity MV brought me to this game, and an OST CD set is currently on its way to my mailbox.- The path the story was taking. Afew points had me going "…really?", but by the end I was hooked & rooting for the good girls.- …Okay, maybe the Yuri as well.So-so:- Gameplay. It's okay. I have lots of small issues with it, but it was enjoyable enough to play inbetween story stuff until the credits. There's post-game stuff to do, I'll likely give it a try but dunno if I'll complete all of it.Disliked:- It's nice that the Tea Party conversations are infinitely rewatchable, but I'm really missing a similar feature for the story scenes & videos. At least the latter can be viewed outside of the game with abit of effort, but having a "Cinema" option or smth like that for rewatching everything within the game would've been superb.- That it's already over! I'm hoping the Trinity DLC makes it to Steam eventually :(. I guess there's still stuff to grind & achievements to hunt down, but that seems alot less exciting without the usual story stuff inbetween.Notes (played on Linux via Proton, YMMV):- The game refused to recognise my controller of choice (PS3 DualShock3) no matter what I did, even though it works fine in Steam Input & other games. Ended up using a Switch Pro controller. I suppose this is an issue with how the game is getting its inputs?- I've had two crashes while playing, one of which took down my AMD graphics driver along with it. There are autosaves though, so not much progress will be lost.Overall, I think this game deserves a gold star.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to get all the achievements before I talked about this game. I played the game’s demo in July, and I really liked what I saw, even if it was all in Japanese. I was fixing for a good action RPG to sink my teeth into, and I wanted it to be great. It was more of a “good” than great though, and although I’m not too happy about the price, I’m happy I got to play it to the end.  Crymachina is a very short and sweet game—I finished the campaign in about 15 hours. The presentation isn’t the greatest; out of all the 15 hours, I think I spent only 5 of them actually playing the game and the rest reclining back watching Leben and her newfound friends chat about life, the meaning of their existence, and their ideal relationship partner. If you look at it that way, it’s a 10-hour visual novel with a lot of cute optional conversations locked behind a game with a combat system that is so average it genuinely hurts to play. Don’t get me wrong, the game is easy enough even without using Casual Mode. But my main gripe with it is just how off-putting the combat system is. It has a nice base, it feels like they tried to encapsulate the feeling of other ARPGs like NieR:Automata yet failed to understand what made them smooth and fun to play to bother with the story. I liked the idea of a combat system revolving around the use of perfect dodging to effortlessly dance around enemy patterns and gain bonuses for doing so, but the game itself makes it difficult for you to do that. The game’s vibrant lighting and effects for both characters and enemies are demerits, obscuring enemy tells and making it difficult to register how fast enemy animations are. Combine that with a rather strict perfect dodge window (not as strict as the Japanese demo, thank God, but still warranting the player to be on the ball) and it’s a recipe for disaster. It warrants a lot of focus and struggling with the controls that story-goers shouldn’t really have to struggle with. By comparison, countering is a weaker option. Most attacks you’re meant to counter you can dodge anyway for a better reward. Which leads to another issue—the lack of visual feedback. Countering attacks feels very flat. Because of how in-your-face the game is with all the special effects, it’s difficult to handle multi-hit attacks effectively. It’s easier to mash and hope for the best, but even then, you run the risk of botching the timing and getting hit with attacks that will surprise you on how much damage they do. Also considering that you don’t have mercy invincibility when you get hit, there’s always a threat of getting hit or stunned by one or multiple attacks you didn’t visually register hitting you (enemy aux units are like, the biggest offenders) until you realize you’re suddenly at 0 HP and now your chosen E.V.E. is taking a dirt nap. Aside from all that, the sentiment and auxiliary unit subsystems are unique, but add a false sense of depth. They’re strictly for defensive utility or DPS, not extenders for your ground or air chains. The enemies are too spongy and heavy outside of Weak state to support that, I guess. The system basically boils down to just landing and looping your charged attacks and cashing out with your finishing move. Ami is especially good at this—I’ve reason to believe that she might just be the strongest character in the game due to her generous armor frames and high damage. A maxed out Ami trivializes the post-game  simply because she can run her game faster than the enemies can in both gun and axe mode. She’s truly the epitome of grace. At its best, I felt like a rebel E.V.E. fighting tooth-and-nail against machines who wish to rob my family of a happy ending they deserve. At its worst, I felt like I was going to die from Centrifugal Syndrome. But the game is truly carried by its story, characters, and music. Sakuzyo brought a whole suite of bangers with him to enhance the atmosphere, and it gives the game much-needed emotion in both story and combat. Every member of the voice cast gave it their all in this game, but the performance of Tono Hikaru (Enoa) was especially standout, given how she handled her character’s development over the story  provided the vocals for 95% of the tracks in the game. The story won’t win any awards; it’s kind of campy and the models in cutscenes don’t emote much, but it does present themes of existentialism and purpose in its own way, and I’d say it’s worth buying just for the story and gals-being-pals humor alone.All in all, it’s a surprisingly good bargain game with an unfortunate premium price-tag that doesn’t justify its content.  I recommend it, but only if it’s at a ~40% or more discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick and surprisingly addictive dungeon-crawler with lots of mazes, simple rules, high strategy and low luck -- you only die when you've made a blunder, or backed yourself into a corner by poor planning. This may seem like a simple hack-and-slash, but it's not. There's almost no luck and a surprising amount of planning involved. Each dungeon is like a puzzle, and might take 15-45 minutes to complete. You start each dungeon as a lowly level 1 character. Kill the monsters in a certain order and gain the power-ups at the right times and you will be able to defeat the boss-monster and thus "win" each dungeon.  if you randomly charge in like a hack-and-slash game, you won't maximize your powerups and you won't have enough health to tackle the tougher monsters. Same if you spend the power-ups too soon. If you don't defeat the tougher monsters, you don't gain the experience-point bonuses to increase your abilities enough to tackle the boss-monster. As you complete dungeons, you can unlock other character classes (again, you start each dungeon back as level 1 and the layout of each dungeon is randomly generated each time).Since there's very little luck involved in combat, most of the time you will know the results of a combat before it happens, and can choose to either delay it until you are more powerful or press on. The game UI shows you in advance how much damage you and your opponent will suffer each round of combat, and thus allows you to predict the result of each combat. Choosing to use magic glyphs and potions can also modify how a combat turns out. Therefore you only die when you've made a blunder, or backed yourself into a corner by poor planning. The art and story in a tongue-in-cheek way poke fun at the Fantasy Role Playing genre. The game is supposedly based on the old networked Rogue game but I can't compare the two since I never played that. The graphics are simplistic and from a decade ago, but they get the job done and don't detract from the enjoyment in any way.EDIT: about the only negatives are that the class challenges are somewhat hard and might put off beginners. Also some of the Explorers Giuld puzzles are more like chess puzzles, in that one wrong move and you can't beat it. Again, give the DDwiki a look before giving up.

_childDocuments_.review: I met the Devs at GamesCom 2014. Around noon on Friday they sat me down in front of a PC and had me try the game - apparently I did well (I looked at the goblin before attacking it and noticed it had first strike). After a merry but short romp through the introduction dungeon, which ended with a green blob of slime eating my poor adventurer, I went on to explore the rest of the Indie Megabooth. Friday night though, before I went to sleep, I knew there was a bit of unfinished business: I bought the game, and not just because the developers are great guys (but that too).The game delivers what it promisses: bite sized adventures you can play during a break. The other day I had 15 minutes to spare: 10 of those were used by a berserker clearing a swamp of monsters.It may look like a simple game, but it has a suprising amound of depth, with many abilities, items and other things that lead to multiple ways to tackle dungeons and may have you adapting your strategy based on what you encounter.And there is a lot to encounter. Just when you think you have seen all the races, seen all the classes, you find one more. Then you check the journal and see just how much you haven't seen yet (I found it more fun not to check how much I am missing so as not to spoil the pleasure of finding something new).But how do you play? Simple: you select a dungeon to explore and write an adventuring permit. The permit is the "character creation" process of that dungeon. For example it could say: To [dungeon name], For Generic Adventuring, Race: Human, Class: Warrior, Equipment: starting adventurer's kit. Then you would play the dungeon with a simple lvl 1 human warrior.As the game progresses you unlock more races, classes and can provide better starting equipment and other bonuses, making each run unique.So what are you waiting for? Your kingdom needs you! Oh, you need a permit? To: Unnamed Desktop Dungeon Kingdom, For: Kingdom Administration, Race: Human, Class: Gamer. There you go, your permit to play the game.And yes, the alpha version is available for free to try out :)

_childDocuments_.review: "Normally, with puzzle games, if it seems too hard then you're generally just doing it wrong. With Desktop Dungeons, it's just too hard." — Kakie, Corsual Live ViewerI have a confession to make. I'm not proud of it, but I haven't finished Desktop Dungeons. I strive to complete all of the games I review prior to writing, but in this case the cross was too great to bear.My failure came not through lack of trying — I tried for many, many hours — but from an overwhelming level of difficulty. Not the bad kind of difficulty, where cheap opponents consistently barrage you until you die hurling an overpriced controller against the nearest wall, but the good kind of difficulty, that will see you thinking — really thinking — about every move you make, every time you make it, lest your adventure come to a inconveniently early end.Fortunately, I appreciate a challenge. Hell, I crave it. But in the end, it turned out that there was more to accomplish, collect and unlock in this roguelike dungeon crawler than I could ever hope to discover in just 2 weeks, and so, I began my review in advance.WITHOUT FURTHER ADO...I first saw Desktop Dungeons while watching MANvsGAME; Danny Baranowsky and Grant Kirkhope, who composed the soundtrack, were there alongside one of the core developers, Danny Day.They discussed many of the basic game concepts; the randomly generated dungeons and roguelike nature, spell-casting warriors, the coming mobile release, the difference between a harpsichord and clavinet and the origins of Granny Kirkanowsky.Listening in, amidst the constant laughter, I quickly learned that DD has something of a cult following that grew around an alpha build released to the public years back and available free today, which led to it winning the IGF Award Winning for Game Design. Immediately, I downloaded it to take a look.IN THE BEGINNINGThe alpha turned out to be a crude version of the one MAN was playing. It looked very different — the hand-drawn art wasn't present, instead offering a more traditional pixel art style, and the entire progression mechanic was missing, so choosing a dungeon was as simple as selecting a race, class and difficulty.Though I was watching MAN play a clearly superior version, I still felt entirely engaged playing the alpha due to the 'roguelike' nature of the gameplay. Every dungeon was different, and though my imminent demise was almost always a single click away, the ability to head straight back in, new knowledge in hand, to a completely new dungeon, maintained my interest throughout the entire night.That's when I made my purchase, gained access to the browser-operated (sans-soundtrack) beta and began to compare.NEW IS ALWAYS BETTERAfter a brief serving of story and a short tutorial explaining the basics I was directed to my very own kingdom, a world map of sorts, comprised mostly of open space and human inhabited houses. After completing a dungeon, more buildings appeared. An elven habitat, a mage tower, a church...I quickly realised that the original 'choose race, choose class, choose difficulty' menu featured in the alpha had been replaced here with progressive RPG elements via the kingdom, including a huge host of quests, and that unlike the alpha, races and classes here required an unlock before they could be used.The game continued forward, revealing multiple new features. Gold could be collected from dungeons and kept afterward, and then used to purchase preparation items that could be used in future dungeon attempts, or saved to unlock new buildings in the kingdom.Eventually, I was introduced to the tavern, which served as a hub allowing access to multiple dungeon types. It was here that the largest difference between the alpha and beta made their appearance — there's more than one dungeon type in the full version. A lot more.DON'T PISS OFF THE DEITIESThat's when things started getting tough, and it was at about that time that the full Steam release arrived, this one complete with Granny K's masterpiece soundtrack.I was happy to learn that the progress I'd made in the beta was saved, and too, that even though I could now play the full release on Steam, I could continue to do so from my browser if I chose. Everything is saved online, so portable gaming is a legitimate option. A good thing, too, as Desktop Dungeons lends itself perfectly to quick gaming when you've only got 10 minutes to spare. Come on mobile version...Where was I... oh, right. It's hard. Even the normal dungeons are hard. And the hard dungeons are a lot f@&ing harder. God only knows if there are even harder dungeons around the bend, but if there are, you'll likely need God's help to complete them. Well, at least one of the Gods, anyway.Yes, yes... I know. Terrible segway, yada-yada. Gods are the key to victory in many of the dungeons, yet they're also a leading cause of death. The decision to adopt a deity is usually a hard one — on the one hand, they offer amazing buffs and bonuses that are generally the key to victory, on the other, they'll restrict you in various ways, punishing you severely for whatever they deem misconduct — though mastering their ways is essential.THIS IS THE GAME THAT NEV-ER ENDSThat's where the other 'game mode' really helps: Puzzles. After unlocking the Explorer's Guild building in your kingdom you'll have access to a series of puzzles - dungeons that aren't generated randomly, but instead, have a single specific solution that you must discover in order to succeed.They double as great ways to learn more information about the various items, weapons, spells, deities and conversion materials on offer, and though not everyone will need them, they're highly advised if you're having difficulty completing certain quests or dungeons.And that's everything I know. Almost. I know that of the nine classes I've unlocked there are another nine to go. I know that of the four races I've unlocked there are another... actually I don't know how many more there are. One, at least. I found him once — a Halfling trapped in a dungeon within a dungeon who nicked my last potion— but failed and haven't seen him since. That's a lot of the fun in Desktop Dungeons; every dungeon is different, and you never know what you're going to get. If you like The Binding of Isaac, or Spelunky, or more appropriately, Rogue Legacy, which offers a similar style of 'progressive roguelike' gameplay, then there's a great chance you'll love Desktop Dungeons, too. It's as hard as the others — perhaps even harder in its own way — but if you're not one to shy from a challenge then there's a lot to enjoy.
