_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely great little game. The writing is cute and humorous, the music is fun and the gameplay itself is a combination of puzzle, mini-dungeon crawler and roguelike. It doesn't take itself too seriously but there is a lot of hidden depth in a seemingly simple idea. The addition of a daily dungeon and weekly reward gives more incentive to someone trying to build up their kingdom and there is always something to do.The final sets of main quests are incredibly challenging but it's so very satisfying to finish one of them. One last thing I'll say that I really like about the game is that, aside from making silly mistakes or a situation of bad luck (both will happen sometimes), death feels like a learning experience. You now know what *not* to do. And each little dungeon dive is a short trip so it's great when you want to play something but don't have a lot of time.I have played this game a lot, not sure how long since I tend to leave DD up for hours while doing other things, come back, play a dungeon, and tab out again. I'd say 100 hours at the least, probably a lot more.UPDATE: I finally 100%ed this little beast at exactly 1000.0 hours (looks nice and clean but as I said above there's no telling how much of that was active playtime, but a large chunk at least). After doing so and really learning all the mechanics and developing a sort of "master strategy" for my playstyle, I can easily call this one of my top 5 games, if not my favorite game of all time from a pure gameplay standpoint. Almost a year has gone by since then and I've frequently had the itch to load it up, but there was nothing else to really do anymore, somehow! It's accessible but it has so much hidden depth that really shines as you get deeper and further into the thick of it. All these little factors add up to make DD a really great experience that I can't recommend enough.  But fear not! There's a fan expansion out now, that's supposed to be even harder that the original and while not made by the developer, its approved by them. I have never been more excited to repeatedly die horribly. See you on the other side!

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing and enjoying the earlier version of this game while at work a couple of years ago (2011), and  it's nice to see that the paid version has built out the features nicely without losing sight of the original design. Don't be fooled by the cutesy artwork either - under the brightly colored hood lies an engine made of pure unadulterated mathematics. Do you fight the stronger enemy while you are lower level, earning extra xp you may need later? Or would that fight require you to eat into your valuable potion supply? The answer is right in front of your eyes, 95% of the time, it's up to you to figure out the optimal path if you can. Or, have a calculator handy.I'm not joking about the math either. This game is like a combination of Soduko, Minesweeper and the popular roguelike Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (I mean this in the best possible way). That's isn't to say that the rpg theme is painted on. On the contrary there is a satisfying asymettry to both the challenges you face in terms of levels and bosses, and also to the way the various classes and loadouts need to be deployed in order to surmount those challenges. The number of abilities and potential interactions, combined with a high degree of randomization, means that things stay interesting and fresh.Expect a game to last anywhere from 5 or 10 minutes from the early levels/challenges and upwards to an hour when attempting to successfully navigate some of the later dungeons, where a single miscalculation or wrong move can snatch sudden defeat from the jaws of victory. The logic and mechanics are incredibly tight (using unexplored space as a kind of resource is a genius mechanic IMO), and the fact that you now to get to build out your own kingdom as your acquire resources just adds another element of fun.Awesome game! I can't wait to see what happens next with the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played lots of games in my lifetime. And I don't think I've played any other game that's more boring than Desktop Dungeons. _childDocuments_.review: Deceptively difficult puzzler that looks like a roguelike but plays very differently. You start with a level 1 character in a single screen random dungeon and have to level up and collect gear to defeat a level 10 boss monster. This has the usual fantasy trappings of wizards, warriors, elves and undead, but the gameplay is almost pure resource management, where exploration is an important "resource" because uncovering hidden tiles is the primary method of healing and recovering spell points.The basic puzzle loop is pretty simple but DD has a LOT of ways to mix things up: spells, items, classes, races, deities, status effects, quests, theme dungeons, an upgradeable towns, there is a ton of content here.  A single run might only take 10-20 min, but at 22 hours of playtime I've only unlocked a little over half of the games 16+ classes and haven't beaten any of the "hard" dungeons yet.Graphics are a mixed bag. The in-game graphics look perfectly good and distinct and I like the monster designs (Meat Man is a personal favorite). The town graphics have a painterly look where the style reminds me of a cover of a Terry Pratchett novel, that doesn't quite work for me. It's kind of muddy and confusing and you only learn where things are by trial and error. You never spend more than a minute or two in town before/after a run, but some cleaner lines / darker outlines / better labels would go a long way to improving the town interface. I'm on the fence about the cartoonish/grotesque art style for the portraits: I love that every race/class combo has a male and female portrait variant and the art is good, just some of the designs are a little creepy and bug-eyed.Overall though the core gameplay is extremely well designed and satisfying and TOUGH. The first couple of dungeons are casual but after that you really have to plan and optimize and carefully conserve your resources in a bunch of directions, and DD is really good at leaving you a single XP / HP / gold away from success. If that kind of demanding mental juggling around every step sounds satisfying, I encourage you to take a trip into the Desktop Dungeons.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't find the few mechanics in this game satisfying.It's a bit weird to be told you've lost the game on the first click, and  be sent into a tutorial, which has overblown music like the world was about to end. The gameplay is like learning an awkward version of chess, as you have to consider each move carefully even if you're not near an enemy. Simply walking around the dungeon can mean you lose, even if nothing attacks you. As far as I've seen, the enemies are unable to attack you first, so the fighting is a bit flat.I didn't like how the difficulty revolved around recycling all your items and trying to remember which tiles you already stepped on, because you only regenerate health (and recharge ranged attacks) by stepping on tiles that you've never stepped on before, so the healing potential is wasted if you step on them at full health. You need their healing potential to recover after fighting low level enemies so that you can level up to beat the dungeon boss. Part of the problem is that you can only see the tiles immediately around you (or ones you've already stepped on), so you can't even plan ahead - essentially soft-locking you if you don't end up strong enough to defeat the boss. You're more or less forced to buy "preparations" just to slightly increase your chance of winning, and get punished for experimenting with different strategies because the meta is narrow, and restarting costs you the preparations again.As the meta involves pacing around the dungeon while counting the tiles like a mentalist, I didn't feel any immersion - the game breaks the fourth wall constantly which doesn't help, and fights just involve a mouse click or two. I thought there must be something fun about this game, but I don't get it. When exploring a dungeon I feel like I'm messing up an awkwardly made puzzle, and that's the entire game. I'd rather trade the intensity of picking your steps so carefully for the animating flow of a real-time strategy game. Why wouldn't I play something more fleshed out like Age of Empires 2? Even Celtic Kings had an RPG mode that felt more natural. For £11.99 it doesn't offer much in the way of mechanics, and seems game-breakingly difficult.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't know much about this game nor did I know what to expect when I installed it but safe to say I had a blast playing the game! I'm not super into it yet since I think I only just got the tavern but from what I played I had a blast! I mostly played as a wizard as made classes are always THE class I play during DnD sessions and this game to me perfectly captures that vibe of a DnD session with the random NPC's you talk to, the classes and the world plus dungeons themselves. It all feels neat. Not to mention the whole game has a vibe of an old pc game circa early 2000s, something in the vain of Plants vs Zombies or Zuma or Bejeweled and so on. I highly recommend this if you're a fantasy nerd like myself. I'll be coming back to the game pretty frequently that's for sure. Bravo!

_childDocuments_.review: In the game, players navigate a dungeon filled with monsters before battling a final dungeon boss. The game has qualities of a puzzle as players must find the best methods to use items, spells, and upgrades to reach the final boss without losing too much of their character's health. -WikipediaThis game looks and feels very simple at first since you only need mouse1 when clearing those dungeons out of those filthy monster scums. But the thing is, you wont get far if you try to kill every enemy that crosses your path just by smacking their goblin faces with your mighty sword. You need to think a few steps ahead and make a gameplan about how to get the best use out of your items and not waste any tiles while trying keep you health and mana high enough to be able to keep pushing forward. _childDocuments_.review: Best game ever. Think Dark Souls, with more capra.More seriously, Desktop Dungeons is essentially a math puzzle with a lot (emphasis on "lot") of mechanics interplaying, leading sometimes to awesome victories or terrible defeats. While dungeons run may be sometimes unsolvable -there is randomness in some aspects of the setup after all- achieving victory exploiting all the ressources available to you can be exhilarating. If you ever wondered what could happen if a developper had a neat puzzle idea and spent 3 years figuring out how to exploit each and every inches of its inginuity, instead of leaving that work to the players, this is what would happen. Word of warning : having Steam listing the game under "casual" reads like trolling. Expect to spend an hour per run once you hit the hard and vicious dungeons.I loved the freeware version, and cannot see me stopping playing the complete one anytime soon. If you love maths, this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Calling this a roguelike doesn't do it justice, it's no more a roguelike than Minesweeper is. Each dungeon is a different puzzle that need to be solved in a more or less specific order. It didn't hold my interest since my expectations going into it were misaligned, but if you like puzzle games there seems to be a good amount of depth here.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Every dungeon is a boss, and you will feel awesome for beating it.  The metagame and each bout of play meld beautifully, as in that winning is fun on its own, the metagame is super motivating, and completing a metagame sidequest does not conflict with the fun of the level, which is to make your brain burst.  Endless race/class combinations, hours upon hours of content.EDIT:  This is still the most amazing roguelikelike game I've ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: My bad.Somehow believed this is RPG with some puzzle elements. Looked nice at beginning with building own kingdom and such.Sadly i was very wrong - it is ultimately quite hard puzzle game that played and look bit as RPG. Whole gameloop is about NOT fighting enemies, dungeoning and loot but to figure out perfect order of things like turn enemy to stone for chain of XP and bonuses gain. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the old Desktop Dungeons v0.2, so I thought I should try the new one.The concept of 10-minute roguelique is awesome, and with each unlocked class, the game makes me adapt my strategy to the new class.This version has some nice additions, such as the "puzzles", which are non-random tutorials and challenges.The art style has been redone, but I liked the clarity of the low-res version.The dungeons are more varied.I haven't seen any altars yet but I guess they might unlock later on.Some of the spells have been made more complex, unclear and weird. For example, the fireball spell now has 3 effects, even though the glyph tooltip only lists 2 of them. Burning enemies are supposed to receive extra damage when attacked, but strangely they also receive damage when I attack someone else.The spell descriptions and effects tooltips are sometimes misleading or unclear.The added music is pretty nice. There are various annoying bugs in the menu. For example, the "cloud save" button is greyed out, with no indication whatsoever on how to fix it, and the "login" button does nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very well thought out game if you like complex mechanics that require advance planning at every stage. The game play is nice and balanced, once you get the hang of it's unique mechanics for healing and mana regen. That said I like a dungeon crawl game where exploration is not a game mechanic, so while I like the game for my tastes is's not "fun" when idly killing time, which is the metric I am rating on. So this can be taken as a positive review of the game being that it's well done, with a negative recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: You start at level 1 in a one screen dungeon, and try to get strong enough to beat the lvl 10 boss.In the meantime, you will have to explore, get equipped, beat lower level foes to gain experience and get stronger.During the process, you will constantly juggle risk vs reward since every decision you take will probably burn some precious  ressource or some other. You will always run the risk of driving yourself into a corner.But since the dungeon is quiet short, any mistake will only set you back 10-20 minutes at most and you will itch to try again one more time.As you chain the  dungeons, you will be able to unlock new classes, races, loot, dungeons and options. Each of these expand the ways you might tackle the next dungeon, adding variety and more difficult decisions to the mix.I found the process very addictive as you always have the impression to improve in meaningful ways; and each run is short enough to fit in a coffeebreak.In short: very enjoyable game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a puzzle game. There's no role playing and no significant strategy involved.  Every level is a variation of the same puzzle. The dungeon consists of one tiled screen that's dark. Your character always start at level 1 and must beat a high level dungeon boss. The puzzle is how to level up your character, with limited resources, high enough to beat the boss. Sounds interesting, but there's only one way to do it: beat monsters with higher level than your character. You have a selection of spells, traits and tricks for this goal, and once you figure it out you just have to repeat it. I found the way this plays to be anti-intuitive and contrived.  It's not a terrible game but I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons draws inspiration from roguelikes, but is at its heart a giant math puzzle. In each match it is up to you to explore the dungeon carefully, attempting to defeat the strongest foes you can without dying because you get bonus xp for defeating monsters that are higher level than you. Each round starts you back at level 1 with your chosen race and class, and it is up to you to become strong enough to take on the boss of the dungeon without running out of health and dying first. It is a very addictive and fun game, and I completely finished the original version (a freeware game you can google up), unlocking every class and race. This version is a pretty massive update that adds a lot of new features, a new soundtrack by Danny B, the guy behind Super Meatboy's soundtrack, and a complete graphical overhaul.

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is a great game that fittingly belongs on the desktop although at first glance may look like it is better suited to playing it on a portable device. Dungeons generally take 10-20 minutes to complete (or fail) but the base mechanics are addicting enough that I did not find myself saying 'just one more', sessions ended only while glancing at the clock and being surprised enough to force myself to stop. This is a surprisingly deep experience for a somewhat simplified dungeon crawler. Not only are the layouts different each time you start a dungeon (even the same one multiple times) but there is quite a bit outside of these in building up your kingdom and unlocking classes and races. The dungeon mechanics themselves are for the most part pretty standard - move, attack, kill, level up, repeat. The twist here is that as you explore, newly discovered tiles refill your (and any damaged enemy) health and mana bars. The impact of this was lost on me at the lower levels, but as you progress you will find it is impossible to explore the map and plan all your moves ahead of time. There are some abilities that help mitigate this but for the most part, each step is a resource not to be wasted and a wrong turn can mean the difference between leveling up or running out of options seven levels later while fighting the boss.Here lies the first of my two main issues with the game. I have had dungeons where the first half of my exploration resulted in dead ends or creatures far above my level 1 hero you always start as. This can be frustrating as it means you lose out on health/mana regen later on when those tiles could have been useful. I readily acknowledge that this is very much part of the game and there is strategy here above what my compulsion for exploration allows, but it can be hard not to feel that such runs are pointless to pursue.My other issue with Desktop Dungeons has nothing to do with gameplay - the writing takes me completely out of the experience. The game world seems steeped in lore and interesting hero / creature design, yet all the dialogue is extremely casual and self-referential well beyond the tongue-in-cheek point. It's too bad, and is one of those situations where a flaw is almost made worse by the amount of potential it has. I would have preferred the tone to get more serious as I realized how deep the experience could be, and not the other way around. That may be personal opinion, but I really feel as if it is an area of missed opportunity in an otherwise enjoyable and lasting experience.Overall, I would highly recommend Desktop Dungeons to anyone looking for a game that satisfies in a way games like Binding of Isaac or even Spelunky does, where it doesn't matter if you play 5 or 50 games a session and can come back the next day and still find fresh gameplay waiting. The excellency of the procedural generation (which is greatly designed, no randomness here is used as a crutch) is exciting in its balance of interesting and clever levels, and even though the difficulty gets quite high early on you will most likely be able to find fun with it no matter your skill level.---Desktop Dungeons---+ Addicting base mechanics+ Deep experience tied to player skill progression- Some runs can be a letdown at the very start- Writing direction is not for me at allIt is my opinion that you should buy Desktop Dungeons anytime it is $12.50 or less!

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorites but I feel this a very tough game to rate. I cannot think of any other like it and it succeeds on so many levels that I am blown away by the amount of time and energy it must have taken to create this. That being said many of my friends would (and have) toss this aside very quickly. The best comparison I can think of for this game would be chess, crosswords, or suduko not because this game operates by the same level or rules but because of the amount of mental energy required to play well (or poorly but with maximum effort in my case).On a high note this game does an excellent job of rewarding progress. Even nearly 80 hours into the game I am still unlocking new aspects every couple hours. The high difficulty factor and this make every finished map lead to both a sigh of relief and quick inhale of anticipation as to what might be next. There are not too many titles you can find that can or will provide this.The game is a puzzle/roguelike/rpg with a steeeeep learning curve. It goes from fairly easy, to somewhat challenging to difficult to "okay quit smacking me in the balls" tough in a span of about 2 hours or playtime each at which point the challenge continues to escalate as you progress through each map after. I personally enjoy the challenge but I think this is a balancing issue that is likely to turn away alot of people before they really get into the game. This is a shame because of the amazing amount of possiblities and strategies you can and will need to master to get through it. I have to grudgengliny give it a slight knock for this.The only other major criticism I have is that the tutorial is a bit limited. In a game that gives you such progression the mechanics of many of the aspects are not clearly explained. There are puzzles that come with many of the unlocks that are obviously suppose to help out with this. Unfortunately they are pretty limited (and freakin hard as hell themselves) and do not provide you with much help. This can add on to the frustration level pretty damn quick.The graphics are obviously not the draw here but the cartoony and light-hearteness of the game provide a nice counterpoint to the toughness factor. All in all if you own or play mostly titles that contain the tags "board games, tcg, puzzles, strategy, tactical" there is a really good chance this is a gonna be one of your favorites. If your looking for something light-hearted and dislike high difficulty you are likely better off walking the other way.  Objectively I rate his high for orignality and length of content as well as awe-inspiring game design and detract slightly for the poorly explained mechanics and balancing issues.7/10bump this to 9/10 if your a fan of puzzles and high challenge...

_childDocuments_.review: Do not spend money on this. You can find vastly better stuff for free. It feels like an unpaid job to play it. Get a real game instead, for example Death Rally Classic and any of the Creeper games (Creeper World, Creeper Academy, etc.)Some games are fun and others sap fun out of you. This one saps the bajebus out of you. It also robs all the enjoyment of the power curve by off-setting any resource improvements you might gain. For example, once you get the blacksmith available, the enemies power will get increased so that you end up weaker than in the beginning if you do not take the upgrades. The change is that the enemies have higher levels stats out of nowhere.Most of your gameplay experience involves comparing numbers in a badly camouflaged spreadsheet. A newsflash: they pay people for doing stuff like this at work. And they pay you because it F-ing sucks.Do not let the cute graphics fool you - this is a number matrix game about MATH. Why? Because it is much easier to program a turn-based game where you merely change a couple numbers every now and then. It is a stretch to call it a game, as it is a static obstacle course with minor randomization added in.This kind of number-crunching was a passable in the 1980s and even back then people were quick to move on to more graphical and fun games. The reason games like this are still made is because they are easy and quick to make with modern game maker tools. To underline this point, the game was originally made with GameMaker, only to switch for Unity later.Oh and nice job bullying the League of Epic Heroes out of the market with legal threats. The gall of a devs making generic turn-based RPG to claim originality. The same dudes had no qualms taking the tileset made by the Spelunky dude. I would call that a double standard, though that would imply this game meets one. What a drag of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface this seems like it could be a somewhat simple and casual dungeon crawler roguelike, but upon a closer inspection this is actually a calculus puzzle roguelike presented in a dungeon.Each dungeon has a set number of enemies at various levels, and powerups scattered about. You are expected to navigate through the dungeon and kill the enemies that you come across before exploring further, since exploring dark tiles gives you back health and mana. Being tricky with the spells you collect is encouraged, as you will need to challenge enemies of a higher level regularly.Exploring to find all the powerups first will result in failure as there will be too few black tiles to use for recovery for later battles.Skipping enemies too often will result in failure - you are required to engage with enemies several levels over you in order to ration necessary recovery tiles.No matter what you do, sometimes the randomized dungeon layout, enemy placement, or powerup placement will just spell out your doom from the start.The game does offer some tutorials on how to use abilities to their utmost potential, however it is mostly unintuitive and reliant on a bit of luck when used in a live run.This game has the veneer of a somewhat casual experience, however the truth is anything but. It's far more methodical and calculating than the artwork or dialogue might lead you to believe. I can't say I enjoyed the experience. 4/10

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is a puzzle game that takes elements from rogue and condenses it to a single screen experience. You pick a class, buy some starting items and venture forth into a randomly generated dungeon. Your "hero" always starts at level 1 and you have to find a way to make the best use of experience boosts, glyphs, items and gold to beat the boss (or bosses) of the level. If you're successful you bring back treasures that will help improve your kingdom and allow you to discover new dungeons and monsters.The goal is to use your resources to beat higher level monsters and get the experience boost you need to level up high enough to strike the boss. Uncovered tiles regenerate you and your foes, so waste as little as possible. Keep weak monsters around to strategically level up mid-fight and gain a full heal. There are lots of strategies and once you master them you can tackle any dungeon with any class. The mechanics are very deep and the advanced dungeons can take you one or two hours to beat them. Some later dungeons also abandon the idea of a single screen map and will offer two or more screens to play with, or challenge you with shifting walls. There's even a minotaur that chases you.I've been playing the game since beta and there's still more content for me to uncover. The newly added daily challenges adds new motivation to keep playing the game and the absolutely fantastic soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky has been a steady part of my music playlist since release. If you like puzzles and you like strategical fights then this game is a must buy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent puzzle game.  It's really a puzzle game more than it is anything else.   I'm going to recommend this game with on big caveat attached.  With all its frills, and new graphics, this version isn't all that much better than the FREE version currently available online. Actually the free version is much more pure and streamlined version of this game.  The original is even better in some ways.  All of the extra stuff in the steam version of this are mostly just bloat.  All the "outside the dungeon" town building interface is really poor compared to the version slick a brilliant puzzle game that you are trying to access from the town.  Also it takes quite a while to unlock everything.  I have nearly 30 hours clocked and still have not unlocked all 9 basic classes.  Having to run 2-6 dungeons just to get the 2000 gold for an unlock seems grindy and is something the original free version lacks.  So what is improved over the free version?  The graphics are greatly enhanced.  The Deity system is better handled although they are a bit too powerful in the sense that using the deities is often key to conquering higher end maps.   The biggest upgrade is the amount of new diversity added to the maps.  There are just more scenarios and variations applied in each new challenge.  If you enjoyed the original desktop dungeons, this one takes what was there and adds to variety 100 fold.  With puzzles, challenges, interesting bosses, 2ndary rooms, and much more. So yeah its good stuff, but I feel it's a little odd that some of the simple purity of the original gets a bit bogged down in some unnecessary bloat in its steam version.  And they should patch in reduced town upgrade prices.

_childDocuments_.review: You start each dungeon/puzzle at level 1 and have to fight your way through monsters until you can fight toe to toe with the boss. Despite being "puzzle-ish" there are a lot of different ways to beat a specific dungeon, even if it does not seem like it the first time you play. Fighting a monster takes away health and mana, though you can replenish it by exploring. However, just make sure to consider in which direction you want to explore the dungeon, as the precious tiles run out faster than you think. There are also a lot of different items that you can unlock, which will help you to smack those monsters around. And to spice it up, you have also 9 gods to choose from. Each one will alter your play style, as they reward and punish(!) various actions. One god is easy to learn, but tough to master, but to use more than one and know when to worship which god will take time, but will give such a huge reward!In addition, there are some fixed dungeons included, which only allow for one single execution of steps to beat the challenge. They are very smartly designed and will teach you the mechanics of the game (if you are observant). Very well done!10/10 Definitely recommend

_childDocuments_.review: This game wants to be a difficult puzzler where you have to use your limited resources just right or you won't have enough health/mana/potions/faith/regeneration/equipment/spells/gold/shops/etc to survive a dungeon.  That would be fine in constructed levels, but when highly randomized, it's like trying to solve a Rubik's cube blindfolded.  Sure, SOME people CAN do that and LIKE doing that, the rest of us, not so much.The dungeons are also too long and involved for this sort of thing.  It's fine if you spend a few minutes, make a mistake, and then get nothing, or even net lose gold for your troubles, but if you spend tens of minutes on a dungeon and mismanage one thing, or worse, didn't mismanage anything tactically, but the game WANTED you to strategically tackle the run differently to maximize every last scrap of resources (attacking a big monster that you can't kill to weaken it, then when you're almost dead, killing a weak monster to level up and get a full heal, then going back and killing the big monster--which is exhausting, stupid, and "gamesy" to have to set up), or even worse, get into an unwinnable situation through sheer bad RNG. But worst of all is losing when the game actively DOESN'T TELL YOU what it wants, expects, or the limits it's set.  Two examples: puzzles unlock early in the game and award 300 gold.  I had about 400ish gold on hand and beat the puzzles.  Then my gold turned red for some reason--oh, NOW the game tells me I can only hold 500 gold and I have to spend some upgrading buildings or I'll lose the extra as soon as I enter a dungeon.  OK, I'll upgrade a building, but all buildings cost 1,000 to upgrade at this point in the game.  So I couldn't hold the extra gold, couldn;t spend it on anything, and the game just took it away, gee thanks.But what made me uninstall and leave a negative review was the Glowing Guardian God.  Suddenly, without really telling me what;s going on (I did read all the text it bothered to show), now I'm worshipping a god in the middle of a dungeon run.  He grants this power and that power by spending faith, OK.  Nowhere does it warn me not to drink potions, but apparantly, this god really hates it when you drink potions and it makes you lose faith points if you do that (but doesn't tell you that's why).  I worked all the way up to the boss, and in boss fights, you have to manage your potions just right to win.  I was about to win the fight, drank a potion to heal up and my god got so mad at me that he took away all of my equipment without warning.Can't defeat the boss now, so I retreated.  Normally you can sell off your gear at the end of a run for some gold, but since my god took everything away from me, I lost everything that I looted and everything that I paid for before the run as preperation equipment.  The run bankrupted me and I only had 21 gold left in my kingdom afterwards, not even enough to go on another run with full equipment.So here we are, rage quit, rage uninstall, rage review.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Desktop Dungeons since the alpha, signed up during the beta, happily redeemed my key on Steam and have put in countless hours. It's genuinely one of the best puzzle games ever made - it has a roguelike sheen and borrows heavily from Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (which is my roguelike of choice anyways) but it follows a certain iterative structure, and builds into something that requires a lot of math, resource management, and long-term thinking with short-term heuristics on trying to figure out the best choice when you don't have all of the information in front of you. It's genuinely good, more than well worth the price point, and I'd suggest it to anybody who asked and try to push it on a few people who didn't either.Don't go in expecting a formal RPG - it does get hard, fast, but it's much much more forgiving than it seems, and while the learning curve is steep, it pulls you right up along it. I would only refrain from recommending it if you're looking for not even a more casual experience, but just something that doesn't require you to do a weird amount of math on the fly. Otherwise, it's a game that could happily belong in everyone's library.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you love roguelikes? Do you like puzzle games? Then this game is totally for you. Desktop Dungeons combines both roguelike elements and the puzzle genre to create an immensely captivating and addictive game. As the game is heavily influenced by roguelikes, then you'll already know that the game will be extremely hard. You'll certainly crave that "... just one more dungeon" while you totally ignore that you should've be in bed several hours ago.Yes, the price might put some people off, but you'll certainly receive days (or even weeks) of challenging and fun puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: Rogue-Likes and Rouge-Like-Likes alike all tend to feel alike. Generally in these genres, you hack and slash your way to death with nothing left to really prove except for the knowledge that comes with drinking a suspicious looking potion and losing all your health to a single swig. You take these tips with a grain of salt as the variability to your death changes with each play-through...Although I use the term "play-through" lightly since you never actually get through some of the more hardcore rogue-likes without hours and hours of dedication to understanding the game's many quirks and traps. Desktop Dungeons feels like a solid blend of Rogue-Like and Puzzle with a welcome sense of progression as you earn gold and unlock new classes and races along the way. All of that mixed with the ability to spend 10-20 minutes on a single session is also entirely welcome. The puzzle-like aspect of the game is a great mix to the genre. Instead of spending your time focusing on surviving until your next death, you know exactly what you need to do: kill all of the enemies. The helpful levels that appear next to the enemy names allow you to expect what's coming whether its a victory or a disappointing failure. Rogue-Likes are always known for their randomized nature with their random levels and random encounters; Desktop Dungeons has these to an extent but when you're level 5 and you're about to swing your sword at a level 9, you know you're not making a sound decision. The screen also turns red when your next move is fatal, which helps quite a bit as well. The progression in the game also allows for a sense of accomplishment. No longer do you feel that sense of loss when you lose everything you worked so hard to get. Each "dungeon" is its own instance and if you know you're about to fail you can easily just retire and keep all your money (the items you acquire get sold for more money) which can then be spent on upgrading classes, races and even buying gear to aid you on the next quest you go on. Along with multiple locations, there's plenty of different quests and challenges you can attack. Each class has its own set of challenges that give you bonus money and there are also general challenges that give you more gold just by doing things like spending a certain amount of gold or piety during a quest. This game is certainly recommended if you enjoy the difficulty in Rogue-Likes but like to spend a casual amount of time slowly increasing your stats, or in this case, your kingdom.

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is the answer to a question virtually nobody has ever asked: "What if Minesweeper was a real game, and not just a tool for teaching people how to right-click?" Combining classic Rogue-like trappings gives the game real longevity, and character options and overarching progression do even more. If any of that sounds like your jam, Desktop Dungeons is easy to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee time rogue-lite strategy. 634 hours and I'm still playing it so that's value.You'll like it if you like strategy that often forces you to pivot effectively, simple math, play styles that change based on class, race, deities, item and skill availability, map layout, badges you want to earn, and boss/miniboss toughness.There are plenty of let's plays if you want to know if it's for you, but the gist of any session is:Pick a map or quest to tackle -> Pick a race (of 7) & class (of 20) or a monster class (of 5) -> pick your item loadout -> commence. In each dungeon there is a set number of various monsters from level 1 to 9. You spend your time leveling up off monsters and preparing for the level 10 boss (or bosses) by buying items, picking up glyphs, gold, and potions, and worshipping deities (while not pissing them off). There's also an Extreme Edition mod made by the community that is very fun to play and expands on the game a lot with tonnes of new maps, classes, items, and badges to earn.For roguelike buffs, this is not a roguelike. It's more of a roguelite. You can bring items out of a dungeon for later runs. Your character isn't preserved between runs but to say permadeath is really disingenuous.

_childDocuments_.review: I acutally wouldn't consider this game a roguelike. While it does have the trappings of one, such as leveling, equipment, classes, gods, etc. it plays more like a puzzle game. You enter a one-screen (sometimes with a basement) dungoen with one or more bosses hiding in it. Your objective is to kill all the bosses. However, you will have to level up your character enough in order to be able to stand a chance against the boss. You do this by defeating lesser enemies in a logical order, using your class and racial abilities. Enemies don't move, so you have plenty of freedom to think out your moves. Strangely enough, you gain HP and mana by exploring the dark areas of the screen, so you'll have to manage this resource carefully.Overall, this game fits the bill for those who like puzzles, but also enjoy random elements and roguelikes or rpgs. Don't expect an exploration-based experience, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview:Though Desktop Dungeons does have a high learning curve, it is still an addictive and well-designed puzzle roguelike that will keep you coming back for more to defeat its nastier challenges.  As you defeat dungeons and complete challenges, your kingdom will grow, unlocking more races, gods, classes, and items to choose from or find in the dungeon.  The story might not be the best, but the writing is hilarious and should easily keep you entertained, on top of the deep and interesting gameplay.Gameplay:Like I said, everything is a resource, including gold, level-ups (they fully heal you, in addition to giving extra stats), items you don't use, and even exploration!  This is the source of the puzzle nature of the game, as maximizing the utility of your resources to defeat higher-level monsters is essential for defeating the harder difficulties.  Every dungeon has one or more level 10 bosses, who must be defeated to win.  These bosses are appropriately epic, sporting significantly higher stats than the other dungeon inhabitants, so much of the challenge comes from getting to the point where you can take them on.Desktop Dungeons includes a large variety of dungeons and challenges of varying difficulties that will keep you coming back for more.  In true roguelike spirit, all dungeons are randomized each time you attempt them.  While the normal dungeons may just feature a set of monsters and a level 10 boss, the hard and vicious dungeons all have their own gameplay gimmicks which make them feel unique, like separate challenges.  In addition to the standard dungeons, there are also a large number of challenges and puzzles to complete to improve your skills and unlock items.  I can't say I enjoyed the puzzles as much as the challenges and dungeons, but the puzzles are completely optional.As you complete those dungeons, you will obtain gold which can be used to improve your kingdom, unlocking new classes, races, and preparations for dungeons.  These preparations can be used to aid future dungeon runs in certain strategic ways.  For example, you can guarantee that you start with a fireball, a useful preparation for the sorcerer.  By doing so, however, you give up the ability to increase your stats through a different preparation.  These preparations provide a good amount of strategy to a run through carefully planning which ones you will need to defeat a certain dungeon.  They also cost gold, which can be daunting for new players.  However, preparations are never actually required to clear a dungeon, and one preparation even massively increases the gold that you receive from clearing a dungeon successfully.Music:Desktop Dungeons has a pretty good thematic soundtrack by the same person who composed the soudtrack for Super Meat Boy.  There are over 20 tracks, many just to set a nice atmosphere for a given dungeon.  I personally still haven't gotten tired of the music, and I've played well over 100 hours of the game, another testament to how fun and addictive this game is!Graphics:The graphics have a nice, distinctive style, and are pretty good for a roguelike.  However, the gameplay is what makes Desktop Dungeons good, not the graphics.Conclusion:Desktop Dungeons is one of my favorite games, with nearly unlimited replayability and deep strategy.  Most of the negative reviews here focus on the difficult gameplay.  If you want a sense of about how difficult the normal-hard dungeons are here, check out the award-winning alpha version, which is available for free online.  Personally, I think that the difficulty is one of the best aspects of the game.  If you're like me, finally beating a difficult dungeon with a certain class or restriction, is an extremely rewarding experience.  But if you expect a path to beat the game without learning the strategy, you will be disappointed.  The game could be better at teaching you that strategy, but there are guides out there if you get stuck.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game for many many years now, courtesy of a dear friend of mine, on GOG and played it for a long, long time ever since it came out in 2013. It was my first exposure to indie games and the general innovative drive that isn't as constrained as big companies tend to be to get nods from big bad shareholders.So, intro aside, what is this, exactly?It's a pretty unique single screen (though with multiple floors) puzzle roguelike that requires understanding many underlying factors to win besides the usual HP and MP scores, from the best order to engage the enemies in (enemies are a limited resource that also needs to be managed) to which deities are present in that particular dungeon. Despite the apparent simplicity at face value, (from the graphics to combat), as with most things worth one's while, there is a very deep, satisfying rabbit hole to fall into.There are several classes to unlock and use, as well as races (or kin, if you will) to populate your fantasy kingdom with, again, with very interesting unique abilities and synergies to discover and even create - perhaps an unconventional combination will become your favorite!There are also spells you can use and items you can unlock to find in later dungeon runs and they significantly modify how a run goes. There's just a lot to discover and even 10 years since its launch (and with a wonderful remake fast approaching) there is still not (and likely never will be) a brain teaser as creative, challenging and satisfying as this one here.Even with the upcoming remake, this version remains well designed, playable and relevant, with a vibrant modding community behind it.A true indie gem that is well worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for many hours before being on Steam.If you've ever played a roguelike Role Playing Game(RPG) you'll know they are amazing time sinks.  Indeed, most RPGs are time sinks.  Desktop Dungeons takes the basics of RPGs and condenses them into one screen full of adventure.  These play out as puzzles as much as an RPG.  You can be done and dusted with a dungeon in only a few minutes, yet they are full of the usual RPG elements.  Potions, gold, shops, stat bonuses, gods, monsters and level ups.  Your goal in each fixed dungeon is to kill one or two level 10 boss monsters.Difficulty in Desktop Dungeons is one of the highlights.  Each map and element provides a serious challenge to get to the end result of killing the level 10 boss monster.  It is not at all uncommon to fail.  You have to balance exploration so much so that it can feel like minesweeper.  You have tough choices to make and the key to this being such a great game is that your choices actually matter.  That makes the dungeons memorable and fun.Another nice thing about Desktop Dungeons is the way it ties the dungeons together.  As you complete the basic dungeons you unlock lots more content.  Humour in game is also quite well done without being overbearing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty good game if you're interested in strategy that leans into the puzzles/sequencing side. It's a good game, but not a traditional roguelike so don't expect that. It doesn't really have a heavy RPG aspect where you have a character/roster that you can make lots of progression. The progression elements are very simplistic, almost mobile game like. The humor is excellent!I give it a 6/10, it's decent and well-made, but to me it's not a game that has a great deal of depth to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Because Steam has the unfortunate thumbs-up-or-thumbs-down system, I will give this the thumbs up.Starting out, this was enjoyable. It got better as things opened up: new maps, enemies, classes, races, etc. Areas were doable even if you weren't lucky, they just required more care and thought. But once you get to a certain point, it seems more about how lucky you can get. Bosses become ridiculously overpowered, and many enemies have deleterious effects should you dare attack them -- which you often need to do to progress. _childDocuments_.review: A mix of rouglike and puzzle game. As a ruler of  a kingdom you send adventurers on quests into different dungeons. Before each quest begins, you select a race and a class, which determine the way you must play to succeed. Dungeons are turn-based. You explore each dungeon, finding powerups, equipment, magic, shrines and of course monsters. Defeating monsters gives your hero experience, which lets you defeat more powerful enemies. Between quests you upgrade your kingdom, which adds new classes races and items to the roster and unlocks new challanges. "One more turn" syndrome is present and strong.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: More annoying than fun. As others have said, it's a hardcore puzzle game with little room for error on each level. You need to figure out the set piece of moves that will allow you to beat each level. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible bite-sized dungeoneering gameplay. A tight focus on simple exploration and combat with enough ticks and modifiers to proudly wear that "roguelite/roguelike" descriptor. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Finally picked up Desktop Dungeons after years of meaning to. The alpha version of this game got me through high school computer classes. Sorry I didn't give you my money until recently devs, but this game ♥♥♥♥♥. Buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Boardgamers, this one's for you! Have you ever gotten murdered on turn two in Dungeonquest? You have a level three monster at rank one in the dungeon in Thunderstone Advance and you draw four regulars and two torches and realize that going to the dungeon is folly and remaining in the Village means that big nasty is going to raid? Welcome to Desktop Dungeons!  It seems to me at least that the developers of this game were at least partly inspired by these two punishing but eminently fun boardgames. A few reviews here with 90 plus hours have rated it a thumbs down and mostly because of the random difficulty. But intrepid adventurers, these poor folk just don't have the wisdom to understand that a large part of the charm is retelling/rethinking about the hilarious ways you got your face punched.How can you NOT love a game in which you have to defend your fledgling kingdom's petting zoo! And let's face it, killing a banker is at least a metaphorical high. [Official disclaimer: I do not advocate the actual killing of non-pixel bankers].There are fun references to Lord of the Rings, Super Meat Boy [copyright infringement: likely as it states in the game], Monty Python, and who knows what else!If you are looking for a grimdark "serious" dungeon crawler then look elsewhere. But, if you love the feeling of overcoming the dreaded bankers, goats, and other nefarious creatures and can accept that most of the time you will get pwned and can laugh about it, get this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Hmph, only 17 minutes of playtime for Desktop Dungeons? As a transformer, I know that's plenty of time to form an opinion on this game. After all, I'm far smarter than any puny human.Let's talk about the gameplay. The concept of randomly generated dungeons is intriguing, and I appreciate the turn-based strategy mechanics. The retro-style graphics may seem outdated to some, but I find them charming in a nostalgic way. The game's soundtrack could use a bit more variety, but it's still enjoyable.Overall, I give Desktop Dungeons . It's a solid indie game that's worth checking out, especially for fans of classic dungeon crawlers. But let's be real, it's no Transformers: Devastation. That game was a masterpiece. .
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I remember being in awe of the game innovation. Your enemies are numbered between lvls 1-10. You start as a level 1 and have to fight them.Each one is worth xp, the higher the kill - the higher the xp.Weapons, spells and strategy are needed to eliminate them. Starts simple, develops complexity as you go.Your health and mana regenerate from exploring the darkness.You unlock new races, gods and classes with quests and gold.The game structure has solid early, mid and late game content.The difficulty ramps up as you go - the wikipage and forum have solid tips and guides.Graphics and movement are neat.Mouse and keyboard with shortcut keys.I have spent hundreds of hours playing Desktop Dungeons.It's definately worth playing!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game since alpha and the base gameplay was addictive enough back then. The puzzle and dungeon mechanics work together beautifully and I often find myself emotionally invested in working out a solution. You will not regret this purchase!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of a casual single-screen roguelike really appeals to me. I played an early, free version of this game that I really liked. But the paid version, while more polished, feels stretched too thin. It just feels like the game doesn't have enough content for its length, and needs to be shortened by 30-50%.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: The completely random level construction method leads to a complete loss of control over the difficulty of the game.Simply put, this game has a spell where after petrifying a small monster (without gaining experience), the next kill experience gains+50%. Monsters are classified into different levels, with lower level monsters having less experience and higher level monsters having more experience. So far, it is still normal.However, first of all, the experience card of this game is very dead. You must use this spell multiple times to be at the same level as the boss, otherwise you will find yourself two or even three levels lower than the boss. Secondly, this game upgrade has a huge improvement in attributes. That is to say, if you are lower than the boss level, you will not be able to fight at all. If you cannot fight, you will have to run away. This cost benefit is equal to 0, and you will also lose the money you spent on buying things.Then there is also a very treacherous situation. The initial map of this game is covered by the fog of war, and the character's health and mana are restored by exploring the map. If you don't hit the discovered monster, you will lose blood and mana. That means you can't plan your route at all, you can only rely on luck. Often, it's difficult to kill monsters in front of you, and a bunch of level 1 small monsters emerge from behind. Then, the remaining big monsters are generally one or two levels higher than you, and you can't beat them at all.Having said so much, even the game's spell drops are random. Sometimes (a lot) you don't even have the experienced spell in the entire map, and you don't even have to gamble on luck. This map will definitely not pass, even if you open the entire map at the beginning and plan to pass, because you don't have enough level, you just can't win.Sure enough, there is a reason why this game is free. Steam has never given me any fun games for free.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game many, many years ago when it was a simple grid based romp.Was really excited to see a bigger, campaign based version come out on steam .. that was .. until I played it ..All the fun is gone.It's buried in items and rules and this and that and uugh .. Which I hate to say 'cause I really wanted to love this game.

_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I think the number of hours I spent in this game says it all, but I can really recommend this game.It is unbelievable how much content this relatively simple looking game has to offer and how even after hundreds of hours you can still find new synergies to boost your gameplay even further. A definitive recommendation for everyone who enjoys puzzle games!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: It's an addictive little game... I intended to play for maybe 20 minutes, just to get my feet wet, and now it's hours later.Desktop Dungeons is a combination dungeon crawl + city building game. The storyline is simple, but you're not here for the storyline; you're here to kill beasties. And there are beasties aplenty available. Each dungeon is randomly generated, so there should be nearly infinite replayability even when you reach the upper echelons of the game.Definitely recommend this as a time killer.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is what you get when you distill the roguelike genre into a single screen puzzle and it is incredibly addictive. It's a great game to play in a 10 minute break and thanks to the village based meta-game aspects you are always working towards unlocking something new that adds further variety to the already copious amount of content.As an added bonus you can link your steam version of the game to their servers and even play in a browser and pick up exactly where you left off and vice versa.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended!  This is a great bite-sized puzzler with an rpg/roguelike theme.  It is math and planning intensive, especially as you dig deeper in the game.  For me, a single round can take anywhere from 10 minutes to an hour depending on the challenge I'm tackling.  This game is very polished and held my attention again and again throughout its Beta and now in release, even in a Steam library of hundreds of games.  I always feel like I can get through one more level, earn one more item, or unlock one more badge with another round.  It has the best addictive game qualities combined with the need for a serious strategy and strong tactics to be successful.  Again, if this description sounds even vaguely appealing to you, I would give it a try!  You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Boy-oh-boy, this game will kick your butt.Now, that isn't necessarily a bad thing. Desktop Dungeons is a difficult game, despite its casual exterior, but it is also incredibly addicting. You will want to come back and give that dungeon that massacred you another shot, and doing so is very easy (as soon as you've gotten past the slightly-too-long tutorial section). Essentially, you pick your race, type and starting equipment, and then off you go. There is a lot of hidden depth in this game and it can easily suck up hours of your time. The price is right for the amount of content available, and I can heartily recommend Desktop Dungeons. Just be prepared to die. Lots and lots and lots.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who went into Desktop Dungeons never knowing what Rogue-like game ever played like, I was a little worried at that it wouldn't be my sort of game. After just on around 40 hours of game time now, I can say that this game is incredibly addictive and fun thanks to its smart progression, incredibly polished systems and charming art/music combo. It's described as a game you can play during coffee breaks, but I'm personally taking around 40mins to 1 hour to finish a dungeon properly as it can sometimes take some brain-raking and planning to overcome the obstacles in front of you. What does work really well for quick burst though are devilishly challenging puzzle challenges. These double as advanced tutorials and are almost a must for anyone wanting to really know what the game may expect of you.All in all, a really challenging but incredibly rewarding experience so far. Nothing better than feeling stuck on a dungeon having a solution swirl itself into fruition, leading to that immensely satisfying "aha!" moment. My favortite part for sure.Highly recommended! Great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: The game is annoying and not as "deep" as it wants you to believe. Worst thing of all though is how you can just be doomed by a certain class pick and have no realistic way to complete the run because the random boss counters the class you picked.Also they absolutely ruined the game by tying the puzzle challenges to progression. The old version where you could just progress by doing dungeons was much better. The new kingdom stuff is terrible. The gold management, banking limits, weird overworld dungeon progression, tons of random messages you have to click multiple times to get rid of, kingdom item management... none of it is wanted. Should have just focused on the core game and not all the kingdom nonsense.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: A simple little entertaining game.  It doesn't quite reach addictive status, but it's well worth the couple bucks it costs to play.  The simple gameplay makes it fast and fun while the random dungeons allow repetitive gaming enjoyable.  I love the style of graphics: cartoony and simple.  Throughout the game are little quests and achievements that actually add to the game.  The problem is some of the content is useless.  Most notably are the number of gods that have more negatives than positives when selecting them as your chosen deity.  Players do not have to chose a deity, but it doesn't make sense to have them in the game if they aren't going to be chosen.  Despite this minor annoyance, it's a great game to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great mix of roguelike and simple math-puzzler. The gameplay is simple and quick, with just enough strategy and randomness to really evoke that "just one more turn!" feel. Though the "grind" to unlock new content and build up gold can sometimes feel like a bit of a chore after a while, I nonetheless got maaaaany hours of fun out of this before it started to wear on me. There's enough variety with puzzle modes, challenges, and difficulties so that there's almost always something to strive for. The gameplay is pretty basic—check out the free alpha on the dev's website if you want just a sample—but the full version adds puzzle modes, achievements, an upgradeable town, and other features to make it a worthwhile purchase (especially if you can grab it on sale!).

As more is unlocked to help, more is unlocked to hinder.  I've followed this game since it was in it's Alpha stage and am happy to state that the finished product is more than just a prettier version.  It possesses more depth and challenge than the original.  I will be sure to unleash the updated addiction upon my friends who fell prey to it in it's Alpha form.As far as gameplay goes, it is a turn based dungeon crawl in which, for the most part, you are the only character that moves.  It utilizes multiple character classes and races each with their own perks and disadvantages.

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeon is a unique blend of casual puzzler, rogue-like dungeon crawler, and turn-based strategy game. _childDocuments_.review: This is quite possibly one of my favorite puzzle games of all time.   At first it seems rather simple - your goal is to take a level one character and find a way to kill the level 10 boss at the end of the map.  The challenge comes in how you do it - the amount of XP and healing items are limited, so every step counts.As you progress through the quests, (which are nothing more than fixed starting criteria) you'll unlock new items, characters, classes, and gods to help (or hurt) your progress through each map.If you're looking for a well-paced evolving challenge, I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: A challenging, but likable and quite complex rogue-like dungeon crawler with village building and quick missions well suited for coffee break activity.At first the dungeon quests seem simple enough, but after the tutorials they reveal their dastardly nature. You can't just go about killing anyone you see in any order or you'll soon find out you'll be totally outmatched by the dungeon boss. You must plan your advance and maximize your xp in a chess-like manner to even have a chance of winning. Frustrating at first, very rewarding when you get the handle of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a roguelike. It's a clever puzzle game disguised as an RPG. While it has potential, it falls short in that single mistakes, or just a badly placed bad guy on a random map level can cause you to lose the whole map, regardless of what else you do. The Good   - This is a truly hard game. If you like hard puzzles, this gives it in spades.  - The artwork and voice work is nice.  The Bad  - This game is frustrating when you lose making no mistakes. That's fine in real life a game shouldn't have unwinnable situations unless it's the Kobayashi Maru.   - Despite having multiple characters, playing gets grindy really quickly. You either get a good random map or a bad one.   - You lose your character and money spent each round. You level up by buying houses which allow you to buy add-ons.   - All these taken together give the game a pay to win type of feel like many casual games, but isn't one. I wanted to like this game, but after playing I found myself both bored and frustrated. For some people this is going to be a good game, for those looking for a rogue-like, dungeon crawl, this is not that.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

Solving something always rewards. Many progression aspects for further gameplay.+ Mechanics: Everything works as it is meant to be. Didnt encounter any bugs. Puzzle system is superb!Cons:- Sometimes a randomly generated dungeon might be too hard or impossible to solve. (Even tho' you can exit the dungeon forehand and carry your earnings, even losing is rewarding.)- Even the game is cool and all, i find its price a little bit much.If you want a good puzzle game (with rpg-roguelike spice on it), this is the game for you. Dont miss this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best roguelike game I've ever played. It's incredibly tightly balanced and strategic, leading to it often feeling very puzzle-like.A single game only take 10-15 minutes, and after every one I want to jump back in and play another. You're constantly unlocking new races, classes, dungeons, and items, which leads to TONS of replayability and variety.On top of that are tons of incredibly interesting mechanics - expolring Fog of War is how you regain health/mana, making it a critical resource, and how you manage your 6 inventory slots is crucial.Anyone who even remotely likes roguelikes should get this game - it's absolutely incredible.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potentially to really be amazing.  I WANT it to be amazing.  The fundamental flaw is that it is simply too difficult for the casual (and in my instance, hardcore) gamer and you often waste time trying to beat a level that is straight up unbeatable.  Thanks to random generations, you can find you have shot yourself in the foot many turns ago when approaching the boss and there is nothing you can do but quit for a measely 25g or so trying to climb your way to the next 1000g upgrade.  I do understand it is a roguelike and the purpose is to die often but the agony of defeat and the time you just wasted zaps the fun right out of the game.  Unless you really want a difficult challenge and are ok with losing because you made a mistake 15 minutes ago on a 20 minute level, then by all means pick this up.  If you want to constantly be calculating moderate to heavy math every turn as if you are playing sudoku and chess simultaenously, pick this up.  If you want to relax and have fun, move on to something else.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons: An RPG/Strategy hybrid that's actually a puzzle game in disguise. The game has an unforgiving learning curve and doesn't get much easier as the game progresses, but each level is oh so satisfying to beat. There are lots of hours of gameplay from a deceptively simple title. Personally I love the extremely lightweight game design and how it uses simple concepts to make exceedingly challenging scenarios.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: A challenging dungeon-crawler roguelike that refuses to hold your hand. Action economy is key, and I've had a few moments where I should have done more math & thinking. Although I'm only a few hours in it feels like there's a lot of depth to the content in this game. If you like roguelikes with a VERY steep knowledge curve you'll enjoy this one. It probably improves from the "desktop dungeon rewind" reskin, as the visuals feel a bit dated but that wasn't an issue for me. The reason I'm giving up on this game for now is that it's just too punishing and would be much more enjoyable to me with lower difficulty options.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons features a highly addictive gameplay loop that revolves around quick dungeon crawls and strategic decision-making. Each session is short yet challenging, encouraging players to experiment with different character classes and tactics to overcome obstacles and defeat enemies. 🎮🔥 The game's retro pixel art style adds charm and nostalgia, reminiscent of classic roguelike titles. The colorful and detailed pixel art graphics create a visually appealing experience that pays homage to the genre's roots while incorporating modern gameplay elements. 🖼️🎮  While randomness is a core aspect of roguelike games, Desktop Dungeons' reliance on procedural generation can sometimes lead to frustrating or unfair situations. Players may encounter unwinnable scenarios or feel hindered by luck-based elements, impacting their enjoyment of the game. 🎲😕 Despite its accessible presentation, Desktop Dungeons has a steep learning curve that may deter some players, especially those new to the roguelike genre. Understanding the game's mechanics, character abilities, and optimal strategies requires time and patience, potentially alienating casual gamers. 📈🤔  While the game offers a variety of character classes and gameplay mechanics, the environments themselves can feel repetitive over time. Players may find themselves exploring similar dungeon layouts and encountering familiar obstacles, leading to a sense of monotony in prolonged play sessions. 🏰🔄 Desktop Dungeons lacks a robust sound design, with repetitive or generic sound effects that fail to enhance the game's atmosphere. While not a critical flaw, the absence of immersive audio elements detracts from the overall experience and leaves the game feeling somewhat lacking in auditory depth. 🔇🎶  Desktop Dungeons offers a compelling blend of addictive gameplay and retro aesthetics, making it a must-play for fans of the roguelike genre. While its randomness and learning curve may pose challenges, the game's strategic depth and charming presentation make it a rewarding experience for those willing to delve into its dungeons.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic roguelike. Brutal and unforgiving, but incredibly rewarding and engaging to learn and play. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I had already received my money's worth before I even started playing this game. Desktop Dungeons, made by the studio QCF Design, originally came about as a freeware "alpha" title, full of challenges and surprises, and that version of the game is still available for download today. I played the alpha for countless hours, so I was in their debt and did not hesitate to make the purchase.Rebuilt from the ground up, Desktop Dungeons now features more content than the most tenacious goblin could ever hope to shake a stick at. The developers would like you to believe this is a "quick play" sort of game, but make no mistake, it's going to snatch the afternoon out of your hands and devour it like a ravenous dog. The intense challenge of the dungeons demands your complete attention if you are to succeed. And when you do, hundreds of other dungeons await their turn, eager to throw another horde of savage beasts at your hapless wizard's forehead.The presentation of it is astonishing. The dialogue is superbly written, and the characters all have their own portraits, including - and this is the best part - every possible race and class and gender combination that your character can have. That makes at least 200 different portraits for your player character alone. It is clear that QCF went to great lengths to ensure their brainchild would hold up to the scrutiny of video game critics.I suppose you could find some fault in the game's storyline, but it really doesn't beat you over the head with it. It's only there to move the game along, and works just fine for that purpose. If you like puzzles, or role-playing games, or unique blends of the two, I would highly recommend that you take a look at Desktop Dungeons.

_childDocuments_.review: A rougelike-like game made by developers with a firm grasp of both geek culture and gameplay mechanisms. It provides a constant stream of challenges lasting dozens of hours, and it is fun with a capital H. It includes pop culture references about everything from Evil Dead to Office Space, menacing bankers, and nightmare fueling goats. Also, just like in reality, having a spoon at the right moment might save your life.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Nice puzzle game, in dungeon crawler RPG form. You start each dungeon at level 1, and the goal is to power up enough to kill the boss. But you have limited resources. You only heal by exploring unexplored tiles or leveling up (or chugging potions), and you only level up by killing things (which usually depletes health and/or mana). And monsters and items don't respawn or anything like that. So you have to be smart about how you go about killing things, and in what order, and so on.You can also unlock new classes and starter items and such to take into the various dungeons, and there are special challenge dungeons, and some tightly calibrated puzzle levels. It's pretty engaging overall. Made me late to class because I lost track of time.Also the music in the dungeons is pretty great. And the tutorial system is extremely well done. It throws you right into a dungeon that's designed to teach you how to play as you go, without any explicit instructions. And then once you complete it (or, I bet, if you die), it gives you the option to continue on to the rest of the game or to go into some actual hand-holding tutorial levels with explicit instruction.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: This review is mostly for people unfamiliar with Desktop Dungeons. If you played the free alpha, then you already know whether you like the game; this new version features many improvements, but it's still the same type of gameplay.Anyway, the second video (with the gnome wizard runthrough) does a decent job of showcasing game mechanics. Your goal is to explore a randomly-generated dungeon and ultimately to defeat a high-level boss monster. To beat the boss, you'll need to have leveled efficiently. This (usually) includes killing the highest-level monster that you can at any given time, since you get bonus XP for killing a monster whose level is higher than your own. That's pretty much the core of what makes Desktop Dungeons interesting: you're always trying to beat a tougher monster. The way you do this varies tremendously; there's a long list of things that can help or hurt you, and you have to deal with whichever ones happen to be in the dungeon you're exploring. It's this variation that keeps the game interesting hours later.Bottom line: I don't often write reviews. I like Desktop Dungeons enough that I felt I should take the time. I highly recommend this game.
