_childDocuments_.review: This game is a big fail for me, for a simple reason: success or failure is based on luck at more than 90%. The "strategy" to apply is globally pretty basic and depends on your calculus skill: mine is kinda slow but infallible so there's no way I can die (except on a few Boss fights where escape is not possible), but the level drags for too long.And if you fail at calculus, the game tells you if the next strike will kill you, so you can't die anyway.So the main issue is that you meet enemies randomly but you can kill only enemies of your level (or 1 above, sometimes), and to heal you have to explore new squares. This means that if you meet only too high-level enemies (and not fight them because you cannot win) before finding the low-level ones, you're going to not have enough health regeneration left to beat the level. And there's nothing you can do to avoid that.There's 1 class (out of ~20), the fighter, that can see where the unrevealed enemies of his level and below are. With it, the game makes sense as you can plan your exploration accordingly to maximize your healing. But with other classes, it's just a flip of the coin, with a lot of calculus in the middle: not exactly fun.I've read the FAQ for newcomers which states the UI should show how many strikes are needed to kill each enemy. It's actually not there, and it's a pity because it'd have removed a lot of tedious work on our side.Moreover, finding the God altar early or late in the run alters a lot the difficulty, which increases even more the luck factor.Except that, the game is well made but there's basically no exploration nor progression in the dungeons as they are only 1 big square taking only one whole screen with no sensible way to advance: there's no room, door, or even corridors, or anything that looks like a classic dungeon crawler; it's just random walls here and there.I got some fun out of it for a few hours and got the game for free, so I can't complain too much, but I really cannot recommend it.- many classes with many different abilities and quirks- If you know how to calculate, then it's almost 100% luck-based (except with the Fighter class)- If you don't know how to calculate, this game must feel very strange- If you're not fast to calculate, a run is closer to 30 minutes than 10, which is way too long- Dungeons are randomized but they all look the same anyway so it doesn't bring much gameplay-wise- The game description states that it's a roguelike and there are many ways to die, but actually, there's no character to lose (so no permadeath) and it's almost impossible to die as we can escape at almost any time (except against the Bosses sometimes, but you can calculate if you're going to win or not before engaging them)- A lot of bonuses bring absolutely nothing: for example, you get +10% base attack, but often even getting 3 or 4 times this bonus won't change the number of attacks you need to kill the enemies; so the extra damage is useless most of the time.

_childDocuments_.review: While ostensibly a roguelike RPG, each dungeon is basically one or two levels, so it's ideal for short gaming sessions. The main thing that makes this one interesting is that combat is basically deterministic; you can predict the outcome of each fight pretty accurately, you don't have to worry about getting screwed by the RNG at a critical point. The thing is, this may not sound like a big difference, but  it completely changes the flavor of the game. Instead of an RPG, it ends up being more of a puzzle game, where the objective is to figure out how to maximize XP gained and minimize the waste of health and mana, by deciding where  to go and what to fight next. Adds a sort of minesweeper aspect to the roguelike gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence about whether to leave a negative review, or just leave it review-less.  While Desktop Dungeons is definitely a bad game with redeeming qualities of meh-ness, it isn't a terrible game, and is a far cry away from being the worst game out there.The best part about the game (for me) is it's insane difficulty.  It's not so much an uphill challenge, as an actual balls to the wind, sheer drop, roof climb, which I'm always a huge fan of.  Now that could be a bit of a turn off for those who frustrate easily, and it's worth mentioning that there's an achievement for spending a 100 hours on failed dungeon runs,The worst part about the game is the insane repetitiveness, oh sweet lord the repetitiveness.  The game has a lot of surface variety with the races and classes, but is almost completely lacking in depth.  The Developers appear to have been somewhat partially aware of this fact, and added some text humour into the dungeons.  Sadly that wellspring of meta in-jokes dries up all too quickly, leaving a long slog of samey sameness to dredge through.Since you restart every dungeon with a level 1 newbie, the challenge aspect is ever present which is great until things start to feel boring and repetitive, then that challenge aspect starts working against itself, drawing out the mucky, sludgy, absolute drudgery of the repetitiveness.Game mechanics are simple and straightforward, if a bit on the shallow side.  There are spells and abilities (called glyphs) and deity boons that initially present some interesting synergies and exchanges with class selection to spice up tactical play.  However there are far too few glyphs or boons to do anything complicated, or truly synergistic with, and this severe lack of depth only exasperates the repetitiveness problem.Lately, I've been going through a lot of my older games, and crushing through all their achievements to raise my perfect games score,  I'm not a particularly huge completionist, but the number of unfinished games on my account has been starting to get me down a little bit.  Like an assembly of unpainted Warhammer 40,000 miniatures standing regimentally upon the shelf, slowly gathering dust, faintly mocking, and silently asking: When?Truth be told, I didn't expect Desktop Dungeons to take 25 hours to complete in it's entirety, or rather semi-complete.  There is still that 100 hour achievement (mentioned in the second paragraph) and one hidden achievement that was unashamedly included in the base game, but is locked behind a DLC paywall.  There are a lot of really scummy Developers who do this, typically big Publisher Developers, which is why it's so jarring to see a small indie company doing it.  Especially considering the good humour in the game leads one to believe the Developers might be decent folk.  Alas, it seems that Developer greed truly knows no bounds.Regardless, I'm very glad to be putting this game far behind me, 25 hours was 20 hours too long for this level of repetitiveness.  You'll likely see about 100 hours of "gameplay" tagged on to this game after this review, which "spoiler alert" will be from me running the game in the background to get the 100 hour "Masochist" achievement, and most definitely not because I had a change of heart about the game.  I did wishlist the Goatperson DLC which I'll probably get if I can grab it for £0.50 or less, in the meanwhile I'll consign this game to steadily growing list of games that require DLC to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hard. I'll say it again for the people in the back, THIS GAME IS *HARD*.If you like games that have a hint button, or a little sparkle after 10 seconds to point you in the right direction...This is NOT that game.This is FUN but challenging and brutal roguelike/roguelite. This game will give you some cheeky text, some cryptic hints, and a very very quick tutorial. But it does NONE of these things while holding your hand and telling you it will be alright. You will gain things from and between dungeon runs that carry over and make the next run just a teeny (teeny tiny) bit more doable. For a game from 2011, it reminds me of some great Popcap games, like the original PvZ, while having much more complex depth and endless puzzles. People saying it's not really a dungeon crawler, it's just a puzzle game hiding... This is a true-blue roguelike, not some quirky spin on the genre. It's turn-based tactics and every dungeon is randomly spawned so you never know what you're going to get to aid you. Or murder you. Not every dungeon can be beat *with what you have right now in this run*, and that's the random nature of it. Not every spell or item spawns in every run. It would have greatly benefited from a combat log, it's absence is very strange for a roguelike, but alas, it doesn't have it, so sometimes you're left staring at an abruptly-ended run wondering how that monster just killed you when you thought you were perfectly healthy, and there's no good way to figure out why except to think real hard before clicking out. Actually one of the nicest gifts from the devs is that the monsters don't move around. Everyone would lose a lot more runs if these monsters chased you down, too.For some perspective, I play a lot of roguelikes, I think I'm decent at puzzles. After 50 hours, I've only unlocked 8 out of 16 classes, 6 out of 7 races, and a fraction of the building upgrades. Every class and race has it's own mechanics, some are familiar and intuitive, others are tricky and it's only after a few runs and the right glyph (spell) on the board that you realize how *good* they are. Sometimes you find random rooms in a dungeon and these are definitely puzzles, and you may not figure it out this time. At least one of your attempts to figure it out might kill you. Puzzles inside puzzles.There are lots of mechanics at play. There are lots of tricky, clever ways to combine tactics. Over a few losses you will learn them. Over many you might someday master them. Either way, you will die a lot. And it will feel really good when you win. If you really like roguelikes, original genre/style roguelikes, this is one of the best I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: Written after only 3 hours of playSince I'm giving this a positive review I want to bring up cons before pros, of which I only really have one.This is more of a puzzle game than a rougelite, the problem with that is its unbalanced, even on regular difficulties - if you don't already know the advanced player strategies, and get bad RnG you easily end up with maps that aren't winnable unless you look up the wiki and invest time learning them.Generally speaking I'm fine with this, the exception with this game being because there's not enough information until you're knee-deep into things. When I looked up advanced strategies I noticed this saying frequently: if you see X or don't see Y then just restart. This means every game you have to not only tread very carefully and make your choices consciously - you also aren't guaranteed for a win with near-perfect execution of advanced strats.The tutorial is very misleading because of this difficulty, the tutorial holds your hand and walks you through the basics before switching entirely into the "teach without teaching" type of tutorial - which I like better but its jarring and the game seems to suddenly spike because of that.__That being said, I like enough of the pros to keep coming back to this, its challenging and offers a simple twist on typical rougelites that make you think about taking on fights very differently from just "locate and kill weak enemies" - no, you HAVE to get clever and work up a way to defeat the strongest enemy. Desktop Dungeons doesn't rely on novelty as much as most rougelites do, the main things to look forward to are simple applications of concepts you've already seen before -in the form of new classes, altars, and items - and now they're unlocked for you.The graphics aren't anything special, but it does have a style to it and it works well here.The music is forgettable, I'm already tempted to mute it entirely and listen to something else but I'd like to see if they use better music further into the game, we'll see.The puzzle system I actually like, they're designed to make you question why one strategy didn't work and another one did, this is what I was referring to in the cons about "teach without teaching" and these puzzles are clever ways to teach players the advanced mechanics.There is no terrain, not really anyways, everything is either a wall or is empty space to be filled by you, an item, an enemy, etc. They don't get messy with it .Enemies spike in power faster than you, level one enemies are fine while you're level one, but don't get me started on level 9, just getting to them let alone the fight is usually the best puzzle it offers.The spells are neat, they always look simple and they always do what they're instructed to - nothing is really beyond the grasp of the player as far as I can tell.____There's a new mechanic I just started crossing called altars, or gods/worship. Struggling to figure this mechanic out at the moment and unlike the previous puzzles the hints seem cryptic, I'm left feeling as though there's info I'm skipping or a strat that I haven't figured out or found yet, because I've been able to solve everything else without the guides up until now.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This is not really a dungeon-crawler... it's an RPG MATHS PUZZLE GAMEI realised the following things when I started unlocking their 'puzzles' which are basically advanced tutorials that don't do any hand holding.Everyone keeps going on about how awesome this game is, I like it too, but it's not what' you would normally expect froma  dungeon crawler, please let me explain.... forewarned is forearmed....1st, This is not really a dungeon-crawler... it's a PUZZLE GAME It uses a lot of maths type puzzles - you need to figure out how many minions to kill so that you can level up, and how to do it efficiently... killing higher level baddies gains you an exp bonus, but you need to do it as much as possible so you don't lose XP from minions that are now "lower"... you need to snowball your XP. Levelling up gives you 100%health and mana, and you have to exploit this all game so that you don't use too many potions.... you'll need them for the boss in the level.2nd, because it's only 10 minutes, things have to be simplified. You move around on a checkerboard style tabletop. revealing a tile (standing next to it = gaining visibility of the next tile) will restore some health and mana.3rd, this is not a 10 minute game. You can play a dungeon in 10 minutes, sure, so you can play in 10 minute sessions, this can be a positive... but "just one more, it's only 10 minutes" will quickly translate into hours of game play.4th This is a Rogue LITE - it does have a progression system where you can unlock new classes, abilities, etc between runs, in a similar way to Rogue Legacy. [A true rogue-like features permadeath where you lose everything and start again at level 1.]For those that like this game, it's addictive. Look at people's play times, the ones that have reviewed this. there are some who have 15-30h, then there are those with 80-120 hours, and the odd one over 200h - that's about the point where you beat the game, from my understanding / reading on the wiki.Do I recommend this game? That's such a hard one. Yes, If you know what you're getting into when you buy it, but the Store description is deceptive, and doesn't really explain just how this game works, and I was dissapointed about that, I wanted more 'hack n slash', and less 'calculating the next 7 steps to level up without using that mana pot' So for me, Although the game itself seems solid, I do like it, and I will play it some more, but I already know I won't clock it if it requires 200h it's a No.

_childDocuments_.review: SHORT VERSION: Do you like highly-difficult thought-based games? If so, get this game.LONG VERSION: Despite the developer's claim that "reviewers have trouble with genres", the core genre is simple: At heart, Desktop Dungeons is a strategy game. Success requires careful management of limitted resources. There are plenty of RPG elements in the game, but RPGs are typically centered more on their story, which, lets face it, isn't exactly this game's strong point.Each dungeon has a simple goal: Defeat the boss(es). This is, of course, easier said than done.As mentioned, fulfilling that goal will require very careful management of your resources. Obvious resources are health and mana, but there's also item slots (you can only carry so much stuff), blankspace (exploring unexplored parts of the dungeon regenerates health and mana, but re-exploring already explored parts does not), conversion points (turn items into something else), levels and experience (levelling up fully restores health and mana, which is highly abusable), gold (for buying stuff!), and piety (too complex to explain here). In addition, your class (as well as many other factors) helps define just how efficiently you can use these resources. For example, wizards use less mana for the same bang, monks regen double health from blankspace, and fighters gain experience much faster. Mastery of the game will come from a thorough knowledge of its mechanics, intelligent use of resources, and at times, a bit of luck.It's worth mentioning that this game is HARD. The learning curve is very steep. While you are guided through the basics via tutorial, the rest of the mechanics will need to be figured out on your own. Do not expect to win every time. (However, also notably, this difficulty rarely stems from randomness issues; a highly skilled player should lose in only the worst random situations)This game is also humorous. In fact, it's rarely NOT humorous.

_childDocuments_.review: It's so close to being good. But the developers don't seem to understand what direction they should take their game, leading to it suffering from a bit of an identity crisis and feeling rough around the edges.- The Gods system. An otherwise simple and easy to understand game is ruined by the cluster♥♥♥♥ of gods. There are like 6 of them, each with ~10 different rules about what they punish, what they reward, and by how much. The worst part is that none of this crap is documented in-game, which alone turns Desktop Dungeons into one of those abominations that requires a wiki tab constantly open by the side. Developers also never even attempted to make the gods fair and balanced (not that I believe this is remotely possible), leading to the player being punished for touching the Pactmaker altar either too early or too late (only one of the many, many examples of the broken mess of a system).- Items carried out of a dungeon don't persist between games. There is just no reason to forget about the backpack items. This is sloppy development.- Betting on the boss is a horrible mechanic and has no place in the game. Yes, I know 5 gold is nothing. Yes, I know that the +150 is almost guaranteed. Yes, I know it's a no-brainer. It is fundamentally a bad mechanic. Have the dungeon be a one-off endeavor, with no risk of losing the 5 gold (or any gold) and no "betting". Have a dungeon run be only an upside for the player. Then the game will more closely resemble the "coffee break" type you advertise.- The meme quest dungeons are horribly unfun and horribly undocumented. Yet another case where the player has to have the wiki open on the side.- Other random "gotchas" such as a second boss popping up when the first dies and similar surprises. Undocumented things that punish the player for not having the wiki open beforehand.Stop trying to trick the player. Focus on depth of gameplay, rather than adding more crap like the gods and new classes and whatnot. Make the game easy to learn and hard to master.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say? I really loved the style of artwork portrayed in this game. This game initally starts off very addicted and emerssive. But that only lasted for an extremely short amount of time, leaving me unfulfilled and extremely unsatisfied with my purchase. It's not the gameplay or the game mechanics fault this time as to why it got old fast. This time the culprit was the difficulty. After the inital first few dungeons and extreme enjoyment, the game throws you in a hell hole of a metaphoric toxic goo and pretty much tells you to learn how to swim through it without dying. The tutorials they "offer" (using the word "offer" very loosely) are not very great tutorials. Instead, to them, the tutorials are basicly just slimmed down dungeons with specific situations with only one SPECIFIC way out to complete with no instructions whatsoever. This makes it impossible to progress further into the game, which stunts the enjoyment to a grinding halt. This COULD HAVE been forgiven if they decided to put a difficulty mode choice option somewhere in the game but that exists just as much as their tutorial instructions do. I would have never paid 15 dollars for this game, had I known that the replay value (do to difficulty) was shorter than a first round knockout match between Mike Tyson and some random crackhead midget. This game is worth maybe about 2 dollars at this point. In my opinion, if the developers were to atleast put in a difficulty option, the gameplay value and price value would rise tremendously. And that's just putting a band-aid on a large cut that needs surgery. That wouldn't REALLY solve the problem here. I DO love a challenge. But I would like to be given a competent tutorial so that I can actually enjoy the game as it was intended to be, which is "difficult", NOT impossible.This part here is specifically to the developers:You have a game with a mass amount of potential but you guys need to put more effort into this game. It's not just about making it more aesthetically pleasing from your free game version. You need to step up to the plate and make this game more user friendly. We need a way better tutorial system because the tutorial system in it now is horrible. And I'm putting it as nicely as I can without allowing my affability make me cringe too much.In conclusion:I only hope that I can enjoy this game and be able to recommend it in the future. I really do.

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is a rogue-like miniature RPG unlike anything else that could fit that description.  The game advertises that it operates primarily in 10-15 minute instances, which is appropriate, but not necessarily accurate, as the serious player will quickly discover that you will be well rewarded in later levels by careful consideration and chess-like strategizing.  The aim in each dungeon instance is to clear out the dungeon boss by leveling up, acquiring items, and making use of every possible resource at your disposal (including the unexplored areas of the dungeon: every new tile revealed restores health and mana) - which is deceptively easy in earlier stages, but will prove frustratingly difficult in later levels.  Think of it as much as a strategy/puzzle game as an RPG - and an excellent, if unorthodox, example of all these genres.  If you're on the fence try the alpha - available free at the developer's website - for a taste of what the game offers: the full release is both more accessible at first and more difficult at last, while providing more control over your circumstances at every step of the way.  Whether you are a casual gamer looking for a new fix, a hardcore gamer seeking new challenges of your wit and will, or simply a conoisseur of the quirky - I cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I really dislike this game and I'm still recommending anyone who might like it to buy it!If you're a fan of Mobile phone games in general and puzzle games or town building games in particular but hate the horrid monetization that often accompanies them then this is a game for you.If you also like quirky dialogue and a cute and well detailed medieval/fantasy setting then that makes it doubly worth an investment both of time and money. As others have said:  In fact it's the first game I've ever gone into and reported a tag for. The RPG tag is direclty misleading. Your heroes don't permanently level up with you through the dungeons, any items or spells you find are not accompanied with you at the end of a stage, your choices don't really matter and ultimately it's intended that you complete all stages that you have with different heroes that are more apt for each particular environment.  Each hero always starts at level 1 in each stage.Every stage is intended to be possible to complete by anyone with enough smarts or enough time to poke around in the dungeon long enough to figure out the sequence in which you're supposed to beat each foe. There is no AI, no adaptation to be made on the go, no backtracking possible, no real way to reverse mistakes except to fail and redo them.This is a game of stages.  Each stage made more complicated by the levels and numbers of monsters you face and your own towns development which allow for different heroes to be brought into the stage with different items attached to them based not on what those heroes had done in the past but what buildings you've bought in town. The progression of the town is managed by the design, i.e. you can't mess it up to the point where you can't progress anymore and you can't really specialize in something you find very interesting, because tier leveling of buildings is much more expensive than just buying new basic buildings. This coupled with the handholding advice you're given means you'll generally be going on a path of the generalist and as a new building (or later upgrade) is unlocked, a new challenge appears appropriate for that upgrade. It's a very casual game made to entertain you and make you think a bit. Probably good on a train trip or long plane journey as you listen to some music. According to other reviewers the difficulty ramps up but for various reasons in the way exploration and healing works that difficulty will become very complicated but ultimately linear and non-complex. This is because you heal with each move and so moving without doing too much combat is a waste of potential healing. As such the puzzle's are made with this in mind. In essence this means that exploration is opposite of rewarded; it's punished. This also limits the complexity of the puzzle.If you're a fan of what is essentially a Sodoku-esque (but infinitely more complicated/varied) puzzle experience with a fog of war coupled with a casual town building mini-game then this is for you. Since in that way it's very well made.

_childDocuments_.review: Like most adults who work for a living, I have very hard limits on what I am willing to spend on particular items. Take a bottle of wine, for example: I've found that there is no difference between a ten dollar bottle of wine and a thirty dollar bottle of wine. Anybody that tells you otherwise is trying to impress you. With wine, you get very little return on your investment past the 15-20 dollar price point. There's a reason that many sommeliers refuse to do blind tastings, and that reason being that sommeliers have all agreed to subscribe to the same groupthink that says X vintage and Y grapes grown in Z reason are superior, and none of this information would be available to them if they were prevented from looking at the label on the bottle. Have you ever met anyone who's a certified "master sommelier"? They're truly insufferable people. The next time you meet one ask them a question about wine - any question, it doesn't matter how dumb, will send them into a desperate panic while they fumble to form an opinion, any opinion, about the matter in question. It doesn't matter what their answer is becuase they will be certain to couch it in arcane wine terms like "tannins" and "finish" and other completely subjective abstract concepts that you won't understand.Desktop Dungeons is like an overpriced bottle of wine. Sure, the label is fancy and the guy trying to sell it to you is telling you about how great it is, using words like "replayability" and other nonsense, but as soon as you taste it you realize "hey, this tastes just like a $5 iphone game?"Just look at the screenshots. There's a reason that they only expect you to play this in ten minute bursts. $15 is just way, way, too much.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying I have nothing against the concept of blending genres. It can work and if done properly it can create a game far greater than the sum of its parts. , a game which attempts to combine a rogue-like dungeon crawl with a puzzle game, could definitely have worked, if only the elements it chose to borrow from those two genres were actually compatible with each other.Allow me to explain by way of example. As part of the puzzle aspect of the game, your hero only regenerates health and mana when exploring new areas, not when backtracking over old areas. Blind exploration is dicouraged, as doing so at full health means wasting precious healing. This forces you to think about where you want to go next instead of just going out willy nilly. I know it sounds like I'm praising the game and the truth is it could have been a good gameplay mechanic......IF you had any way of actually KNOWING where you should go next.Unexplored areas are always completely blacked out, and since the dungeons are randomly layed out every time you have no way of knowing where you should go next. The fighter class mitigates this somewhat by automatically revealing the location of enemies that are your level or lower, but that hardly helps out the OTHER classes and even with this, you still have no way of knowing where to find valuable power-ups, equippable items, or spells.The whole game is like that. In fact the greatest challenge in this game is not any enemy, but the game's own vague rules. I talked about this a little in my review of  but it's even more true here: we really,  need to be given accurate, real information for a game like this to work.For example, there's a speed stat that determines who attacks first in combat, but you can't actually see what your speed stat is. You can see that some enemies have first strike, but even enemies that don't have first strike and which you would expect to go after you in the combat order - like warlocks and zombies - can often end up going first... sometimes. Other times they go second, and since you can't actually see your speed stat or the enemy's the whole thing just comes across as arbitrary.And that's why this game fails on both fronts. The puzzle aspects are too strictly demanding and the punishment for even one single misstep is too harsh, so the game fails as a rogue-like. At the same time, the rogue-like aspects add too much randomness and too much hidden information, so the game fails as a puzzle.The worst part is the game has no idea. It demands care, but then forces you to go out blindly, and then punishes you harshly for doing so. It tells you it's all your fault when you fail (and you will) with condescending messages and taunts, but really it's no one's fault because everything is entirely luck-based.Like I said, the idea of combining a rogue-like and a puzzle game is not entirely terrible. It could have worked, it just didn't in this case. Maybe some other game will come along and get it right. But this one ain't it.My Rating: [2] BAD

_childDocuments_.review: This game pulls you fiercly through fun and challenging tutorial levels to throw you straight into the shredder afterwards. Maybe too much RNG actually.Key takeaways:- you'll always be underleveled and on the brink of dying- you don't/can't/won't find the items and/or enough gold you'd really need- you never have enough potions (late game issue)The mechanics with gaining extra xp using certain spells is annoying and the only way to get a high enough level to not get one-shot by the boss. It rarely works because of the RNG. I often had to fight a level 10 boss with ridiculous resistances and HP as an underpowered level 7 or 8, chucking 1-2 potions after every strike just to die close to victory, or explore most of the map just to find enough low level mobs to get me even started - as fighting level 2 monsters is instant death at start.Getting strong enough in a run to beat the level boss(es) is based on luck. _childDocuments_.review: A well-crafted roguelike with persistent elements, a fun if ignorable story, and a zany sense of humor. _childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, this is a great choice for a resource management puzzle. It may take the structure of a more traditional roguelike game, but it feels less so about making a character build and more so about squeezing every inch of value from the board to beat the boss. This includes more traditional resources like health, mana, and experience, but also includes things like divine favor, black-space, and even enemies themselves. There's a variety of classes, and each one encourages different playstyles relative to the core loop.Presentation overall is nice, with the distinctive soundtrack the atmospheric soundtrack. Writing is generally unremarkable, satirical humor that feels hit or miss, but that's not what you're looking for here. I mostly played this version out of fear that the remake might be too much for my laptop.

_childDocuments_.review: With its bite-sized dungeons and puzzle-like approach to combat, Desktop Dungeons offers an intriguing interpretation of the roguelike genre. For those who like to plan and solve problems, the strategy and resource management mechanics in the game present a special challenge. Replayability is ensured by randomly generated levels, and the gameplay is kept front and center by the minimalist aesthetic.It's important to remember that some players might be turned off by the game's challenging learning curve. The initial learning curve for the mechanics and strategies can be steep, which can make early playthroughs potentially frustrating. Additionally, even though the art is straightforward and practical, not everyone will find it visually appealing, especially those who favor more intricate graphics.In general, Desktop Dungeons is a niche title that appeals to players who enjoy gameplay that is challenging and strategic in nature. It stands out for its distinctive mechanics and approach to the roguelike genre, but a larger audience looking for a more approachable or visually immersive experience might find it less appealing due to its learning curve and simple graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is digital crack. I've already put a ton of time into it over the past few days, and I can see myself putting in a ton more.Think Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup meets Munchkin meets Minesweeper. Much like a traditional rogue-like, you are tasked with creating a hero of a specific race and class, and then venturing into a dungeon to kill a boss and retrieve its treasure. The dungeons are single-screen (hence the title) and quick to get through, but the bosses are quite tough to kill, and playing this game like a traditional rogue-like isn't going to get you far. Rather, the game's classes, items, and glyphs (spells) encourage experimentation, and you'll need to rely on strategy (and maybe a little luck) to get through each without dying. The interface and graphics are simple, but the underlying combat and leveling system that will determine your success in each run has a lot of depth. The meta-game progression here is handled really well, too; clearing dungeons will net you gold for more classes and items to take into each dungeon, but the game does not drip feed you resources on failed runs, much like other rogue-lites. This means that the game will introduce more mechanics and complexity as it goes on, but you have to actually earn it first. This makes clearing the bite-sized dungeons all the more gratifying, as your victories actively allow you to add more stuff for subsequent runs.The quick-pace of each run means that the losses are easy to shrug off, and the wins encourage you to go for another run. Even early in the game, there is enough randomness and surprises to keep things interesting. I picked this up for free, but I would have gladly paid full price for it.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique game, and one that never ceases to entertain. Also quite hard, but that's the joy of it. It's one of these games where dying is always your fault, and you get the satisfaction of learning after every run. Victory is in your grasp; it just takes practice. I play plenty of games, but I always find myself coming back to this one every once in a while. Just a quick dungeon run.A couple of warnings:- Known what this game is. It is not really an RPG, and what little story there is isn't really substantive. No, this is a resource-management puzzle game with roguelike elements. It also feels both casual and very difficult, almost like a crossword puzzle.- Take. Your. Time. Yes the dungeon runs can be completed quickly once you're experienced, but that doesn't mean you can just go around killing all the enemies you see. You have to choose battles strategically, go for higher-leveled enemies, and clean up the weaker monsters later.- ***Completionists beware***: This game is very difficult to complete 100%. Completing some of the "Very Hard" dungeons and getting all of the achievements is just insanely difficult. Fortunately, you can play in the standard dungeons forever and still have a great experience.

Playing somewhere between a puzzle game and a true roguelike, it's got a surprising amount of depth and resource management to it. If you like puzzle games, RPGs, and aren't scared of a little bit of arithmetic here and there, you may just find a new treat here.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: This game plays much more like a puzzle game then it does a rogue-like. Yes you can get advantages in your city and build up, unlock new classes, and level up your adventurers guild to unlock more areas to play. But the actual gameplay... It is incredibly unique.Just not the rogue-like and combat oriented game I am looking for. It's more like... minesweeper with monsters. Or math with graphics.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Much deeper than I expected on the surface, the puzzle mechanics in this game can get quite involved when set up right. With that said, I actually the individual challenges for classes and faiths are more fun and interesting than the "normal" levels themselves. I'd originally bought this because it looked like something simple and lightweight I could boot up quickly to do while waiting for other things to finish, something I could play for 5 or 10 minutes and immediately step away from.It's less a matter of the game being difficult, and more the fact that I always try to optimize my next move no matter what...and there is a lot to think about when planning your next step as you get deeper and deeper into the mechanics. Certainly worth the price, but provides a very different experience than what I expected, so I would suggest keeping that in mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: It is like a game of complex chess with a dungeon master. 9/10 amazing.I would've liked more flow to the story, the 4th wall breaking cheapened the experience, the story itself lacked a strong motivation, but the story elements were very interesting.I want more. I want shared puzzles, I want to spectate other people's games, I want to have a rewatch button at the end where I can admire my work.Amazing replayability and I will buy the sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: very meaty game this. it took me quite a while to 'learn' it - using the fog of war as a resource, not killing everything in sight (as enemies are also a resource), and all the neat little tricks you can pull off using the spells and God bonuses (the game has a puzzle section that works as a sort of tutorial to learn how to think about the maps in a more strategic way - tho beware, the puzzles are not straightforward). I never thought myself a fan of puzzles, but I find that the puzzle aspect of this game has really drawn me in. Imagine rogue crossed with one of those logic puzzles you find in crossword magazines, or indeed windows minesweeper, and you'll get the idea. The maps increasingly mix up the challenge and you are forced to vary your character builds to progress so it is probably not a game for someone who always sticks with a mage, say, or rogue. I really enjoyed the variety and it will encourage me to mix it up a bit more in other RPGs and roguelikes. The graphics are fun in a kinda plants vs zombies way. A bit grotesque and ott. Yes, a fantastic game.  A real surprise not what I was expecting at all, but what I needed.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: A classic puzzle roguelike that still stands up as an enjoyable experience years after release.  While a nearly deterministic combat puzzle once all the pieces (monsters, items, shops, spells, shrines, etc.) are explored, the act of exploration is itself a resource to be managed since it governs health and mana replenishment.  As a result, you're always balancing risk and reward.  Do you progress the puzzle now, spending health and mana to fight and gain experience, or do you explore, wasting regeneration but potentially discovering a more efficient way to level up?  It's a solid gameplay loop.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game when all it was, was a free demo a long while back. I was super excited to see it roll past my queue and immediately put it on my wishlist. I've got 5 hours in on steam so far and I'm probably gonna dump a lot more. There's so much more than what I remember and the pixel art is fantastic. Well worth getting!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for many reasons: the gameplay is both tutorial and punishing, the variations are numerous, the wit and animations are enjoyable, and outside of the explorer challenges there are many ways to "win" if you pay attention. It feels like a puzzler and an RPG combined, easy to pick up and play for <1 hour but tough to complete, you need to adjust your approach to every dungeon based on what you get and when (this is one of the great variables, the unknown of when items appear and how to adapt based on your character, deities, spells, etc.).I have spent a fair amount of time on this game, although to be clear my account reflects a lot of  hours where the toddler or something else distracted me and I was AFK, sometimes overnight or whenever I could find the time to pick up the game again. It is made to approach dungeons carefully and you are rewarded for considering your moves. It has been enjoyable and I look forward to more time unlocking all of what this has to offer but am confident it is worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: I re-install this every few years just to putz around. The game can be a little bit unforgiving sometimes, but it has charm. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Wow! Very smart, and very good. Flashbacks to OG Zelda. If Link grew up in a town of other nerds who wanted to clear one screen of baddies at a time. Except now with more powerups and many other tricks hidden up their sleeves. Every level's a mini brain teaser. With so many game mechanics to exploit. It's the baby bear of strategy. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Well, let's see. I've owned this game for 17 days and have 52 hours of play time as of this review. I think that ought to say something. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Well suited to lighter play sessions, Desktop Dungeons is a fun game with plenty of variety in playstyles to keep it from getting stale. While the "story" isn't exactly a driving force of literature, it provides plenty of opportunities to ease players into options as they unlock them and become familiar with the overall mechanics of the game. These range from challenges with guaranteed layouts, dungeons more suited to specific classes, or even just bonus quests that require clearing a dungeon with every class of a theme. As a whole, all these mechanics allow people to get as invested in the game as they like. You can try and use every possible avenue to turn a difficult run into a victory, or you can stack the odds towards yourself with preparations and hoping for a strong start. I can safely say while not for everyone, Desktop Dungeons is a great pick for those who like short snappy play sessions with careful decision making. It's good at what it doe, so as long as you understand that you'll have a great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful puzzle game, dressed up as a turn based roguelike dungeon crawler. This is a remake of the free game also called Desktop Dungeons, with much more content and higher res graphics. The free version is also very good, if you are unsure whether to buy this you can try out the free version. The remake is superior in every way. Lots of content, lots of variety, very smart stuff. One of my favourite games ever.There are a lot of (genuinely different) classes, and a lot of (genuinely different) maps, of varying difficulty. There is random level generation, and It is possible to maneuver yourself into a dead end. Actually it is quite easy to do that when playing badly. Levels start out unexplored and are randomly generated, although some things never change, like plant levels have lots of plants, there is always a fire run, and so on. Exploring heals you, but also your enemies. You level up by killing enemies, which also heals you. The goal is to beat the boss. And while this starts out pretty simple on easy levels (just kill some dudes, explore to heal, kill more dudes, repeat until you are high enough level to beat the boss), it gets harder quickly, and you need to develop ever more complex tactics to eke out victory.One slight annoyance is that most levels give a small permanent bonus for beating it with each class. So if you want all the bonuses, you have to beat even the easy levels with every class, which is tedious. And you have to beat even the annoying levels with every class, which is pretty annoying. But there is quite a bit of variety, so it's possible intermingle these tedious parts between more interesting content. And if you haven't played the free versions for weeks before playing this, this wont really be a problem because it will be quite hard to progress for a good long while.It's really very good and if you like puzzle games or roguelikes you should buy it. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is a very peculiar game which plays like some kind of puzzle game.One half of the game you are buying upgrades in your town which will aid you in future adventures.And the other half is you adventuring into caves and dungeons to slay the biggest baddest baddie available and return with the loot.You are tossed out on a map which you explore square by square. _childDocuments_.review: Desktop Dungeons is one of my favorite games.  The mix of roguelike and puzzle gameplay is extremely well-balanced to a satisfying difficulty combined with near-endless replayability.You control a hero exploring a randomly-generated dungeon, gathering powerups, equipment, and spells (glyphs).  The enemies are purely reactive: they only damage you in retaliation to your attacks.  This mechanic sets Desktop Dungeons apart from most roguelikes, and your ability to plan ahead results in gameplay comparable to a puzzle game.  Situations can become increasingly complex as you progress further and obtain more unlockables (such as the various gods you can worship in the dungeon).You (and the enemies) regenerate your health and mana through revealing unexplored tiles, allowing you to recharge between encounters.  Your resources are all finite, so you can't simply grind your way to victory.  Instead, careful play is needed to gain bonus XP from killing higher-level enemies without exhausting your ability to recover before you face the boss (or bosses).The skill ceiling is extremely high, and the more difficult scenarios are quite brutal.  When you first start playing even the easier "Normal" dungeons will provide a challenge.  You can tilt the odds in your favor by spending kingdom gold (essentially your winnings from successful runs) on preparations that should make your hero more effective.   I will note that the most difficult dungeons are unnecessary to complete the main storyline, but beating them unlocks powerful items as well as four monster races. Dungeons are reasonably short (my runs are roughly 10-40 minutes depending on the situation), but the game is extremely replayable.  The wide selection of classes, races, and items allows for a wide diversity of viable builds.  I have played over a hundred hours and completed the main storyline, but it will be quite some time before I feel that I have exhausted the postgame content.  The Enhanced Edition additionally introduces a 'Daily Dungeon' feature allowing you to compare your results to other players.

_childDocuments_.review: The First time I ran into this game was years ago when it was a contender in the Independent Games Festival. I remember downloading other contest entries as well, but the alpha of this game was the one that really grabbed my attention. I spent hours upon hours playing the alpha and was really excited when I learned that they were making a full game out of it. I didn't buy the early access version, but I followed the development closely. When it finally was officially released I bought it immediately and boy was I surprised. I had expected a graphical overhaul and the extra features, but not to this extent! There was just so much more to unlock and do. The devs had upped everything to eleven. New monster types, afflictions, gods, character classes, races, secrets, challenge dungeons, tutorials, the list just goes on and on.The full release really pushed this game to new heights, at least for me. What had been a quick puzzle fix was now a fully fleshed out puzzle game with a mischievious art style and depth like never before + the ost by Danny Baranowsky and Grant Kirkhope is great!I highly recommend this fantastic game. The sheer amount of gameplay variation and replayability this game offers in such a tight package is nothing short of impressive.P.S. I realize this isn't really a full review, but more of a memoir of a Desktop Dungeonist.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you're into logic/puzzles, math, and rogue-like elements, the games don't get more entertaining than this.  The Good: -The necessity to use different strategies and builds depending on the levels. There's no single strategy that will beat the game for you.-The difficulty is almost spot-on throughout the entire game. It's only easy in the beginning. By the end it's brutally hard, but you feel accomplished.-Fun in small spurts or for long periods of time.-There are a ton of upgrades that keep the game fresh.The Bad:-The more you lose on one level the harder it is to remain patient and play well (more of a personal flaw, but it applies greatly here).-The randomness of the "boss", glyph drops, enemies, etc. can break/ruin a run for you.  Takes some luck on harder levels.Verdict: If you can deal with feeling dumb as you try to figure out the best strategies and are patient enough to not blow a fuse as you repeat levels multiple times, the game is great.  The upgrades keep the game and strategies fresh and you feel great accomplishment as you make your way through the harder levels.  For the price they are asking, you get great value for your buck.  I'd give it a solid 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Very high replayability. Slightly overpriced for the average gamer. A slight grind to unlock all areas and characters.This game rewards patience and good decision making. Have a plan and execute - or learn to adjust to the randomly generated dungeon. Either way, a worthwhile experience when the price is right.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying; this was the first game that actually got me interested in the genre of Rogue-likes. Previously I had played around with Vulture for Nethack, The Binding of Isaac (although it doesn’t necessarily fit my idea of Rogue-like), Don’t Starve, and some various flash games that just never sparked interest. Now here is what Desktop Dungeons does right- Great for beginners:If you're willing to waltz throught the tutorial, which I recommend you do, you'll begin to believe that you understand the game a lot more than you do, but the tutorial drops you off at a point where the learning curve is much less steep.- Captivating and Hilarious:Each of the missions that you run through, each have taken me around 3-5 runs before completion, have left me thirsty for much much more, and considering the expandability of your kingdom and the available upgrades, I believe I haven't even sank my teeth into the first quarter of this game and I love it. Going back to the tutorial,  the narrator is hilarious and there are always little things they add into the game that make me giggle. Never a full on guffaw, but a solid giggle. - Difficulty:Beyond giggling to the moon at the minor jokes that are at hand, Desktop Dungeons has set an immense level of difficulty, which parallels its learning curve. If the dungeon begin to feel too easy for you, go ahead and try out the puzzles up the mountain, I promise it won't be at all a cake walk. The puzzles really make you go indepth with the mechanics of the game and how each item affects how your character attacks.And here is what I think has gone wrong (only one thing) - Price:I don't believe the price point is necessarily a fair one. The only reason I have this game now, is because I got it in a humble bundle, which is still going on until 7/12/16 where I paid a little over half for this game, and plenty of others, rather than its full price. I don't think I would have bought it otherwise, but I believe if you're on the fence about buying it, you absolutely should.
