_childDocuments_.review: is like an adorable kitten:  Small and cute.This time, the franchise's yellow kitty PC is a pirate on a quest for the North Star.  Said kitty is of the bloodline of the Seekers, a group of sages who searched for the North Star and then locked it away for safekeeping.  The reasons for hiding the star quickly become more Tolkien than Disney.If you played the first two games, then much will be familiar.  The franchise is a kid-friendly action RPG.  Your kitty gets melee weapons, a quick swap to an equipped ranged weapon, and magic to cast.You roam a world map with locations labeled as if the world were a real map, plus you can consult an actual map that marks locations of stuff and keeps track of overworld treasures you have yet to find, and dungeons you have yet to complete.  Overworld locations look like cardboard figures standing up from a flat map.True to the pirate theme, you quickly pick up a cute little ship.  It sails at a nice fast clip even without the acceleration button.  Of course, there are enemy ships stationed in many places.  Dodge the enemies, though, and the entire world is open to you, with no gatekeeping other than some barriers that your ship's cannon has to take down, and, of course, enemy levels.Enemies roam the world, and are usually easy to dodge.  Most enemies respawn after a game reload, including on your death.  At first, this is slightly annoying, but the constant respawn also gives you a reliable means of low-tedium grinding for levels.  You also eventually find a tower that gives you an endurance run for lots of quick XP.Level gains account for most stats, but equipment upgrades can help you edge past the bosses.  You also can gain duplicate equipment that gives you an instant free upgrade of some item.Leveling up also slowly unlocks slots for helpful trinkets and blueprints to upgrade your ship.Naturally, enemies have a variety of different attacks and attack patterns, a decent variety to them.  Ranged attacks and swapping out equipment help at lower levels.Bosses usually require dodging their attack patterns and finding the right equipment and spells to survive them.  If you're not at a good level to have a real chance of beating them, the boss health bar is labeled with their approximate level.Save points are well-distributed and usually easy to reach, with the stretch into the game's finale clearly labeled as a point of no return.  Save points are also instant-refreshers, and work on both you and your ship at the same time.  Death just kicks you back to the last save, sometimes the game's autosave at critical points.Equipment and spells can be upgraded.  The gold you loot is used only for upgrading equipment at the smithy.  Spells are upgraded with magic crystals found in treasures.One thing that helps you gain gold for upgrades is a bounty system in the main port's tavern.  Some bounties are from bosses you'd be fighting in the main storyline, but most are on sidequests.  They are helpfully laid out in level order.Levels come fast and easy.  Enemies actually scale up slightly in power with you, including in XP given.  You'll never one-hit the earliest enemies, but they become easier as you find and equip items and spells.  Gains with levels also inch up, so you gain more at level 50 than you do at level 10.Sidequests also help with finding interesting loot as well as XP and gold.  This includes a couple large and challenging optional bosses to fight.Lore loosely links all three games.  It's not necessary to play the first two to understand this game; you get some of the basic lore during the game anyhow.  However, a linked saga is slowly being written, and with a sequel hook that might be the finale to the franchise.This game sorta feels like a disappointment coming off of   That game was huge, spanning two continents and two anthropomorphic animal kingdoms.  Plus, it had swapping between two characters, cat and dog, which facilitates local co-op play.  Co-op is in this game, too.Here, though, the main game has less than ten hours of play.  I finished the game in fifteen hours, getting most of the sidequests aside from trying and failing against the two largest and most difficult optional bosses.  The $20 base price tag is too pricey for that length.  Wait for a sale, or at least grab the bundle discount if you've played any of the other two games.Hopefully, the disappointingly shortish length here is due to a desire to push to the grand finale of the franchise and do something big with it.Meow-while, the game has all the gentle humor and warmth of the other two games.  The devs have seemingly pounced on every single op-purr-tunity for kitty puns, with a few rodent and dog puns and other animal references thrown in for good measure, not to mention many pirate puns.  One antagonist group is a crew of rodent pi-rats.The save points are especially cute, consisting of a parrot and pillow your kitty takes a quick catnap at, and labeled a Rest Beakon.  That parrot squawks if combat is near it (and saves are disabled until things calm down), and you can attack it.  NPCs can be attacked and complain about it.My only complaint here is that the game is too short for its price.  Toward the end of the game, it looks as if there'll be a bigger boss to fight and the franchise comes to its finale ... only for a swerve at the final boss and a sequel hook.But the devs have a winning formula going with this franchise and its style and its world, and hopefully they will come up with a worthy conclusion to this adorable game series.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Cat Quest 1 and 2 then you will enjoy Cat Quest 3 as it still holds the same humor and charm the series is known for. As for the length of the game it does feel shorter and I think that has to do with three major factors: less dungeons, less quests, and much faster movement around the world map. For the dungeons and quests part it feels more like there was a focus on quality over quantity this time around. The dungeons feel like there was more effort and thought put into their designs and the quests feel more like complete quests. What I mean about quests as that in previous Cat Quest games you will have a questline that ends up being multiple quests instead of one single quest where in Cat Quest 3 instead of opting to split a questline into multiple quests you get one single quest.While I would have enjoyed a few more quests and dungeons (bonus side dungeons not tied to any quests at all that challenge the player and have great loot as a reward would be great) I am satisfied Cat Quest 3 does not feel as repetitive as Cat Quest 2. To clarify I have played Cat Quest 2 on the Switch and the Xbox before playing it on Steam. When I went to beat it on Steam getting hyped for Cat Quest 3 to drop, I found myself getting burnt out on it, so the focus in Cat Quest 3 to be more quality over quantity I feel is a step in the right direction but isn't quite a perfect balance just yet.The thing that disappoints me the most is we get some new characters: Kidd Cat, Mage Bonny and Mama Milka which is great but, I do not feel we get enough with these characters to truly make them shine. I would have liked a little more story and development put into them to better know them.To comment on the faster movement around the map, this game gives you a boat at the beginning of the game meaning you essentially get the equivalent of water walking in Cat Quest 1 and 2 right at the start to use where in 1 and 2 you got that ability late into the main quest. It makes since being this game is focused around being a pirate and the entirety of the world map is yours to explore fairly early. Of course some spots will be much more difficult to explore first as I found out the hard way trying to go to a dungeon with level 60 foes while I wasn't even level 10 yet. I found myself having fun just sailing around exploring instead of doing the main quest I was tasked with, I actively avoided it.I enjoyed my time with Cat Quest 3 and while I feel it could have added a bit more to do I was satisfied with my playthrough of it. I am looking forward to the future of this series to see where the bigger narrative of the series goes. Apawcalypse when?

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a bad game. I like this series. It's very casual oriented, which fits me just fine, even if I don't care for the cat puns. But I think the developers have stagnated a little, even if this is possibly what the majority wants.+ More of the same, good presentation, decent casual gameplay.+ Some promising additions, like the new 2D "dungeons", but there isn't enough of it and it's very simplistic.+ Decent amount of variety on all fronts, even if everything has the same basic core, you will be engaged the whole time.+ Well presented map with quest icons.- Ship controls without gamepad are infuriating, and even with it, far from elegant, with you having to do loops around enemies that have figured out the secrets of autoiming turrets. Then again, if the game had good controls, the ship combat would be even more trivial than it already is.- Camera on the main map feels weird, the position is too close to the ground, giving you this weird feeling that they tried to make a blend between 2D and isometric, which is obviously impossible - compare with the isometric camera in first game, you can see yourself and the enemies a lot better, here, everything feels a bit squashed, like 2D sprites in original DOOM or something.- I didn't really care for most of the loot - I just settled for one melee weapon and a pistol, I only changed melee few times, until I got the ultimate weapon, and I've only cared for few basic stats for my armor. This could be because I'm playing basically the same game for the third time, but it rarely gives you incentive to change your loadout, but when it does, it's more annoying than anything, because there is no quick button to switch weapons etc.- While the story isn't more important than gameplay, it clearly matters, but it feels more simplistic and plain than ever. Again, maybe it's just because I've played it before.- No replay value for me personally - the gameplay is so basic (nothing wrong with that), it gives me no pleasure to just do it again. I care about the content, and after consuming it all, I'm done.This game cannot compete with many others on the gameplay front - it's way too simplistic, and devs don't seem to have the incentive to change it. At the same time, there are some ideas (like enemies that are weak and resistant to certain types of attacks), which unfortunately aren't expanded (no quick way to switch weapons, no loadouts, at least I didn't notice anything).I have spend 24 hours in Cat Quest 1, 36 in Cat Quest 2, and 11 in this one, without the desire to play it again. I didn't feel bored, my opinion is mixed, and I'm only giving negative, because but I think the overwhelmingly positive rating is inflated by the fans of the series and the devs aren't in such a good place to receive just endless praise.If you're content with what you got, that's fine, and you can eagerly await 10 other sequels, as the developers have no doubt found their retirement plan, but I want more. Those games aren't that special, and the devs risk milking them to death.

_childDocuments_.review: Wait for a big sale, 3 is hands down the weakest entry in the series. Yes, it is fun and addictive like the other two, but it is lacking in content and just feels empty compared to the other two. This should be around half the price or less than it is listed for. For context:Cat Quest 3 has 24 dungeons, 28 side quests, and 96 pieces of equipment. Cat Quest 1 has 52 dungeons, 62 side quests, and 66 pieces of equipment. Cat Quest 2 has 73 dungeons, 67 side quests, and 101 pieces of equipment. It is not hard to see that 3 is lacking in content and stuff to do. 12 of the side quests are bounties that don’t take very long to do. The other side quests and dungeons are very simple as well, so it’s not like they can use complexity or longer as an excuse. On top of that, the ship combat added very little if anything. It is much faster and easier to bait a boss ship, including the duck, over to the shore and just fight them on foot. The ship is good for moving around the map but using it to fight is a waste of time. I hope they put the time and care they put into 1 and 2 into the next game. If they put out a lazy attempt like 3 again, they will lose me and probably many others. It took me 10.5 hours to 100% Cat Quest 3. (Game Does Not have challenges) It took me 18.5 hours to 100% Cat Quest 1. (Includes Challenges as part of 100%)It took me 12.5 hours to 100% Cat Quest 2. (Does Not include Challenges as part of 100%)I bought and replayed 1 and 2 on steam to get times. I may do the challenges on 2 to compare it to 1 as well. 2 feels like the complete Cat Quest experience. Keep in mind that I have played 1 and 2 a few times before on console, so a new player to these games may have a higher play time due to exploring. Likewise, if I replayed 3 and didn't have to explore, then i'd expect the clear time to be lower even. After replaying 1 and 2 again, 3 just feels empty and small compared to the first two. The devs need to replay the first two games and see all the effort they put into them, because they took the easy way out with 3 in many ways.

_childDocuments_.review: Update, as of original review, I have now 100%'d the game.The game's main storyline is perhaps around 2-3 hours. The side content is probably 2-3 extra, and that isn't really accounting for player skill either- I have 11 hours of gametime and when I posted my review initially after 4 hours, I had only beaten the game, not gone back and done side content. Most of the side content is vague unlike previous installments, and this game leaves it up to you to go out and look for everything in every tiny corner of the map. Regardless, the game can leave you feeling lost and clueless at times, and fully expects you to use your ship to solve problems if you're too weak to fight something. It also fully intends for you to exploit the combat system for you to turn any disadvantage (including 5-15 levels of it), into an advantage.However, despite it's lack of content, and it definitely just feeling like a significantly shorter Cat Quest 1, even having less content and map size than the first game in it's trilogy, the game does make up for it in spirit, gameplay, and charm.I do recommend this game- However, please get it while it's on sale. ^^;Original Review, before update:Pros:- Same charming humor as the other two games.- Multiplayer.- Combat feels fluid, and is an improvement from the second game, but it has flaws.- Graphics keep the same charm as the previous games while improving upon them.- Music and story are fairly good.Cons:- The map size is significantly smaller than Cat Quest 2- It appears to be similar in size to the OG Cat Quest.- The story appears to be a lot shorter than previous entries- and there are very few side quests- most of which are hidden or sporadically found while exploring.- The game's combat is very easy to break- similar to previous entries, though unlike them, you'll find that one of the first few weapons you get does this for you.- The game somehow makes itself feel like more of a grind than the previous two entries as well- this is perhaps due to it's lack of areas to explore that aren't related to the main quest and lack of side content to aid your leveling. Conclusion: Play the game if you like cats and beating stuff up, I guess. Don't play the game if you care more about how big or how long the game is.

Then I discovered the story of an adorable cat and stories starring them in a 2.5D open world that gives you the freedom to explore as you prefer on land and sea. In each region you will find dungeons, enemies, treasure chests, characters, clues and secrets that you can discover by investigating or solving puzzles.Also fun thanks to the clever writing work full of jokes. (Cat language)And this is where the best part comes in, as players have the freedom to make the combinations they want with weapons, spells and armor. With special mention to the variety of bosses and at the same time they will put a smile on your face due to their design..Speaking especially of Cat Quest 3. This time it is in Gatoribe, highlighting of course the hordes of rats that follow the orders of the Pirate King. Regarding combat, it can be divided into two parts. The first would be the naval combat, which at first may seem somewhat repetitive and even annoying, but as you equip and reinforce your ship it becomes more satisfying.-I'm not interested in the cooperative mode, but it's very friendly- to defeat more complicated enemies more easily and even plan strategies. Like one attacking from the ship and the other staying on land for greater effectiveness.The New Game+ option will always be available with your level and equipment..This very feline action RPG was released on August 8, International Cat Day, a celebration that highlights the importance of these enigmatic felines in our lives. Have a meowfull game!

_childDocuments_.review: (Up-to-date as of September 6th, 2024: review might be changed as the game receives new patches and updates. go to bottom for summary)I've played both of the previous titles prior: couldn't beat the final boss of CQ1, and accidentally started a New Game+ on CQ2 before I realized there were dungeons after beating the final boss on that one, so this is the first in the series that I got 100% on. While numerous changes gave way for smoother sailing, it still purr-vided quite a challenge (no, I'm not apologizing for puns; the series is full of them and I love it)Quite notably different from the previous titles, the setting is nowhere near Felingard, meaning the devs had to make up more of the setting from scratch than the previous installment. There's still a few cameos and allusions to characters and quests from earlier games, but the distance allows for even a wider range of characters to appear, the previously introduced cats and dogs from the previous game being accompanied by not only rats but also boars.The available equipment makes a significant difference to the gameplay: while wands are mostly untouched, melee weapons now feel much more distinct based on whether they're swords, axes, or the newly added claws and shields, with the addition of combo finishers to all weapons and the defensive utility of the shields making the most notable difference for close ranged combat. Ranged weapons get the addition of guns, which often have unique attacks when you use the last bullet in a clip (at the cost of not being able to shoot for a while after using all the bullets in your gun).The ship is a powerful addition to the player's arsenal, although it takes quite a bit of getting used to. with the right upgrades, you can sail circles around enemies while taking potshots at them from behind, but unlike most games that feature naval combat, your cannons are a single front-mounted turret with a 180-degree range of rotation centered forward, meaning that its easy to accidentally get enemies in your blindspot if you instinctively try to go for a broadside barrage (Windward players be warned; this got me a fair few game overs)There a good amount of puzzles and treasure hunting, as well as dungeons that switch the 2.5D controls for 2D minus the ability to jump, making for very interesting boss fights that use attacks beyond what you'd usually find from regular monsters throughout the series. Whereas before you'd expect a thunder boss to simply spam Lightnyan and regular AoE attacks, now you can get several unique Metroidvania-style attack barrages accompanied with electric guitar riffs while you try to block or dodge waves of thunder magic.TL:DR: If you enjoyed the other Cat Quest games, this is a must-play. Combat mechanics are greatly fleshed out and made me decide to revisit the older games after so much time

_childDocuments_.review: (Edit: I played on Normal) I can’t say the game isn’t fun, but I feel as though this game removed a lot of what I liked about the other two entries. Overall, it’s a 6/10 when the other two were 8/10 (cq1) and 9/10 (cq2). I spend too much time moving around the map and finding myself doing very little fighting. When I do fight, I’m beating enemies that are 10 to 15 levels above mine with little difficulty, and the final boss was laughably easy as I beat it 12 levels under in 15 seconds. I love the guns as they added a new way to play, but with how few enemies there are, I never felt like playing range had any downside as I never got surrounded, and I was often doing the same or more damage ranged. I don’t know how this game took so long to make in comparison to the others, yet it feels so empty; imagine  if the second game had half the quests and a tenth of the dungeons with the same amount of walking. Finally, the enemy variety does not exist. You have a small guy with a sword, the guy that jumps and smashes, the guy that charges at you. That’s most of the enemies, and only two non-boss enemies cast spells/spell-like abilities. Frankly, wait for a sale when this game drops 50% or more.

_childDocuments_.review: As with the previous installment, I played through the entirety of CQ3 with my significant other. We had a great time, but didn't enjoy CQ3 quite as much as CQ2. In general, CQ3 offers a more refined, but also rather streamlined experience.In particular:- CQ3 cuts a lot of filler content. There aren't quite as many quests, dungeons, cutscenes, dialogues, thus less reasons for walking back and forth. Some of the overarching themes and enemies (dogs, catnip, wyrms) have mostly been dropped.- It feels like there's less puns. This may be an issue with the (pun-struggling) German translation, and even then, I'm still unsure whether that actually is a good thing.- You can explore (and see) the entire world from the beginning and, by ship, you have a quick means of travel. This, alongside the fact that a larger part of the map is water, makes the world feel smaller than it is.- Ship travels and ship combat aren't particularly fun in local co-op. Both players control the same ship in the same way and there is no need and no chance for teamwork. For best results, one player just doesn't touch the controller during these (extensive) parts of the game.- There are no level markers on dungeons. Once you accidentially overlevel by going the wrong way, the later game becomes too easy.- The tactical combat system with precisely telegraphed attacks has been replaced by a mostly generic ARPG one. You can now win most fights just by button mashing. It doesn't help that the FX became so intrusive that it is hard to see what is going on in a fight.- Previously, enemies were recurring all over the game and you did learn their unique patterns at one point or another. With CQ3, enemies don't recur as often, and every enemy is just an exchangeable sprite you mash down exactly the same way as all the others.- In total, CQ3 feels smaller than its predecessor, though it probably isn't if you only count quality content. We took 16 hours for an all-achievements run of CQ3, as opposed to 20 hours for a similar run of CQ2.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Played Cat Quest from the first one. Cat Quest 2 being my (still) favorite. Cat Quest 3 improved on a lot of aspects but downgraded on just as many. I still believe this game is fantastic and is totally worth the money, so if you liked the previous games, you will probably like this one too.The aesthetics of the game have improved both in art style and tower dungeons / caves layouts. Some are 2.5D while others are side scrollers and are also themed. The main quest line boss fights are unique visually and a lot of fun. The downsides is that the dungeons are extremely short, most tower dungeons having 5-8 rooms and maybe 4-6ish enemies occupying them and then the boss room. Both the diversity and quantity of enemies / dungeons / caves are severely lacking in the dungeons and overall world map, making the game feel empty compared to the other games. And while Cat Quest 2 seemed a bit bloated with these things and a reduction isn't technically a bad thing when being replace with quality over quantity, there still just wasn't enough in this one.The melee has been improved, in my opinion. (I hated most melee in the first two games but absolutely loved in this one.) The range combat in general was lackluster with the exception of one gun. The wands for the most part were the same with a different element. Nothing like the crazy wands from the second game and the guns are pretty much the same. Range combat was boring and didn't feel like it was a necessary addition to the combat rotation. Which brings me to the magic. Magic was also lackluster. Most spells were the same fire out balls of this element and boring. Ice spike was the only spell I used other than healing. There wasn't any reason to use the other magic spells or range weapons due to how nonessential they were. I really wish they were fleshed out more and made more interesting but they just felt flat.Ships were fun. I had a blast with it. unfortunately, again, just like with the ranged weapons and magic, it seemed like a half fleshed out mechanic. the main event for ships consist of 3 boss ships, 1 bounty ship, and the 1 bar mission. After that there's not much for you to do with your ship.  So overall, it was still a great experience. I really do recommend the game to those who've played the previous two. So while i think they have upped the quality in the dungeons, boss fights, melee, and general aesthetics of the game, i also feel that range combat, magic spells, and the ships were taken in a good direction, but they ran out of time or budget to fully see them through and became a shadow of what they could have been. So while there is a sense of lacking while and after the game and it feels almost incomplete in a way, i still got satisfaction from the game.I finished this game 100% in 14hrs. it probably would have been a lot less but I like to explore right off the bat which led me to boss fights that were 30 lvls over my own. had I followed the story as it was more intended I probably would have finished around 8-9 hours.So again, I recommend the game, but know that it is short and maybe a bit empty. And as a "Pirate" themed game, I really wanted more out of the ship and gun play. Maybe they'll update it with more content in the future. I'd even pay for DLCs if they expand those things I feel are lacking. Can't wait for the next one!

_childDocuments_.review: Cat Quest III manages to improve many aspects from the previous games, while also sacrificing other aspects of it. But those changes actually don't make the game be bad, since the game is actually good.The equipments system got a revamp. Now most weapons and equipments offers an unique benefit for your build, and special effect, making each weapon and equipment feel unique, compared to previous games, where they were mostly changes on base stats. That also means there's fewer weapons and equipments to find, but with the addition of new weapons types, like guns, claws and shields, further makes up for that.And to further add up to this, relics were added to further give special effects to your character. Want to deal an extra attack when hitting a opponent with your sword? Equip a relic that does that.The equipment enhancing system got an upgrade too, making it a lot more easier and less annoying to upgrade and strengthen your equipment. And upgrading your equipment is something you will want to do eventually in the game, because the game gets harder as you progress, so all the boosts you can get are handy.Instead of being a mostly dungeon crawler with many quests for you to do, like the previous games, this game is mostly about exploring the game world. The camera view further reinforces that, by giving you a better view of your horizon, and what is ahead. Sailing was also added so you can ride your boat through it and blast pirates with its cannons. And yep, you can customize the abilities of your ship, as you find their blueprints. The sacrifices done to dungeons can be seen while playing the game, because they feel short and poorly designed.The worst thing added was the bi dimensional dungeons, where you can only travel to left or right, and has to activate stairs and doors to go to the next floor. I can understand that that was done to make boss fights harder, but the restriction in movement is still very annoying.Beside the poor dungeon design is rather annoying, the Infinity Tower was added as quite a fun arcade you can do, which seems to... Have infinite progression..? Anyways, last time I tried, it managed to get the monsters tougher as I run through the waves, not only making it handy for getting gear and golds, but also for leveling up the character (up to when you're able to).The boss fights also are better now, with bosses having more new and dangerous attacks. They even have desperate attacks being used as their health drops. That makes so you keep your attention up during the entire fight, or else you'll end up dead.The game also features fewer quests compared to previous games, located at specific places. Instead of quest boards offering quests, you most likely trigger them by speaking with npcs in the overworld, or npcs you talk with to do some job, like refine your equipment and stuff.But the best thing added to the game, which I can believe will be speed run strat, is doing bounty quests at the tavern. I say that because beating the bosses listed in the tavern will award you with lots of golds, which allow you to upgrade further your equipments.As for the plot, the game plot feels very straight forward. The way it's presented, you don't really need to play the other games to understand part of the story, beside it would be good to play them just to further add up to the knowledge about the game world.A downside this game has, is that there's a few moments where you might need to change your gameplay style, to use certain equipment to deal with your opponents. Generally, that happens on the bi dimensional dungeons, like one where you need to equip a shield to deal with the monsters, since it's impossible to dodge their rolling attacks. Good thing there's a limited number of times that happens (It's just 2 dungeons).Anyways, this game is good. It also features coop too. Since it's your Starbear and the Pirate Cat Spirit journey, it's good to see that you can hire some purrvateer to be your second player character, with full equipment customization.Feel free to get it. And if you got a friend or familiar to play with, you're probably lucky.Happy sailing.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this game is shorter than its predecessors; however, it's a much better game for it.I've played it through several times now merely on the fact that its pacing is snappy.There's always something to find behind a corner—a chest, a puzzle, a quest, a weapon. _childDocuments_.review: Cat Quest III is the long-awaited third game of the Cat Quest series, this time now taking place in the Purribean, and to put it simply, this is yet another improvement from its predecessor.The story is more enticing, with characters that are more unique, the animations are amew-zing, and the gameplay is a massive cat leap from the past two games, featuring more gear of different types that do many different things, making for a fun time creating different setups to fight different enemies and bosses, all of which have different sets of attacks to learn now! They have removed the telegraph from attacks, which while makes some attacks unpredictable at times, adds more challenge and it just makes learning the different enemies and bosses' attacks more satisfying. All of this even applies to their addition of ship combat, which is pretty fun as well!However, there are a couple things that irk me...first off, there are no warnings on levels, meaning you could enter a cave and end up running into high-level enemies by mistake, albeit they can be easy to avoid. Another con is that this game feels somewhat shorter, only being prolonged by hidden treasure to curiously wander for.Thankfully, these cons are massively outweighed by how much of an upgrade the combat, looting, quests, and story got, as if the previous games' elements weren't already great before! Once again, this is a fantastic RPG game and I highly recommend this series to those that enjoy cats in general along with RPG games too! :3

_childDocuments_.review: Review of Cat Quest III **Cat Quest III** is an exhilarating and charming addition to the beloved series that continues to delight both new and returning players. Here are some highlights: ## Engaging Gameplay - **Open World Exploration:** The game offers a beautifully crafted **open world** filled with diverse environments, from lush forests to bustling towns, inviting players to explore at their own pace. - **Fluid Combat System:** The real-time combat is **intuitive** and **dynamic**, allowing players to execute combos and dodge attacks smoothly, making battles both exciting and strategic. ## Adorable Aesthetics - **Charming Art Style:** The visuals are vibrant and whimsical, featuring adorable cat characters that are sure to warm the hearts of players. - **Delightful Soundtrack:** The music complements the gameplay perfectly, enhancing the overall atmosphere and providing a fun backdrop to the adventure. ## Rich Storyline - **Engaging Narrative:** The storyline is filled with humor, heart, and plenty of cat puns, making the quest enjoyable and entertaining. - **Memorable Characters:** Players will encounter a cast of quirky characters that add depth and personality to the game world. ## Customization and Progression - **Character Customization:** The game allows for various customization options, enabling players to tailor their feline hero to suit their playstyle. - **Skill Trees:** With various skills and abilities to unlock, players can develop their characters in a way that enhances their unique gameplay experience. ## Conclusion **Cat Quest III** is a delightful journey that combines humor, engaging gameplay, and charming visuals, making it a must-play for fans of action RPGs and cat lovers alike. Whether you're a seasoned player or new to the series, this game promises hours of fun and adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Way, way, waaaaay too expensive. The map is very small (smaller than the cat quest II), there are very few dungeons and they all look the same, there is no memorable sound design, there is no voice acting. This feels more like a flash game than a fully fledged PC game. It is simply too expensive to recommend. I had a good time playing it on the couch with my wife, but not only is the story trivial and oversimplified (even for a kid), but the gameplay is similarly trivial (even for a kid). If you are at  or above the level of the enemies you just button mash away. If you are not, your skills don't matter because enemies have apparently infinite health if you under leveled.The positive changes are that you can equip two weapons and swap with them, you have several spells, and you have a ship. All of these are great.Nevertheless, I don't think it is fair for this game to ask for more than 5 pounds. It is practically the same price as Cult of The Lamb, the latter being an objectively superior game in terms of content, gameplay, sound design, story.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I played 1 & 2, if you told me I'd buy Cat Quest 3 day one, I would never have believed you. I mean sure they looked good - in a "babby's first ARPG" way - but not THAT good surely. Welp, I bought Cat Quest 3 day one, and no regrets.About the only complaint I've seen people voice is that it's "too short", but that ain't strictly true. It's quickest 100%, sure. The campaign is tad longer than #1 & a lot shorter than #2, but it has the very good taste of NOT making a bunch of NG+ / Mew Games necessary for 100%. You can get that in your first run / in about 10 hours. Which is perfect since that's about as long as the loop takes to wear out its welcome.Length aside, this is arguably the best game in the trilogy from a gameplay perspective. Don't expect something extremely different, it's extremely familiar. Camera angle is different so you can see far north / have this sense of scale, you cannot fly or teleport, you get around on your ship & yes of course there is naval combat. It is pirate themed after all. New camera angle does take some getting used to, everything else feel perfect from the get-go.TLDR : you already played 1 & 2 and liked them? do buy this, you will like it.You have not already played 1 & 2? buy the whole trilogy, you will like it.Here's hoping CQ4 will have the quality of 3 combined with the scale/size of 2.I'm off to whistle the sailing theme for a week, GLHF.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Cat Quest 2 (cringe inducing puns and all), then you'll enjoy this.  I played Cat Quest 2 and 3 coop with a friend of mine, and we had a fun time with both games.  Our playtime of Cat Quest II was 14.25 hours, and that's with us completing all of the side quests.  Our playtime of this game was 10.1 hours, which again was with us completing all the side activities.  So, this game is shorter, easier, or both.  However, I wouldn't say that's a problem.  But on the subject of problems, I don't really have any major ones, but there are a few minor gripes I have.There's no equipment loadouts in this game.  It'd be nice to be able to swap back and forth between different sets of equipment without having to just re-equip each piece individually.The "dungeons" and "caves" almost all look the same.  There's like 1 "dungeon" in this that is noticeably different from the others, but I would've appreciated a bit more visual variety amongst the "dungeons" and "caves" you explore.I was really expecting the final boss to have 2 phases: 1 which you fight on foot and another you fight on the sea while you're piloting your ship.  That didn't happen (or at least, it didn't happen in the true ending route).There's not really much to complain about with this game.  While I wouldn't say anything about it is outstanding, its a perfectly functional and enjoyable little title, and it does feel like step up from Cat Quest 2.  I am curious how they'll step it up for Cat Quest IV (spoiler: the true ending strongly implies that the devs will try to make a Cat Quest IV)

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good Cat Quest game, just... not as good as CQ2.I played this directly after CQ2 and I missed a lot of what CQ2 had; they say the overworld map is bigger, but a LOT of it is just open space, ocean between places; most of the spells are forgettable, and equipping them is more awkward than CQ1/2; there's just a lot less places to find and explore, probably coz so much of the map is just open water, and what is there is super-obvious because it's "not water"; the ship and the ship combat are very simple and not a major addition ....just go in circles a lot... and don't really involve "upgrading" anything, just finding and equipping blueprints; the story is even simpler and kind of hackneyed, with overly-simple, derivative characters... I could go on.I also didn't like the parts that force you into a side-scrolling action event when you don't have a way to jump. One boss is the absolute worst example, because you absolutely MUST use a shield, apparently.Instead of scattered challenge shrines, there's one central place that does endless timed combat waves for random loot, which wouldn't be so bad except you can only really complete one or two of the collection achievements there, which means hoping you randomly get what you need every three rounds. I do like the design of it well enough for the CQ setting, but as an "only real challenge shrine" with only random loot, it's a bit of a let-down.But it's an "okay" addition to the CQ series, and keeps the story moving forward. I would suggest getting it on sale, though; thankfully, I got it 17% off and already had $12 in credit, so it only cost me about ~$5, and I beat it and found and did almost everything in ~13 hours.Here's hoping maybe CQ4 takes a page from Skyrim and the like... big, open world, tons of places to explore and things to see, all sorts of characters to meet and things to do. Skills. Crafting. More than one should expect from a CQ game, I know... but I'd at least like to see a step forward from CQ2, and not just a step sorta-sideways.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely adored this game. Nearly all of my time spent on Cat Quest III was on my Steam Deck, while I was on the road.This is my first Cat Quest game and was pleasantly surprised, especially with the combat and some level of build crafting. Though once you get a specific armor set and some relics, you're going to be overpowered and unstoppable; Your choices at the end will mostly boil down to "become super strong" or "become super tanky and kinda strong".I enjoyed the art style - the storybook aesthetic really appealed to me. Though at first I was slightly confused at the world-map open world, it slowly clicked and made sense eventually. Exploring the world with the ship doesn't take too long, and there isn't that much scattered in the sea. Don't expect a huge amount of scattered icons and "goodies" on the map, a lot of it is handcrafted and useful to you.As for the story, it's not deep, but I don't think it's bad either. In the end it does its job enough to make me feel kind of warm and fuzzy inside. There's not enough games that just make you feel good throughout your swashbuckling adventure - this one does. The numerous puns present in the dialog and item descriptions are also welcome, and they surely made me chuckle on a few occasions.The bounty system made me think there were going to be more bosses in the story but for the most part, they are the story bosses. Some of them are optional, but the coins you'll get from them are kind of necessary to make progress less painful through upgrades, at least on the Normal difficulty.As a whole, I thoroughly enjoyed Cat Quest III. It's on the shorter side, but I didn't really feel it's briefness since I was usually on the move. But for those that really sit down and take-in their games, this might feel much too expedient. Even so, the short time I spent with it was a lot of fun. I'm excited to try the NG+ mode some day.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is in mind with my best friend that i played it with.You will never feel bothered, really. You never have to look what you did in order to track your progress, it's very fluent.  Go into any dungeon, see if you can complete it and if you don't, just go somewhere else first.Scaling here is not exponential, it seems. I, as a level 22 should'nt be able to slay a lvl 40 boss. I absolutely did. What i expected was a lot of deaths, trying to get past something i shouldn't be able to. As a lvl 30 just running through a lvl 60 dungeon, which is the highest in the first playthrough is not really a problem here. We could defeat the Piratking when we haven't even been going forward the main questline. Just sailing around. Having fun. I didn't want to break the game, so we did not kill the king in that moment.But all the enemies here are no problem at all. The only problem that you could encounter, is that the ship goes down in an instant. That's it. But you're as fast as high lvl enemies, have high dodge rate and just take no damage if you wanted to. Take 2-3 hits, you still are able to dodge away, heal and go back. They don't immediatly heal when they are deaggro'd. So you can go back and forth, if you wanted.Bosses don't really feel like bosses. It's much harder having a load of enemies in one spot than beating the endboss. What's even the point of having those, then? At least provide a challenge, like the rubber ducky of death. As i said before, you can just go through much higher level dungeons than you are supposed to, making that not challenging as well.Resident Evil Revelations like scaling. Have a 10 level enemy higher and you're in big trouble, have a 15 level higher, almost impossible, have a 20 level higher, yup. You're doomed. That's what i like to see when dealing with levels. Exponential growth. Here, you can go as a level 22 through level 40 dungeons as if it's no problem and they give much more exp as well. You level faster by wanting difficulty than you can say "boring" when that same level is now just going at it and punch through.All in all, great game. Great story, if i wouldn't be able to time travel by looking for challenges. That's a me problem, tho. Great story, nonetheless. Weapons feel good, especially shields are very funny to work with. My favourite is the fire shield, that just throws fire at the enemies, when blocking their attacks. Fun gameplay. It was good. Really. _childDocuments_.review: Cat Quest 3 is a delightful continuation of the beloved series, offering a purrfect blend of humor, adventure, and engaging gameplay. Developed by The Gentlebros, this installment takes players on a high-seas adventure with a pirate twist, adding a fresh layer of excitement to the familiar open-world catventure.Storyline and CharactersThe game kicks off with a dramatic cutscene where a kitten, marked as a Seeker, is set adrift after a pirate attack. Raised by Captain Cappey, the protagonist embarks on a quest to find the legendary North Star. The narrative is filled with whimsical humor and quirky characters, making it both engaging and heartwarming.Gameplay and MechanicsCat Quest 3 introduces new gameplay elements like sailing and naval battles, which add depth and variety to the exploration. The combat system remains intuitive and satisfying, with upgradable gear and spells enhancing the player’s experience12. The open-world design encourages exploration, with hidden treasures and side quests that keep the adventure lively.Visuals and SoundThe game’s vibrant art style and charming character designs are visually appealing, immersing players in a whimsical world. The soundtrack complements the adventurous spirit of the game, adding to the overall enjoyment.Pros and ConsPros:Humor and Narrative: Perfectly spaced humor and a compelling storyline.Gameplay Mechanics: Smooth combat, upgradable gear, and the addition of a pirate ship for exploration.Visual Appeal: Bright, colorful graphics and charming character designs.Cons:Multiplayer Limitations: No online multiplayer, only local co-opOverall ExperienceCat Quest 3 is a fun-sized action RPG that manages to be both approachable and deeply engaging. Whether you’re a longtime fan or new to the series, this game offers a delightful adventure filled with charm, humor, and plenty of feline fun

_childDocuments_.review: My impressions of the game changed a lot throughout my time playing, and CQIII went from being an okay game in the series to my favorite one.- better graphics, smooth combat/gameplay, stunning visuals- I'm disappointed there're no longer emoticons above characters like there were in CQII- map is much smaller, feels more like "small open world of archipelagos" than "vast open seas"- loved certain ideas/concepts/gameplay in quests and areas of the map- loved the puns (like always)- don't like lack of dungeons- not a lot to do (much smaller amount of quests, more tasks to complete in each; very few caves/dungeons other than main quests)- quests, dungeons, combat, tasks mostly limited to a small number or confined to specific locations  - (in previous games, could enter what felt like 20-30 dungeons/trials in a single landmass - lots of options for lower/middle/higher levels - they were more clustered than isolated although they were all spread around the map)  - now feels like at most 2 dungeons/caves on 1 island, and less than 10 in the entire map- chests almost entirely confined to rewards from completing quests and finding hidden secrets (I like hidden secrets from discoveries; I don't like struggling so much more to find items compared to previous games - I used to just go to the closest dungeon in either location or level difference and just complete them to get rewards)- it felt like I had to keep actively searching for more things to do vs just exploring the world and finding things naturallyOverall, my initial impressions were that it was worth the wait, and I had a lot of fun...but it was partially an empty experience. I felt like I was missing (out on) something a lot of the time.- CQIII might be my favorite in the series. A lot of the critiques or things I didn't like initially didn't bother me as much after I had completed most of the game.- I still love the improvement in graphics and the quality of life features like being able to switch weapons without going into the inventory menu to manually switch it out, and also the manual speed up option for almost all of the dialogue and cutscenes. (This was one of the things I wish had been available in the previous two games, but I'm happy we have it now.)- One of the things I still don't like is the removal of emoticons, but I do like the shaky text that comes up when there's an extreme reaction to an event or news so the game doesn't feel completely devoid of emotion.- The map being so much smaller doesn't bother me as much anymore since it's much easier to figure out where everything is and to travel all around the map in a short amount of time. (I do wish we had teleport points though.)- There were a couple concepts and side quests that made me love this game. One was the  castle in the upper left of the map and the other was  in the format of a .- I still wish we had more dungeons since there would've been more to do, but I think I actually prefer having fewer quests that last longer vs having many short quests. I loved all of the questlines, compared to the previous games where there were a couple I completely hated.- I still can't believe that the Gentlebros gave us GUNS but it makes purrfect sense since we're pirates and I love the combat mechanic they have.- I loved the other gameplay mechanics implemented for the concept of pirates like being able to steer the ship we stole and shoot cannons and add upgrades to it, and also the bounties, which were more long-term goals to complete alongside the main quest.- I don't like how slow it is to move in water, although the plus side is we can go in the water from the start of the game compared to later on in the previous games.- (After completing everything: I also miss the  casually floating by in the background or just appearing out of nowhere and also  just vibing in the middle of nowhere at the most random times.)I think I would initially rate CQIII a 7/10 but I would bump it up to 9/10 after completing everything. I still wish there was more content but I'm really happy with what we have. My favorite parts were the changes to combat in terms of having different types of weapons and being able to switch between them, the pirate ship and bounties, and the quests.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a great game, even if I enjoyed the first two more. It has less content, but I feel like that's fine, in my opinion it was still worth the amount I paid for it. The ending felt a little abrupt, but I'm sure there cooking something good for the Apawcalypse. Cat Quest IV perhaps? One common complaint is that the map is smaller, and while I learned the size of the map is technically bigger than before, it's clear others have noticed the seeming lack in content compared to the first two. I have also noticed this, but I can still enjoy it even with fewer content, but it sort of feels more like a spinoff than a mainline game. Still, there are some major improvements. The graphics are incredible, much better than the first two. The combat is also as good as last time, which was really good. I really enjoy the shield gameplay and the boat stuff is cool too.      I also like the direction it's heading in regarding the lore. It felt like a natural continuation of the last two games and leads into the eventual Apawcalypse well. I also figured going back to every island to check everything off would be more annoying, but in the end it didn't take too long. The gentlebros easter egg was also awesome, finding the one hole in the seemingly arbitrary boundary was an incredible feeling. I just wish there wasn't another arbitrary boundary after that, how cool would it be to be able to sail out into the open ocean far away from the Purribean without anything stopping you. Well, there might need to be a system to get people back if they get lost, but I feel it would still be worth it.     Onto another somewhat mild complaint, I don't like how the bird poop trinket wasn't hinted at at all. Considering it's required for 100%ing, it feels like the intended way for someone to get this is to just arbitrarily know that if you keep hitting the bird you'll get it. I had to look up a guide to find it, so I guess people could just do that, but it still feels flawed. My main complaint with the game would be that it lacks a sort of Cat Quest charm that came with the last two. Of course, most of the mechanics in the last games are here, it plays like a cat quest game, but that wasn't what I was talking about.     Stuff like random invisible paths, gold chests that couldn't be opened until you fight a random mimic on an island, a cave that only has one starter enemy, luring you into a false sense of security, but the enemy is actually level 200 and a superboss, that stuff is just gone from this part. Well, saying it out loud, some of that sounds like it could be annoying to a new player, so I see why it might have been cut. But still, it feels like a bit of an insult to have lonely isle back without anything notable on it. But who knows, maybe one of the new caves listed on the roadmap will happen to spawn there...    One more thing, but this is cat quest, where are the Quests? I know they still sort of exist, but the fully existing quest format, be it from a quest board(my personal favorite), or a random NPC, quests just felt more official and more fleshed out in the other games. Back in the other games, questlines like the Kitmas Storyline, the Banished, and Pundoras Box were some of my favorite aspects. Quests here just don't feel as deep as they used to be. But, I guess the old quest structure could get pretty repetitive at times too...    But looking past that, Cat Quest 3 is still a great game and I believe it was worth the price. And I know whatever the Gentlebros are cooking for the sequel is going to be great, even if I might not get to experience it, but that's a different story. Still, this is a solid lineup in the Cat Quest series and it was worth the wait. But if you do make Cat Quest IV, can you drop the Pirate theme? Honestly it was getting kind of annoying by the end. Still, great game.

_childDocuments_.review: Addictive. The dopamine drip is just perfect. It's definitely not as long as cat quest 2, but just as fun. Lots of build variety. Always something new to play with. Their shield mechanics are very interesting - you lose your roll distance, but when you attack with shield and hold, you will block while holding - to block you have to attack. That alone was interesting, but then you have gear which damages enemies when you heal, and also heals you when you block. It's an interesting combo, and some enemies will just murder themselves on your shield if you time it right with long/quick hitting combo attacks. The pirate ship stuff is just ok and wasn't well implemented in coop - both players can control all of the ship at the same time, causing some tug of war. We had the most fun with one player driving and aiming, and the other choosing what ammo to fire and when. The game definitely starts out dumb dumb easy, with bosses and elites basically having one highly telegraphed attack pattern, but once you get deeper in to it, the boss/elite mechanics get more interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Superb and endearing action role-playing game that maintains the comedy and straightforward game play that define the series. _childDocuments_.review: Cat Quest III fixes all the issues I had with the second game, and is just really well polished and enjoyable throughout. It iterates on the previous formula with a new theme; it's an ARPG where you play as a cat with a companion who has a dubious backstory, you hack and slash your way through an overworld (with caves and dungeons, with the addition of 2D levels), increase your gear levels, find new stuff and generally explore the Purribean. The game is full of cat puns as always, and is just a joy to play.- Combat is just as good as always - although I note the complete removal of telegraphing system- Excellent music- Controls are great, as always- Inventory management is much improved- The fixed the major problem with CQ2 - having two player characters on screen at once when playing solo. Now there's only one of you, which is way better- You can swap between ranged and melee at any time- The game tells you how many of the treasures you've found in each area/cave and how many pieces of equipment you've found- All the bosses, and a few other NPCs, have bounty posters in the pub- There are multiple accessory slots for your character and ship to customise your build- There are now some 2D levels in interiors, which adapt the overworld combat style very well- The boat / land transitions are seamless, and it works really well with the combat formula- Fun writing and interesting side quests- Great map- Boat combat is simple and fun- The camera is at a much lower angle than previous games which felt quite strange to start with - it's mainly because of the boat, but it could have switched between the two depending if you were on land or not- Most of the bosses happen in small 2D spaces, which I really didn't like- Although the game is excellent, I still feel like CQ1 was the best in the series - but I think that's because I just enjoyed the original combat system the most
_childDocuments_.name: Cat Quest III

_childDocuments_.review: Cat Quest as a franchise is an interesting case of seeing a dev team grow their skills over time and I fully recommend playing the whole trilogy back to back.Cat Quest 3 in particular shows a number of innovations in both the graphics design and combat overall. This is such a visual step up from 2 it's not even funny and 1... well it's not fair to make the comparison I want to there. For combat, the trinket system opens up new build variety and playstyle customization and the guns feel right at home as a physical ranged option. All the weapon types feel different to play (and even weapons in the same category, going back to the guns) and have their own niches.The story feels more "focused" overall, with every main quest and much of the map space tied to the different pirate factions all searching for the North Star Treasure. Sidequesting is a bit lighter as well to compensate for the reduced scope, but a full "Platinum" run still took 10 hours.At $20 it isn't a bad pickup and replayability will only get better if/when the "Mew Game" options like Cat Quest 1/2 are added for challenge runs. For now, there's a challenge mode horde/boss rush if you don't want to commit to a full New Game+ run.

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved cat quest two this one will be a bit dissapointing, but it is still an all right game.The Game has fun gameplay but the balancing is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AWFUL, half the time you are either way overleveled or way underleveled and the games instructions on where to go to continue quests will leave you running into enemies you are either not prepared for or crush in seconds. I understand that the devs wanted a "you can go wherever you want approach" but then halfarsed the execution of this, at least give me enough quests that I can do in an area so I am leveled enough to go to the higher ones. Then on the flipside as in this game seemingly nothing scales properly you go to other areas and absolutely crush everything even things leveled higher than you (or so you'd think). At the end of the game the last bit is surrounded by level 50 enemies, we cheesed those to get through (we were somewhere in the 40s) and expected a nice hard fight for the ending.... nope the bossfights at the VERY END were easier than the ones surrounding them that we had to cheese, HOW DOES THIS MAKE SENSE? If you want a fun co-op game and haven't played cat quest 2 then play 2 instead of this, it will save you some frustration it is also open world but has a MUCH better flow.Recommendation: Buy on sale/play CQ2 instead

_childDocuments_.review: The best Cat Quest in the series at the moment.Difficulty ★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆☆ (without using nerf items always a too easy)* improved visuals* new puns* biggest map technically* more freedom to explore the open-world than on the prequels* new weapons and fight styles* new sea battles * coop mode (as usual - hope they patch it in to CQ1 too)* a lot of side quests* secret mirror lets you cosmetical change your looks w/o altering effects (awesome!)* infinite tower (dungeon) to test your might* game feels shorter than the other games* world feels smaller (reasons: less dungeons, a lot of water, faster ship travel)* new game+ level gap is automatically chosen (bad idea)* boss fights are most of the time too easy from their game concept* yet again the story and music are not the strong point of the game but both fulfill their purposes good enough* no coop ship control (why not let the second player control tower and fire, the other steers)* max mana is 21, which looks odd on the screen. Make it 20 or 22 please In the prequel you were allowed to choose the level gap of enemies manually, which was way better to start a more interesting run. Now your level cap is raised by 100 and the enemy level 80 each NG+ run you start. Which is leading automatically to an overpowered player the more runs you play. To nerf yourself you have to intentionally use items that debuff you (3 items exists to do that) because the game is (currently) missing a pro mode.The tower is a pretty cool idea. Due to the NG+ mechancis you will automatically get better each NG+ run (which was probably the whole level gap idea of the devs?). And due to some certain items in the game you can virtually get lower the longer you play until you reached max level with your cat and equipuement (lvl 999, 21 magic orbs, level 3 magic). Yet again, magic is overpowered like in former CQ games and key to get very far down in the tower (unless you are max level). I currently reached 179 at lvl 999 and now I am stuck due to the fact that you don't gain lvel ups anymore that help you to grind deeper than usual. This is a bad design. Game should give your virtual refills. So actually if you go for a true hunt for deepness, try not to be over lvl 940 if you ask me.From the visualy and the overall quality Gentlebro did made a big leap this time. And CQ3 is definitely way better than the former games due to a lot of new game mechanics and sidequest ideas that were not so repetitive this time. But the whole game feels shorter than the prequels, unfortunetally. Still had a blast playing it and can recommend it without any doubts. If you are looking for a coop game (couch coop or Remote Play Together) this is also exactly what you are looking for to enjoy with a friend.
_childDocuments_.name: Cat Quest III

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin...I've fallen in love with Cat Quest since the first entry, the story is always wholesome (albeit not very memorable, it's a nice feelgood story though) the art is always beautiful, and the combat is always just complex enough to keep you interested.There's no deep RPG mechanics here, no Diablo/Borderlands like itemization, and the visuals are nothing to brag about, but if you liked Cat Quest and Cat Quest 2, Cat Quest 3 is more of the same but in a good way!The camera is a little more zoomed in that usual, but you get used to it quick, and there's some mechanics not explained well in the game (equipping a shield makes you roll slow, equipping claws makes your roll very fast, etc...) and there is variety between areas in the game, you have your tried and true map like overworld that you walk/swim/use your pirate ship on, you have 2D side scrolling areas, and you have a genuinely great throwback area that I will not spoil here.Items all feel unique with their different special effects and attributes, but one build I felt was particularly broken was a heal build. I became invincible so to speak, at the cost of attack damage, but that build made the game far too easy.all in all if you loved the first two games, I can guarantee you will love this one!

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Cat Quest series since the very beginning, I was definitely excited when I heard that a third game was being released.  I remember rushing home from work on the day that Cat Quest II came out, so that I could download it and immediately start playing.  Truthfully, I am a big fan.One of the things I love best about this series is that it takes cute cat humor and blends it with a genuinely good action RPG experience.  Cat Quest III carries on that tradition in grand fashion.  The new pirate theme allows the game to feel distinctly different from Cat Quest II, which really makes the game stand out in the series.The story, as in the previous game, relates back to the others in the series to form a sort of continuous storyline, however no knowledge of the other games is requires to thoroughly enjoy this one.  It's this kind of attention to detail that makes indie games like this stand out in the very large, bustling crowd of titles coming from small developers.Finally, for those complaining about the length, this game took me just short of 15 hours to complete, which is right in line with what I spent on Cat Quest II.  Overall, I feel absolutely satisfied with Cat Quest III and can't wait for the next installment in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally don't understand why people are losing their ♥♥♥♥ over the fact that it's shorter than Cat Quest 1 and 2. I'm so sorry that not every game you purchase from an indie company made up of under 15 people is not 15-20 hours long. Keep in mind Cat Quest 2 had a lot of updates to it once it came out. They'll probably do the same for this game.     While the game is short, I don't really see it as a negative and i don't really think that's what people should be focusing on, especially if you're a longtime fan.  There are improvements to art, combat, cosmetics, character design, and character movement in CQ3. Imo it's been really heartwarming to watch them grow over the last 7 years. Not to mention the bigass map and the fact they added a boat mechanic! I also really loved how they tied in the lore to CQ 1 and 2. (lol)     My biggest complaint from CQ1 and 2 was the excessively repetitive grind for levels, armor, and 100%ing the game. CQ3 still has a grind, but it doesn't feel as painstakingly long. Is that "grind" shorter than the other CQ games, and other games similar to CQ3? Yes. But I don't really think we should expect a 20 hour equipment/achievement grind from a game about a little yellow cat going on adventures. I really don't get the intensity of certain people's hate for this game, it's literally about a cat. It's not that deep.     Additionally, I feel like the shortness of it and the simple style makes it open to wider audiences, specifically younger gamers. Considering it's also on the Switch, I think it wasn't a horrible move to make it accessible to both veteran gamers and littles.      And of course, the price. Yes it's $20. It was made by like 8 people, and they need to feed themselves.       One thing I will say is the weapons felt a tad unbalanced. As hilarious as it was to watch a cat use a machine gun to kill his enemies, it was... the ONLY weapon I used. The magic also felt wayyy too expendable. By the end of the game you can just strike them 5x and blamg they're goners. I'm not too mad at this tho because of the setting to go back and replay the game at a harder difficulty. It's also helpful in the  The storyline was also a little chaotic and confusing at times, but I also kinda vibed with it because it went with the "chaotic pirate we-do-what-we-want" essence of the game. Excited for more from Gentlebros. Keep in mind everyone hates the most recent sequel installment until another one comes out, then everyone will love CQ3 lmao; keep moving fwd <3

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put, this is a fun, childlike game. It has the same charm as the previous two titles, plus adds in the ability to more easily traverse the entire map by giving you a life raft and a ship. The addition of a pirate ship is fun and some of the new weapon, armor and item mechanics are unique. This said, however, in this installment you really need to feel comfortable punching above your weight class, using tactics such as attack and retreat to defeat enemies easily 20 levels higher than you at times. I'm currently level 47 and a certain location can help you power level to make things easier. Also, the addition of easy water travel has you moving more erratically throughout the world than perhaps is desired. Either way, the developers have delivered a new flavor to the franchise and is worth checking out. If you're new to the franchise, I'd recommend starting with Cat Quest 2. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first two games, you'll probably like this one. I was a fan of both, but each had some weaknesses: a lot of travel time (especially before gaining abilities that let you explore the world freely or getting NG+), a TON of dungeons, sometimes needing to grind xp/gold to advance, and potentially repetitive gameplay. CQ3 is beautifully polished and refined; you start out free to explore the world (after a very quick intro island), can get around FAST, and enemies are more sparse (less grinding and dodging packs), but varied. The new mechanics (pistols, equippable trinkets that grant various effects, a speedy agile pirate ship) work well and are fun. AND, most importantly, it's very fun, filled with silly puns and characters (including rat/rodent ones), callbacks to many mainstays of the series, and has the sweetness of the first two.I saw folks talking about it being short, but I think we need to distinguish between a game not taking a very long time to finish and a game that feels unfinished. I finished the game in 8 hours, but CW3 felt satisfying and complete. It didn't feel like anything was cut or missing from the game (even with yet another cliffhanger ending).I think it may be my favorite of the series so far. It's a bit different, but all the changes are for the benefit of the player, imo, and show a lot of careful design choices. Also, if you really want more time with the game after finishing, NG+ is still very fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Cat Quest so far.  While it's shorter than the previous two, it's also much, much richer.  The combat is much improved, with several types of weapons featuring unique combos and the addition of a second ranged weapon you can swap to on the fly.  New to CQ3 is the ability to equip trinkets that add additional perks, some from previous games and others that are all new.  Enemies are more varied to boot, losing the extremely telegraphed danger circles of the previous titles and instead signalling through animations and sound.  While it's still on the easy side, it's altogether more engaging than the series has ever been.That's not to ignore the puzzles dotted around the map and the much streamlined quest system (which no longer requires you to return to the questgiver between every step, thank you Gentlebros!)  This is the smoothest, prettiest cat on the block now.All of this polish does come at the cost of a reducing playtime.  I finished the game in seven hours, but I say bring on more seven hour games of this quality over the repetitive bloat of Cat Quest 2. _childDocuments_.review: So after a long time Cat Quest 3 is finally out, and this time the theme is Pirates! Your new cat hero wakes up from a slumber and guided by a little spirit is looking for the treasure of the North Star while also facing the tropps of the Pi Rat King. Being a Pirate of course we have a ship to guide which lets us travel real quick across the various islands in order to pursue our quest and we also have guns on our side which is basically works as our ranged attack option, together with some magic wands and of course our always very reliable magic attacks. The rest of the game follows the same formula as always, run around beat some enemies, explore dunqeons, complete quests, gather equipments to create your favourite build and keep going until you reach the end. If it ain't broke don't fix it and surely Cat Quest 3 follows this logic to a T. The only issue I would see in this game is that the emphasis on boat exploration make it feel like the world is a lot smaller tha what we had before purely in the principle that there's more water than earth around, we also have only one major town where you hang out to power up your equipment and magic, and speaking of magic I had a really hard time finding out currency for powering up my spells to the point where I could only max out 3 of them. It's probably to balance out the powerful damage output that comes with a magic build but I feel like the game was a tad too stingy on that front. It took me 10 hours to beat the game with is almost half of what took me to get all the achievements in Cat Quest 2. The developers already let know that the game is going to get some updates and some new dungeons added but I get why some would feel like this is a lesser game from its predecessor due to it's shorter length and the world feeling a smaller than usual. The small world also made me feel like the level scaling was a bit all over the place, I ended up doing a lot of sections underleveled which led me to try and play it as defensively as possible in order to not die quick due to the damage I was taking, mind you the game is still not that hard so if you really want a challenge I recommend going with the hard difficulty out of the game. Honestly despite the fact that this game feels like a blueprint for something bigger that needed to be scaled back for some reason, I still had fun with it and I'm glad Cat Quest is still around to give us a cozy cat puns filled action adventure time. I hope that an eventual Cat Quest 4 can smooth out the sharp edges of this game and combine everything that made all the previous games fun in a neat little package

_childDocuments_.review: Great game that knows exactly what it wants to be and delivers fully on it.Presentation and story are endlessly adorable, replete with positive messaging and never-ending animal puns.My best frame of reference would be a Kirby or a simplified Zelda.  You run around, hit enemies, deliver stuff, solve easy puzzles and get rewarded with equipment that lets you hit harder, faster and more interestingly across melee, ranged and magic.Enemies telegraph attacks very transparently and only ever combine up to two attacks - meaning kids should get challenged but not frustrated. The puzzles only ever have one level of abstraction.If you absolutely want to force difficulty, you can do that too by doing areas you are vastly underleveled for - but the game guides you (including by an actual mechanic) on a very relaxed progression path.On a side note: I was especially impressed that you cannot seem to sequence-break any part of the game - I did try basically anything I could think of on new game +.Worked well on an X-Box Controller (ship controls are mildly frustrating), cannot vouch for keyboard + mouse.Took me about 11 hours to fully complete the game with all achievements and another 3 for the new game + run.I can whole-heartedly recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: I find myself torn when reviewing this game. _childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of the Gentlebros Developers. The first two Cat Quest entries into their 9-pawrt series were so much fun. I am 35 and these games are a nice reminder that its okay to go back and enjoy a simpler, colorful time in my life. Cat Quest 3 has improved on basically every aspect of the first two games. While the game is shorter (same length as Cat Quest 1; about 5 hours), it does introduce New Game + for people who want to experience it over and over again. Each new game adds more difficulty to the game, ala Dark Souls style, by ramping up their level scaling, as well as allowing your gear and spells to obtain higher levels. Combat is a major upgrade, in that you're allowed to swap between a melee and ranged weapon by the click of a button, as well as the typical four-button spell system from the previous games. Dodging is still there, and now with certain weapons, you can pull of timed blocks as well. Honestly, i don't expect much future content outside of "Mew Game Plus" (which lets you choose modifiers for a new run that hinders you or helps you and allows for exclusive rewards), but thats okay. This is a game i can easily see myself picking up time and time again, especially when i need a pick-me-up. Thanks again, Gentlebros!
