_childDocuments_.review: Well I wanted to like this game and thought I'd give it a chance once it went on sale, and frankly yeah I can see why it's got mixed reviews. Uncharacteristically I'm going to need to start with the setbacks on the game because they're the most deleterious part of the collective experience for what, from what I've seen from trailers, is marketed primarily for its  and what it lets you construct.Picture: you've just bought a game titled  that promises capabilities of building wacky war machines of all shapes and sizes, of robot dogs or centaurs or funky spiders, you see parts or potential to recreate something cool you saw, like slamming a car on top of your torso and calling it Megas XLR, or using funky spider legs and big railguns to make an SSC Death's Head. BUT FIRST... you need to do the tutorial for piloting mechs, during which you use a small premade set of mechs for a couple of missions, the first couple of which deliberately prevent you from using certain buttons to practice or discover. Only about after 1-2 hours of that, THEN you finally get a tutorial on how to actually customize your machines. Throughout all of this very little opportunity for experimentation is allotted to the player, and the limit of what your first "custom" mech will look like is basically the same as the default one except with maybe a square piece of armor and an L-shaped piece of armor slapped onto it I Guess. You CAN dismantle the starter models to experiment, sure, but unless you play missions, you won't be able to access the options to buy/craft components from your list of discovered pieces - of which you basically can only expand by picking up enemy drops. Making matters even more convoluted is the fact that the pieces you gather can vary in  (supposedly on the latter, I've yet to find anything yet from all these drops that's larger than S) and even more screwed up is that you can  individual parts to raise their stats - If the goal here is to make builds interchangeable or to encourage experimenting with various different robot shapes, why would you add that as a factor? All through this, the method by which you "grind up EXP" is to go through campaign missions, which really highlight the snails pace at which it narrates your efforts to defend earth from teleporting angel-robot hackers or something. At the very least all the post-killing-everything chatter gives you plenty of time to scrub the entire battlefield for the part pickups and EXP-crates that "train up" your mech's parts.The promise of a game that prides itself on making custom mechs requires you to grind for it, and nowhere are there features to meaningfully share designs or experiment in a sandbox build-mode to see exactly what kind of crazy leg-trains or hamburger mechs you can make.Now you'd expect a game called  to have good tools for making your mechs, right..? Unfortunately the interface is heavily saddled with presumption that you're going to be using chiefly a gamepad for it. Nowhere is there options to map your keys to functions, and instead the keyboard binding seems to just interpret specific (undocumented) keys to certain buttons (I remember something like pressing Shift randomly and it doing something that would've been mapped to my B button on a menu for example.) While this is semi-acceptable for the gameplay loop of actually piloting the mechs, any depth the mech-construction tools that are given to you are saddled with requirements and expectations of using controllers - expect many sliders you have to LMB/RMB to adjust, imprecise HSV color pickers you need to finagle with analog stick + LT + LB?? and long, LONG lists of potential parts you can only sort on filters that won't even be relevant for what is seeming to me like the first 30 missions of the game! (Again! I haven't found a single part that isn't S.)Even more cursed is how the filters for things like Accessories in the Builder and the Research Center aren't even consistent! For whatever reason the creator lets me categorize the parts by things like armor/decoration/lights/etc, but instead when I'm trying to make another copy of a matching Left Shoulder Pad or something, the only things I can sort on in research is  And now I need to sift through an ever growing stack of randomly, opaquely-named Delta-Codpiece Plates to find that matching Shoulder Pad I'm trying to create.Also all made more infuriating is how information regarding certain weapons, body parts, and components are conveying multiple sentences of information on how they work with the . For all I know this might've worked much better with the native language where individual kanji can probably impart a lot more information than letters, but to my knowledge literally the only place to read part information in a sane multi-line block is on the mission-complete screen for drops - where you can't even get a point of reference for how the piece even looks. Also some descriptions just flat-out lie to you what they do, and other aspects of the UI, like the mech's "radar map" of stats are completely nonsensical (I stack 3 bazookas onto a build and it has an "A" ranking in ATK, but then suddenly I add a shotgun and it becomes a "B"? What?) And what the hell is RES? I'm still not even sure why torso even have stats correlating to Boosters when they don't seem to change the listing in the lower-left for Boost duration/power, and apparently the accessories for thrusters that say they "improve boost duration and power" are just flat-out lying - but then apparently the Kinetic Shields and Electromagnetic Shields actually work?? With almost absolutely no preparation and just making missile-boat stacking wide monstrosities that ram into stuff with drills, I consistently get S-Ranks on almost every mission I do on Normal. Maybe I can progress faster if I graduate to Hard, but the thing is that the game's mechanics are described so opaquely on whether things I change actually matter or not, effects on weapons are conveyed so slowly, and because for whatever reason your  are your most important vital organ, is that it's an experience I really don't want to engage with more than I can tolerate. Supposedly just stacking a bunch of accessories on every part does a big part towards increasing your durability (big deal if you're like me and enamored by melee mechs since there's mech contact damage - Forward Facing Drills on my arms  seem to work the best given they don't force me to flail my arms around wildly.) Making weapon copies of the exact same gun on top of eachother (to conceal it's actually six quantum-superimposed shotguns instead of just one) feels like an exploit but gets brutal results where I just one-shot most things my size.You get droves of purple powerup dice to basically cover for any deficiencies your design might have, and there's cases where I've wiped out entire starting waves of enemies before the level intro dialog has even finished. In at least one case in Mission 30, something I did ended up breaking one of the AngelMech's "teleports behind you" scripting and they were just stuck walking in place, unable to be damaged by anything.Whew ok this game some props:RanOutOfLetters.

_childDocuments_.review: So, CMW was a game I was REALLY looking foward to. Let me explain why I was disapointed, as an EDF fan.I played EDF with my friends a LOT, and when I saw a Mech game from the same company, I instantly got super excited because I thought we where going to play "EDF but with Robots".When I saw the negative reviews, I though that it was just a bunch of people who never played EDF, and complained about the game look and gameplay.But when I played it myself, I understood.DON'T expect this game to be as polished as EDF. Yes, the same company, managed to make a game overall worse then their other games, even though some stuff could have been literally COPY/PASTED into this.And why do I compare it to EDF so much? Because it's literally the same kind of game, from the SAME company.What do I mean? Lemme explain:-The animations are super robotic, stiff, even for HUMAN characters. And I mean REALLY stiff, as if no effort was put into it.-Map destruction is awfull. The buildings don't break parts and collapse like on EDF. Here they just receive damage, and when enough damage is received, they just enter through the ground. They don't have not even half of the same dynamic destruction EDF has. And for a mecha game, that is a REALLY  turnoff.-Enemies just "pop" when you defeat them. On EDF, they have sometimes partial destruction, and their bodies remain on the battlefield. Here, they sometimes lose an arm or something, and just disapear after an explosion when you defeat them. It's NOT the same level of satisfaction of when you kill something on EDF.-Mouse control full of deadzones and awfull.The point is, this game doesn't have the level of satisfaction that EDF has when you play it.Even though EDF still looks kinda outdated, it feels smooth and fun to play. Everything that happens is really satisfying and exciting, while Mech Wars is just.... bland.Yeah, you can make cursed and fun robots, but why does it metter if when you gotta play the game, it is just boring and bland?It makes me really sad... no, actually, it makes me angry. Stuff that could've literally have been copy-pasted from other games, and they still managed to get it wrong. I wonder if they can update it in the future. But right now, don't waste your money on it. Go buy EDF 5 or 4.1, which is way more fun to play.Might go back to it if they get a 75% promo in the future. But right now, it's simply... dissapointing...

_childDocuments_.review: There are basically 2 things going against this game right now: 1) The price tag: as of time of writing this game is going for 45 usd, which is way too overpriced for a game like this. This is a 25 usd game, wait for it to go on sale if you want to pick it up2) It released in the same year as Armored core 6, and thus invites comparisons that it has no way of matching. This game isn't AC6 and if you go in expecting AC6 but with lego style customization you will be sorely dissapointedApart from those two issues, it's a charming little game with a fun core gameplay loop where you go on missions to gather more parts to build better robots to go on tougher missions with. The missions are easy enough that you don't feel compelled to ignore cosmetic appeal to pursue max meta, but at the same time it's difficult enough that some thought need to go into your robot. The customization really is the key selling point here, it's freeform enough that you can replicate the look of any robot you imagine given enough time, but if you just want to build a robot that can carry 10 miniguns in a hurryt, you don't need to fiddle around too much to get just that.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited for this game and really want to be able to recommend it but I can't as of right now at least. The customization is fantastic though. Really hope they try this again one day and build upon that. I'd honestly be okay with this game if they just gave you everything all in the beginning and it was just a mech building / testing simulator. The biggest issue for me is the aiming. I have permanent tendonitis so I struggle to make precise motions with just about anything but this is probably the worst offender I've dealt with. The targets are absolutely miniscule and the control stick sensitivity is all over the place. Mouse isn't any better cause THERE'S A DEADZONE ON THE MOUSE. Who does that?! You can sort of get used to it but the effort plus just how many enemies there are in each stage just absolutely destroys my hands.Besides that, the gameplay is an absolute slog with unskippable cutscenes and essentially the same mission 15 times in a row in the same areas to start with. The enemies just either move / shoot toward you or the dummy you can activate and that is the height of their intelligence. I wanted to at least unlock a bunch of parts so I could make a goofy mech and the missions DO kind of pick up after a dozen or so but I was too exasperated by that point and sort of lost any momentum I had for the game. I did actually get to try out some interesting configurations but it turns out a lot of the leg pieces are buggy or broken. Like the tank treads get stuck facing certain directions sometimes. Makes me sad.I really do hope they make a sequel to this one day, it's a great idea and parts of it were implemented really well. This just isn't the one.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun, but ruined by some flaws.1. Poorly port to PC. The menu control is frustrating. And you can't fine aim in game. (My mouse is working perfectly)There is a chance to freeze the game in intermission menu, you can only terminate the game by task manager.2. Lack of content. From the same developer of EDF, I had already expected the same play style. You customize your mech, take a sortie, destroy and targets, and so on. Some how the execution is poor. I don't know how to explain but it felt more boring than EDF. The atmosphere is not filled with different emotion like EDF, nor full of cold calculation like Armored Core 6.3. Super heavy grinding. Even you want to customize your mech, you have so few parts to start with. To unlock new parts you can only beat a level and get random loots. This exhaust the passion of the player so much.4. Graphic quality. The game requires less than 6GB. Even EDF requires more than 20GB of disk space, while its character are not able to be customized like this. A mech game with so many parts only have 1/4 of the size of EDF, it is certain to be bad.I hate to say it but this game does not worth its price. It would be considerable if on 50% off sale or lower.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning, this game is not playable with m/kb. The devs very clearly have never ever played a game using mouse.There is forced acceleration in this game called "Variable Perspective Speed". The lowest setting is 1. If you move your mouse slightly to the side, just wiggle it back and forth, you will suddenly immediately make a 90-180 degree spin.Its like the devs thought people wanted extremely low sensitivity in a very small deadzone center screen and the second we aim outside that we want EXTREMELY high sensitivity. its some weird controller logic, and it makes it unplayable.I am an EDF lover, i am okay with yanky ♥♥♥♥, I was looking forward to trying out the customization etc, but the controls are so god awful I honestly couldnt get through the tutorial and even get to trying customization. You'd rather be playing Counter-Strike with a 1990s ball mouse that had its ball previously rolled in soda to get all sticky and ♥♥♥♥ than try to just look around in this game.Oh its also worth mentioning the game does not support 2560x1440, it jumped from 1920x1080 to one of the 4k formats (cant recall which).If the devs decide to stop their experiment with the worst possible implementation of camera control ever then I'll revisit this title. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fairly in-depth mech customiser that manages to hit that sweet spot between customisation and over-complication without getting so demanding that it turns some away from itself the way games like mechwarrior do. It's a lot of fun, it's simple, and you can choose between difficulties so as to not lock any good times behind any kind of "skill wall" or deny any more serious players their challenge. It's only flaw (if any), is that it can start to feel kind of generic what your approach should be (hint: overwhelming firepower) for any given situation, but in a way that also means the different approaches a player can build their mech to take should all be at least decently effective. It also means that if you think for yourself and keep trying new things instead of just hoping the game will tell you what loadouts to use, you won't get bored for quite a while lol.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr Wait for a sale and some patches, and this game will be great with friends.---------------It's not that this game is BAD, it's that it's currently nonfunctional. There's myriad problems with controlling the camera; though the devs thankfully fixed the mouse look issues you still can't easily look at your mech in the hangar, for example. The game doesn't properly register some inputs, a lot of the "how" of mech weaponry is not well-explained at all, and the menu controls are much jankier than they are in EDF.Here's the thing: If you're an EDF player coming to this game, you know that D3's games are just *like this*. They're janky, there's always SOMETHING wrong with them on release. This port will almost certainly get cleaned up through a combination of patches, mods and configuration options that come together to make something that's at least sort of playable and, with the right combination of people, some of the best multiplayer you'll ever have. It's just that right now, this isn't that game.If you really want to play this game but don't want to risk wasting your money, I would wait for a sale because by the time the game goes on sale for a fair amount off (I'm talking 40-50% minimum), a few things will have happened:- EDF 6 will have released, so interest in this type of game will spike for a bit- The game will have been patched, likely multiple times more, to address bugs and grievances- The reviews will have balanced out a little, with more recent reviews giving an assessment of what it's like post-launchI'm pretty confident that this game will get there eventually. I can see just from how little of it I actually got to play that the potential for this game to be really good is buried in here somewhere, it just needs more time to bake. I had fun with it, I just wasn't able to do the things I wanted to do with it when I tried it.I'm being an apologist for a game that had serious issues on launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I decided to give this game a solid go before coming here to make this review.Aside from the insane price tag this game has, this is by far the worst game I have played, and i go into details why i think that.prepare yourselves, text wall ahoy...Firstly, the campaign is... awful, I got to around mission 5 and was already disinterested in it, it's difficult to connect to any of these characters throughout the game. more so when in all the 40 missions they repeat so many lines that are the exact same lines... again and again. which can really grind your gears after awhile.The story is rather strange and seems to throw itself off the tracks around mission 30 in some weird twist.But as for context i leave that up to you to find out, no real spoilers for those who care.but i will say the ending was horrible, and i now have a permanent frown on my face when seeing it or remembering it...Then there is the Grind!, you want to repeat missions to farm for some gear at the early stages of the game, as any good gamer who would know this is help make tough missions bearable, however all missions take forever to finish up when the last hostile mech is destroyed, which is fine i guess if you don't pick up all the loot boxes throughout the whole fighting. but when you already have grab everything you could be waiting 45 seconds to a minute, or more.Also the AI is terrible, and the friendly AI just as bad if not worse, they are pretty much worthless in terms of combat ability and half the time getting in your way and dying instantly to you, or to the enemy cause they as are weak as the starting mech is, as for hostile mechs, some don't even see you from certain distances, and well, AI is Janky, when in combat, just hold A or D and circle them, you will win 99% of the time.Leading off from that, the bread and butter of the game is the mech creation, Now at first it's boring and empty, you can't even make anything interesting. cause you have jack all to start with, but you do eventually get enough to make something interesting (waaaaay down the line), However there is a downside with all this,*EDIT* the actual creation of your mech is actually pretty good, i did make a decent looking mech which i was satisfied with in appearance,  But it just gets messy quickly after awhile though, after adding more and more to it. that is the only really upside about it is the freedom of what you can put on (almost).*Now after awhile you start to collect lots of things and you might noticed quickly that there are many types of the same thing.because say, we got this 1 gun. now lets make that in 3 different sizes. now give them stars for tiers. you now have many  different versions of the same type of gun. in a list. with everything else with the same format of small, medium and large. and 5 tiers. cluttered together. it's a complete nightmare to navigate through it and half the time it picks something else from the thing you wanted! Janky as hell and the filters barely make it any better, (they only allow one filter at a time?!)Moving along, in the main menu (why it there and not together with the mech creation is beyond me) there is also RnD where you can make items but only items you have collected from drops.or captured mechs (not worth trying to capture just don't do it) but here is something strange about it.you earn funds, and materials. 3 of which you might never actually use.because only small made objects only go from 1 star to 5 star.but medium goes from tier 3 to 5 ( if i remember correctly?) and large 4 to 5.Which means you can't even use half of the materials with bigger versions parts which are really expensive to make, but really just play nightmare you only get large and medium size parts there, HOWEVER...medium and large mechs you pilot are painful in a lot of aspects. sorry more downsides again.being in a massive mech you find out your just gonna get shot in the legs and die extremely quick, cause your movement is awfully slow and painful, and well your a massive target who can not avoid damage.you also will have hell of a time hitting small targets, even with your lock on ranged missiles, they don't seem to work well being on a huge mech.So only small mechs really have any advantage or rather any chance of getting anywhere without being destroyed to quickly by small swarming mechs, or massive weapons from afar.Speed and movement is your only defence, like Armored Core! treat it the same way. then we come to talk about game play stuff, half  of it i kinda already covered up above by mentions.lets just skip the rating system, i don't think anyone knows why you get given S rank on everything.However let talk difficulty.The game goes  ahead and states you don't even want to touch nightmare mode due to being difficult.Those who played EDF like me, would look back and think on the good old times playing EDF, like this would hit that spot where the difficult is rough and harsh and make you want to push yourself to your limits. . . sorry nope.The nightmare difficulty is a straight up joke in comparison to EDF.I went from the recommended normal difficulty to nightmare and smashed through nightmare with a small mech with ok-ish guns and with minor issues to be found, you only need 1 mech to do these too, rarely would you need a second back up, cause your first was destroyed by that random insta death laser from janky mini bosses. it was disappointing really, i wanted there to be new enemies or more in total, but no, same enemies and same numbers as it were in normal difficulty.I only had one issue on one mission in nightmare.And that is only cause it was a defence mission which you gotta protect buildings and getting swarmed all around in the desert, but that also cause those buildings die in like a few hits so you have to be quick with dealing with all hostile mechs.if anything the enemies on nightmare just seem to shoot 4 times as quick, move 4 times as quick and have 4 times as much HP, which is not really any harder honestly? ( at least for small mechs anyway.)Also if you wanted to play multiplayer with randoms you won't, I have checked many times and never see anyone in there, that or the servers don't exist or people really just don't touch the game, a wise choice move by them! unlike me. . .I'm going to end this review here, I think I have said enough to get the point across. Save your cash lads and lasses. this is not worth getting, I'm going to go cry myself to sleep now.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended with a BUT. In my opinion grab this ONLY if you're in the niche area of customizing mechs and doing crazy things with it, otherwise you might not enjoy it. This isn't Armored Core too to the point where a lot of stats matter when building an AC. Also do consider the price range depending on your region and the replay value; the game as of now only has 40 missions and 10 DLC missions unlike EDF's usual 100 missions, with two other difficulties unlocking and giving you bigger-sized parts after clearing the campaign.As for the gameplay in general, there's a lot of jank going on and there's a lack of enemy variety.Hopefully much later on they'll patch in some more missions. But if you prefer stuff like MASS Builder or Gundam Breaker 1-3, you can easily spend hours making your favorite mech or your own creations once you've gotten used to its customization system. It had a pretty bad launch but the devs are continuously working on the game for improvements, and most of the problems from back then have been already patched.

_childDocuments_.review: If you know D3, you know their games are almost always janky in some way, and they seems to have a habbit of reusing assets repeatedly, buuuut> The camera controls are very inconsistent. Sometimes it moves just fine, sometimes there is extreme delay in starting and stopping movement>Some of the weapons require you to be sighted in to use. While some are strong, they all run into the issues above with the camera, making accurate aim attrocious>The movement is snappy. Not as in it feels good, but it snaps from one pose to annother, with very little smoothing between animations>At launch the game was very sparse with rewards, now the rewards are.. serviceable, but the actual items you get rarely feel like they're exciting or fun. Most being just a +1 version of your starter gun>Melee is awful. Just full stop. Instead of actually feeling like your swinging a weapon it plays a preset animation set and locks you to it.>The locations are extremely unvaried, even for a D3 game. If you've come to build a mech and have a ton of fun, might be your game.Start on Hard if you want the tutorial missions to feel somewhat threatening and want to feel like you're not an unstoppable murder machine.I will say the moment you lower your guard something will tear your arms off, and the game fools you into thinking it's overly easy so they can tear your arms off.Options wise, the games a port. _childDocuments_.review: *With the latest patches, aiming with the mouse is in a better spot then it was during launch. So a lot of reviews about the mouse acceleration and dead zone are a bit outdated. Just go into the setting and set "Variable Perspective speed" to off.If you are the creative type that like to build and create elaborate things while also wanting some kind of playground to use said creation, this is the game for you. If you can dream of a mech design, chances are you can make it in this game. Want to make a mech with more Dakka then Gundam Heavyarms and Full Armored Unicorn? It is very possible to do so in Custom Mech Wars. 6 Gatling guns, 4 Bazooka, and enough missile pods to fire a 30 missile volley with each lock on, what you can make and do is near endless. Now for the con. If you are just looking for a shoot'em up type of game or horde shooter, this game is not for you. This is not Armored Core 6 nor is it Earth Defense Force. The best way I can describe the gameplay difficulty is, Child friendly but can get frustrating at times due to damage spike during higher game difficulty if you aren't prepared. Highly recommend skipping to hard mode as soon as you have your custom mech loadout up and running. The game on Normal is just dull.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite having a different title and settings, this is still an EDF game and you're still fighting bugs(the computer kind)The game is building mechs with the vast customization and testing it on some mission/scenarios. The main gameplay is the mech building not the mission/scenarios. The missions helps you collect parts and stuff, you can "capture" the mech you fight on the mission too(capturing the whole mech only to get 1 part of the mech is lame).Story is there for flavorings on doing missions, music and sounds are pretty good(hopefully the bug where sound didn't play if there's too much thing happening is fixed)ControlsIn missions/battle : If you've experienced playing fencer in EDF5 without using exoskeletons and doing fine you won't have a problem with the controls here.In menu : sucks major balls, especially when building mechs, you can't use your mouse to pan around/zoom the mech you're building using the mouse, keyboard only sucksThere 40 main story mission and 10 dlc mission all of them is very shortThe main meat of the game the mech building. There's no stopping you from building anything(except if you didn't have the parts yet). You can individually color every single part of the mech, there's even a texture modifying to make your mech looks shiny like a mirror or weathered and battered. But there's still a limit of stuff like 10 weapons of each type (there's 4 type : main, lock-on, melee, auto)I reccomend this for mech builder enthusisast, if looking for main story/coop experience i don't reccomend this game

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people are ragging on this game for technical reasons, and some of them are right. The deadzone on the mouse is crazy bad.However, the game runs smoothly, and it's FUN! Not in a challenging way per-se even at high difficulty. Combat is pretty basic to start with. Point and shoot, launch some missiles, kill all enemies. Typical if you've played EDF games. The damage system is cool, and like most mech games you can lose arms, etc to damage. What I truly didn't expect is that if you get destroyed you can just hop out and run around until you get a new mech delivered to you. I like that WAY better than how EDF does it where you spend the rest of the mission stuck on the ground hoping someone comes and picks you up.The customization is truly where the game shines. It doesn't care about physics or clipping. Want to have a massive shield on your chest that blocks your face but has a giant cannon coming out? Go right ahead! Want a weapon to float off to the side, disconnected from the body? DO IT! Complete mech customization is here, as long as the weight of everything isn't too heavy for the legs.Naturally this makes for truly cursed builds if you want, or you can be more reasonable. One thing I've already found is there really isn't a limit to the number of weapons you equip. If you want 40 guns all firing when you pull the trigger, you can do that. It does however make the game pretty easy when you do that.Overall, on a day one game, It's pretty solid. The multiplayer lobby has been having issues, but that's typical day-one launch stuff. I got into one game and had a blast. Single player is just the same missions just like EDF.

_childDocuments_.review: The straw that broke the camel's back:  If you make a private, friends-only lobby, this game will spam invites to people who don't have the game, but not to ones that do.  Like, this is just rank, amateur code.  It is fundamentally broken bull excrement.  You can't trigger this yourself, it's gonna do it when it's good and ready.But there's so much more broken with this thing.  Look, folks, I had desperately high hopes for this, I may even have done a few lines of copium, but I've just spent 10+ minutes going down my friendslist and apologizing for the spam.Straight up, this game isn't just janky, it's shambolic.  It's got ambition, sure, but if there was no UI testing at all I wouldn't be surprised.  Who needs to test menus to see if they work?  NOT THESE GUYS.  Testing is for nancies that like fancy things like "working code" and "functional experiences".Menu systems don't always respect the buttons you press.  If you get partway into a chain of context-sensitive actions (changing your colour, accidentally selecting the chat menu for instance), you're stuck until you bang enter enough times to get through it.  It won't let you back out... reliably, anyway.  It felt like programming by first-year students, the arrogant sorts who claim they can make a game in 30 seconds but can barely program "Hello World" without syntax errors.Keybinds are really limited. If you don't want to use WASD for movement, then you better have a controller because that is literally your only other option.  Though all the support buttons (dashing, etc.) those were easily changed.  So I have no idea what anybody was thinking.  Was there thinking?  The only thing consistent about this game is how inconsistent it all is.As for the game itself, if you are driving vehicle-types in combat and keep holding forward, but turn rapidly, sometimes you are now moving backwards.  You can quickly release W and hold again and you're back to being forward, and yeah okay sports cars and trains as "legs" are kind of outside the normal realm of giant robots, but if you're going to put it in, make it work right.  In the grand scale of things, fine, that's not the biggest sin, but it's the little cherry on top.  The *details*.The graphics?  Right, EDF's graphics weren't great.  These are worse.  Fairly bland terrain, unremarkable cities, buildings that maybe shake a bit as they sink into the earth, not even leaving a heap of rubble behind.  Maybe all the effort was invested on the robot parts, but two fewer parts for scenery that was worth looking at would be okay.There are systems that aren't even explained.  "Hey, we've given you the means to capture robots!" they tell you.  But never say how it's done.  Somebody on the forums figured it out, it involves a weapon swap-up.  Great.  Good information to know, should the game have mentioned it.Positives:  uhh, you can build yourself a robot.  And you can be pretty silly with it.  Though since they don't start you off with a lot of parts, you're basically going to staple legs to train cars to start off with.  If you have a dream vision of a robot to build, just hang on to it and cherish it.  You'll unlock parts over the course of your gameplay, maybe you'll get it then.MAYBE this game will get patched up, maybe.  D3Publisher hasn't done that sort of thing before, but there's always a first time for everything.  But folks, this game, right now, is rubbish.  I don't like dunking on things like this, but it seriously needed another several months of severe UI testing, and I really want stern words with the guy who thought randomly spamming invites was a good idea.  By "stern words" I mean I'm going to do some shouting until I get it out of my system.Maybe get it on sale.  Maybe they'll have patched up the worst of it.  But right now, you have absolutely got to be mad.  I've gone past the two hours limit and am asking for a refund anyway.

To me, the appeal is the mech builder. This isn't mass builder, but the customization is solid and you can make some pretty unique stuff. The core gameplay is a bit bland, but it's more about collecting parts and capturing enemy mechs so that you have the most toys to work with when building. If you put enough weapons on your mechs, the missions go pretty quick even at higher difficulties. Weapon progression is pretty good so far, although the variety isn't crazy early on; EDF fans should be used to this.Given how fast the devs patched the launch issues, most of the jank with the game will probably be ironed out over the next several weeks. _childDocuments_.review: This game gets a lot of negative reviews but I think it's largely misunderstood. More than anything, it's just a more expensive and HD PS2 simple series game. Rather than people who only like EDF 4.1 and 5, this is more in line with the first three titles and will be enjoyed by people who specifically want the janky charm of the simple series. Yes it looks like a PS3 game, the gameplay isn't too much to write home about and it's repetitive. To me that sounds like the perfect PS2-era shovelware for the modern day and I'm really happy to be able to play something like this today.If you want a proper good mecha action game then look elsewhere. If you want something really stupid but focused on one experimental and weird mechanic then you might like this. I would much rather spend £40 on this budget title than £70 on whatever new AAA wank just came out. Budget AA games costing more is just a sad fact of the industry, where they don't get the attention that AAA or indie titles get. I hope that the reviews don't put them off of making a sequel that irons out some of its problems.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not EDF. This game feels like a tech demo.Technical issues:The game has a bit of a rough translation. The dialogue seems okay but some of the menus and especially the settings can leave you unsure what a setting even does.The game has hard-coded joystick dead-zones and acceleration. That is fine if your playing with a controller. But have you ever tried use a mouse to aim with joystick dead-zones? You can't, it's an awful experience. If you do plan on getting this against the communities better judgment I would forget that this game even suggests it supports mouse and keyboard, this game is only playable worth a damn with a controller.Gameplay issues:For reference I completed 10% of the levels before refunding the game. With that in mind, almost every single level boils down to "kill 10-20 robots over and over in waves until the game decides your done".Ignoring the issues other people mention regarding the irrelevancy of the different weapon types themselves (I don't understand why the grenade launcher even exists), having such small packs attack you AND having them spawn randomly on the map means if your playing on normal you may actually spend more time flying from pack of enemies to pack of enemies then you will spend killing them.Conclusion:The concept of this game could be fun, it just feels unfinished. EDF shows us a game can have each combat boil down to "fight a horde of mobs" and be fun, but the hordes being only 10-20 units big in this makes the whole thing feel like a joke. You never have the massive spectacle battles that makes EDF so much fun. Increasing the wave count by 10-20x might help, along with making the mechs slower and the maps a bit more interesting. On that point, the maps are exceedingly dull. I could ignore that if the gained performance was going towards something else like having massive amounts of enemies on screen. The reality however is that mostly you fight a fairly small amount of units at a time in these vast barren wastelands.Bonus note:What is with the size scaling in this game? Like sure, you could just scale mechs up or down to have "bigger or smaller" mechs. But if you add things like trucks and trains, then let us get out of our mechs, it just goes to show how completely bizarre the size scaling is. I put my mech on the back of a truck, got out, and realised my human character was taller then the truck.

_childDocuments_.review: -at full price. Get it when it's at least half off, preferably more. In American dollarinos, it's maybe $20 at best, and that still might be a generous estimate for some folks.To summarize since this review's gotten too lengthy: customization good. Gameplay/graphics/UI bad. Has the opposite 'problem' Armored Core VI has/had, in that it's  easy. Waaaay too easy on normal difficulty even. Get it on sale if you like tinkering. I did, but I still feel like I should have waited for it to be cheaper.Because yes, while I did sink nearly 19 hours as of writing into this game, that does come with the caveat that I'm a bit odd. You look into my workshop submissions, you will find a few dozen submissions to Trailmakers alone, that is to say I like games where I can tinker and build something within the game itself that can then be played with in that game. I'm a glorified digital toymaker in that regard, and with that in mind the customization system of this game is just as the ads would tell you: that is to say, robust.It starts with your standard customizable robot affair, you get a mid-sized roster of frame parts ranging from the expected (different types of torsos, humanoid arms, heads, etc) to the strange (you likely saw them already in the ads: passenger train cars and sedans are available as legs). From there though you can slowly acquire a roster of not only weapons but different accessory additions that can be attached to certain points on your frame parts, then moved/rotated within a fixed area around those points, with the accessories themselves further able to be resized. They even went as far as including not only outright shaped pieces among the accessories, even dummy cockpit pieces straight out of Robo/BattleTech, but a bare biped frame set for the explicit purpose of creating your own unique mech using those available part accessories. Depending on where you place them on the extremities, they'll even flex and move with the limbs.You go through the community screenshots tab of this game, you'll first see a prominent expy of a Macross Tomahawk/BattleTech Warhammer, then mechs and 'bots from no small amount of other properties, Armored Core VI, a lot of Anime, D3's own Earth Defense Force series, even Gipsy Danger of Pacific Rim makes an appearance. Someone else even went and modeled the Sedan legs to resemble one of Toyota's old AE86's, why? So yes, the 'mech customization is great. Brilliant even, if I'm to go that far. So where's the problem? The story was mostly fine. Not great. Passable, up until what feels like a forced sequel hook at the end.  Gameplay wise at normal difficulty at any rate, the enemy and even allied AI are  the brightest bulbs in the pack. What's more I'm told the harder difficulty settings just introduce harder-hitting weapons on your foes, and more of them: more enemies that try to beeline right for your 'bot and blindly shoot at it, at best maybe try to back away to take advantage of the range of their weapons, at worst stand still and take pot shots when you get in range.That's it.(At base,) 40 timed missions of wipe out every rogue mech in the field, who spawn in with a red glowing effect that can be fired upon before they fully spawn. Maybe a handful of missions where we also defend something from those rogue mechs where, honestly, after awhile our weapons are more of a threat to whatever we're defending than these poor bots themselves.Speaking of weapons meanwhile, unlike accessories and more like the frame parts, weapons are  resizable. This isn't too much of an issue, per se; it's when you want to rig, say, missile launchers to your default-sized mechs that some scaling issues become scathingly obvious. Yes, there is an entire frame made to support these super-sized in relation to the frame parts but most of the time missile pods alone will be the size of your mech's entire dang torso and half the legs even.Thankfully, and apparently, you can mix different sizes of part on your mechs, including the weapons. Whenever you can acquire larger parts at any rate. Bringing me to another point, the lack of indication in-game on where or how you can acquire the larger mech parts. I'm assuming at this point it's harder difficulties but at that same point I'm debating if it's worth it for some folks to even redo the missions over on Nightmare at all. Not a good mindset to have when the big selling point of the game is ludicrous customization using those parts!Now, what else can I nitpick...the voicelines seem like a good start. Once you got a good 'mech built you can start wiping out entire waves of enemy mechs in a snap. If you're  to follow the story that may not be a good thing: sometimes you can defeat waves before the previous lines of dialogue finish, triggering  lines of dialogue leaving whatever the last person had to say floating off on the wind, never to be heard/read unless you decide to return to the mission later for some reason.Speaking of dialogue, and I never thought I'd say this, but there's no dub option: your choice, if you can't understand what's being spoken, is to either read what's being said or pay attention to what you're doing so you don't accidentally shoot one of your allies in the knees. Your allies whom, much like the enemy mechs, appear to be made of tissue paper in the face of your weaponry, especially if they catch a good salvo from your guns.It's with all of this in mind, the A"I", the weapon nitpicking, the voiceovers, the gameplay, the PS2 era graphics and destructo physics even: all of this goes on to make me question who in their right mind decided $50 was a fair price for this hot mess of a game? Even the customization system, the main thing that I  like, when rolled in with everything else it makes the whole thing look like someone's proof-of-concept project. A mostly finished, but definitely unpolished proof-of-concept project. Guns when attached to the arms rather than carried by the hands for instance don't use the arm for aiming: they pivot, often weirdly, in the direction of your reticle. Sometimes when pivoting the camera all the way down so you're looking up at your creation in the hangar, the camera will refuse to come back off the floor, instead requiring you to reset the camera's position relative to your creation. Some folks have likely already mentioned this, but you get at most three weapon 'groups' that are mapped to buttons, one dedicated to your main guns, one dedicated to lock-on/subweapons, and one solely for making your mech's arms swing wildly if it's carrying melee weapons. There's a fourth hidden weapon group for main guns when you have to zoom in your camera in order to fire these particular guns: they also fire all your other main guns at the same time, and they often don't have the same range as the guns you can only fire when zoomed in. That's right, crazy amounts of customization and yet no one thought to give players the ability to map weapons to different buttons.So one last time, to reiterate from a layman who's not played any of the EDF games but likes games with customizable vehicles/bots: if you  like games with customizable vehicles/bots, get this one when it's steeply discounted. Steeeeeeeply. If you don't, and if you wanted a nice action game to whittle away a few hours, ehhhhhh...look elsewhere, this ain't it.

_childDocuments_.review: After Playing all 40 mission of this game I will give my opinion on several negative points I experienced from the game in my opinion.-Mouse aiming need some worksThere still some problem with trying to aim with mouse in this game. It's hard to aim precisely because there seems to be some kind of dead zones when aiming even when "Variable Camera Speed" is turned off. I think it is a bug since aiming while in pilot mode feels a lot smoother than in the mech.- Enemy lack quantityThe AI in this game is pretty dumb which is fine since that is expected from a game of this nature, so I expect the game to make up the lack of intelligence with numbers. But the game only spawn a handful of enemies at times instead of spawning everything at once on each waves. While the Medium and large mech enemy quantity per waves is alright, the small mech especially in the first 10 mission, is too few in number. They mostly die in one hit anyway so I feel like spawning more of them would pose no problem for a bit more challenge.-Enemies just appears out of thin airI hate it when I was in the middle of a fight when suddenly a new enemy appears out of thin air right in front of my face. I saw a lot of instances where they drop down from the sky, why not have all of them spawn like that? It's a lot more better than enemy just appearing from thin air.-Leg parts get destroyed too easilyIn this game your mech and the enemy mech get instantly destroyed if your leg or chest part is broken, which makes sense and fair. Except the developer forget the fact that legs part makes up 50% of the mech size, except when you use tank legs. So when you get shot at, 50% of the time it's the leg part that got destroyed. Chest parts doesn't have this problem since they are smaller and usually the arms or head parts will block the shot. This is especially the case with Medium and Large robots since everything and everyone will always go for the legs first. For a game about customizing your robot as you like, being restricted to using only tank legs just for being able to survive playing the game on higher difficulty than normal seems pretty restrictive. I think legs part need to have their HP buffed.Overall I enjoy building my mech, but playing the game is another matter. Out of 40 missions, only the last 10 missions is the one I enjoy since there's more medium and large mech to shot at. But that doesn't justify this game price.I still stand by my opinion that you should wait for this game to go on sale before buying it.

_childDocuments_.review: I got through the first three missions before coming to the conclusion that this is simply a low-quality game which is not worth putting time into, let alone the fifteen dollar sale price.To be clear, I did not have high expectations for this game; all I really wanted was the ability to create a highly customized mech and use it in gameplay in some way.  I suspect that if I had stuck through further into the game, I would have gotten a plethora of weapons and mech parts to customize with, but the experience of progressing was a boring slog.The worst part of my brief experience was that each mission consisted entirely of running up to practically stationary enemies and shooting them, waiting two minutes for trite dialogue to play out, waiting two more minutes for an unskippable cutscene, and then one more round of shooting.  Another unskippable dialogue later, the mission was over.Just about everywhere the developers could have put in effort, they seem to have decided not to:-The voice lines were entirely in Japanese, and English subtitles had frequent typos or simply did not appear.-The lore and dialogue completely lacked substance, and the frequent interruptions to exposit or for characters to talk were just that: interruptions.-Movement felt like it was coded to allow you to move horizontally, boost vertically, and fall to the ground when you stopped boosting, and nothing else.  No effort was made to make the units feel powerful, fast, or heavy, or to make movement feel fluid or fun.-There was a weird acceleration on mouse movement that could not be turned off, and while aiming didn't matter much, it was frequently off-putting.-Just about every element of the game menu, level design, and general game design made the game feel small and artificial; it frequently reminded me that it is a small, low-effort game, and I never felt even slightly like there was a larger universe that I was experiencing.-The customization itself is awkward and difficult; you cannot move the camera to better see what you're doing, and among other things, when I tried to place weapons in the hands of the default humanoid mech, they were stuck at an odd angle and did not respond to the rotation sliders.I don't think that this game is for anyone, and even if it was offered for free, I do not think it would be worth the time it takes to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game, and if you enjoy mech games or Earth Defense Force, it's worth a look. The customization is pretty vast and the options can range from awesome to silly.It has some flaws you should note if you want it though. To use a gamepad, you have to force a Steam override. It's frustrating that you need to do this manually in 2023, but here we are. Don't bother with keyboard and mouse, they feel pretty bad.The controls feel... off. No matter what I do, it's hard to really feel in control. It's like the game enforces a wide analog deadzone and has a pretty sharp movement sensitivity. You can turn the latter down, but the former is hard to work around.While you can mount dozens of weapons, you have almost no control over how they're grouped. You get a primary fire, secondary fire, melee and "critical" button. Weapons of the first three categories auto-assign to that group, and every one on your mech will fire when you push that button. The "critical" button lets you pick exactly one that only works when you push that button.That sounds like a lot of negatives. But to be frank, that's all of them that I've found. The rest of the game is a good time and I enjoy it. If you can get past these problems, you'll have a great time. If the devs fix them or someone makes a mod for them, all the better.

_childDocuments_.review: EDITED after 30hrs of playOne of those "Gets better after 20 hrs" games, wait for a discount.The graphics are a step down from Sandlot's EDF games, often in barren landscapes and cities that feel made out of cardboard boxes. I find this excusable considering the complexity of the mechs, but others might be turned off. Controls are excellent, thankfully, you'll need as much responsiveness as possible for this 3D bullet hell. Gameplay is simple, kill every enemy. If you've played 90's Doom you'll have a good grip on how to maneuver here, and it works well enough. It's fun to visibly dismantle the larger enemies and one-shot delete the smaller ones. I previously complained about how parts damage affects gameplay, but there is a workaround not explained in the game. As your mech is damaged, accessories attached will break off. These accessories take the damage for your more vital parts like the legs and torso, so the game is actively encouraging you to almost scratch-build your mechs, covering them in layers of accessories. I'd prioritize the legs and torso, as your mech will instantly explode when those parts are destroyed regardless of remaining health.Where the game sort of falters is that it has the density and difficulty of EDF, but not the absurd weapons of EDF to counteract what you will face. Anything more flashy than a simple gun has limited ammo and will run out quickly--and there are no reloads in this game. If you run out of ammo, the gun will never fire again for the rest of the mission. In order to win you have to prioritize the very plain guns that you must stack in the dozens to get any reasonable damage output without running out of ammo. Another complaint is that like EDF, the game expects you to spend an absurd amount of time grinding missions, only here instead of you playing because the missions are fun you're playing because resources are extremely scarce and you want the money to build the parts you need. It's fun to build parts and assemble them to mechs, but not when you constantly run out of cash and ore to make them or can't even afford them after 10+ missions.One last complaint is that the game should have taken a tip from Mechwarrior. You can mount DOZENS of weapons on your mech, but it's a bad idea to have more than one low-ammo weapon because you can only pick one weapon to separate from the others. Mechwarrior already solved this problem by having weapon-groupings, multiple weapons that are paired to fire together. CMW instead says all or nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: fun game but has got a lot of polishing to do.the current main issue is the absurd mouse acceleration issue, this single handedly makes aiming a chore and is probably responsible for at least half of the negative reviews.As for graphics, this uses the same engine as EDF 5, which deliberately had reduced graphics as there were quite literally hundreds of insects with their own corpse physics to simulate, however there are not hundreds of enemies on this (at least so far as of level 12)calling this game EDF meets AC6 only works on paper, in action, its combat doesnt quite match armored core, and feels a bit more like EDF where you fire blindly at all the enemies.the progression feels like a mix between EDF 5 and EDF IR where you can find weapons in the battlefield and upgrade, but you can also get resources which can be used to craft specific weapons of specific rarities, so if you have lots of spare resources around, you could craft a part that you already own, but craft it at a higher tier.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to rewrite my review to give a more accurate assessment of how i feel after playing for a few days. So first thing i want to say is that the aiming acceleration can now be toggled off, they released a patch a day after the game launched that fixed that issue. So comments mentioning that specifically as the reason for disliking the game should be seen as outdated. Now for the review.Overall, i would say it is a great game in a niche market that had a rough launch due to some unfortunate oversights that are being corrected. The customization is pretty fantastic and is pretty much as advertised where you can build basically anything you feel like. The weapons are varied and all have a niche they can play with your typical distribution of good-meh-stupid quality of weapons from the EDF series, or you can just do what a friend did and attach six swords to the legs of your spider mech and call it a day.The game had a bit underwhelming combat at first, but honestly so does every EDF game and it takes a bit for it to ramp up, which shouldn't be a shock to any EDF players. It does get harder and its not particularly hard to lose a mech at any given time from my experience, even on normal. It is mosty a horde based game where you have an ungodly amount of ammo for basically every gun in the game, with a few exceptions, and you go around either killing mechs or defending things by killing mechs. It is not a super technical game, and you can make it as hard or as easy for yourself as you really want to. You have 5 mechs per mission and no penalty for them blowing up besides a lower rank at the end of a match (sometimes, damage taken seems to be less important here for scoring) so go nuts. You can call them in pretty much on demand and swap them out at will, they wont repair but they will rearm so its a good idea to swap around if you like using giant laser cannons.There is a few things the game also doesn't tell you about, like the Research Center (where using materials you get from completing every mission you can duplicate or build better versions of the parts you get in battle) and how you can capture mechs while on foot (with a limited number of shots). Another big one is accessories, many of these can provide actual functions like shields, armor, or even stuff like night vision, extra flight time, and higher resistance to stagger. I would recommend to everyone to explore everything in the game for yourself as it may prove useful.Overall the game has a great foundation and is worth the time if you love creating wacky vehicles or strapping 10 rocket launchers to the roof of a bus and calling it combat worthy.

_childDocuments_.review:
Take customization to the extreme with the Omega Customization System and battle with one-of-a-kind combat units in this all-new third-person shooter mecha game.

Not being restricted to bipedal builds, you can freely customize your mechs to include multiple heads, legs, and arms in whatever positions and angles you choose. Depending on the parts you use, the parameters will vary wildly, so you can build mechs with whatever abilities and fighting styles you wish!

Arm your custom mech to the teeth with every weapon imaginable and blast your way through oncoming enemies. _childDocuments_.review: I was negative on this new version of FX at first. The slightly improved graphics, the collectibles/room display, and trophy collecting are all nice bells-and-whistles, but they didn't do much for me. I already had a majority of the library for FX3 and wasn't enthused about repurchasing everything, even with a 50% discount on packs I already owned. During sales, the discounts do stack on top of each other and cut down the repurchasing price to about $1 per table, which is fair to me. The pinball pass subscription is still a terrible value though and should be avoided by everyone.The biggest benefit of this new version is that it's better as a free game than all of the previous versions. In past games, the only way to play tables you didn't have was in short trials. This FX has an event system that allows for 3 to 5 full games (with rule sets like a distance/flip limit or one-ball) of tables you don't own every day in a limited time rotation. That's enough for me to feel like it's worthwhile to recommend this over FX3 to anyone looking for PC pinball.

_childDocuments_.review: edit 10-13-23: It's been 6-months(April 13th, 2023) since Zen released FX4 and the game is still unoptimized. _childDocuments_.review: Pinball FX developed and published by Zen Studios earlier this year is another digital pinball (emphasis on digital) experience from Studio that has been in the game for quite some time.  At the time of the writing of this review a total of 120 tables have been released thus far into this experience. Pricing at time varies, some as low as FREE (some tables do come with the program, but others go up to $14.99 US, and if you buy all the DLC, it can cost you a whopping $499 big ones. So it would be my suggest to purchase what you want on deals and piece-meal your collection together over time.29 - Williams Tables23 - Marvel Studios Tables21 - Star Wars Tables18 - Zen Studios Original Tables6 - Universal Studios Tables 3 - Dreamworks Studios Tables3 - Game Night Pinball Tables   3 - Gearbox Studios Tables3 - Legendary Tables3 - Star Trek Zen Pinball Tables 2 - Peanuts Pinball Tables2 - South Park Tables1 - Nickelodeon Studios Table 1 - Paramount Studios Table 1 - Hasbro Table 1 - Brace Yourself Games TableA fair amount of the tables are carry-overs from previous renditions of the franchise with some new additional content brought into the mix. It appears that Zen has been making quite a few deals to produce these tables for what they are. I like the idea of partnering to develop new content.The overall ideas for each table for the most part look great and add some nostalgia to the game play, but again like previous games, the physics and angles still seem a tad off to real play pinball, which is fine I guess, this game makes no real claims that it can go toe-to-toe with a real machine, but overall, I find it a bit more frustrating than entertaining in my personal opinion.The UI itself for Pinball FX seems fairly straight forward offer several quick navigational options at the top of the screen (HOME-MY TABLES-TOURNAMENTS-EVENTS-COLLECTIBLES-SHOP) as well your personal profile (fully customizable) and Settings.  On the HOME screen you are provided view of your room (more on this to come later in the review). The MY TABLES section contains a complete list of the actual pinball games you own and allows the user to filter yours games down by various means, which comes in quite handy if you do own a lot of tables. TOURNAMENTS offers the user some opportunities to compete with others through various modes where you can either play a tournament or create you own.  EVENTS offers a place to compete for a season(s). COLLECTIBLES is probably the coolest new feature, but you gather these collectibles as you play your tables, each table has 5 and you place them MY TABLES ROOM or TOURNAMENTS (again more to come on this). SHOP offers users the opportunity to purchase BUNDLES (table packs), PINBALL COINS (money you can buy to purchase a PINBALL PASS or PREMIUM COLLECTIBLES for your room. The PROFILE section the user can customize their leader-board avatar (still looking for a better phrase here) and track you PROGRESSION for ACHIEVEMENTS (all 19 for the game) and TABLE AWARDS (these are tracked in sections like Brace Yourself Games Pinball, DreamWorks Pinball, Game Night Pinball, Gearbox Pinball, Hasbro Pinball, Legendary Pinball, Marvel Pinball, Nickelodeon Pinball, Paramount Pinball, Peanuts Pinball, South Park Pinball, Star Trek Pinball, Star Wars Pinball, Universal Pinball, Williams Pinball, and Zen Originals), and PINBALL PASS can be check for status, PERSONAL DATA allows you access to the PRIVACY POLICY and a place to MANAGE YOUR PERSONAL DATA, and last, but certainly not least, the COLLECTOR LEVEL (gives you a way to track the collectibles).Another feature the franchise has given us is the opportunity to play these tables in what we call "Cabinet Mode" and in this mode if you have the proper equipment and/or know-how to to make your own, you can indeed play these tables on your very own pinball cabinet. This is a wonderful option to offer, although like in the previous versions of the game, feels a bit unfinished as I think the developers should be creating back-glasses for the tables and just them incorporate into the cabinet mode, but thanks to the wonderful community this ecosystem has, makes this mode a success in configuring back-glasses and adding the various whatnot's you may need to get your cabinet working. I also feel like Zen taken a big step forward in the fact that you don't have to send pictures of your cabinet to Zen to use cabinet mode, all you need to do now is just activate it. Again, I cannot say enough about the amazing community that has rallied around this game, they are what makes this game survive in my opinion.There is also quite the controversy surrounding this particular installment of the franchise in that it was first released on a different ecosystem, which may or may not have caused the riff within the community when Zen chose to ask its faithful customers to re-purchase all of the tables (most already own a fair amount of these tables in previous games), but again, I don't know the full story (nor do I care at this point, they can do what they do and its ultimately up to the customer if they will reinvest their hard-earned cash (in an otherwise rough time for most consumers this seems a bit of a stretch), but I can see why they chose this, at least partly, Zen has introduced a room idea to this game where you more or less get to decorate your said room with the various accolades and goodies from the games you play, and offers a SHOP to purchase more unique items to make your room what you want, and while this does offer some appeal, for the pricing on the tables, I am not really certain it is worth it, again my opinion.I have no doubt my review will have plenty of scoffers, but hey, its my own and no body will buy my review or change what I feel about it. It is a game and that is all.  Hope to see you all on the leader-boards.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played all of the pinball games/tables from Zen Studios prior to this game and as someone who has experienced all they've had to offer I can say this game is the worst iteration of pinball I've ever played. Pinball FX3 was already a downgrade from Pinball FX2 but this is so much worse than that was... The ball is slow and drifty. The Ui is absolutely awful, from the menu to the camera controls. There are bugs still present in the game from early access that haven't been polished out. Lastly this game is a cash grab through and through. All these downgrades I've mentioned were done to save money and almost all of the DLC was ripped from the Virtual Pinball website or ported from their previous games, meaning adding these tables is very minimal effort/cost. You can tell this is true not only by testing the corresponding tables in Virtual Pinball but simply by comparing the physics in Pinball FX3 and Pinball FX, they are drastically different. Too different for a product boasting accurate physics for over a decade. My advice is if you are a pinball enthusiast either put the effort in to properly use Virtual Pinball, buy Pinball FX3 before it gets removed from the stores, or my favorite option just pirate it. I have a modded XBOX 360 with Pinball FX2 and all the DLC including the discontinued Rocky and Bullwinkle table.

_childDocuments_.review: While I miss the league seasons mechanic from FX3 I find the continuous stream of events with different challenge conditions on a variety of tables to be a lot of fun in the new FX - and I enjoy the collectibles a lot - there are a ton of collectibles. The collectibles feature and the broader array of events are the selling points.  If neither interest you then perhaps it won't be as compelling to make the switch from FX3.  Some things need to get fixed, such as collectibles not being synced between devices - but overall enjoying it.  I am able to have an enjoyable experience on my steam deck although I did need to tweak the settings to reduce shadows and effects a bit on the deck to get smooth game play. Purchasing the tables we already have on FX3 again is annoying, although the 50% legacy discount for tables already owned is helpful.  Some may prefer to wait to get those tables until deeper discount sales are available but not sure how long that will be.  I ended up buying all the tables to be able to enjoy all the events in the new FX ecosystem.  The new pinball pass is an option but if you know you will play for a year or more then just buying them at the discount is more cost effective than the subscription.  There are enhanced graphics - particularly animations.  If you are a purest who is not a fan of animated elements that probably won't be a compelling argument for the new FX.  If you like seeing all of that, well there is more of it in FX.  I enjoy it.  Physics are supposed to be improved but I honestly don't really notice that. _childDocuments_.review: Update: 29Aug23I'm changing my original thumbs-down into a thumbs-up, but with qualifications.  Basically, I'm enjoying the game and believe that most pinball fans will find enjoyment here.  Also, Zen Studios have added a selection of post-process upscaling technologies since release, including DLSS 2, FSR 2.0, and XeSS... which really helps with maintaining a decent framerate while enabling raytracing and HDR.  The "custom" camera options are still extremely limited.  The cabinet mode still tanks in performance when using a second screen as a backglass.  Yes, there are problems and missed opportunities.  However, there have also been tangible improvements and some great Williams tables have been released that I'm having loads of fun with. If I were rating this release on a 10-point scale, I'd say Zen has reached a solid "7" at this point.  ------------Original Review (April 2023)TLDR: Bring some stonking good PC hardware for the raytracing & HDR benefits, otherwise you may as well stick to FX3 for the time being, until further optimisations are made.My vote could go either way on Pinball FX at the present moment.  My own *personal* experience would lean toward a highly-qualified "recommended", but only because I have a rather powerful gaming PC and an HDR display that can do this title justice.  I have an 11th gen i7 processor and a RTX 3070Ti GPU with a 144hz Gsync 1440p HDR display... which is upper mid-tier hardware atm.  I can run Pinball FX with Raytracing and HDR enabled in Portrait/TATE mode at @100-120 fps.... at 70% display scaling (1080p effectively).  This isn't as bad as it sounds, because it would seem that display scaling doesn't affect all rendered elements in a linear fashion.  The playfield texture resolution, for example, seems to maintain 100% (or close) resolution even at 70% scaling, so it's really only the 3D ramps/rails and raytracing elements that seem to lose definition with the reduced scaling.The point is - expect that you'll need to compromise on some settings if you have anything less than an RTX 4090 gpu.  To my mind, 60fps is simply not good enough for natural-feeling pinball.  You will probably have to turn down some settings to hit a smooth, flowing, responsive FPS.  I find that it needs at least a more-or-less consistent 90 FPS before it starts looking/feeling good.  120 FPS or higher is buttery smooth.  And of course, you need to have Vsync disabled, or you will feel the input lag.  Which also means that your display will require variable refresh rate  (VRR/GSync/FreeSync) or you will experience tearing.  Some of this is not Pinball FX's fault, to be fair.This new Pinball FX has exactly 2 things going for it, as compared to the previous Pinball FX3: raytraced lighting and HDR support.  The updated physics are... fine... but I thought they were fine before.  If your PC hardware doesn't have some serious heft to it in order to push raytracing and HDR... well, then... you might as well stick to FX3 imo.But, with raytracing and HDR enabled.... wow.  I mean, it really is quite visually stunning!  Being able to play my two favourite IRL tables of all time in Pinball FX (Twilight Zone and The Addams Family), in portrait mode, with raytracing and HDR enabled.  That's the stuff of my dreams - it's really, really excellent.  I would massively recommend THAT experience.  But you won't get THAT experience unless you come packing a behemoth of a dedicated PC gaming rig, and that's the main reason I can't give a thumbs-up right now.Pinball FX doesn't currently support AMD FSR 2.0 (or higher - 3.0 is releasing soon) and it doesn't support DLSS.  So, enabling raytracing on support hardware will cut your FPS *BY HALF* -seriously!  It feels like a lot more people could enjoy these tables the way they're meant to be enjoyed if this software were to support current upscaling technologies.  Also, Pinball FX claims to finally support custom camera settings for each table.  That's only slightly true.  The settings are incredibly limited to just a few broad camera tilt adjustments at the moment.  That's not proper custom camera support.  Pinball FX claims to have cabinet settings for a separate backglass and DMD positioning.  But if you enable it, the application drops from fullscreen into borderless windowed mode, meaning you're stuck with Windows always-enabled Vsync (input lag!) and a 60 FPS cap.  Lame!There's a lot of potential here for the developers to implement performance-saving image upscaling methods, more granular display settings, proper custom camera settings, and more.  If they do, then I will change my review and give my full heartfelt recommendation.  But, as it stands today, proceed with caution.  There is some absolutely awesome pinball available in here - but have you got the rig and the display to access it?Update 17 April 2023:  A lot of other reviews seem to find the pricing contentious - particularly regarding payment for updates of tables already purchased in Pinball FX3.  There is nuance to this discussion, so I can respect their opinions here.  Personally, I do wish our purchases were cross-platform - other companies manage to accomplish that in this era.  But, my personal opinion is that I do find the "Legacy Upgrade Bundle" 50%-off upgrade offer for those of us who owned FX3 tables to be justifiable.  For example, a 3-pack of upgraded Williams tables works out to being just under £1.50 per upgraded table with the legacy discount.  I would pay that amount for the amount of upgrade work that has been done - not necessarily for the physics tweaks, but for the lighting/HDR/raytracing upgrades.  For now, I've upgraded all my Williams tables and have no regrets about that - they look and play awesome with respect to the caveats mentioned in my full review, above.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a minefield to review, I'll start easy. _childDocuments_.review: Having played many hours on Epic, I'm so happy to see this launch on Steam. The biggest draw to Pinball FX is the updated physics system coming from the prior entry, Pinball FX3. While much of this may feel minor at first, the ball behaves far more consistently across different tables and the challenge on the non simulator pinball tables (i.e, Zen Originals and franchise crossovers) is much faster and weighty. Graphically, it is a solid improvement if you have a capable PC. The ray-tracing is nice, although not mandatory. It is much improved over its early access performance, and I now get around 90FPS with max graphics settings at 1440p with ray-tracing enabled. Hey, it's just nice to see those reflections on the glossy board :-) The elephant in the room is the lack of DLC carryover to the new platform. While unfortunate, I believe this is a passion project geared towards enthusiasts. Recreating each table takes time, so does implementing ray-tracing, updating lighting, and ensuring all of the prior systems work with how the ball and flippers now behave; this is no small feat. Given the DLC packs which discount purchases of updated tables if you already own them on PFX3 (See the legacy bundles), I think it is fair. Zen have provided multiple ways to discount tables and assist long-term players in the transition to the new system. No, you don't *need* to update to Pinball FX if you are happy with Pinball FX3. Keep your purchases there and keep enjoying the game! Those tables are still great. However if you are an enthusiast, you will enjoy playing these tables with their updated physics along with the already hefty amount of new content. I have particularly enjoyed Wrath of the Elder Gods, Grimm Tales, World War Z and the new William's tables (Addams Family, finally!). Two thumbs up from me. Zen have really pulled through after their rocky launch on Epic and I'm excited to see how this platform develops for years to come. Between the Punishinly accurate Williams simulations, the video-gamey Zen Originals and numerous franchise crossovers, I believe Pinball FX has truly become THE hub for Pinball, no matter how you engage with the game.
