_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Good but not good enough (yet)Many of the reviews here fall into 3 camps:1: People who refuse to pay anything for “remastered” tables. I understand feeling fatigue after having bought “the same” tables multiples times on Pinball Arcade and FX3 (and earlier iterations thereof) across multiple platforms. But the tables aren’t the same. They’ve been “remastered”. I’ve no issue with buying remastered tables IF they represent a significant improvement and provide sufficient value for money. Zen are offering a 50% discount on “legacy” tables for people who bought them on Pinball FX3. The question is whether the remastered tables 50% better? Personally I don’t think so. 2: People who say Zen are nice guys who worked hard on the remasters and should therefore automatically be paid for said work. Zen aren’t a charity. They’re owned by Sabre Interactive who are part of the Embracer Group. Zen are not nice guys (would nice guys release the manipulative and microtransaction-laden Williams Pinball app or put out passive-aggressive tweets blaming customers for their inability to implement cross platform purchases?). Also, how hard they work is irrelevant. What matters is whether the end product is good enough and represents value for money. 3 (overlaps with 2): People who bought tables from Epic and had them ported across to Steam. Their positive reviews may be coloured by the fact that tables were cheaper on Epic Game and because Zen gave many of them a significant number of free tables*. You may be getting a much worse deal than those people so bear that in mind.  That’s my preamble done. Now I’ll cover the pros and cons of Pinball FX tables for me. I’m not a pinball expert (far from it) and other opinions are available. Btw, please let me know if I’ve made any factual errors and I’ll happily correct these.Pros:- There are plenty of tables to choose from. - There’s a good mix of tables – some are based on real-life one and some are Zen originals. - I haven’t tried every table but had fun with several and most folk will be able to find something they enjoy. - You get free access to all of the tables for a day so you can try before you buy. This is to be applauded. - I’m not a pinball expert but the new physics seem perfectly fine and arguably represent an improvement for some (but not all – see below) of the tables. - I’ve been playing with ray tracing on nearly max settings (apart from my monitor is only 1440p and isn’t HDR) and the graphics seem somewhat better than in FX3 - I’m very impressed with the visual aesthetics and general inventiveness of some of the new Zen-designed tables such as Wrath Of The Elder Gods and My Little Pony. - You can filter the table list to only show tables you own (something that the main competitor Zaccaria Pinball doesn’t let you do)Cons:- Whilst the visuals have improved, the change isn’t massively noticeable for me. I honestly can’t tell what difference ray tracing makes. - No VR support. That would have constituted a major step forward and made it worth paying for the remastered tables.  - Steam Deck is not officially supported yet.- Improvements in the visuals and physics have come at the expense of significantly higher PC requirements. Bear this in mind if you’ve been enjoying playing FX3 on a lower spec system.- The new physics make some of the tables feel worse than they did in FX3. I’m thinking of Sorcerer’s Lair and the Wild West one. Tables like those were designed around the older physics and now they don’t flow as well. Certain shots are now more difficult and there’s a tendency to lose the ball more easily in certain circumstances. This makes some tables feel less fun which is why I don’t think they represent good value for money for those upgrading from FX3, even at 50% off. - The UI should be more streamlined. It involves too many clicks to do certain basic things like restarting a game. - There’s no option to turn off the annoying menu screen music. - The UI should be more customisable. For example, I’m not interested in tournaments or collectables or the trophy room (they look ugly and cheap and nasty) so I’d like to be able to hide anything to do with those because it’s just distracting clutter. - There’s a distracting pop-up at the bottom right of the home screen. It’s essentially an advert for new tables and tournaments. There’s no way to disable this. If you’ve paid money for tables you shouldn’t have to look at adverts. - I don’t like the background to the Williams tables and it limits my enjoyment of them. Give us the option to have a black background with no distractions please. - The volume of different tables is quite inconsistent (the King Kong one was very loud) and there’s no way to save settings on a per table basis so you have to faff about with settings more than you should.- They should let you set your favourite camera angles and only cycle through those instead of having to cycle through every one of the angles every time which is annoying. - The voiceovers/callouts are a bit of a weak point for Zen. They can get very repetitive and sometimes involve some very dodgy and distracting accents. - I’ve spotted a few minor bugs and glitches. Others have reported flipper lag and some game breaking bugs. I haven’t encountered this (as far as I can tell) but possibly worth noting - you can look at the Steam discussion board for more details.- FX3 has now been abandoned and some of the bugs that were reported will never be fixed. Who’s to say FX wouldn’t suffer a similar fate in future?- I’m not too interested in leaderboards or competing against others (mainly because I’m not very good) but in FX3 it was easy to see how your scores compared against your friends scores. It’s not as obvious in FX and I see that as a step backwards. - Zen has very little competition and perhaps that’s why in some respects they seem to be resting on their laurels. The main competitor is Zaccaria Pinball. That came out years ago, has a much smaller dev team and introduced a lot of excellent innovations that Zen still haven’t implemented. For example, Zaccaria is much more customisable. You can tweak every aspect of the physics, the table lighting, the room lighting, the table glass, the ball skins and the flipper colour, etc. It also lets you run tables from the command line. This lets you bypass all the distractions of the menu and go straight into your table of choice, with the settings of your choice straight from your desktop. Zaccaria has also had VR support for years. (Btw, I’m no Zaccaria fanboy – there are plenty of issues with that too and the devs seem to have given up on it sadly) Not sure:- I’m not too interested in tournaments or online versus play so I can’t comment on whether those work or how well. - Imho certain well-designed achievements can help you get a better understanding and appreciation of a table, e.g. by getting you to play in a different way because you're focused on a particular outcome. Sadly there are only 10 achievements and they’re for just trying out different things like entering a tournament, which I’m not really interested in. Apparently each table does have it’s own set of goals which is good but I haven’t looked into these yet so can’t comment.

_childDocuments_.review: Pinball evolved over the years from simple electro-mechanical tables, to solid state tables, to the modern computerized tables, and along the way they grew more ambitious and more complex. Pinball FX has followed a similar path. When it first started it did nothing but it's own original tables with it's own engine, that they felt wasn't good enough, so they then created FX2 with an updated engine. But, they then decided that they wanted to recreate real pinball tables, and they knew that their engine wasn't up to that task, and thus FX3 came about with a further updated engine. But, in the meantime, real pinball had also advanced, and now tables eschew the old dot matrix displays of the past  in favor of video score screens that play actual video and graphics. And that's how we got here, Pinball FX, Zen's newest update.But hopefully this should be the final engine change, as this time they realized that rather than keep fiddling with their own engine, they're using Unreal Engine going forward. This way they can concentrate on the pinball, and let someone else worry about the engine. Some people have complained about them changing engines again, and say that they're just doing it to milk customers again by making them pay for their tables all over again, and while I have some issues with their pricing mechanics, they didn't do this for that reason.They did it to have a definitive version of FX, one that can be used for pinball tables of any era, and they HAD to update the engine if they wanted any chance of convincing companies making modern pins, companies such as Stern, Jersey Jack, etc. to license their tables to Zen, because getting a license would be useless if the engine couldn't handle recreating the tables. And the new FX is great. It plays well, and the graphics are excellent. I know some people have complained of numerous bugs, but I've encountered relatively few. There's always things that can be improved, such as some rough aspects of their UI, but the games themselves run smoothly and largely problem free.The main issue that many, including myself, have with Zen is over their pricing issues. They used to sell the tables individually, and us old timers bought many of the tables as single tables, but then they decided to stop selling tables individually, and only sell them in packs of three. When we upgraded from FX2 to FX3, they didn't charge again for the tables, and just let everyone carry the tables over from 2 to 3. But, now they're saying that they're not doing that for FX, because they had to port the tables over to the new engine, and that required time and resources to perform, so they can't afford to do that for free. But, they said they would have Legacy packs for us to cost us less to buy the old tables in this new engine.But, the problem is that they changed the old tables from single table sales to the bundles, so even though we have the tables in FX3, they don't count unless you bought the bundle and not the table individually, which is leading to some weird pricing issues. For example, two weeks ago, I bought the Williams Pinball Vol. 2 Legacy Pack for about $3.35, which worked out to roughly $1.11 per game. Fair price I thought. But, last week they had a bundle of 3 Star Wars tables where I could buy the bundle direct for Pinball FX for around $6.75, but the Legacy Pack price was something like $8.89 for the same three tables. Needless to say, the pricing is very screwy if you're an older player.If your a new player though, those issues don't concern you, and you shouldn't let the reviews by salty older pinheads dissuade you from getting the game. It's the best digital pinball around, with lots of great tables, and they're going to be adding many more. They have classic Williams tables, but they also have lots of fun and clever original tables as well. So, if you enjoy pinball, Pinball FX stands alongside Zaccaria Pinball as one of the best digital pinball simulators out there.

_childDocuments_.review: It's certainly not perfect, but after all else is said and done, the truth is that  sets the standard for all other virtual pinball games to follow.There are a few nits I'd like to pick.  The various Zen original designs, both those based on licensed properties and originals,  are more inconsistent and they often fail to include classic, traditional elements.  Having said that, there are well over 100 tables available and it would be silly for someone expect all of them to be great.  The 30-ish Williams tables are my favorites overall but there are a few that aren't so good there too.My biggest complaint is that Zen seems to be gleefully following in the footsteps of Farsight's  when it comes to choosing which Williams tables to release.  I'd much rather see them prioritize tables we didn't see in Pinball Arcade.My second biggest complaint is that Zen seems to think Pinball was invented in 1985 or thereabouts.   None of the Williams recreations are from before that, and Zen's original tables generally look contemporary in origin. There are a lot of classic Williams tables from the mid 70's through the mid 80's that Zen has ignored so far, and there's no reason they couldn't do some new designs in a retro late 70's or earl 80's style.  It would be nice to see Zen pay a bit more attention to what many consider to be the golden age of pinball.

_childDocuments_.review: Preface: I have over 2000 hours on Pinball FX2 and FX3, combined, and I have another 1600 on Pinball Arcade. Safe to say, I've a fair bit of experience on my belt not just by playing these games, but in bug-hunting as well. I can also say that I've received codes from Zen in the past, and I've purchased their products since the beginning of FX2 here on Steam, so I've played a lot more for my money's worth.This review is not a flat, outright, "Yes" or "No" recommendation. There are obvious flaws in this game, and unfortunately so given the state of some tables. I want to write with as much of a genuine take on this as possible. Right now, I give this a solid 7/10. Not as great as FX3, still needs work, but has a lot of potential with the new engine. Is Pinball FX better now than what it was last year? A definite yes. My build is borderline minimum, running a GTX 970 and an i7-6700k processor. Pinball FX runs very well on my system, much more so than how it was during Early Access. Tables like World War Z and E.T. were absolutely horrendous. I've seen many improvements, and it'll get better as they optimize for Steam Deck, Cabinet Mode, and the eventual Switch release.Is FX better graphically? Personally, yes, but the first several Williams Volumes are up for debate. FX3's graphics already look great as they are, and a step up from FX2. Repurchasing on looks alone is already a tough sell. You'll really need a keen eye to tell the differences.Is FX better physics-wise? Yes and no. No, because Williams already uses the new physics found in Classic Single Player, so that's already the baseline. Yes, because in originals like Infinity Gauntlet, I can feel the difference in the interactions. What I can do in Williams tables with specific flipper tricks, I couldn't do in FX3's originals, but can now do in FX. Both FX2 and FX3 use the same engine, and some of the physics changes between the two intertwine using the same model. Pinball FX's new physics model is a complete revamp; the older originals need retuned, and we have a different ball game. Know that there are some issues that need ironed out in recent remasters like Sorcerer's Lair and Fish Tales, and the list of remasters yet to be done from FX3 isn't as large as before. Who knows; we might end up seeing some returning from FX2.Is it worth repurchasing all tables immediately? Not necessarily. People have different budgets, and I did not start out with a complete collection of FX2 tables right away. That said, how much a table is worth is entirely up to you. The "no backwards compatibility" take is quite the sting to the wallet, especially with new tables coming out at $5-10 per table, and Indy being $15. Discount details below.I feel for the people outside of the US who suffered from the pricing increase. As a US player, I'm not personally affected, but for people in other areas like Europe and Brazil, definitely. I highly encourage those seeking repurchases, and likewise, those not wanting to pay as much for new tables like Twilight Zone, to wait for discounts. I've observed the FX3/FX bundles Zen put out to lessen the pain of repurchases, and 50% is the base discount for FX3 owners of any given pack. Oddly enough, this includes Indy. This discount STACKS multiplicatively with those that take place during any given sale -- take the traditional Summer or Winter Sale, as an example. Time will tell what will happen when the first discounts roll around on Steam; therefore, watch.Bug fixes: I checked back in SteamDB regarding FX2 and FX3. We never got many patches or fixes between the two games, and I wonder if their previous engine had something to do with that. For those who are not aware, I maintain an unofficial Master List of issues, with the vast majority of them reported towards the Williams tables. A good majority of issues on the Williams tables in FX3 are now resolved in FX, but there are still plenty of bugs, especially game-breakers, that desperately need fixed. I've seen a faster rate of fixes here compared to the previous engine. With the Switch release coming up in July, I imagine more fixes are headed our way between now and then, now that most of the remastered titles are out there. There will be plenty more fixes even after that, and I want Zen to communicate as much about this topic as possible.Censorship on Williams: Completely GONE. Zen got in trouble with the ESRB for Infinite Minigolf on Switch, and they can't afford to make that mistake twice putting things in that might bump up FX3 age ratings. This even includes a censorship toggle, which we got here on Steam. We wouldn't see games like Dracula, Jack*Bot, or anything else that might have warranted a bump in the ratings. Purely on consoles, and much rather make the leap now than have repurchases sting more later on in FX3's life. FX3, to me, felt a lot more like what we've seen previously in FX2. Overall, the same game, but with additional challenges, powers, "matchup", custom tournaments, and new physics on Williams. Zen Pinball 2 on Mac is further proof from what I've seen on some videos. While FX seems a lot like a rehash of what FX3 has to offer, this is only the beginning.Is Pinball FX a terrible game? No. Is it top of the charts, year 1? No, given the state of the game as of writing. I remember how FX3 was during the first few months of launch, and reviews weren't as pretty there, either. Will it get better over time? Absolutely.Again, I tell you: Watch. Zen is in this for the long haul.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam Deck Preview Here: Let's get straight to the point; Zen Studios has delivered another solid Pinball offering with excellent licensed tables and in-house creations. They have built a better Pinball FX3, and technically the latest installment is superior to its predecessors in almost every way. Additionally, they now include instant access to Cabinet Mode, which works well for owners of Virtual Pinball Cabinets. There are also updated physics to mention, and the exclusive tables for the new game look gorgeous! The biggest problem that most Pinball FX enthusiasts will face is that they own up to 80% of the tables and have paid only a fraction for each through the various Pinball FX3 sales over the last five years. There is no way to move these tables to the latest platform, which is just another barrier to enjoying Virtual Pinball. Don't get me wrong; it's not like Zen will pull Pinball FX3 from Steam and somehow remove the owner's access to the tables they already own on the previous version. They are just creating a distaste for PFX3 owners and potentially confusing prospective consumers for the new version of Pinball FX. It's bittersweet that such a solid offering can drag itself down by not giving the most loyal fans a path to bring tables forward and take advantage of the apparent benefits without repurchasing every table. The alternative option is to spend endless money purchasing monthly or annual access to the tables, which is nothing I am interested in. These access passes may be a good option for others, and I will encourage everyone to play these tables as they see fit. In the end, I'm going to hold off for the tables to go on sale and pick the ones that I don't own first and slowly ( and cheaply) pick up the remaining tables that I deem worthy of a second purchase.Enjoy!🎮eeFoGee🎮

_childDocuments_.review: The ultimate pinball game has finally arrived at Steam. Do I recommend it? Oh yeah, without a doubt. There's some old tables remastered and some new ones. Some of them are awesome, the others frustrating, but overall great. I like diversity.Let's first talk about the elephant in the room. There's a lot of reviewers saying they should get the tables for free. I'm really baffled by that. I've never got any game for free. If I wanted a remastered version of the game I had to bought it. You usually get a loyalty discount, like it's the case here, but that's about it. The price tag is high if you want to buy all of them at once, but it's about 3 euros per table which I think it's reasonable. And of course I've bought the whole thing. I know I'm going to sink hundreds of hours into it, so it was a no brainer for me. I've made a mistake only once and I'm still salty about it. Back when Pinball FX2 was out I didn't know I won't be able to buy the rest of the tables after certain date. I would be happy to buy the tables I'm missing, to complete my collection, even though I have all the missing ones in FX3. *Please ZEN unlock that option just for a day :)The game runs smooth. The physics is quite different, so it will take some time to get used to. Some tables are easier in the old game (the ball is really bouncy on some of the tables here), the others in the new version (I've found Williams tables in particular way easier now), but it's fun to learn new stuff.Also if you're on the fence, if you should buy the game or not, you actually have every table unlocked for the 24 hours when you first start the game (I think only Marvel tables were on time trial for me). Definitely try before you buy, so you won't regret it. I think that's a great move by the developers.Now let's talk about the cons. There's one thing that I personaly don't like and that's the achievements. I know I'm probably alone on this one, but I really miss those. There are only 10 general Steam achievements now. You'll unlock 8 of them about 15 minutes after starting the game and leave the other 2 unlocked forever.  But that's not the biggest problem I have with it. Pinball FX2 and Pinball FX3 had the best trophy mechanics in video games. It was what got me into pinball in the first place and why I've left so many hours on those games. The moment when the whole table suddenly paused and that shiny medal spun into view was the most satisfying thing in gaming. _childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like with the new Pinball FX!   I'm glad this has finally made it's way to Steam and that Zen offered to transfer purchases from Epic over here.  I've really been enjoying the Event mode with Grand Tournaments for trophies and other tables to push toward season long collectibles.  One of the best parts is getting to play some new tables.  There's both new Williams tables and new Zen original tables based on their own IP and some classic IPs.  Another nice thing is finally having unified physics on the Williams tables.  In FX3, the different Williams Volumes had different physics.  That's unified now so they're all the same.  Of the new tables, The Twilight Zone and The Addams Family are standouts.  We've also got Bride of Pinbot, Swords of Fury, Champsionship SoccerThese are consistently rated as two of the best pinball tables of all time.  Hopefully we'll be seeing some of the other Bally and Williams classics like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Doctor Who, Black Knight, Centaur, Banzai Run, and PinBot soon.One of big under the hood changes is the move to Unreal as the game engine, replacing their in-house engine.  There's some small lighting improvements, but it's similar.  I think the main benefit will be freeing up their developers to focus more on building tables instead of maintaining a game engine.Overall, Pinball FX has been a lot of fun to play so far.  I'm looking forward to seeing what's coming in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: I got my game codes via Zen Studios; I bought all the tables during the 2022 Holiday Season on EGS, so I'm grateful of them doing that, as well as the discount for the Pinball FX3 owners. Still my opinions are going to the point and fair.The Good:It's still Pinball FX in terms of gameplay, with harder physics as the physics are now closer to an actual pinball. Pinball FX more exclusive tables compared to Pinball FX3.The tables come in a pack (or individual for the licensed Williams/Midway tables) instead buying "tickets".The Williams tables exclusive to Pinball FX are beloved classics with World Cup Soccer (MUCH better than The Pinball Arcade's reskin), The Addams Family, and Twilight Zone.The presentation's decent; it's the same presentation as Pinball FX2 VR and Star Wars Pinball VR.The Bad:You can't enter initials for the DMD tables like you could in Pinball FX2 and Pinball FX3, thus missing out on the end game DMD tables or the Williams tables. The "enter initials" option is just entering your username, instead of the three-letter initials. It removes the satisfaction of getting a top score, as well as missing game game over screens.There are still bugs to be had for the tables; the Pinball FX Discord and Steam forums have posted bugs. Perhaps bugs are present for some of the lesser-played tables as well? Each and every table needs a much closer look to see if there are soft-locks within the designs. Hopefully, all the soft-lock bugs get ironed-out for a better experience for the more skilled players who notice certain bugs.Not a fan of the subscription model, especially now, since you can buy each design, thus removing the point of the subscription model. I have a feeling there will be upcoming sales, besides the 50%-off discount for Pinball FX3 design owners.More of a complaint about Pinball FX3 than Pinball FX, but for Pinball FX2 owners, none of the Pinball FX2 tables count as "bought" from Pinball FX3 on the storefronts from all gaming platforms, thus you have to be careful about purchasing previously tables on here for Pinball FX2 owners. I'd recommend going for the Pinball FX bundle and only Pinball FX, not Pinball FX3. So yeah, for the tables that will come to Pinball FX you bought as a Pinball FX2 owner, will have to be repurchased again, unfortunately.The presentation could be more simplified; it has the Pinball FX2 VR presentation, which is decent for VR users, but not for the legacy Pinball FX users. Hopefully, there could be a VR option to purchase for Pinball FX, much like what Magic Pixels did for Zaccaria Pinball. I don't mind the presentation, but I think until a purchasable VR option is implemented, the majority of Zen Studios Pinball users would just prefer the icons at the start screen like the other games.Overall, Pinball FX is a solid continuation, especially if you started out with Pinball FX3 and purchased all the designs from FX3. Zen Studios, even given previous faults, is still one of the best companies to handle and continue on with digital pinball. Could it be better? Of course! The foundation is still present with Pinball FX.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE 4/7/2024: To everyone experiencing flipper delay and lag, I figured it out. You absolutely need vsync turned off, as that made the biggest difference for me on the responsiveness. After fixing the controls, I went ahead and reached top 10 all time high score on Sorcerer's Lair. Now I finally have a chance to actually judge the game properly, and it's still... not quite there. The physics is def the biggest change compared to FX3. The ball feels way heavier, and you will notice it when you keep missing certain ramps that you definitely know you would've gotten in FX3. Some tables have their slingshot physics completely changed too, from a soft bounce in FX3 to a hard launch here. But the biggest one I noticed is the ball sometimes bounces WAY harder than it should. A typical technique to cradle the ball is to have the ball bounce off the flipper and hit the underside of the slingshot, so you can catch the ball. Some tables (trials) would see the ball completely bouncing out of that space now. Though the flipper responsiveness is good now, the wonky and inconsistent physics is still an issue. The other disappointment is how this game does table achievements. There's no display of medal anymore, it's just a small notification on the side, like the kind of desktop notifications you get on your PC. So getting an achievement no longer feels like an event. Like FX3, each table only has one achievement to get, only this time the achievements are not even linked through Steam. The last thing is the customization display feature is a big meh. I just don't care much about displaying things on shelves. I'd prefer the way they've been doing it in the new Pinball M, where you can customize the tables themselves, the flipper skins, the ball skins, and customize the lighting and particle effects.UPDATE 4/3/2024: I found out that this lag issue does not exist on the PS4 version of the game, so it looks like this is yet another example of a bad PC port that I hope they patch.3/4/2024: I typically don't write reviews for games, but I wanted to speak up about this one, since I've played and bought pinball tables since FX2. My issue is not about repurchasing the tables. My issue is SOLELY on the performance. There is a clear lag on the flippers. _childDocuments_.review: You can view my 3D in VR gameplay here: I'm not sure why Pinball FX doesn't officially support VR. It's running on the Unreal Engine and the Unreal Engine natively supports VR. Other than working to make sure the menus are okay in VR and the camera views are okay for VR, there wouldn't be much work to bring official VR support to Pinball FX. You don't even need to support motion controllers!In any event, you can forget about official VR support or Praydog's VR injector (who knows when if ever that will be released to the public), because you can already play this in full 3D in VR using the Universal Unreal Engine 3D fix that utilizes the Geo-11 3D driver. The only thing you need to do, besides download and install the driver in the correct game directory, is to force DX11 by typing -dx11 in the Steam launch options. Lastly, you need software to view 3D in VR such as Virtual Desktop, VRScreenCap, or HelixVision.Game looks great in 3D in VR. Just a few minor issues that aren't even worth mentioning. Once you go 3D in VR, you won't want to play pinball again in an outdated 2D screen. Ran fine on my RTX 3080 for the most part.

_childDocuments_.review: The majority of negative reviews are cost related, but I've already crossed that bridge. I bought every table that was available at the Epic launch, plus Honor and Legacy and all of the new Williams tables. To Zen's credit, they did a fantastic job of allowing people who purchased tables during early access to migrate them to other platforms - something which I greatly appreciate - but there's no escaping that Pinball FX4 is just not a well made product. Every change they made is conceptually misguided, and due to a galling lack of effort put into the table "remasters" all play worse than their original counterparts, with the possible exception of the early Williams tables - and even that might be generous.The promise of updating old tables with the exceptional physics from Pinball FX3's Williams Vol. 6 DLC was incredibly exciting, but the reality we got is something entirely different. Recreated tables have become more Zen-like and less arcade faithful, while old Zen tables feel lousy due to not making enough changes to accommodate the new physics engine. It's really the worst of both worlds, and to see Zen throw out the most faithful simulation physics ever created breaks my heart as a pinball fan. Despite being a recurring theme of early access feedback, no work has been done to bring back the more realistic experience - and it this point it seems unlikely to ever happen.Adding insult to injury is:I don't agree with the take that Zen are greedy. While it would have been nice to continue forward-porting tables forever, asking you to pay for a remaster doesn't ultimately strike me as unreasonable. The problem is that the remasters aren't good. Williams tables play decently even if they're a downgrade from the new Williams physics, but classic Zen originals were not given adequate retooling. Wild West Rampage is the worst, it feels terrible compared to the original release, but even the less bad remasters never rise above the level of "okay". They all feel janky, like someone recreated a Zen table in Visual Pinball without considering that Zen's tables are designed around a very specific, somewhat nontraditional physics model. You're almost guaranteed to encounter a bizarre physics interaction in every round.If you just want to play the new Williams tables, you'll have a decent enough time. I haven't encountered major issues with any of them beyond feeling more streamlined than a real arcade machine. Yet I highly recommend avoiding anything with a Pinball FX3 equivalent. You'd be paying more to have a far worse experience. The new Zen tables are a bit of a wash too, they at least work well with the new engine but none of them have struck me as particularly remarkable.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot more time on this on the Epic Store, but wanted to post a review now to add some good vibes here. This is hands down the best virtual pinball experience there is. You like pinball? Get it. It runs great on the Steam Deck, especially in handheld mode. Of course, desktop mileage will vary depending on settings/resolution.The tables are diverse, ranging from classic reproductions/simulations of real tables to "fantasy" pinball tables based on themes and franchises. You also get a nice variation of play-styles from lane-heavy tables to drop target focused and everything in between, mission based or high-score chasing, etc.You can buy tables to own, play daily events for free, chase "F2P" rewards, or pay a "gaming as a service" model. Whatever your "flavor" or preference you will find it here. I have been playing Zen Pinball/Pinball FX since it's inception back in 2007. While there were some missteps in the series, this one feel like it hits all the sweet spots, and is a great step forward in physics and graphics.REGARDING ALL THE NEGATIVITY:The biggest issue people have is the "buying tables all over again" if they already filled their catalogs in the past versions. I understand the pain on the wallet, as I have done this about four times now. However, I also know that making money with digital pinball is extremely difficult. Asking Zen Studios to credit us all tables from past versions is basically asking them to go out of business. We know this is true, because it happened to everyone else (R.I.P. Farsight Studios, Sierra, LittleWing, Pro Pinball, etc.)It seems many have forgotten (or never knew) that in the original "golden age" of pinball, we paid $30-$50 PER TABLE! And those tables came out every year or more. Pinball FX gives us new tables frequently, and they are all great quality (more or less). Paying $5-$15 per new table is a steal, really.Zen Studios has done a great job crediting "founders" with credits to move platforms from Epic. I got my codes in a timely and personal manner. I felt this showed great customer service. Also, Pinball FX does not lock you into the F2P or "gaming as a service" mechanics, they gave players the option to engage however they want. I would definitely be upset if they forced me to use those, but they don't. I think it very impressive how they seamlessly offered all options. My ONLY criticism is that after more than two decades, no one has yet to match the physics of the Pro Pinball series. It's one of the greatest mysteries of the virtual pinball industry. That said, I am happy virtual pinball is alive and well.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a rewriting of my original review.  Since that time I've come around on my thoughts of Pinball FX.  Overall it's an excellent pinball simulator, with its excellent graphics and physics.  To readdress my original problems with the game:1. Input lag - I was able to overcome this with my 60hz IPS monitor by using the in-game 120 fps limit and disabling vsync.  Between these two setting I find the input lag to be nonexistent, or at least it's no longer noticeable and the flipper response is always consistent.   BTW, screen tearing drives me nuts but fortunately using the 120 (or higher) fps limit seems to be as tear free as vsync. 2.  Image quality - I run an overclocked i7 10700k with a rtx 3080 ti driving a 25" 2K 60 hz IPS display (all this is primary used for VR flight simming).   The visuals of the tables is really well done with all elements being realistically rendered.  For my computer I've found that the best IQ is had if using none of the scaling options.  I've found too that my monitor suffers slight ghosting which at times is noticeable, thus some of the IQ degradation I was originally noticing was solely do to my monitor.3.  Ball plunger mechanics - you are forced to twitch master the fractional second of a button press that yields a starting plunger skill shot.  Too bad the mouse can't be used to pull the plunger back to the precise position you want before releasing it (like The Pinball Arcade did).  Dang, I'd LOVE to have this mouse controlled plunger feature!In the end, Pinball FX does deliver an excellent pinball experience.  But if you want an authentic pinball experience, you will have find an arcade with real life tables and go there to play pinball.  In the meantime though, having Pinball FX on your PC is an acceptable substitute (but IMHO definitely not a replacement).   Go have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: There are still 21 tables from Pinball FX3 that are not available in this new version of the game, including many of my favorites. To have access to all of the tables, players will need to continue using Pinball FX3, despite the release of this new version. It is not yet possible to "fully migrate."This means that players will have to remember which tables are available on which version of Pinball FX and they will also need to remember for which game they happened to buy any of the tables that have overlapping availability. Nobody from Zen has suggested keeping an external spreadsheet handy to look up the necessary information when players want to launch a specific table, but it would be a good idea.The insanely ironic thing about the various tables being exclusive to different versions of Pinball FX is that it creates the very situation that a game like "Pinball FX" was aimed at addressing. Right now, there is not one unified platform from which all of someone's Pinball FX tables can be viewed and launched. For the player, it would be better if the tables were just their own titles on Steam and if none of the Pinball FX lobby-like launcher "games" existed at all. At least that way, Steam would be a single place from which all of a player's tables could be viewed and accessed.The absurdity is that Zen could reasonably release a new game that isn't really a game, but rather another lobby-like launcher. From this lobby, players could view and launch all of the versions of Pinball FX that they have collected. If the lobby also displayed which pinball tables were available and owned in each of the Pinball FX games, then at least players would once again have a unified place from which to access all of their Pinball FX pinball tables. It would mean having a lobby-like launcher that launches other lobby-like launchers that themselves launch pinball tables, but at least then there would once again be a unified home for all things Pinball FX.In short, Zen has created an absolute mess with this release.And honestly, the overarching meta-situation might not even be the worst part because the new Pinball FX isn't even very good. Here are some complaints:Local scores can now only be viewed from within the tables on their respective dot matrix display. For seemingly no reason, Zen has decided to remove the option to show local highscores from the main menu. If local highscore chasing among hotseat friends or family members is what you're after, you have no reason to consider this version of Pinball FX.Tables previously owned in Pinball FX3 must be purchased again to be played here. There is a decent discount available to owners of previous titles looking to migrate their tables to the new game, but only if the tables were purchased as part of a bundle and not individually. Despite this supposed olive branch, being asked to pay for titles that were already paid for - even with a discount - is brazen and unconscionable. Besides the requirement being offensive, buying previously owned tables on this new version is also a bad idea, since they'll play worse on this platform than on Pinball FX3 (see below).Optimization is poor. The game takes substantially longer just to boot than FX3 did. Enabling raytracing on a 2080 lowers the frame rate to the point of unplayability. Even without raytracing, tables feel sluggish compared to the same tables in Pinball FX3. To be fair, this might just be a "feature" of the new Unreal engine behind the physics. But regardless of the cause, old tables feel worse here. Others have suggested that the legacy tables simply weren't designed with the new physics in mind, which seems totally plausible to me. Still, it doesn't just feel like the table layouts don't match the ball path. The whole thing just feels worse overall.Table Nudge can no longer be mapped to same stick as Manual Pull. I have no idea why that limitation would exist, but it does.The main menu is bad looking and more difficult to use than it was in Pinball FX3. I wasn't ever a huge fan of FX3's interface, but I would gladly stay in that environment forever if the new interface is the alternative.Given Zen's history of recharging for the same tables across versions and game platforms, spending hundreds of dollars on tables for this bad feeling, poorly optimized version seems foolish. It would be silly to think that Zen won't find a plausible-seeming reason to release an even newer version of Pinball FX in a couple of years and expect players to fork over new cash for whatever tables they might soon be buying (I suggest calling it "Pinball FX X: Super Definitive Hyper"). At that point, anyone who buys a bunch of tables now will be stuck with a lose-lose proposition: stay in this bad version forever or pay big bucks to escape it.This whole mess leaves me with a bad taste in my mouth.I wish I didn't like pinball so much.

_childDocuments_.review: I was prepared for disappointment with this new version of Pinball FX, so I can at least say it met my expectations. What was a pretty fun, if expensive, series of pinball games has become even more expensive, lifeless, and has apparently sold its soul in the name of pure profits.Look, I understand, pinball is expensive to make, especially for a niche audience. You might not be able to afford giving players tables for free based on what they bought in previous titles. I also get the meh-fest that was Zen Pinball Party on mobile, where many tables just don't really have a long lasting impression on you and the controls can be troublesome. But there is a line you don't cross, at least with me. The moment you add a premium currency to the game, on top of your existing money-sink, AND have a subscription pass that can only with bought with funny money that doesn't even unlock all tables for play, that goes far enough to cross that line twice over.It doesn't help that the one sample table I got to play is just absolute garbage - visually, it all blends together way too much, the theme of the table is one of the most basic themes one could suggest, and the controls... Oh, My God, It's a special kind of bad when I can routinely hit certain shots one moment but the very next the game just decides its not your day - this has happened twice in the span of 15 minutes of play, where shots I could make accidentally over and over suddenly refuse to be made when it counts, blowing two otherwise flawless runs of their respective missions.I hate saying this, but this is by far the worst game in the series. AVOID AT ALL COSTS.

_childDocuments_.review: There is not a Meh choice for recommending the game, so I must go with No.The only aspect that matters to me, is the physics, as everything else was already solid enough in Pinball FX3. Zen screwed that up with Pinball FX. This Pro physics in-between Pinball FX3 Zen physics and Williams Classic Arcade physics just doesn't work. In Pinball FX3 Williams Classic Arcade on the later Volumes e.g. Universal Monsters, the physics was getting really good and realistic playing. It still needed some work i.e. it had exaggerated bounce like a heavy rubber ball and not really any micro-bounces, but they gave me hope that they were on the right track. The news that all their tables in Pinball FX were going to get "realistic" Pro-physics, got me really excited... until I actually played it. The ball doesn't play like a real metal ball, the bounces are unrealistic and just plain weird, and the flipper tricks feels at best like an approximation by someone that has never played real pinball... you can e.g. do a live catch, but it just feels wrong.Either way, I'm still buying their new Williams tables to support them out of appreciation for what they have done over the years. I though never play them more than an hour or two before I get frustrated and bored (because they play too easily even with the wonky physics). The originals, I can't play anymore, because modes and missions are too repetitive and games last forever (which was already the case in Pinball FX3). What I ideally want from Zen before I'll take their game seriously again (and enjoy it), is to bring their Pinball FX3 Williams Classic Arcade physics back to their Williams tables. They were on the right track with those physics, but then they threw it all away for their unified frankensteined Pro physics... that just doesn't work.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE:The game is still not totally awesome, but it is the best pinball simulation out there. While several tables suffer from minor bugs and the German localization is a joke (seems to be machine-based with constant errors and even bad grammar that is hard to understand), I love pinball and like the game. Yes, it could be better, but it could be worse too...Overall, if you don't expect a perfect product and love pinball, this is for you.===========I love Pinball FX3 and 2 and have played about 530 hours in both games. I didn't like Zen's move to be Epic-inclusive for some time (a year or so), but understand that they had to do it because of financial reasons.Now that FX is finally available on Steam I was excited and had my wallet ready to buy all tables at launch, something I had done in all those years of FX2 and FX3. But the wait was not worth it.Table physics are better and more realistic now, not just on real-life machines (Williams tables etc.), but on all of them. This is good if you are a pro, but not the best decision if you are a casual pinball player. Your scores will be so much lower than in FX2/FX3 because of the increased difficulty. Moreover, the video game-like physics of FX2 and FX3 perfectly fit the Zen Originals, Star Wars, Marvel etc. tables (all but Williams tables)...now tables feel odd, you no longer make shots you are perfect at in FX2/FX3...and some tables are even broken as certain shots are either impossible or way too difficult to make. Thor is one of my fav tables. I am a rhythmic shooter that goes for back to back lightning strike combos in FX2/FX3. Missing them is almost impossible...but in FX the upper-left flipper does not let you hit the ramp on the right side (needed for the lightning strike combo)...or the ball goes down again...or you press A to do the lightning strike, but it does not count as one:On the one hand, pro physics are great, but on the other one, parts of the non-Williams tables don't work properly, are way too difficult or even broken.+/good:1) Physics in general, especially on Williams tables2) There are new tables available3) The graphics with raytracing (good computer required)~/average:You have to buy all tables you own in FX3 again. It's understandable though as nobody works for free.-/bad:1) The whole idea to launch FX instead of keeping FX3 and releasing new tables for it2) Bugs everywhere, some minor, some game-breaking3) The new physics don't always fit non-Williams tables, which ranges from too difficult shots to broken gameplay (Sorcerer's Lair, Thor etc.)4) Overall, the tables sound good, but the volume differences are too big. One table has soft music, loud sound samples, on another table it is the other way round...you have to find the best setting for every table, but cannot save them individually. There are some tables with soft overall volumes, you crank up the speakers, but the next table is way too loud....the tables are not balanced or professionally mixed.4) UI and menus: I prefer FX3. In the German localization a lot of menus have shortened text that looks odd. Filtering tables and tournaments is tedious and fiddly.5) The German localization (tables) was not good in FX2/FX3 is still not good, but slightly better6) Option menu: You cannot even assign buttons freely, but have to use presets. A to shoot, B to change camera like I'm used to from FX3 is not possible.Conclusion after 15 hours of gameplay:o Play Williams tables as they are awesomeo Play all other tables in FX3/FX2o Wait for fixes, then buy what you like for FX

_childDocuments_.review: I'm nearing 1.5k hours played on FX Pinball 3, and I was looking forward for a considerable update with new tables.  This feels like two steps forward, fifteen steps back.The first glaring issue is that any table that you previously owned will not port to this one, and since the vast majority of the tables are the very same ones I've already bought, the idea that I have to buy everything again is very hard to swallow.  They do have a "legacy" discount for a great number of said tables which gives you 50% off, but it does not cover the entirety of the 100 tables that I already bought in Pinball FX 3.But even if I did buy evertyhing back, the game engine itself is spotty.  The physics feel different, more "floaty", and I even detect a modicum of delay between my button presses and the action on the screen.  Furthermore, my RTX 3070 does not seem to cut it if I put the game to it's best graphics setting, which is even more odd. I need to tune things down to a point where the game looks worse than it used to look like on Pinball FX 3, so that makes no sense.  If I don't do that, I get a few frame skips, hiccups and so forth, which has considerably hindered my typical scores I can get with the previous itteration of this game.The second, even more irritating feature is the push for people to use game passes instead of buying the content.  A full unlock of every game will ask you to shell 22$ CAD (I'm estimating 15$ USD) for monthly access and several hundred dollars for a yearly pass.  Consider that most streaming services ask you for about the same amount and it's not hard to choose between, say, Disney + or Pinball games.  The value of subsciptions is well established out there, and Pinball FX is an outlier in low ROI.So the cons are: Iffy game engine, all your previous purchases don't count for much, different physics and very pricey model.  The Pros? RTX is very much welcomed, you can add chromatic aberatiion, and there's a few more things here and there that, if it worked properly (and I expect they will if they make tweaks to the engine in the future) would make this even better looking than its predecessor. You also have a vertical screen mode out of the box, however you can have that unlocked with Pinball FX 3 if you go through a few hoops with the publisher.My conclusion is that if you have any amount of money put into Pinball FX 3, stick with it.  The new tables that are offered are nice, but not enough for me to deal with the downsides, which is a shame becuase some of these looked very promising.This is a hard no for me.I wouild actually subscribe to this if the price was WAY better, and would likely learn to deal with the other issues if I could port my old games for free (which again, are the majority here, and I own every table there is in FX 3).

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)Introduction:Pinball FX, developed and published by Zen Studios, is a digital pinball platform that offers a captivating and immersive pinball experience for enthusiasts and casual players alike. With its wide array of beautifully designed tables, realistic physics, and engaging gameplay, Pinball FX has become a go-to destination for fans seeking the thrill of pinball on various platforms. As a pinball aficionado, I have spent numerous hours flipping the virtual silver ball, and here's my in-depth review of Pinball FX.Table Selection and Variety:One of the standout features of Pinball FX is the extensive collection of tables available. Ranging from classic designs to licensed themes from popular franchises, there is a diverse selection to suit every player's taste. Each table comes with its own unique layout, objectives, and special features, providing a fresh and exciting experience with every new addition.Realistic Physics and Gameplay:Zen Studios has managed to recreate the essence of real pinball machines remarkably well. The ball physics feel natural and responsive, accurately simulating the unpredictable bounces and trajectories characteristic of traditional pinball games. The flippers respond with precision, allowing for skillful shots and strategic nudging to keep the ball in play. This level of authenticity enhances the overall enjoyment and satisfaction of the gameplay.Table Graphics and Immersion:The attention to detail in the table graphics is impressive, with vibrant colors, dynamic lighting, and intricate artwork. Whether it's the whimsical world of a fantasy-themed table or the iconic characters and locations from licensed franchises, the visual fidelity draws players into the pinball adventure. The dynamic camera angles and interactive elements further contribute to the immersive experience.Table Objectives and Challenges:Each pinball table in Pinball FX offers a range of objectives, challenges, and mini-games to keep players engaged and motivated. Achieving specific targets, unlocking bonuses, and activating unique features add depth and variety to the gameplay. Mastering these objectives can be both rewarding and challenging, ensuring that players have a reason to return to their favorite tables for continuous improvement.Leaderboards and Multiplayer:Competing for high scores is an integral part of the pinball experience, and Pinball FX excels in this aspect. Global leaderboards encourage friendly competition among players, fostering a sense of community and camaraderie. Additionally, the game supports multiplayer options, allowing friends to challenge each other's scores and engage in head-to-head matches.Customization and DLC:Pinball FX offers customization options for players to tweak their preferred table settings and game preferences. Moreover, Zen Studios regularly releases downloadable content (DLC) that introduces new tables and updates to keep the content fresh and exciting. While some DLC may come at an additional cost, the variety and quality of new tables make it a worthy investment for devoted players.Conclusion:Pinball FX captures the essence of pinball gameplay with its realistic physics, visually stunning tables, and diverse range of themes. Whether you're a seasoned pinball pro or a newcomer to the game, Pinball FX provides an addictive and enjoyable experience for players of all skill levels. With regular updates, a thriving community, and the ability to customize your pinball experience, Pinball FX remains a top choice for those seeking pinball excitement in the digital realm.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess the (accomplished) goal of Zen was to make one of the laziest releases (cash grabs?) ever without being completly dysfunctional.  Not a bad game in the core gameplay, but the amount nothing but the bare minimum regarding  everything else is quite offensive.The game has some changed physics, I suppose. Or the tables are just set up steeper since PFX3. Or everything is just a little more "bouncy", iDK. But without fine tuning of the tables this sucks a lot of fun out of some of the old ones. Also it causes countless things that, as far as I remember, never were an issue before. Like hitting the hangar in the middle of the Force Awakens table when launching a ball.New game modes probably are just there to be able to claim there is something new. How many of you are going to make a game plan on how to reach the highest score with as few button presses as possible? Not many I suppose! So for the majority this is pretty much the same as the 5 minute and distance limit modes.PFX claims to have steam cloud saves. But it really doesn't. I have no clue what it saves but certainly not the 'effing GAME PROGRESS aka unlocked garbage!Unlocking things is no fun at all. It wasn't in PFX3 either, but at least they did try a little harder. You unlocked (not always great) artwork. Possibly original even for the Star Wars and Marvel tables. Now its mostly just some 3D models that are mounted on the tables in one way or another anyway. How lazy can you be ZEN? I get it, it doesn't matter gameplay wise but if your're asking premium prices (again!) maybe consider delivering something! And if you don't, why showcase it with that garbage room? Wouldn't it make more sense the other way around? Move stuff out of that trash can to pimp up your table? Oh my, why do I think about this? For sure nobody at ZEN did!So there must be at least some some qol changes, right?Does the game save brightness settings individually for each table? Nope!Does the game save popup score settings individually for each table? Nope!Does the game save selected "superpowers"? Nope! (it did in 3, didn't it?)Does the game... -   NOPE,  STOP ASKING!!!Is the volume of the tables all over the place? Yes!Can I at least turn off the (imho horrible) menu music? Of course not! This would directly conflict with the as lazy as possible policy!Maybe get the new tables if you're a pinball addict but play the older ones on PFX3! Like I said, this is a lazy release. You'll probably shake your head a lot in disbelief why so many simple things are just not there / possible / glitchy /  worse than earlier entrys of the series. And what is there is sooo uninspired that I wonder why they even bothered at all. Like the camera movement showing your unlocked garbage.PS: I can't complain about performance issues, at least not since the DLSS patch.Edit: To be fair, there are old tables I enjoy very much in this version. Doctor Strange for example. On the other hand this is the third release of the table and still the view of the upper left flipper is obstructed.Edit: Since my review they made it possible to disable menu music. Also they keep adding fixes to old tables originally from PFX2/3 . But I still prefer to play them on PFX3!

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following Zen Studios since their very beginning and I can tell you that the road traveled by this Hungarian company, which started in 2003 with a team of only 4 people, is immense; the work accomplished, immeasurable.I cannot advise you enough to take any outrageously unfavorable feedback with highest caution. Such reviews do not do justice at all to the long and hard work provided by the people who have been working on this colossal (and yes, I choose my words carefully) project, and are an insult to all the sacrifices endured to reach this point of excellence.It is, of course, easy to criticize what we consider to be insufficiencies. I mean, I completely agree that any good review should mention the negative points. However, it is essential to remain fair. To only focus on the alleged flaws, without ever mentioning the exceptional qualities of the game and its unique character, is not right. To make unfounded accusations against the designers, imputing them motives, is simply scandalous.This pinball simulation is a masterpiece. Of course, it's not perfect yet, a few issues persist here and there. But I have been playing the early-access version for more than one year and I can tell you, this Steam release is beyond expectation. The tables are numerous and play smooth. Most of the legacy tables have been remastered, the last ones will eventually come. Each of them  now has its own illustrations on the 3d-modelized machine. Input lag is completely gone, and the graphics are breathtaking.I can assure you, playing this game 4k@120Hz on a vertical 55" oled TV is an amazing experience. The number of tables available is crazy. It costs about 3-5 € per table (with a few exceptions), but two are free and legacy discounts give you 50% if you own the PFX3 counterpart.Most importantly, what you are seeing now is only the beginning of a great journey. The Unreal engine will keep improving and the tables will not have to be remastered from scratch ever again: this is the reason why this game is named Pinball FX, instead of Pinball FX 4. The number changing is over. And Zsolt Kigyossy's dream has finally come true: Pinball FX is the definitive, ultimate Pinball game.

_childDocuments_.review: The majority of negative reviews are regarding the fact that you can't import previous tables from existing games. I think that's a fair reason, but I only had a few tables of FX3 on my switch so for me it's not a problem. The reason for this is because they rebuilt the tables from the ground up, which I find to be a valid reason as well. Others apparently disagree. While the game isn't bug/nitpick free (I'll get into that), if the lack of imported tables is irrelevant to you, then yes overall I do recommend it. I think the other major complaint is the "pinball passes" - but the idea is sound. You don't need to pay for a pass but it's an option. Buying tables outright is obviously the better choice if you don't need the variety. That being said, here's my gripes and observation.First of all, I'm not a fan of any game that loads in, asks you to hit a button, and THEN loads in the rest of it. You don't pick an account or save, and yet it doesn't load everything until you hit A to begin. Silly and unnecessary. Overall the UI leaves a lot to be desired. A lot of real estate on screen to show examples, or explain things better that just isn't used. It isn't "new player friendly" in my opinion, takes a lot of trial and error to even realize what's happening while playing. I wish it had a better practice mode, helping you with things like specific skill shots.The collection room is cool but navigating it is clunky and weird (can't place Jaws stuff next to TNG on the shelf!). It's fine for frequent players, but it's a bit lackluster. Same with explaining how tables work, Why they use pictures instead of video examples is disappointing. Why can't I tour the table myself, instead of getting a generic scroll of it on repeat? There's so many tables I played that I haven't seen what the upper half of it looks like.I do have the settings on max and have a decent computer, and the lag issues are very rare. Once in a while the paddles don't respond right away or there are frames dropped. What's frustrating about it, is that it's pretty consistent when it happens. On certain tables if I drop frames, it's at the same point, which makes me think this is an issue that can be fixed. That being said, I haven't tried it on lower settings so that might be enough a solution.There's also a "plunger camera" that activates sometimes, and it's always annoying and there's no way to disable it. I'll be picking my starting mission for the Star Trek TNG table, and it'll zoom out to show me the bottom of the table (thanks?). Also no way to choose your camera modes until you're playing a game is also a strange choice. You can adjust the "manual" camera while choosing the table, but there's a dozen or so different views that you can't access until you are in game actively playing. Events are a fun way to play random tables you may ignore or may not own. I do wish there was a consistency or indication of difficulty. Some tables will have a high score goal with only one ball, while other tables will want you to play for 5 minutes and you can reach your goal within the first 30 seconds. Also when starting this game for the first time, you have 24 hours to play pretty much all tables (marvel/star wars are trials) - USE THIS TIME! You may find some of the things you love aren't great tables, and other ones you didn't consider are way more fun. I purchased the TNG DLC first time playing it, and it's my least favourite table. Meanwhile I have fun with the Jurassic Park tables way more than I thought I would.There are lots of types of tables, but the big differences lie in Zen vs Williams tables. Williams seem to be based on real tables, and are definitely "harder" because of it (I do like the factoids they give you about them). Zen are more digital based tables (all tables do have digital effects added in tho) and are easier. There is a pretty toxic discourse within the community whenever this is brought up as well (it's pinball people calm down).So yeah pinball. Pretty cool I guess idk.

_childDocuments_.review: First, let me note that my review is based on the experience of using Pinball FX in Cabinet Mode on pinball cabinet with a beefy PC using an AMD GPU, with a 4K 32" main screen in portrait mode (playfield), 1080p 22" backglass screen, and 7" LCD for the DMD. I use a standard USB interface for arcade buttons (Launch, Left/Right Flipper, Left/Right Nudge, and 4 front-panel buttons), and I have a 4-way arcade joystick (in place of the plunger) for navigation in menus. My playfield is topped with tempered glass, and I use a wireless touchpad/keypad for any extra input that may be necessary. I do not use any sort of front-end besides Steam Big Picture. With all that being said, I can speak with confidence to the fact that Pinball FX is pretty great in Cabinet Mode, with some minor caveats. The visuals are excellent. I do not use Ray Tracing (GPU is a half-generation too old for that) but 4K on High settings looks fantastic. I haven't experienced any lag with flippers, but that may be because I'm using JoyToKey and treating input like keyboard presses instead of joypad/button input. Yes, you will have to re-buy old tables that get remastered. I have the entire Williams and Zen Originals collection on Pinball FX3, and it's a bit of a bitter pill to have to re-purchase for the new version if you want the remastered tables all in one place, but considering that there are a lot of tables that haven't yet made it over to Pinball FX, and some that-- due to licensing-- may never make it (are we going to see the Alien bundle, or the Bethesda bundle?) I still find myself starting up Pinball FX3 sometimes when I want to play those tables, so I'm not too aggrieved at the inclusion of FX3 tables in Pinball FX, and since they're being somewhat generous and giving owners of the previous versions a nice discount on the remasters (if you pick the proper bundle), and that is further reduced if you wait for weekly sales, I daresay you could populate Pinball FX with all your favorites from FX3 for a lower price than expected. Physics do feel different in FX versus FX3. Some tables in FX are just plain HARDER because of the physics. Monster Bash, one of my favorites, is a bit more punishing in Pinball FX because some of the shots are harder with the new physics, and the ball has a tendency to shoot right down the middle a lot more often, so you'll need to get good with nudging... Which I am not, yet. My major complaint is in the main menu. In Pinball FX3 you can navigate with Direction Keys/Dpad, Enter/A, Shift/Bumpers, and Escape/B alone. In Pinball FX you NEED to have either a mouse pointer, or a Menu Button in order to access the Settings, which is the only way to exit out of the game. This is very awkward compared to FX3's setup where you can hit escape on the main menu until you get a window asking if you want to exit; No mouse or menu button required. Honestly, if it weren't for this awkward need for a mouse or Menu button to enter the Settings and choose Exit, I wouldn't need to have the keypad/trackpad at all for gameplay sessions! In Pinball FX, if you hit Esc, you get a sidebar menu that doesn't really do much good for those of us in Cabinet Mode. And this leads me to my next topic: Button assignments.In Pinball FX you must select from some pre-set choices for button/key assignments. It's not fully customizable. This is why the aforementioned game exit issue remains an issue: I can't simply tell the game not to assign Escape to their stupid popup sidebar that I never use, or reassign Escape Settings, or anything else. I'm stuck with the configuration they give me, which means I have to tailor my JoyToKey settings to fit them, not the other way around. It also means I need a unique profile for Pinball FX that is different from the standard one I've used for every other game, including the competition's Zaccaria Pinball. Even Pinball Arcade, that sad no-man's-land of virtual abandonware, works better with the pincab controls and plays nice with the "Esc to exit the game" standard. I strongly desire Zen to give us FULLY customizable controls, not just a selection of pre-made schemes. The Cabinet Mode in Pinball FX is way better than the one in Pinball FX 3, though still not quite to the standards of Zaccaria Pinball. You'll still (at the time of this review) need to do the heavy lifting on getting the backglass images and making sure they're in the proper PNG format, named correctly (Table_##), and in the proper folder. And you'll still need to go through the setup, as in Pinball FX3, to position the backglass and DMD. However, the positioning is MUCH easier in Pinball FX, as they have a little light-up border-circling thingamabob that shows you where you're moving the windows, and it works very well. In FX3, you had to enter numbers, go back and see how it looked in-game, then go back to settings and tweak the numbers over and over until you got it just right. This new method is MUCH better. However, they still haven't figured out how Zaccaria Pinball manages to place the backglass on the proper screen automatically, without any need for tweaking or moving windows, and that's what puts Zaccaria ahead in the backglass category. The DMD is also positioned in FX the same way, and it's much easier than in FX3. You can have it overlapping the backglass if you want, or sent to an entirely different screen if you have it. You can customize the color, size, shape, etc. as well. If you like DMDs, this is a nice feature to have for Cabinet Mode. Most of the newly remastered tables play nice with Cabinet Mode, with some of the Zen Originals, Marvel, and Star Wars tables still doing the "zoom into the plunger" thing despite setting it at View 1 or 1w, but most of the Williams tables obeying the static setup and honoring your desire for it to play like a real machine instead of a video game version. You can turn off the Zen "extras" in Williams tables if you want to experience the original physics and mechanical effects on those tables, and I prefer it that way. I don't want cartoon characters running around on the table in Monster Bash, thank you very much. I like the charm of the old original effects. In the Zen Originals, Marvel, Star Wars, and other tables you're stuck with the extra effects, but they use them well enough in those that they're not annoying, and sometimes kind of fun. My only problem with most of Zen's original tables, including Star Wars, Marvel, Family Guy, Bob's Burgers, Garfield, and more, is that they very similar in that they rely too much on ramps, and not enough on bumpers. Some tables, you'll find yourself stuck in a loop of shooting into a ramp, watching the ball go all the way around the edge of the table, and empty out on your flipper lane ready to line up for another ramp shot that will do the same in the opposite direction. It gets dull when you compare it to the Williams tables, which have a lot more tricks, bumpers, layers, and lanes that don't turn into big looping table-wide ramps. Tables like Wild West Rampage and Sorcerer's Lair show a lot of creativity. Tables in the Marvel & Star Wars packs often feel like they're all the same, but with different pictures and voices. Still, there's enough good stuff in here, including newer tables like Twilight Zone, Addams Family, Bride of Pin-Bot, and some good Zen Originals, to make Pinball FX worth having on a pinball cabinet setup. My advice is to wait for sales, buy the legacy bundles, and be patient. They're still improving the game, with plans to do things like add the backglass images automatically (I've even heard talk of animated backglass, which would be AWESOME), tweak the controls, and expand the library of tables significantly. It's a free game that comes with a couple good tables, the Pinball Pass is a decent value if you don't want to buy tables, and they're doing sales to make the crossover less costly. I'm willing to keep going with Pinball FX and see what happens.

_childDocuments_.review: Pinball FX is a must-play for any pinball enthusiast or anyone who loves fast-paced, thrilling games. From the moment you launch the game, it’s clear that the developers have poured their hearts into creating a polished, immersive experience that pays homage to the timeless appeal of pinball while introducing modern innovations that elevate the game to new heights.The physics in Pinball FX are incredibly realistic, capturing the essence of how a pinball moves and reacts on a physical table. The attention to detail is remarkable, from the intricate table designs to the vibrant sound effects that echo the nostalgic clinks and clatters of a real pinball machine. Whether you're a seasoned pinball wizard or a newcomer, the controls are intuitive and responsive, making it easy to dive in and start racking up high scores.What truly sets Pinball FX apart, though, is the sheer variety of tables available. Each one is a work of art, meticulously crafted with unique themes, challenges, and interactive elements. The game seamlessly blends classic pinball mechanics with modern technology, introducing dynamic visuals, animated characters, and special effects that bring each table to life. The variety ensures that there’s always something new to explore, keeping the gameplay fresh and engaging.In addition to the stellar single-player experience, Pinball FX offers robust online features, including leaderboards and multiplayer modes, which add a competitive edge to the game. Competing with friends or players from around the world adds another layer of excitement, driving you to improve your skills and achieve higher scores.Overall, Pinball FX is a triumph in the world of digital pinball. It’s a game that beautifully bridges the gap between the classic and the contemporary, offering hours of fun, challenge, and nostalgia. Whether you’re playing for the first time or returning as a fan, Pinball FX delivers an experience that’s both timeless and cutting-edge. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: This is the future of digital pinball, and it is a good future despite some things that still need to be improved. The tables look amazing in the new engine and play super smooth, though you will need newer hardware to take advantage of it. I had to upgrade my video card to an RTX 3070, and once I did everything ran well. The platform itself has promise but there are still bugs that need to be worked out and it would be nice to have more features for tournaments, events, and customization. Zen is committed to working on this so it should all improve. I'm enjoying the new tables and I think they will get even better as we go on. On another note,  I think it is totally fair to have to pay for remade tables, and the 50% discount they are giving is more than worth it. I won't repurchase everything I had on FX3, but I can easily get my favorite tables here or wait for a sale. For those who don't want to move on, I suggest you give some of the new tables a try! Many of them feel like brand new tables, and I never find myself going back to the FX3 versions.

_childDocuments_.review: It boggles the mind how bad the lag in this game is. My computer is no slouch, I've yet to play any games I couldn't run on settings higher than Snoop DoggYet this game, has a 0.5 to 1 second input lag on flippers that just embarrassing. How can this game not have calibration options? I lowered all my settings to absolute rock bottom to the point where it looks like 3D Pinball Space Cadet on Windows 95 and the unacceptable input lag is still there. I've played with keyboard, PS4 controller, Xbox controller, and a whole assortment of random controllers I've collected over the years and the lag persists universally. They really have the audacity to ask $10 a table for DLC in this game when this unplayable lag makes the game not even worth the price of free. It's been 6 years since Pinball FX 3 and the only addition to this game is lag and the ability to repay for DLC.
