_childDocuments_.review: Right, Zen Studios has been and to this day remains the biggest developer of digital pinball games on every major gaming platform be it Steam, Xbox, Play Station, Switch or Epic Games Store. This game offers a lot compared to Pinball FX 3.The first major change is cross platform, This allows me to compete with people from all platforms not just PC players this is huge and will make aiming for high scores much more rewarding as you will be challenged by the entire community not just a single platform it is a chance to truly show your skills.The second part involves the Epic games exclusivity on release. This had to happen because it gave devs access to unreal engine. This is a game changer that not only made the tables look better it also allowed for a better score display. Instead of the DOT Matrix display now zen can use LCD score display and animate score display as well this is a game changer on the long run for if Zen aquires Stern or Jerssy Jacks Pinball licenses they can recreat there modern tables which dont use DOT matrix display anymore.The third change is ray tracing. Cabinet builders and PC builders alike want the most bleeding edge features when available and now they get both HDR support, better cabinet support and RTX this would not be possible on FX 3's old engine and standard PC requirements but now we have a much easier way to use cabinets and full HDR and RTX support.The last thing I will cover in terms of changes is the in-game store. Where Pinball is concerned customization is huge we love customizing we spent a lot of time building cabinets and organizing our gaming rooms devs noted this and made it possible for us to customize our very own unique profiles in-game with cosmetics that can be purchased in-game this makes every individual profile look unique and gives it its own identity.These changes combined make Pinball FX the ultimate platform for the future of digital pinball and this could have been done simply by updating FX 3.PRICING:The pricing model in this game is the same as every major pinball platform on Steam but with a twist. You buy table packs as dlcs. The argument that Steam prices are higher than Epic games is not valid there is a lot that goes on when estimating the price for one steam takes a bigger cut from purchases compared to Epic's cut in fact Steam takes Twice the amount Epic takes. In order to keep the licenses and be able to produce more tables this cost needs to be delegated to players so it makes since that the players pay the extra cost if you dont want or can't afford the current prices you are more than welcome to play on Epic but those want to play on steam know how the pricing works and can afford it. Additionally, if you are a newcomer or unsure if you will play pinball on a daily bases this game introduces a new method of buying tables not present in any other game. The Pinball Pass is a membership that can be purchased and it unlocks 90% of the tables so for a monthly or an annual fee you can have 90% of the table ready to play  not to mention the fact that Pinball FX 3 owners get the tables that were previously on FX 3 at half the original price and people who are switching from Epic to steam are getting all the tables they purchased on Epic for free on Steam making the transition easy pricing wise. This is not a scam Zen studios are doing whatever they can to provide the best fair experience for pinball players worldwide.GAME PLAY:The game runs and plays exactly as it does on Epic games with only 1 issue and 2 improvements over the Epic games version. The only issue which devs are aware of and will fix soon is the fact that your keyboard controls don't get saved you have to edit them each time you log in which takes a minute to do.Cabinet mode is a huge improvement you no longer need to contact anyone one to set it up and the interface is much easier to navigate on Steam compared to EpicRay tracing performance is much better on steam I get an average of 70-90 FPS with maximum settings and RTX enabled while on Epic I barely maintained 60 FPS with the exact same setup.

_childDocuments_.review: The new Pinball FX is an authentic recreation of an overused pinball table.  While I don't suffer with significant performance issues like many others, it's still not a great experience.  The flippers now feel like the springs are stretched out due to them rendering the full physics simulation of them but not having a quality snap back to place when released giving them a sluggish sensation.  Audio mix continues to be Zen's biggest weakness with it being absolutely terrible on a 5.1 system with some tables sounding like an actual table that has blown out speakers.  For Charging previous owners for new tables again they did nothing about improving the voice work that was utterly rancid on many tables in the past, you'd think for all the extra cost they could at least re-record with people other than their custodial staff in their own broom closet.  While the UI was never great in FX2 and 3, it was very functional.  This one doesn't feel good with any control method and takes forever to navigate to what you actually want to do.  To top it off it adds a lot of extra loading even between game over to restart on the same table even when running entirely on NVMe SSDs.  While a subscription pass isn't a bad idea on paper even that is executed rather poorly. Your options are $15 for a month or $100 for a year, making the one year option the easily best value of your money...IF it actually let you access the entire library of tables.  While they do inform you it's for most the tables, the ones not part of it are all the Marvel ones and the Indiana Jones table which is currently 23 of their current total 112, a pretty sizeable chunk.  That's not even taking into account that 20+ of the tables are also on Apple Arcade which is only $5/month and also has another 200some games on the service.All in all moving pinball to the new Unreal Engine with more methods to pay for what you want to play should be a home run, but Zen Studios continues to make progressively odd changes in the execution that continue to feel like a backstab for veterans of the franchise and unwelcoming to new potential customers.

With the legacy discount in addition to frequent sales they can be had for less than a cup of coffee (and not a fancy one either). There is noticeable flipper lag on some tables. Twilight Zone was pretty bad at first and it’s now great to play.New tables are only on FX, so snag it, enjoy the new tables.Initial load times are a little slower, but it’s alright. _childDocuments_.review: Pinball FX is a great game that builds on previous iterations. Some of the biggest improvements you will notice are in the physics department and with the graphics and lighting. I am a seasoned digital pinball player and can tell you this is by far the closestthis game has come to having realistic physics. For me, the physics are what really soldme on this title and I have played it since its first release on the Epic Games Store.When you play digital pinball games, realistic physics can go a long way because it challenges you to make good shots and rewards you when you do but also punishesyou when you don't. In FX3, for example, the physics felt like the ball had a predetermined path(especially on the Zen tables) which is why I played the Williams titles for the majority of my playtime.That is not the case with Pinball FX and because of the physics overhaul, I am finding myself enjoyingtitles from FX3 that I didn't have much interest in before. The second biggest improvement is the lighting and animations that you will notice while you are playing.The Williams tables received a glow update that improved lighting specifically around the flashers which wasvery noticeable.If you are coming from FX3, the physics will feel a lot different at first and it will take getting used to becauseit's a different engine but you will notice how much more "realistic" they feel the more you play.Lastly, the amount of tables Pinball FX offers is actually quite insane. There is something for everyone. For oldtimers like myself, I enjoy playing the Williams recreations the most but because of the renewed physics,I am also enjoying original titles like Crypt of the Necrodancer a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, this an update on my review that I did some time ago. I erased my other review because I think I was a little too haste in doing my review. The ball on pinball fx feels heavier. So much so that playing my favorite board on both of them (Secrets of the Deep) you can feel the difference. The ball came to a complete stop on a flipper. Like as if it defied gravity. Yeah, I know it's not real. But realism is why got this game, no? Pinball fx3 feels like they spend more time tweaking it, and fx feels like they did it just to make it feel different. Did'nt spent as much time with a good enough feel to them. I find myself going back to fx3 more often than this one. It just plays better, and much more fun. Alot more predictable. This version ain't bad. The could of, and should of just made those extra boards for fx3, rather than just relying on unreal engine to do something extraordinary that they already achieved with fx3. Atomiswave , Naomi , two different mames.  Two different Naomi and Atomiswave for vertical and horizontal games with inlays. Not trying to brag, just like the simplicity of pinball fx3 more. _childDocuments_.review: The nostalgia hits strong with this one.Zen Studios sucks for so many reasons, such as requiring loyal customers to re-purchase tables they already own with successive releases of the game, and across devices, particularly if you are a completionist seeking all table rewards to decorate your Tables and Tournament Room. There is a pretty good discount through Legacy Bundles, but with so many tables the cost adds up quickly. Also, Zen aren't the only ones to do this, but locking Steam achievements behind paid DLC is also kinda scummy.For now I'm sticking to tables that I don't already own in Pinball FX3, and I'm also glad FX3 was not made completely obsolete with this new release, as some tables remain exclusive to each (at least at the time of writing this review in Feb 2024). But, having said all that, the pinball experience is amazeballs. You can choose to add extra SFX to classic tables or keep to the traditional experience. I find that while the extra SFX look really great, they can be rather distracting. Some tables pull it off better than others. There is online and offline leaderboards so you can challenge yourself against others. Just the fact that you can play pinball whenever you want is the most important thing you need to know about this game. 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: After having played FX2, FX3, I purchased Pinball FX in the Epic store last year after the initial launch. I am glad it's playable on Steam now as well. Where the William's table are the most challenging, as they are IRL as well, the Marvel tables are the most forgiving and leave some room for human error. _childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid my parents got me a mid-sized Digimon pinball table made by Funrise, Inc. I assembled the table, plugged it in, and launched my first ball. My first shot sent the ball half way up the middle ramp before it plummeted down the board between the two flippers. I felt cheated and robbed.Looking at the DLC page for this game gave me that same exact feeling. Thanks Zen Studios for making me feel like a kid again!On second thought, this is a poor analogy. The Digimon pinball table made by Funrise, Inc did not come with micro transactions or a monthly subscription unlike Pinball Fx, made by Zen Studios. As for "premium" cosmetics, I decorated my table with a Slifer the Sky Dragon Yu-Gi-Oh! card. I placed it near the scoreboard and told my friends that it was a reward for beating my high score. It was tacky, stupid, and made no sense; much like the "premium" cosmetics for Pinball FX.But enough childhood stories. Let's break down why Zen Studios sucks:-Micro transactions that should be called Macro transactions-A monthly pinball pass that cost more than a Netflix subscription and does not include all the tables-A perplexing DLC page that makes Hitman 3, Farming Simulator, and any Ubisoft Game page look tame and sane in comparison-14.99 United States Dollars for one table in the form of Indiana Jones™: The Pinball Adventure (not included in the pinball pass lol)-Any tables you bought previously need re-bought in the new game-Couldn't be bothered to port every table over from FX3 for a definitive experience -Couldn't be bothered to add tables that were in FX2 (you're telling me that Zen Studios were able to work with Disney to get their Marvel and Star Wars tables over, but they couldn't be bothered to work with anyone to bring over the Portal, South Park, AvP, Street Fighter, Doom, Bob's Burger, or Ninja Gaiden tables? Even with Epic Games exclusive money? Go suck one.)-35 GB for a flipping pinball gameTo sum it all up: don't give Zen Studios your money. If you want to get into pinball, but don't want to buy/play on a physical machine, then there are free/cheaper virtual pinball games. I can help you find these free alternatives. I would even suggest the Super Skill Pinball board game to help you "get" what pinball is about; it's a fantastic roll and write game that can be played solo or with friends. It's $20 and comes with 4 different tables (lol again at the $14.99 Indiana Jones table).Keep your hard earned money. In a time where a dozen eggs almost cost as much as the US federal minimum wage (it's actually double the minimum wage for tipped employees lmao), you deserve that money. Not these shmucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, this is the only place to play some iconic Williams tables, let alone future ones.  But those current tables come with issues ranging from scratchy sound and balance, flipper spacing, a complete lack of any kind of table specific options such as number of balls, to the biggest offender, something of a heavy feel to the gameplay.  You can adjust to it, but it's immediately noticeable.And the usual omnipresent Zen Studios games and offers can't be turned off, or hidden.  Selecting a reward to display in your home room requires scrolling past every other manufacturer, as a reminder that your 'collection' isn't complete.  That and the giant billboard in the lower right of the screen.Room decorations can be obtained through playing, and tournaments which allow a limited number of plays per day, in order to accumulate points.  As there is no option to move freely about your Room, it seems like an underdeveloped idea.And I have no idea how you're expected to follow a friend's progress other than a message that appears onscreen if you best their score.  I saw no friend's list options at all, unless I missed them.Zaccaria Pinball's crisp feel and plethora of settings keep it at the apex of digital pinball.Buyer's remorse with FX is somewhat lessened with the promise of future Bally, Williams, and Midway tables.  And there is some fun to be had, but since I must choose between a 'Yes' and 'No' with no middling option, I must currently choose 'No.'

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing Pin FX on Epic Store since early access, player name "Move Your Car". I've installed to Steam simply so I can write this review. I've only really played the Williams tables as the originals feel too slow for me and largely feel like they're made for casuals. These games have their place and there's some good ideas there, but they're not for me. Onto the Williams line up...There's a lot to like in the new FX so lets open with that. There's a few new long awaited Williams tables which is good to see, with more on the way. And Zen have done a pretty good job of nailing the look and feel of the tables and I don't think they get enough credit for this. Advanced players are likely to notice that the flippers are now more capable of performing techniques such as live and drop catches. With RTX turned on the playfields look much sharper and the ball really come to life. Recently added DLSS support is highly welcome as well. After having put quite a few hours into this game it would be hypocritical for me to give this game a bad rating (which I did originally) so I have changed to a "yes" on the recommendation. Its free to install, Fish Tales is free to play in full (highly recommend giving that a go), and you can play a quick demo of all the tables on offer, so there's a risk-free option worth taking advantage of before spending anything. There's a caveat though, so here comes the bad... I've been pretty vocal in expressing disappointment to what I believe to be unnecessary changes to the original rules, specifically pertaining to extra balls, as well as their handling of those changes in terms of communication and patch notes. I've also thrown shade at the QA dept, for releasing new tables with game-stopper bugs.  Zen, you really didn't need to add your own arbitrary extra balls (for score and specials) to the original rule-sets. They were fine as they were. And then when someone demonstrates that perhaps too many extra balls might now be a problem, rather than asking yourself "Are we the baddies here? Did we put a few too many extra balls in the game?" you just went and arbitrarily nerfed extra balls and the way many of the tables worked with highly restrictive EB per BIP limits. All you had to do was remove the unnecessary stuff that you added in and maybe tweak the playfields on specific tables when and if need arises.¯\_ (ツ)_/¯It just feels like sacrilege to be butchering the original rule-sets like this. I think Zen really dropped the ball there. It probably wouldn't bother me anywhere near as much if these tables weren't as precariously close to perfection as they are. Thais my biggest gripe with this game. I get that a lot of players simply won't care about this (especially those of you who prefer the Zen's originals), but if Zen really asked around they'd find the majority of purist and competitive players would agree.That's my final word on the matter. Apologies for my previously overly aggressive explanation of this. I stand by everything I said, just not the way I said it.

That said, their original tables are genuinely great designs the majority of the time, and I think they do a good job with the graphics and music too. I still hate that the MUCH superior pinball simulator, The Pinball Arcade, has more or less died, with Williams licensing their IPs to FX. It's a testament to how good their core design is for Attack From Mars that it's still fun here, but I can't recommend any of the other tables; they just don't feel right. Overall I still recommend FX, and I love the idea of Pinball M as a Mature themed spinoff, but they still need to go back to the drawing board and get the physics down for this franchise to evolve. _childDocuments_.review: Let's address the elephant in the room - This should not be the expected standard, to have our tables from the previous entry carry over. Yes when Zen announced these will not transfer I was like most here 'bummed out', having the full collection in FX3 (100 Tables). The majority of negative reviews presented here is because of this expectation.We still can play all of our purchases on FX3, we have not lost anything.If they pulled the same stunt by removing the previous title with all its DLC's from the Steam Store, unable to purchase to complete your collection then I would be giving them a negative review.As an alternative you can go into a subscription service to access most of the tables bar a few like Indiana Jones.This works out at £12.79 (GBP) for 150 Pinball Coins which will give you 1 month or £83.99 for 1200 for the yearly pass.You are given 1 day free to access majority of the tables (over 100) with all their modes.During early access on EPIC, you had to buy the tables VIA the microtransactions called tickets, I'm glad the removed this model and allow us to purchase the tables directly from the Steam Store Front.Zen have given an discount for the tables we purchased in FX3 at 50% of the cost.So Williams Pinball:Volume 1 which costs £8.50 is £4.25.Also if you've not purchased the table on FX3 it costs £8.50 and you get it for both FX3 and FX.FX uses Unreal Engine, hence this is part of them releasing on the EPIC game store first. FX uses a new physics model they dub , this is great on the new tables and most of the Williams, however the remasters are hit and miss.for example  Magna Saver is wildly unrealistic unlike FX3/FX2VR. The periscope that bridges mid playfield to upper playfield can have the ball fly through geomety, causing the ball to be stuck. (I have video footage of this.). The williams tables have PRO mode physics in which the playfield is tilted at a steeper angle and increased the difficulty from the operators menu. I for one love this mode for the speed and it feels more realistic, I hope Zen will allow us to make custom changes to the playfield's tilt in a custom mode, having access to the operators menu.Each table has Classic (3 ball), Arcade (FX3 style power up's like slow motion or slow down), 1 Ball, Timed (5 Mins), Flips(200 Flip Presses),Distance (set amount of ball travel) and practice (60 Mins Free Play). Only on some tables you have the PRO mode I mentioned above. With all these modes combined they have over 600 Leaderboards that are crossed over from Epic,PS4,PS5,Xbox One, Xbox Series X and Steam. This is great, however I just hope this does not discourage Zen from updating the tables which will have cause and effect on the scores.Magsave is wildly unrealistic and on occasions throws your ball out of control which did not happen in FX3.Endless Tilt on Free table Fish Tales.Timed Mode is inconsistent on some tables like Indiana Jones or Attack on Mars when the ball is out of play and in a cutscene time is paused, however most tables the time continues to count down.Sound issues that are present in FX3 have carried across to FX.Nice QOL improvements, in setting up backglass and DMD allowing the use of arrow keys to position and scale (that keeps it's ratio), rather than typing it.I have a 2 monitor setup, using one monitor as the playfield and the other for backglass artwork and DM.Unlike FX3 table achievements are not tied to your Steam account, only ten generic achievements you can easily get within a few hours play and two of them taking longer, very easy to 100%. One of the perks of FX3 is when you got a table achievement the game would pause and you see the achievement medal pop in centre of the screen, this effect has not carried across unfortunately, but on the other hand you do not have to own all the tables with the achievement to have it 100%.They have brought over the collectables from Star Wars Pinball VR , where you can display items in your collection room, which consists of statues, figures, carpets, posters and cups.Majority of those said items are unlocked by reaching a score, this is accumulated added to your total each time you play, this just encourages you to play that table enough times to unlock them all, rather than by skill of which I would of preferred or at least having the final unlock by getting x sore in one classic play. Going forward I hope Zen can improve the physics per table where needed and fix issues that have been carried over.Be nice to have the collection room to scale in size to how many tables you own.The game for the most part is an improvement over FX3, mainly being the physics of which is a step-up on majority of tables on offer, got a nice front end, HDR support, Ray Tracing and some visual improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Having been a keen pinballer for many years both real and digitally, and played PFX3 to death I was eagerly awaiting the release of PFX since I heard about it's development. What a disappointment it's turned out to be...Not only did Zen signup to Epic's exclusivity rights for a year with this game prior to it's Steam release but they also did not honour any tables owned in PFX3 to carry over to PFX like they previously did with PFX2 when PFX3 was first released. This of course means I have to purchase them all again if I want to play them on PFX, which I think is unlikely even at the discounted rate of 50% off for tables owned in PFX3. This feels like a stab in the back to the community that made them who they are and Zen must have taken lessons from Epic on this because it's exactly what they did too when they abandoned the reboot of Unreal Tournament in favour of selling out with Fortnite several years ago!OK, the PFX base game is free and comes with 3 free tables all of which are available on PFX3 so they're nothing new to me and I don't have much motivation to play them as they were never on my list of 'go to tables'. However, I played for a while and my immediate impression wasn't a great one. I did not notice much difference in how the tables looked graphically but the ball mechanics did feel better, but not by a large margin. You're also given a free 'pass' to unlock  of the remaining tables for 1 day. This is not a perk, it's clearly designed to whet the appetite of players to get them to purchase more tables. OK that's fair enough but it's not nearly enough time to try out all the available tables, and there are a lot, prior to purchasing. Without the day pass unowned tables are available to trial for 2 minutes at a time.There are several other features within the game, like tournaments, events and a 'Pin Hall'. Tournaments can be setup by players and they can chose the tables and the game rules. This was also a feature in PFX3 so again just a rehash of that, there's no real benefit to playing these unless it's a private tournament against friends. You have to own a table to be able to play it in a tournament. Events I'm not sure what they are exactly as I've not played this mode much, I think it's similar to the 'Matchup' feature in PFX3 but instead of playing against people in leagues you play to unlock cosmetic items which you can showcase in your Pin Hall, which is basically the main screen after opening the game. With events you can play a table even if you don't own it as long as it's not a 'premium' event, however, you're restricted to the number of times you can enter each event per day but it seems to be a good way to trial unowned tables for longer than 2 minutes.Overall, as a player coming from PFX3 there's nothing really to get me hooked but for a new player to Zen's pinball you'll likely have a lot of fun. Had Zen provided 1 or 2 brand new tables to play or even allowed me to play the tables I own on PFX3 then I may have better things to say but as it stands I cannot recommend this game. Saying that, I'm bound to delve into it fairly frequently and I will likely purchase the new tables at some point, particularly if they're on sale so I may update my review at various times in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: [offline player, playtime inaccurate]GOOD:+ Greatly improved Williams table lighting effects (non-raytracing user)+ Greatly improved physics for all tables (particularly noticeable on non-Williams tables)+ Works great out-of-box on Linux via Proton+ Lots of new (and even some FX2-only) tables that thankfully aren't Marvel or Star Wars+ Not online-only and/or subscription-only (yet)+ Customizeable camera angle+ Cab support+ It didn't remain Epic-exclusiveNEUTRAL:~ Performance and input is smooth for me (Vega 56, Ryzen 5 3600, 16gb RAM, max settings, raytracing off, 60fps @1080p) but others seem to have noticeable issues. Oddly enough Pinball M *does* have massive input lag on my system~ Not all FX3 tables (or FX2 for that matter) are remade... yet~ Rebuying is required for FX3 owners... BUT there are "legacy" bundles that when combined with seasonal sales reduce the cost by over 80% for most tables. It's not perfect, but considering the cost over the longterm, the overall improvements, and the FX2->FX3 transfer it was worth it for me. I would have spent faaaar more in a physical arcade (or for a single "AAA" title) over the years, so I don't personally feel cheated in the slightestBAD:- Non-table microtransactions- UI is... functional, but more importantly not designed for offline players (lots of big empty "need to be connected..." boxes)- Some showstopper bugs on a small handful of tables (hard freezes, unintended softlocks with offline-only play, etc.)- The whole game room customization thing is laughable. Pinball M's take is a step a better direction with table-impacting decoration changes, but still not "it"- Steam achievements are only tracked when playing online- Some of the "Zen-ified" Williams table effects block the table view or are annoying/distracting- Physics sounds are still very quiet/lackluster even with manual adjustments. The impact this would make if redesigned can't be understated, but it's a pipedream at this point because sound design is neglected industry-wide... doubly so for pinball suites despite what it does for the feel/impact of the physics

_childDocuments_.review: Bearing in mind that I've barely played any pinball IRL due to lack of access to it, I find this to be a blast. I know there was some controversy about having to re-purchase tables from FX3 to play them in this new version, but I'm mostly coming in fresh here. You have a few fun free tables to start out with and see if you enjoy the game's interpretation of Pinball in a general sense. You also get a day pass for completing the tutorial where you have 24 hours to try any of the pinball tables as much as you want. After that, tables are available as DLC, usually in bundles. So sometimes you have to get a couple tables you aren't super interested in to get one you want, but at the same time, you might be surprised by something fun. And there are sales at different times. I like the original tables I've played quite a lot. Some of the licensed ones are fun but can often be missing licensed music or voices so they feel a little cheap. Doesn't mean they aren't fun to play after you get used to it. There are dozens to choose from, some exclusively digital and others more realistic and based on real pinball games. You have some extras like collectibles you can unlock, online rankings, a quest mode, and specific challenges. You can also change the physics between normal and more realistic, which is harder. You also have the option to use Arcade mode where you can have extra bonuses or powers like slowing down the action. It's a large download because it includes EVERY table whether you own it or not, but I recommend giving it a go and playing the free ones for a few days to see if it clicks.

_childDocuments_.review: The old tables finally went on a steep enough sale that I accepted it - a combined 75% from table pack 50% and legacy bundles 50%. However, I still don't recommend most people upgrade at that price. A sale of 90% off would be an okay deal for the minimal work done on the tables. Though these really should be a free upgrade like the transition of FX2 to FX3.The ray tracing features look nice and are limited enough in scope to be performant on RTX 2000 cards and above. I'm running a 2070 Super with DLSS Quality at 1440p and sitting at about 70-90 fps depending on the table. Nothing amazing for the visual quality on display, but passable.As far as the game itself goes, I'm miffed that they dropped support for ultrawide monitors. They claim that they had to pillarbox gameplay to 16:9 because the levels' backgrounds weren't designed for wider aspect ratios, so there were visual issues at the sides of the frame on some tables.So on one hand, they claim they put work into "remastering" the existing tables and want more money for them, yet on the other hand they can't be bothered to adjust or add assets to the sides of the frame on  of the tables. It's not like these backgrounds have much meaningful detail to begin with. To be honest, I'd rather we have the ability to turn the backgrounds off and just see the collectibles room anyway.It'd also be nice to be able to turn off the visual extras like the moving character models. The Williams tables let you turn them off, but none of the others as far as I can tell.To new players who didn't already own FX3 tables, you may think the complaints about the upgrade value proposition don't matter to you. To you I say, keep in mind they'll probably do another "upgrade" cycle with a new release in 4-5 years, like the last two times. I think they've made it crystal clear they want paid minimum-effort upgrades to be the status quo for future releases.Also, a VR mode would be a great addition to this game. I'll accept buying a DLC for a VR mode, as greedy as that is. But for the love of God, don't try to sell VR as a separate game again.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, this is a hard call of a review for me. There are a number of issues noted in other reviews, from the repurchasing of microtransactions at high prices to inconsistent performance. I actually sympathize with many of these reviews at this time, but in my own perspective, I don't have the same issues that some of these purchasers have.While I too have many, many, many Pinball FX tables from over the years, I ended up going with the Pinball Pass on this version and doing the 15 a month subscription. It got me the bulk of the tables I play anyway and introduced me to tables I would have not normally played, so to me that was an acceptable trade. I may slowly build up my collection again over time, but I don't think I'm going to lean in as hard to purchases as I have in the past because I just don't want to buy the content again. I already own it on so many devices it really DOES seem silly to pay almost full price again.Going on to the performance, again, this is a hard call for me. I've seen people mention flipper lag, poor frame rate, and I can only ever see small glimpses of that on my machine. I have everything cranked up to max and I run on an RTX card, so things like ray tracing and high graphical load are not issues for my machine.But, I do see glimpses of inconsistencies even on my powerful rig. I can only assume that a lesser rig could struggle on some of these graphics, even without high end options like ray tracing enabled.After that, let me also note that I really wasn't impressed with the new look of the tables UNTIL I turned on Ray Tracing. Once I did, wow, the whole thing really popped into life in a stunning way, but I also felt like that moment was a bit of a negative. I want to have that same "this table is gorgeous" feeling when I look at the game without something as expensive as Ray Tracing on, and I feel like that is true of these negative reviews too.But, all of that negativity noted, let me get to the positives of this game, because there are many.The selection of tables is huge, the tournaments are interesting, the Pinball Hall customization is fun and I really hope they do more with it as they go forward, and I've been really engaged with the season pass and its very diverse sets of challenges and restrictions. As a player who likes pushing herself with pinball, all of this gives me new ways to try to learn new tricks or new approaches to a board.A few other reviews in here mention the physics behind the ball, and I have to agree with them, I really, really like the physics. They do feel weighty, predictable, and much better than past iterations of the franchise. I've always liked how they treated the ball in Pinball FX, but this game really makes the ball shine. (As it should, lol.) I feel more prepared, as a pinball player, when I approach boards in real life after playing this game.In past iterations, if I'd go play my local version of Twilight Zone after playing the virtual board, it would be similar but not an exact replica. I'd say this engine edition is MUCH closer to the behavior of the Twilight Zone pinball board in my local arcade. For that alone, I'd say this version is a major upgrade.And, as a new platform that has modern game development tools, I'm looking forward to the studio continuing to iterate on what they've built here. It's not perfect, but I think it's a great start and can continue to become better and better as time goes forward, and I really look forward to continue to play this version over my iPhone!

_childDocuments_.review: Download it for the free stuff and the new tables!I played on other platforms (Xbox, Switch, Epic). For high-end PC users, the new Pinball FX is likely a big step up in visual and play quality from the previous iteration - Pinball FX3. For the rest of us, this seems like a lateral change that has added a few new features and taken away a few others. Generally, the challenge has increased a bit with new physics and a few tweaks to Zen's original layouts brought forward into this new version from Pinball FX3.Many of the new tables introduced only in Pinball FX have great themes and vary wildly in difficulty. Also, more classic Bally/Williams tables have been recreated only for Pinball FX, including best sellers like The Addams Family and Star Trek: The Next Generation. With three free tables and a few free seasonal Events as well as free trials for all of the other tables for sale, it is absolutely worth it to download this game and try out the free stuff. That said, this new platform is still missing some desired features and imports from Pinball FX3, and previously purchased tables in FX2 or FX3 do not carry forward, they must be repurchased, though there is a significant discount available. There are also several obnoxious bugs across the many tables, and the ability to nudge pass is not realistic. All in all, though, Pinball FX is highly replayable, with global leaderboards, player created tournaments, and in-game seasonal events. If you are new to digital pinball, you can pick up a dozen tables for $30 or less and get the silverball rolling!

_childDocuments_.review: I hate the physics.  It's like the people who designed this game have never played a real pinball machine.  Might as well forget about things like flick, post and bounce passes.  Ball control in this game is non existent.   One of my biggest complaints is the slings like to throw the ball backwards and down the middle at lightning speed.  Slings in a real machine are designed to kick the ball back and forth between each other and throw the ball towards the outlanes not down the middle. This is why they are positioned at an upward angle, very rarely will it fire the ball backwards and down the middle. Zen clearly does not understand the design process behind them.  Maybe my hate for this game comes from the fact I have 5 real pinball machines sitting in my basement with access to approx 100 other ones. I play a lot of real pinball and this feels nothing like the real thing.  I find most of their original tables to be way too slow. They lack the excitement that draws a player in and keeps them shoveling money into the machine.  Seriously, you have to shoot a bazillion ramps or spinner shots etc just to start a mode.  It's like when they design these things they forgot the average game of pinball only lasts 3-5 mins.  I keep coming back to this game hoping Zen has improved upon it and end up walking away disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Introduction:I have recently got back into Pinball, and have done a fair amount of research.Now, if you want to play digital Pinball, in my opinion you have 4 options really: 1. PinballFX 2. Zaccaria Pinball 3. Buy a Digital Pinball Cabinet or 4. Play some of the small-time games, some of which haven't been updated in several years, or lost their licenses (*cough, cough* Zen *cough, cough*).My thoughts:First of all, I get it took time and effort to migrate all of/most of the tables from FX3 to FX (aka. FX4). However, mechanically speaking, it feels/they feel mostly the same when compared to FX3. Maybe they do feel different to the trained eye, but not to me. So it's really just a graphical update it seems, as there is no real additional tangible value in my eyes to the "new" versions of the tables. They are essentially the same table with a re-skin, no surmountable difference.So some will argue: "Okay, 'cheapskate'...just go play FX3, or another game then." Listen, you special person you, as mentioned earlier, there aren't a lot of options, and FX3 doesn't appear to be receiving updates or new tables anymore. Yes, I can play the "legacy" versions of the tables, but if I want to play new tables I gotta play FX (FX4). Which is fair, they're new tables after all, but that brings me to another issue....the Pinball Pass. Oh joy.So, the Pinball Pass costs around 12.79 (GBP, my currency), which is a lot just for digital pinball tables. For a year that's almost 100 GBP. They even mentioned not all tables are included. Plus, they now have a new game coming out: PInball M, or as me and friends like to call it: Pinball Moneymaker. The point is, the pass is overly expensive, doesn't include all tables and I don't feel is a justified price. Plus, will the pass cover both games, or will they make you pay for two separate passes? I wouldn't put it past them to be honest with you.The last problem is Zen Studios hold a lot of or most of the licenses, and objectively speaking hold a monopoly on the Pinball game genre right now. Zaccaria is probably their closest competition, but as others have said it's not exactly 50/50. Which is a real and serious problem. That, and you have an army of sheep - or ignorant/careless people - who still support them despite their actions and clear negative reputation.Final Thoughts/Conclusion:They should have given all legacy tables for free, or at a super reduced price in one single bundle. Then made revamped tables which they could then justifiably charge for in my opinion. The revamped tables would play differently, to the point where there is clearly a big difference. Regarding the pass, if it cost half of what it does now, included all tables and covered both games (PinballFX and Pinball M) then I would consider it. But right now, they need to really get their head out of their backsides and change things. Although I wouldn't hold my breath.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a fan of Pinball FX since iteration 2, have bought all the tables on multiple consoles, upgraded to a virtual pin mostly to play FX, upgraded my virtual table pc to play the newest version and tables, and I am still highly entertained and love the way these guys do pinball. _childDocuments_.review: Expect a lot of reviews related to the pricing model, some justified.  If you can get past that, you have a really solid, state-of-the-art pinball game that's a meaningful upgrade from FX3.After 100+ hours in FX on Epic and 100+ hours in FX3 on a lot of the same tables, the new FX is my go-to platform and the one I see myself playing long into the future.  The difference is all in the physics.  There's some visual upgrades for sure - which are actually a mixed bag at the moment, because while the game looks great, it's wildly unoptimized - but what's important in pinball is how it /feels/, and FX feels fantastic.  To compare the two, FX3 is fun and springy, easy and arcadey, while FX, to me, feels like far more like playing real pinball.  It's more challenging and realistic, more unpredictable, faster and less forgiving.  The default competitive mode is "Classic", which allows you to play for scores and excludes the powerups that were a necessity in the default mode of FX3 if you wanted to top the leaderboards.  If you're still after the powerups, you can find them in "Arcade" mode, but "Classic" feels great in my hands, and if you want a challenge even above that, there's "Pro" mode on each of the Williams tables with a steeper playfield and tougher rules.  This game is imperfect, and a work in progress (please add proper Ultrawide support!), but it doesn't deserve to be drowned out in negative reviews.  I'll update this with some more detailed thoughts, but if you're any sort of a pinball fan at all, ignore the hubbub and give FX a look.  You'll be glad you did.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoy the Zen pinball games! This one I have been playing since early access about a year ago, and it has been adding a number of new tables, while polishing the graphics of the old ones. Performance has been a challenge, but the latest update has really improved that.  (Although, my rig still can't play the game with more than mid-range settings).So, that's one area that still needs work (performance), but otherwise, if you have not played the older iterations then this is a great time to jump in.  If you have the previous versions, and don't have a high-powered computer, then you might want to wait until you do and continue enjoying the older iterations until you can upgrade your computer. For cabinet owners, I have FX3 installed in a physical cabinet with a separate dmd monitor and backglass monitor.  Cabinet mode for FX3 is simple and works great.  Plus, community volunteers have created software that can interface with FX3 and allow you to run real flipper and bumper solenoids, shaker motors, led lighting effects, etc...The new Pinball FX, however, does NOT have that robust of a cabinet feature-set, yet.Yes, you can have a 3-screen setup with three monitors for the playfield, dmd, and the backglass.  However, these are glitchy at the moment.  Especially the dmd.  It works, then it doesn't work and freezes the game.  Then it works, then it doesn't work, etc...  But, cabinet mode is a work-in-progress at this point, so....Also, as of right now, I am not aware of any way to connect solenoids, shaker motors, led's, etc... to the new Pinball FX like you can with FX3. _childDocuments_.review: I started playing this in Early Access so the 7 hours currently played as of this writing only reflects the Steam version, not the time I spent in the Epic Store version.I've been a fan of Zen's pinball games since Pinball FX 2 and collected every table in FX 2 and FX 3 with the exception of the Williams arcade table recreations--- not that they're terrible or anything, I just prefer Zen's wildly creative originals over faithful digital recreations of classic arcade machines. There's a lot to love in the new FX collection at release, including some new favorites like Kong, How To Train Your Dragon, Homeworld, Wrath Of The Elder Gods, and Curse Of The Mummy. Some of my favorite originals, Star Wars, and Marvel tables have been ported over (the sound design in Fear Itself and Son Of Zeus are particularly noteworthy) as well as the more mid tables. There's not much I actively dislike with a couple exceptions (the Borderlands and Star Wars Classic Collectibles are duds no matter how much I try to like them) and with development as active as it is I'm really looking forward to a continued stream of more new tables.I understand that licensing restrictions means that some tables from older version of Pinball FX will probably not get ported (South Park, Ms. 'Splosion Man, The Walking Dead) and that's a shame but they still work fine in the older versions of the app so not that big of a deal, I suppose.Great stuff for any digital pinball enthusiast.

_childDocuments_.review: I dont normally post a review this quickly, but I'm making a special exception for this one (and I'll make edits later if anything changes, but I'm doubting that's gonna happen).Disclaimer, I've been playing this for quite awhile over on Epic, so my playtime here aint even close to what it actually is.  For those of you that follow me, you may have noticed that I rarely ever speak of this game, despite saying originally that I'd update as I kept playing it over the months.  There's a reason for that.This... is a mess.  For technical and non-technical reasons.First, the issues with Zen.  Awhile ago I posted a topic on the Steam forums for this (well, for FX3, that's where talks about this new one were happening on Steam) about the whole ticket issue, a topic which just blew up right away.  This was a problem that was happening during the Epic phase... it's gone now... but it was definitely foreshadowing, so to speak.  If you've seen weird mobile game currencies, well... yeah.  Basically that.  There was a variety of excuses given there, particularly "well it's the only way it CAN be done", but... I direct your attention to the DLC list here.  I shouldnt have to say more.  And yes, I know there were more reasons given than that.  But that doesnt fly with me, and overall it says a lot about what Zen is up to.Think about it:  they're already asking players to re-buy tables that they likely already owned on FX3.  So they do that, AND then add that nonsense on top?  An infamously greedy concept from predatory mobile games, which are VERY hated by most PC and console gamers?  Yeah.  It didnt bode well, and put plenty of players off of the whole thing immediately.  I cant blame them.That was bad enough.  It was removed though... right?  Sorta.  The tickets are gone, but "pinball coins" are there.  You dont buy tables with those.  Those are used for... primarily for cosmetics, which is pretty stupid.  Like... really?  Who came up with that one?Well, you also buy the Pinball Pass with those.  This seems like a fine idea to me.  I did pick that up.  The idea is that it's 15 per month, and you get access to a bazillion tables.  Again, seems good to me.  These tables are NOT cheap to make.  Not at all. I cant overstate the amount of time and effort it takes to make these things, seriously.  So the whole thing being a bit on the costly side?  Makes sense to me, always has.Buuuuuuuuut... the pass doesnt REALLY cover everything.  Did ya like some of the many Marvel tables in FX3?  Well, the pass doesnt cover those for some inexplicable reason (which I'm going to assume is Disney's slimy influence, because I cant think of why else it'd be).  There's a couple of other things it doesnt cover.  So, you're paying for a "get them all" thing that doesnt get you all of them.  I quite enjoyed some of the Marvel tables in FX3, so this definitely annoys me.There's plenty more that could be talked about with Zen themselves, and with just how they handled all of this.  This isnt all of it.  But there's only so much room here... let's move on to the technical stuff.Firstly, there's the much-touted new physics, supposedly THE reason for the whole thing.  Updated physics means new engine, really.  That's fine, in theory.  IN THEORY.  But there is a problem with this, which became apparent to me pretty much immediately.The old tables... the ones that werent the Williams set... they were designed with FX3.  They were designed with THAT game's physics engine.  Every angle, every target, every ramp, EVERYTHING, set up for that.  I cant overstate just how CAREFUL and precise pinball table design is.  To work right, everything has gotta be on point.So when you take these older tables and give them new physics... they break down.Just as an example, my favorite of the Zen tables, Sorcerer's Lair.  Almost unplayable.  Do you like the far left outlane?  Do you REALLY like it?  If so, this is now the table for you!  A dive into the bumpers is a nearly guaranteed drain into the far left outlane... which then likes to launch the ball with brief ballsave each time.  At one point I had it do this 5 times in a row, despite my best nudging efforts.  It just... keeps... doing this.  In addition, shots that used to be pretty easy are now quite hard.  Shots that used to be quite hard are now pretty easy.  It's a complete mess.  But what the heck did anyone think would happen?  Different physics!  OF COURSE it's wrecked!Now, I will say, the actual NEW tables developed with FX in mind, are excellent.  Zen has a lot of business related problems.  But their actual table design skills have always been superb, and they've upped their game even further with the new tables here.  Seriously, they're grand.  Which makes all these other problems even more irritating as a result, since they're tied to this instead of FX3.ON TOP OF ALL THAT, seen some bugs and weird issues here.  Getting some major flipper lag, which actually wasnt happening for me before, not sure what's up with that.  Seen some outright glitches, like the menus getting stuck.  And so on.Visually, it looks... it's FX3 again.  I'm sorry, but even with RTX I cant really see a difference.  I guess the ball is a little more reflective?  As if I'm going to be noticing that during exciting pinball action.  UI is... it's okay.  Nothing really to speak of here.  The added bits, like the cosmetic stuffs, I dont really see the point of.  You spend most of your time playing tables, not in the funky room.  If this had VR functionality, then I could absolutely see that making sense.  Well, if it had VR functionality, my review would be a bit different.  That would have entirely sold me on it.  But it doesnt (yet Zaccaria DOES have it... make of that what you will).Just... uuuuuugh.  I'm torn on this one.  New tables are super.  Old tables are busted.  Bad business practices all over, but excellent recreations of real world tables.  Which you cant get all at once with the all-at-once pass.  And so on, and so on...Steam doesnt have review scores, so I gotta pick one or the other.  I normally try to be positive in my reviews.  But there's just been too much stupid with this one, and if I'm not being honest about how I feel about it, there's no point.  So I gotta point this one down.  Sorry, but that's just how it is, as much as I hate saying it.Doesnt mean you wont get some value out of it.  Maybe it'll be your thing.  And I'll still be playing it at least for the new tables... probably.  They're still good.  But let this be a bit of a cautionary thing... think before you buy into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing. I tried to see past what everyone said about "boo hoo, my tables won't transfer from the old game." Well, there's so much more to be disappointed with in this iteration by Zen, that I can't justify anything positive.- Flippers feel like wet noodles- Game plays fast and floppy flippers makes shots difficult- Tables look overproduced and cartoonish- Sound was unbalanced and not intuitive to adjust: Table speaker sounds were clear and high quality but I could barely hear the table (Physics?) sounds (e.g. flippers/targets etc.) even with "Table physics" turned up to 10. - Pop up scoring feels more intrusive than informative. No way to turn off? Only adjust limits so it doesn't occur as often?- Unless you buy tables to fill it, your "hub" is  cold and empty. (Which is stark contrast to the warm cozy feeling from FX3)The beauty in a pinball machine is being responsive and immersive and this version misses the mark on both points. _childDocuments_.review: First off, let me start by saying that I adored zen releases in the past, (mainly fx3, the deals they offered on bundles, ease of use and incredibly smooth gameplay) and ended up buying 99/100 tables, though I know there are more from lost licenses I was very pleased with the amount I spent. I never found Indiana Jones to be worth 3x the other tables, so I didnt purchase it. Then we get the announcement that a new, remastered game was coming in hot from Zen studios named Pinball FX that would be exclusive to Epic games for exactly 1 year. Here is where things started to go sour, with no option to move any tables or receive any vouchers from Zen to make the transition seamless. While I understood this gesture, I didnt understand why that also came with an awful version of the game, on Epic. Nearly unplayable. I accepted this and simply moved back to fx3, which I did not mind as I already had quite the collection of games to keep me busy.  Moving forward 1 year, we get the Steam release and to my incredible surprise, the game plays quite flawlessly albeit missing a native resolution (3840x1080, which worked flawlessly in fx3. 2560x1080 is the resolution I use in the meantime, which gives pretty significant black bars on both sides of the screen, and a slight downgrade on the resolution that shows a bit of jaggedness, no matter, the game still plays great). The game also now comes with an integrated orientation swapping setting, which is awesome and actually works on my screen, nearly looks like a full size pinball machine. So after exhausting my 1 day of free pinball pass, which is also a nice gesture, I looked to see if there were any options to swap my fx3 tables to no avail. Again, new engine, physics, graphics, which are all great, so I really dont mind paying for the tables I dont own on fx3 already,  HOWEVER, while this new version of the game is an incredibly well done version of what we have come to love over the years in fx3, I feel like it is pretty scummy to expect any sort of payment for tables that people own on your "abandoned" platform, fx3, in your new game, pinball FX. The people who would end up continuing to support your game into the future, are the same ones you are looking right in the eye and saying "pay again". No thanks. Great game, great remaster, awesome tables, scummy, SCUMMY tactics. I wont be recommending this game to anyone until they find a way to shake the hand of those who have supported their previous iterations for so long.Also, 100$+ for a year of Pinball pass? lol. At 5$ a month I think they would get a lot more looks.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: with the addition of Questlines and general bugfixes I can now recommend Pinball FX, especially during sales time.  There  still some features missing from previous Pinball FXs.  There is no Superscore, no rewind, and the unlockables / achievements are very limited and some don't even unlock properly. Pinball M's campaign mode (another game by Zen) gives me hope they will expand these features in the future. UPDATE QuestlinesBugs include extreme lag, frame dropping (like an entire second of missing frames which means ball drain), controller disconnects (not due to cable, and not able to reconnect in-game),  invisible objects, and broken / mishandled table modes.The physics might be a slight improvement over PFX3, as there some flipper techniques I can perform consistently now such as tap passing and live catching.  If I had to suggest one total overhaul / redesign it would be the camera.  Most of the 10 cameras are utterly useless, and the ones that do sorta work only work on some tables.  Half the tables I can't find a good angle and the so-called "manual camera" is a joke.  Make it like the Pinball Arcade where you have one button to cycle through about 4 different static angles, and forget about the dynamic cameras because they're impossible to use when you can't see the flippers. If I had one suggestion to drive incentive it would be to add a custom physics mode, and perhaps that could be opened up by playing through the tables and achieving certain score thresholds on the different game modes (distance, flips, timed), which don't really have much reason to be played at the moment.  Pinball M had a good idea tying them to in-game assets, but having a custom physics mode where you can play around with things like friction and steepness (see Zaccaria Pinball) could make customers happy as they could fine tune tables to their liking and maybe even start tournaments with them.  This could incentivize gameplay and experimentation, and be another big reason to buy more tables. I hope now that they have an abundance of tables they focus on consolidating their product.  It's certainly been improved since Early Access and I will definitely be keeping an eye on Pinball FX to see if this is the year it finally all comes together.
_childDocuments_.name: Pinball FX

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME! They've given the fan base the middle finger with their greed.I've been playing Pinball FX since the very first game, and I have to say I'm utterly disgusted by this entry. Zen Studios has long allowed your tables to migrate to the new version of the game, but they didn't do that with this one. Even worse, they've apparently jumped on the same subscription-service bandwagon that's ruining everything else on the planet. This is entry in the series is just a giant middle-finger to the fan base.In short - DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME, DO NOT REWARD THE DEVS FOR A GREEDY CASH GRAB!

_childDocuments_.review: **UPDATE 5/26/23**  Still missing the cup and collectibles.  Having more fun playing FX3.  The tables that are in both games run better in FX3.  **UPDATE 5/8/23**  I had a major crash after finishing a game of Marvel's Fear Itself.  After rebooting my PC, I opened up Pinball FX to find all of my collectibles and my cups reset.  I've reached out to support to see if there's any way to get these back.  I can get over re-earning all the collectibles on the tables I own, but it would really stink to lose all the collectibles I earned during my 24hr pinball pass on tables I don't own and my diamond cup from the Clone Wars Event.----------------------------------------------------I've been a big fan of Pinball FX games since the Xbox 360.  I've purchased tons of tables in both Pinball FX 2 and 3.  I've even doubled down on my purchases when I started playing Pinball FX 3 on Steam. This new Pinball FX adds a bit more bells and whistles to what I'm used to with the previous games.  Highly recommend this game if you've never owned a Pinball FX game before.  If you're like me and have purchased tables in previous games on multiple platforms, I'd say give this a shot for a few hours and then decide if you want to invest in another Pinball FX game.  There's plenty of tables that weren't available on Pinball FX 3.  You also get 24 hours to play almost all the tables as much as you want the first time you load up the game.  You can easily unlock most of the achievements during this trial.I'm glad some of the tables that were exclusive to iOS are now available to me.  I appreciate that I can buy a lot of my previous tables for a decent discount, but I'll probably wait until there's a better sale to buy more than the one Marvel pack I re-purchased for this game.  I enjoy the "one ball", "timed" & "distance" modes for the tables.   I also like the events and tournaments.  Most of the negative reviews on here seem upset that you are not given all the tables you've purchased in previous Pinball FX games.  I get that and that's why I'm not ready to invest much money in this game just yet.  Pinball FX 3 is still available to play, so I can always load that up if I really want to play one of my older tables.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, I was going to give this game a thumbs down, primarily due to the frustrating practice of overcharging existing users for tables they've already purchased. As someone who had bought every single one from the last instalment of Pinball FX, the thought of repurchasing them all felt like a bitter blow.However, playing the classic tables with the new physics engine gives them a new life, making me want to revisit them all over again. And the new tables are great. Let me be crystal clear: when it comes down to gameplay exclusively, this title stands unrivalled as the pinnacle of pinball video gaming. Its sheer brilliance and polish are truly worth celebrating, especially considering the niche nature of pinball video games.Despite the glowing aspects of this game, I acknowledge and understand the rationale behind the negative reviews. Many of the criticisms are justified and warrant attention from the developers. Additionally, while the bugs I've encountered during gameplay haven't been game-breaking, they're still worth mentioning as areas for improvement.In conclusion, this game evokes a complex mix of emotions – from frustration to admiration. Nonetheless, it remains a testament to the passion and skill of the developers, and for that reason, I recommend this title to pinball enthusiasts everywhere.

That alone gives me zero reason to move from FX3. I'm not re-buying tables I already own at a slight discount for a tiny graphical change. The UI also feels really clunky and cheap, reminds me of The Pinball Arcade.

_childDocuments_.review: Zen Studios is doing a fantastic job preserving the legacy of Williams Bally tables for people my age who otherwise would have never looked at these things twice. But alas, there are always those in the peanut gallery who can't wrap their heads around the concept of work costing money. "But I already bought these tables in FX3!" they cry, as if Zen Studios should just give them the tables for free after they spent time and money refreshing them and porting them to the new game (on a completely different game engine). They haven't taken Pinball FX3 away from you, go play the old tables on that game if it bothers you so much. Then there's the crowd who can't seem to grasp the idea of system requirements. They're out here in the steam reviews, bemoaning the "laggy" tables. I have every Williams table and about 1/3 of the Zen tables, they all run absolutely no problem. There is a section of these steam page called "System Requirements", give it a read before you write a negative review complaining about performance on this game that you probably spent $0 on. This game is fantastic, and the price model is very reasonable considering the amount of IP juggling that Zen Studios has to do. Don't pay for the membership or in game currency though, just buy the tables directly from the steam page, they go on sale very frequently.

name: The Crush House
detailed_description: Jae has scored the gig of her dreams as the producer on 1999’s hottest reality TV show, The Crush House! The demands are high and the stakes higher as she must cast, film, and produce each season. Play as Jae as you capture the budding romances and explosive drama of each unique season in the iconic Malibu mansion. And no matter what, remember to satiate the demands of your rabid audience or risk cancellation. Each season is unique based on your chosen cast and the ever-changing audience demands. The longer you manage to keep your show on air, the more questions start to arise. What's up with the cast's dependence on Crush Juice? Where does the Success Slide even go? Clandestine conversations and some good old-fashioned snooping will help you uncover the truth.. providing the Network doesn't get in your way. Cast For Each Season's Run Choose between twelve eccentric personalities and find your four-person cast for each season's run. Mix and match conflicting or complementary attractions and watch as tensions run and sparks fly. Quench Your Audiences' Thirst Everyone with a television watches The Crush House! From Foodies and Divorced Dads to Butt Guys and... Pharologists...? With dozens of micro-audiences to entertain, you'll have to be strategic to capture them all. Commercial Breaks Make Cents Entertainment as good as this isn't free, so set down the camera and pull up some tasteful TV ads now and then to bring the cash. Spend that delicious ad revenue each night on new furnishings for the house to mix things up for the audiences and the cast. Uncover The Mystery Explore the house at night while the show's off-air. Break the rules and engage in forbidden conversation with the cast to figure out the dark secrets of The Crush House!

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is great but after 1 season in game, you've seen pretty much everything and the game doesn't actually do a whole lot with the idea of filming a raunchy, trashy reality TV show. There aren't individual cast interviews, you can't really interact with the cast members other than doing "quests" for them, you can't influence how cast members react with each other, and you can't edit the footage you shoot in a way to boost viewership like you would expect a reality TV producer to do. All you do is follow around the cast members and film certain things in certain ways in order to progress. And sometimes it's unnecessarily difficult trying to film everything the game wants to you film in one day. What's worse is it gets really boring after season 1 because despite having 12 different cast members, you will see dialogue and scenarios repeated over and over. The game is more focused on the story but the story that is here is really paper thin. The demo and the trailers teased a dark and sinister "hidden" plot underneath the flashy reality TV show but it's kind of predictable and just not very engaging. Shame too because I was excited for this. Just wish they did more with the concept of filming a reality show.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: • • •  (thefizz.blog)•  After the first season, you've pretty much seen 95% of the dialogue. I don't really understand the point of having so many cast options when they have VERY FEW unique dialogues.•  Once you satisfy your audience, you just kind of sit there and wait for the day to end. There is literally NOTHING to do while you wait. It took around 8 hours of game time to beat the game but like half of that that was either waiting for the day to end, or waiting for the damn unskippable season finale dialogue to end. (which is basically identical every season...)•  You get a choice of two ending, both of which don't really resolve anything or answer any questions, and is instead mainly used as a teaser for the sequel or dlc.•  The gameplay is literally just pointing a camera. Once you figure out what each audience wants, it is just a walking simulator from each spot to the next, and waiting for the audience score to go up.•  Why pay $16.99 when you can just play the free demo and experience the gameplay & most of the dialogue for free? The only real difference from the demo and the full game is the cast options & the overarching storyline, but the storyline doesn't get resolved in either of the endings, and the cast members have VEEEERYYY little original dialogue, so it's just not worth it imo. I don't know, this one just really missed the mark for me. Such a unique concept, but the devs just didn't do it justice. It's a real bummer too because I've been excited for the release for a while. just play the free demo and save your money.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot in theory more than I do in practice. Really conflicted writing this review. The main game mechanic is not about interesting camera framing as much as it's about angling to have as many audience interests on screen as possible, which is fun in its own regard, but filming a fishtank, some art and keeping the camera still to rack up points does not feel that rewarding or entertaining. The props you can buy aren't as interesting as I would have hoped, for a second I thought there was going to be a full blown house customisation aspect to the game, but no, it's just there to make the game easier and unlock a couple funny prop exclusive scenes or dialogue.The writing is funny and charming. The way contestants go around the house and interact in a funny way felt somewhat like those 24/7 Seinfeld procedurally animated streams. The chat is also fun to read. After a few seasons though, about 3-4 hours into the game, it starts getting repetitive but the game keeps its momentum with the weird storyline and sidequests for a while. I wish there were more reality TV tropes like jealousy, cheating and eliminations. The game also could have been a lot more weird. I didn't find the twist or the storyline interesting. Such a fantastic premise, it hurts to see a lot of this wasted potential. I still recommend it. It's a worthwhile 6/10 game. I appreciate the creativity that went into it and live for unique indie gems like these.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept, but I was pretty much over it as soon as I completed my second season (about 1.5-2 hours in). I was already starting to see some repeated dialogue and fulfilling audience requirements just kind of devolved into aimlessly pointing the camera around, finding a triple to boost my score, and then repeating that over and over until I hit the daily goals. In seasons 1 and 2, I would clear my goals with plenty of time to spare and then just sit on ads waiting for the day to end because there was no penalty for it. By season 3, I was just reaching the goals within the time limit, which meant that I was barely making any money and couldn't afford props, some of which are required to complete character quests.I ended up turning down the difficulty to casual just to make sure that I had a enough money to buy things. Since I couldn't fail I would just sit on ads and wait for characters to do the thing that fulfilled their quests if I had any available. I just wasn't having a ton of fun playing the game on either difficulty by this point. And for some of these character quests, it's totally random if they'll do what needs to be recorded or not. Once I saw Alex, whose whole quest was filming him making friends with people, walk around the house and immediately make enemies with every single person, I knew my time with the game was up. I ended up watching the endings on Youtube and, while the game obviously goes in some interesting directions, I didn't really think the juice was necessarily worth the squeeze for this one. Big fan of Card Shark though (one of the dev's previous games)! Looking forward to seeing what you guys put out next.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I have my gripes with this game, I really wish it was more popular than it is. The setting is unique with an original style and interesting gameplay loop that feels like a strange puzzle. The story is clever with some surprising and thought provoking twists but not overly complicated. It is fairly short, I finished my first run in about 7 hours, and it does kind of dip in quality around the middle, but if this game was advertised better I could absolutely see a mad fandom forming. All of this is not to say that it's perfect, the gameplay rubs against the main selling point of recording your own Big Brother style show in that you need to focus on satisfying fans and thus your attention is pulled away from the actual interactions and towards whatever strange combination of decor, camera angle, and positioning would get the most viewers. Every character is fun, unique, and believable, but they clearly only designed one season in a game where a full playthrough expects between 3 and 5 seasons, so dialogue will repeat and interactions will be sporadic and buggy.One piece of advice if you do intend on playing this: If you are in it for the experience of running your own Big Brother style show and want to see the weird and silly character interactions, play on casual, as you don't even need to bother satisfying all the audiences. If you are interested in the strange and difficult gameplay of finding what will satisfy each audience and don't really care if Ayo wants to have sex with Milo or Emile or whatever, play on Normal. Do not play on Hardcore, there is no reason to and it is not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: While I thought the idea of the game was interesting, the art style is unique, and the storyline was decent enough to follow, once you understand the gameplay the game falls flat.
