_childDocuments_.review: My two cents, having finished the game, is that the concept is interesting and that the interactions between characters can be grounded and dramatic in ways that feel really spot on. - tl;dr -Yet, the game is opaque in a way that I wasn't prepared for. It's a game with secrets and to get the full story of the game will take more than mastering its mechanics. I'm still torn on whether or not that makes it something I'd recommend. It ultimately feels like an experience I'm deeply ambivalent about. There is a fun few hours in there, so if the core gameplay loop sounds interesting to you then go for it. It has a sense of humor and the archetypes presented in game really grab your imagination. - Detailed Review -From a story perspective, Danganronpa, Paradise Killer, or Zero Escape this is not. It lacks the world building, stakes, plot, depth, mystery, and sense of exploration that makes those games linger in your memory. Quite the opposite, it can feel random and repetitive at its worst. To be fair, I'm not sure it's really trying to be those games. It was just the impression I got from the trailers. The plot is vaguely mysterious but ends somewhat abruptly. Left with that it can feel rather disappointing, and that's where I was after finishing it once or twice. Having spent some time in the discussion section however has made it clear that there could be more secrets to be found.Some positives about the gameplay are that it does have some interesting systems. You aren't told what viewer requirements are but there is a mini-progression system where if you pay attention to the chat or the icons and their color (the latter of which isn't explained super well in-game) you'll start to pick up on what people want. Audiences are also fickle in ways that mean you have to mix it up and the process of finding the right shot can be fun. I also like that you have to be somewhat aware of the history of your characters during a season. If you want to film a breakup you have to remember who is coupled (the game does help you with this). There's also clearly meant to be a rhythm where you are sometimes recording and sometimes showing ads. Getting that down and trying to get enough momentum going to meet your goals while making enough money can be a fun loop. Also, while the overarching story is pretty thin, it is cool that the moment to moment dialogue of characters can sometimes feel like it's breaking the fourth wall. Though, never in a way that is consequential.On the other hand, while the randomness in character interactions helps mix things up, it also prevents the characters from feeling like they have much continuity. The per character missions help with but don't really address this problem. Across repeated playthroughs you hear verbatim the same conversation taking place but with the lines shuffled around to different cast members. Much ado is made in the marketing materials about differences in personality, but in practice this felt most often like being presented with variations in familiar conversations. In that way, comparisons to the Sims don't really feel appropriate. They also don't actually keep schedules or have totally consistent behavior, but more often feel like they are just moving from location to location for procedurally generated (aka random) interactions. I think this is because the game doesn't try to surface the interactions you need to check off your objectives. Sometimes characters ask you to film them doing something and then seem to avoid those specific interactions for the rest of the season. It means you'll sometimes just be running around looking for someone hoping that they're doing something the audience is interested in, or following a particular character who literally stands in place or walks between the same two locations and stands alone doing nothing (not doing solo activities, just standing there) which, hey...  might just be an accurate representation of what that job is like.All told the core experience is pretty short and can be finished in 4 or 5 'seasons' (each season is a week of in game time), so if you liked the demo and have 7 or 8 hours to fill then listen to your heart. Just go in with eyes wide open, with the knowledge that the narrative is obscured behind secrets that the community around the game has set itself to finding. If you want an ARG this might be for you. What's there to be seen is not entirely visible on the clear path forward the game sets which means you'll get out what you put into this obscure, satirical, and unique experience. For me as someone looking for a good story, it wasn't worth it to keep looking for hidden clues to a mystery that might not actually be a part of the game itself, but your mileage may vary. I recommend it with those caveats to show support for the core idea/gameplay loop, clever writing, and to encourage the devs to keep at it.

_childDocuments_.review: I so badly want to give this game a  positive review. I had an awesome time playing through the game the first time. The mystery was really interesting and I liked all of the interactions between the characters-- then, I found out that I chose what I saw to be the "wrong" ending. I had to restart the whole game, and it felt more like a chore because there was nothing new for me to experience... Only for the ending to basically be the exact same. It was so frustrating that I've refused to touch it since. It's one thing for the endings to be both negative-- but they were essentially the exact same outcome. I loved the vibe of it all, though, I just think that this game needs a hefty content update. I'd play again if there was more to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Crush House is a decent proof-of-concept game, and there's enough content on offer, but I feel this is a game I'd rather play the sequel to. It is, simply put, a bit too simplistic. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as it is a very accessible game; I don't want to harp on it for a lack of challenge, but I can't help wanting a bit more, and that makes me overly critical. So, let me start by saying it is just engaging enough, just silly enough, and just satirical enough to get you through each day and week, but its lack of larger strategic depth left me wanting to find more in the mechanics.For example, looking for shots that fill your audience's thirsts is a decent enough moment-to-moment mechanic, as different audiences like different things. Optimizing that requires knowing how to use the cast and set. However, there's no larger daily or seasonal strategy. You can choose to show ads during the day, but the most efficient way to do this is to complete your daily goals and then just run ads until the time expires. It seems the narrative is meant to do some of the heavy lifting, and that's the excuse for paper-thin mechanics. Still, if the satire is about the vapid nature of reality content, then why not ask us to manufacture drama for the sake of appeasing certain viewers?After all, there's nothing more real in the narrative than letting the player be the thing you are lampooning. If there were mandatory commercial breaks, perhaps you could coach the cast and try to set up scenes: do it wrong and you get an ad smack in the middle of premium drama, do it wrong and maybe nothing interesting happens. Maybe you could set up synergies between the ads being run and the type of viewers you are courting for the season. I'm not saying these are necessary; I'm saying that you can't play the game and not spot places where this stuff could've gone.Ultimately, the game is fine, but as I said at the top, there are a lot of places where you'd like to see the game go further, and because of that, it's a game I'd rather be playing the sequel to. I don't regret my time with it and would like to see it to the end, but I can't muster unqualified enthusiasm or praise for it. If "it's a slightly experimental, low-budget game about filming a reality TV set" doesn't rouse your interest, then nothing else I say will.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: The Crush House is a game with a major identity crisis, it's trying to be many things at the same time and as such falls short of securely executing any of the three.The first thing it is attempting to be is a Pokemon-Snap-like set in a reality TV house, which is a really great concept. You film the contestants in the house and try to meet various audience demands of what they want to see. However, because the game also wants to be a procedural Sims-like dynamic relationship system (see below) you can't always guarantee you'll be able to film a particular thing (for instance, no romance might happen if everyone is enemies that day). Therefore, over half of the audience demands are for completely static features of the house, like the plumbing or gardens. This is sort of funny the first time it comes up, it's silly to be filming a garden while drama is happening, but what ends up emerging is that for consistent results, you end up pursuing the static objectives (if you fail, you get a game over after all), and you mostly ignore the reality TV part of the game and just cycle through the same maximum-points generating spots/camera angles that you've discovered. The second thing it wants to be is a sort of Sims-like dynamic system where people fall in love, become enemies, and have silly conversations while you watch. Each contestant has a relationship with the others, and can be Enemies, Strangers, Friends, Flirting, or a Couple. There are several time-changes throughout the day where this can change, usually through a conversation. The game really cares about this system, and in much of its advertising really pushes the idea that you want to cast the show with certain personalities together that might meld or clash. Unfortunately, this does not really end up mattering and people will get together and break-up semi-randomly no matter what. The system becomes fairly transparent after awhile: the different characters have certain backend traits like "nerd" or "egotistical" and different canned conversations for different situations emerge when those tagged characters interact. I've heard the same breakup routine between two sets of completely different characters, the same flirting, etc. etc. Also because of the proceduralism, each relationship change is entirely self-contained. Nothing else that has happened in the house has any bearing on if two people stay together or break-up, which I suppose is a bit of the satire of the game. If it means to show that reality TV dynamics are thin, it certainly succeeds!Finally, the game wants to be a sci-fi mystery where you are discovering a dark secret truth. This is where the game truly fumbles the most. The way I've made sense of this is that this mystery element must have been added begrudgingly, because the game seems to loathe to interact with it or pay it off in any meaningful ways. I feel like the developers wanted to make a game that was much more of the first two concepts but felt a mystery was needed either for "depth" (which I disagree with, personally, I would have loved that game) or to make it more "Devolver"-y. I don't want to spoil the mystery here, but if you play and you feel excited or interested by the breadcrumbs that are dropped: don't be. Many things are never returned to, and the endings are huge fumbles of potential. There's an ARG element that I haven't interacted with, but I shouldn't need to in order to feel good about a game I've played, I'd hope. I would have rather there been no mystery at all and more energy put into the other parts of the game.I think this is much better as an art show/arcade game. Just have people play through one week, have it get increasingly harder and add in strange new audiences every time (there are a lot of fun ones the first time you see them!), and end it there at a tight experience. This is a game that's worth playing but absolutely not worth finishing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I was actually excited to play this game, as the idea of essentially being the one filming one of those cheesy reality TV shows was an interesting concept.However the execution leaves a lot to be desired. For example, there's a lot of "generic dialogue" that is just reused throughout the game. Essentially just changing around a few wording here and there to fit with each character's "personalities". (i.e making the "discord moderator" guy say "kitten" at the end of every sentence when referring to a lover). There not a lot of actual specific dialogue that pertains to certain cast members or their dynamic with each other.Which is just... Lame. Like I get that the idea is supposed to be "le epic deep and metaphorical story about the tv industry and how they manufacture these actors with 0 personality" or whatever but it's like it doesn't make for entertaining gameplay when you see the same repeated dialogue over and over again. (which I wouldn't be surprised if they literally just lazily used chatGPT to generate a lot of the dialogue with how generic it really is ngl)Another thing that is missing is there's no like interview system, multiple cameras, maybe like microphones, or other equipment to give the feel of this house being specifically a "set"I also really think this game would've been a lot better with voice acting, a lot of the jokes fall flat since you're not able to read everything the actors are saying because you're too focused on getting shots to boost viewers. (Which may be the point they were going for, but I still feel like that effect can be achieved with voice acting)Ok but all this complaining has been about the aesthetic and character stuff. What about the gameplay? Well... It's lame, you kinda just go around get in good angles that'll get the most "likes" from one of the randomly selected target audiences. There's no way to "anger" or turn away a specific audience other than just not doing what they want. A lot of the stuff that results in them liking you is through buying the various props around the set but the only way to gain money is through ads (which are done by just not filming). Why couldn't there be alternative ways of making money? Why not like product placement, I.e film a character drinking a specific soda or something and you'll gain some money from that or keep a company logo in frame and you'll gain a small but steady amount of income through that? Idk, all in all like the game's concept is novel and I like the idea. But its execution is just lame. It kinda reminds me of a less in depth version of the game "House Party" with less character, no voice acting, a lame filming mechanic, and less funny moments.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: The Crush House was my long awaited game of the summer. The drama, the art direction, and the premise really intrigued me. The colour palette of this whole game, and the characters are so colourful in personality. The dialogue is hilarious and familiar - it's that messy goodness that's found in reality television. Had a lot of fun with the unsolicited fights and sudden hook-ups! You can tell that a lot of research was made for the happenings of The Crush House, particularly the viewers comments felt very realistic. A few thoughts on the game  - the recycled dialogue between scenarios is personally okay with me, it gave me another chance to see the full conversation if I had missed it, or the answers would be different depending on the characters, but variety would be really great! I also wish you could review your footage by the end of the day, and see your work come to life. Finally, without spoiling anything, the ending didn't feel like one, and it felt more like a post-credits scene. I was really excited once the mystery was starting to unfold, that I somewhat wish there were a little more. I hope that there are plans to beef this game up, and I really look forward to its growth! All in all, I think The Crush House is a fun game to play particularly with your messy messy friends LOL. I will be running another playthrough! Let's get crushing!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I did have fun, but it felt really hollow at the end. It's been noted in most other reviews, but the gameplay goes stale pretty quick. It'll likely take you four to six seasons to beat the game, but by the end of season two you'll already have experienced everything the game has to offer, save for the story. Problem is, the finale is just a disappointingly cryptic ~30 second cutscene. There's enough kernels of enjoyment here that I'm at least hopeful that there are some post-launch tweaks that could improve the experience a lot, but currently I would tell most people not to bother.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: A great concept, but its execution is lacking. The game suffers from a lack of character differentiation, with characters recycling the same lines and interacting randomly. This undermines immersion and replayability.Suggestions:- Distinct dialogue and actions for each character.- Cast selection that influences the storyline and game dynamics.- A highlights system, where players can create episode reels and an end-of-season highlight reel.- A more engaging season finale, with the audience selecting a winner based on highlights or audience score.- A free play mode where players can cater to selected audiences each season and aim for a viewership high score.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is one of those games that's really trying to make a singular point with its narrative, mechanics, presentation etc.you start out genuinely trying to follow the stories of the individuals who enter the house, and by the time you reach the end, you will totally ignore them as you ruthlessly pursue the exact content your audience craves. I was very pleased when I realised I could film a solid black painting for a minutes at a time, because the motion-sick, art connoisseurs, and slow TV fans were paying the bills that day.cool concept, doesn't outstay its welcome and pretty compelling once you realise how it all works - recommended
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those "I wish Steam had a neutral recommendation" reviews - I just lean more negatively on it than positive. I'll quickly note that I am playing on the easiest mode, if only because I'd like to actually complete the core story. I actually like the easiest mode, but it does take the stake of cancellation out of the game entirely (again, not a complaint but noting for accuracy). TLDR - don't blind buy (unless discounted), I personally find the game too tedious. Game play wise there's not a lot of nuance. Pick up camera, film the cast you've assembled, occasionally throw in a dutch angle or a tracking shot to appease the cinephiles, and then rinse repeat until season end. You have a randomly selected audience to cater to and random events to go capture for said audience. It's a five day shoot with an extended going away day at season end. Oh, don't jump away from that end of season stage, because you will soft lock yourself and have to reload. In terms of construction...I mean it's beautiful to play. The characters have some decent dimension, but like reality TV you're watching hookups and breakups across the house and there's only so many ways you can stay engaged with that. There's a mystery, but you only get glimpses of it in during the first few seasons. The character designs really pop, and you're able to quickly read who everyone is within seconds of seeing them and track them down within the house. Each character has a mini task they want to accomplish, which of course can potentially conflict with not only your current filming shoot but future shoots as you may fail to complete their objective before season end. The music is notable, but deliberately background but you'll clock it just enough to know if the vibe isn't right. The negativity, and thus this negative review, is entirely based on how freaking   it feels. You cannot film every moment you want as you need to collect advertiser money to buy more stuff to fill the house which can only happen if the camera's not running. Almost everything at the house costs over five hundred dollars, with most of it being over a thousand, so you need to split your time evenly capturing the audience and then selling the audience. The audience profiles vary wildly - some are easy (feet pics, general voyeurism) while some are more of a stumble into it (glitches). In order to have the most success, you may have to leave someone falling in love to go film a plant to ensure the gardeners don't leave you or cut your filming day early and grind out ads. If you don't cater enough to advertisers, you don't get money. No money, no new stuff for the cast to do and things for the audience to see to increase their interest. Like if you have people who are fans of fish, and you don't own fish, you have limited options to collect their viewership. So it's not really "you are in control and this is your show" because you literally select four cast members and toss them in with a "let the chips fall where they may" attitude and likely an eye towards their lower back. I think it's a good game, and I think there's a very good chance that a lot of people will have a burning passion to 100% this game and will embrace it with open arms. That person just isn't me, and I will continue to slowly chip away at the story over time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kind of conflicted with the game. I enjoy it for the humor, drama and relationship aspect, and how each NPC interacts with another. But there's happening so much simultaniously, like the conversations, the comments, the challanges, it's tough to focus on one thing or enjoy a moment. And I found myself searching for the candidats, more then actually filming good content of them, let alone following their conversation and lore. I closed the game after one failed season, I was doing pretty good keeping up with the goals but getting stuck between furniture while filming or searching for candidats on one filming day, resulted in the show being cancelled, which was pretty frustrated. If I'll pick up the game again, I think I'll try the easy mode for a while, maybe that will bring the stress level down for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kind of confused by The Crush House. I loved playing it, even when it was a little gimmicky and hard-to-follow (sometimes, the game makes it really clear what you should be aiming the camera at; other times, you're just filming a juice dispenser and hoping for the best). The core gameplay loop is that -- you have some audiences with some preferences and you need to film what they're excited about. Sometimes, this means you're focused on the characters (or, concerningly, their feet). Other times, you're focused on props that you need to spend ad revenue to buy. The problem is, the "ads" system of the game feels incomplete. You just turn your camera off and the ads cycle and the money comes in, so for some players, a lot of days will be "enough tasks are complete; time to collect ad money until the end of the day". I feel like that could (and should) have been fleshed out more.Where I was really disappointed was the core narrative loop of the game. It kept building and building and building and then just kind of ... fell flat. It felt like there was supposed to be an Act III for the game that never happened, and that made me feel high and dry. I'm hoping I missed something or it felt like it would be added later, but honestly, I half expected a screen saying that I did all that I could and that the rest would come out with the 1.0. I don't mean that in a positive way. Plus, the game insists on locking you into the ending (you cannot continue doing seasons in The Crush House once you get to the ending), so I'd have to start a new game if I want to finish getting the other achievements. Doesn't feel great or fun.What I'd love to see:- Narrative conclusion / Act III- Overhauled advertising system- "Endless" mode where you can either pick audience type or numberI liked the game, otherwise, quite a bit (and was willing to overlook the things I didn't like), but the ending really let me down.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, the premise of choosing from a roster of eccentric personalities and throw them in a house together to try to placate different audiences who are looking for maximum drama is a very cool and interesting concept.In the end it felt like it was more about the "The Mystery" of the house, which isn't necessarily _bad_, but the gameplay was far too often encouraging me to leave my goofballs to film things like the pipes underneath the house. After enough hunts that didn't involve cast drama at all, it became clear to me that the game I wanted to play and the game that was made just weren't the same thing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I found the mystery and potential of this game really engaging, but unfortunately, I experienced significant motion sickness while playing. I made an effort to uncover all the secrets and endings, but I still felt confused about the overall story and conclusion. While the game shows great promise, I think it could have benefited from a bit more polish to truly reach its potential.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: August 21st, 2024 edit: Trying to read the dialog & the audience comments is nearly impossible at how fast they're displayed. Mainly because the conversational bubbles barely appear fast enough to read them if you completely ignore the comments, but then you miss the comments which is the audience you're trying to "quench". The days, interactions, and scenarios need to be slowed by at least half.Basically the games art style carries it. Each character repeats the same thing every day. As soon as I got attached to person A dating person B they were already over each other a few moments later. These build ups and fallouts should happen slower, spanning days or seasons.At the end of a season I went to film a finale and jumped because I thought I was stuck on something. Fell all the way off the roof to the pool, which I then had to figure out how to climb back to the roof wasting 6 minutes (your character is picky on what they can climb), because that's the only way to end the day.Your "reward" for finishing a season is non-existent and the money you earn is so non existent it'll take seasons just to buy a few things. I get this is sort of a way to have a progression system, but you want us to watch the same dialog over several seasons, to just unlock a tiki or a pool shower? Too add on, the cast isn't even that big either. It'll get bland after the end of season 2. Another weird concept is that the game paints itself as a "reality tv" game...but majority of it is filming the environment. Not people, or the few amounts of emotion they have.This game needs severe diversity in its gameplay, payouts/rewards, interactions, scenarios/story, & unlockables.This is an amazing original idea with a great color palette, that's failed terribly because of recycled lines, reused scenarios, lack of cast (add a character randomizer at this point because personalities don't really matter and it would add more characters) almost no interactions between the cast besides fight talk and kiss. With nothing to look forward to as a player after season one. Ads pay out, but at the cost of not getting footage meaning you risk restarting the whole day over adding even more repetitive gameplay to an already overly-repetitive game.I'm holding out hope because like I said, this is an amazing idea.As of August 12th, 2024 wait for a 60% off sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I stop filming the couple, who are in the process of breaking up, from the ledge. the libertarians have grown tired of watching fire so the shot doesn’t work as well anymore even at a dutch angle.today I am trying, at a cast member’s discreet request, to not film any butts. this goes in direct conflict with the audiences who only wants to see butts. hopefully tomorrow won’t have a plurality of demands for butts.the conspiracy theorists demand to see more chorby. I could change the tunes to something more romantic but then I’d lose the shot of the flirting duo I’m hoping to see kiss.hopefully someone wanders over to the kiss statue is so moved by art to kiss. if I can film one more kiss I might finish a quest and save the show from cancellation. chorby is watching, the audience is watching. time is running out. I want to go down the success slide. I want to go down the success slide.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited for this game, but now that I am playing the full version, I feel kinda disapointed.The demo rly made me excited for the game, it's just a neat concept that hasn't rly been explored in gaming to the best of my knowledge. Problem is: that is all this game kinda is, a neat concept.I played through one season and got into the 2nd one only to notice that I had kinda seen everything there is to see before I even started the full game, just from the demo.Just to give you an example: At the start of season 1, 2 of my characters got together around afternoon. When I checked their stats in the morning of the next day, they were enemys. If this was a one time occurance it would be one thing but it happens CONSTANTLY, characters switch form friends, to enemys to lovers at basically random. One could argue this is to represent the nature of these types of shows, but mechanically it just feels completly random, whcih I would be surprised if it isn't. Then the characters: their personalitys lead to a few unique voicelines but outside of their design, they all feel kinda the same? they have their traits describing them, but at the end of the day, they all seem to do the same stuff the roughly same amount of times, no matter of they are the "controlling savy businesswoman", the "conspiracy theorist incel" or any of the many other types, they all get into figths/relationships/deep discussions roughly the same amount of time and with everyone equally.Lastly, the actual gameplay: You need to satisfy multiple audiences each day, requiring u to film multiple things at once. An issue with that is, often times u r just screwed if the characters decide to not be in situations where u can do that. like, I had a day where my audience had plantlovers and friends of waterworks as my viewerbase, but because the characters didnt go to the garden or pool as groups, mostly discussing in the house I just wasnt able to fullfill my daily goals. If this was a one time occurance, I wouldnt mind but it happend roughly once per hour(I am not disregarding the possibility that I just got very unlucky, but it is the experience I had so far).Lastly a problem with the filming is that u r often times left with a rather bad looking experience on screen. Character dialogue will repeat pretty fast, at least the general gist of it, but since u need to read it while also focusing on other things, u will struggle keeping up with conversations anyway. The constant viewerwant to look at the characters from REALLY far away or tilting the camera a lot made for a bad visual experience as well.And some conditions can just outrigth screw u. I have a group of 1 girl and 3 guys on my 2nd season run, cus I wanted to kind of try a princess and her suitors kinda setup, but then the viewerneeds wanted girls on screen so I better hoped that one character aint just doin nothing for extended periods.So yeah, long story short, rly neat idea but very disapointed with the rather barebones execution.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable game with fun dialogue. Great aesthetics overall with the colours, characters and animations. I like the urgency of trying to please a weird mix of audiences. I would've loved for the plot to be longer or for there to be more tasks to help the cast!Some of the dialogue gets repeated each season (regardless of the cast selections) which is a shame, as I was expecting each run to be almost completely unique. One important question... why is the watering can $700? I'm poor!!!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: So I wanted to give this game a thumbs up but I can't do that. I love the designs, I love the colors and I love the idea but here are the problems. First off, there is a lot of repetitive dialogue and that in turn makes the character feel dull. They’re all supposed to be unique but they repeat the same dialogue as other characters. Second, the mystery they have ends up falling flat. It’s an interesting idea and I love a good mystery but I was left disappointed. Nothing was explained. But the biggest issue has to be the endings. I won’t give spoilers but they both felt underwhelming. All that build up and both endings felt rather lame.I’m hoping that the developers make a sequel that’s better or update the game because it’s bursting with potential. It’s just missing a little something.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a little bit of a steep learning curve if you play on the game's recommended mode, since it took me awhile to figure out that recording the cast is less important than finding shots that can min max audience ratings. You as the player are somewhat at the whims of RNG as some audiences are easier to please or synergize better than others or what furniture you happen to have. So if you're thinking this game is like the Sims you're going to be disappointed. However strategizing which props to buy, doing the side quests, and creating routes to maximize yours scores feels very fun. Not to mention the game's humor, compelling story, and unraveling the mystery of the Crush House.if I could change a few things I would like to make the days last longer so the game feels a bit less frantic each run and I can follow what the cast is saying, currently I feel like I am missing jokes. I would also like a feature that lets you have some control over the audience you get. Maybe you could be able to lock an audience in if you've fully satisfied their crushes. Enjoyed it can't wait to finish it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: Is the Crush house fun? Yes (it's a hilarious concept!). Is it well executed? To a degree; it looks good, and it's entertaining. However, as others have mentioned, the immersion for the cast is broken when they reuse the dialogue. I've had several different cast members behave the exact same way and say the exact same things, which makes me feel less excited about the replayability or running different casts. Their breakups and friendships also seem super random and not really related to previous actions, which is meh. I'm not sure if that's something that can be fixed, so I enjoy it for what it is. But if anything, the devs really should've put more love into making each character an individual and having more interactions where we can influence the cast and affect the series/show (think of the show UnREAL). Summarized: good concept but a lot more could and should go into it.Also, a pet peeve, but audiences shouldn't ask for cast members that aren't even cast for the season! (Wine moms asking for the French guy when he's not in the season doesn't make sense).(I've played the demo as well.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I gotta be honest, this game sucks. While a cool idea, actually playing it is both incredibly painful, boring, and confusing. Despite what you may think, most of the time you won't even be filming the people because the arbitrary audiences want to see the lighthouse, water, and chill views. The people themselves act incredibly randomly, become friends one moment, then lovers another, and then suddenly enemies, each from a single interaction.From the three hours I could stand, the gameplay loop had become running around filming whatever random stuff the randomly selected audience groups want and the moment I hit the quota I just run ads for the rest of the broadcast. The game will also give "optional" tasks to do various things that vary wildly in difficulty from buying multiple expensive items, filming a single person for several minutes straight, or filming a person exercising for a few seconds. From what I can tell, doing these is required for progressing the story.Some additional nodes. There is an option to remove the quota, but at that point it's barely a video game and might as well load up The Sims and watch them do their thing with no input. Most of the audience categories are self explanatory for what they want, but some are confusing. For example, the only thing I could find that gave points towards libertarians is filming tiki torches. For some reason, when you meet a quota in one category, if you keep filming it you get points spread one to one (rounded up) across all of your other unfinished quotas, making the whole system feel kinda pointless to me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: While I have enjoyed the game, its hard to recommend. I have been having constant performance issues in this game unlike anything I experience in games that are much more taxing on my hardware. Basically any time anything new is loaded the game stutters, and that happens a lot (time changes, new dialogue starts, even switching tabs in the menu). The core of the game is quite enjoyable to me. There are some rough patches, it feels like sometimes you can get pretty unlucky when it comes to advancing the story, and some audience requirements are super annoying. You will see repeated dialogue, but I don't know if that's as much of a problem as people are making it out to be given the story the game is trying to tell. I think without the performance issues I've been running into I'd recommend the game, but do know the gameplay loop is repetitive and the objectives of the game will take you away from just filming a reality tv show.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I thought this game was really fun.  Both of the endings amused me and made me curious if they were intended for hopeful sequel bait, which I think would be cool to see since I'd love to see a sequel that builds on the formula they created here and improves it.I love that this game brought what felt like a totally new, hilarious and sometimes surprising experiences!  I enjoyed finding ridiculous ways to get extra points from different camera angles, etc., some of which were absolutely absurd.  LOL.I understand some people find the later gameplay loops a drag, but I personally only ever found the final day of each season a drag and wish there was a way to speed up the process of the dialogue before everyone hops into the slide!I strongly recommend this game for the 2024 Sit Back and Relax Steam Award!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: Like a lot of the other reviews, I'm conflicted. The concept of the game is 10/10, I'm so in love with the idea that I bought it day one after playing the demo through multiple times, and for the first couple of seasons it really lives up to the promise. But it doesn't take long for things to get repetitive. The conversations are canned, so pretty soon you know exactly what everyone is going to say. The groups you make don't really change the dynamics much.All that said there are some great bones here. The idea is great, the twist is fun (if a little shallow), the audience comments and the ads you play are funny, the graphics are cute, and the gameplay loop itself is fun. 6/10 unless an update changes things, get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: To be clear, I think this is a great game and I enjoyed watching a streamer play it. However, I encountered game breaking bugs like 10 times in the first half hour of play and had to restart each time. Menus like the computer/bed wouldn't open and lock me out, making it so I couldn't pass time. Transition screens would stall and not change. One time the cast just stood around and did nothing with time not passing. Another time, the day passed the moment it started causing me to "fail" lol.I want to play, but I guess it's not possible for me for some reason? Obviously other people don't have this problem so who knows, but I'm not going to sit on it and miss the refund window.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: game menus freeze constantly. in the one hour i played i had to redo the intro 5-6 times because it wouldnt let me do anything after completing the first day. the cast interacts once or twice and then they stand on opposite spots on the map walking around randomly doing nothing. feels like im playing a demo that wasnt even good enough for release. 0/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not what it seems-- even more than it lets on. The gameplay itself is very fun and at a good difficulty level-- I like finding strategies to get all the audience scores filled on time. The writing is hilarious, the art style is adorable, and the mystery element is very intriguing. I love the characters and their designs.I'm also loving the ARG aspect
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I have been really looking forward to this game, but it doesn't really live up to the expectations I had based on the demo. I enjoyed the core gameplay loop presented in the demo, and I was looking forward to seeing the mystery subplot and gameplay further develop, but it never really goes anywhere exceptional.By season 3 I had cast everyone once, and I don't really feel compelled to try a bunch of different combinations of those cast members, as a lot of the dialogue and scenarios are extremely repetitive no matter who you have cast. The core gameplay loop also felt repetitive at this point. I was hoping the mystery plot going on in the background would be enough to carry it once the gameplay loop started to feel tired, but it's a pretty weak plotline. One of the final audience types introduced in season 4 was borderline impossible for me to please, and at this point I was struggling with some combos of audiences and meeting the requirements. I get that the audience system was introduced to add more of a gameplay element to the concept of 'reality house producer', but it becomes way too much of the focus and the cast interactions feel secondary, which is unfortunate because that was the main draw for me.I didn't experience any bugs really, but frequently I would go up to cast members to film them and they just wouldn't interact at all. Overall, I think it's still worth a purchase if you enjoyed the demo and concept, and the price is good for me so I'm not going to give a negative rating, but I definitely enjoyed it less than expected and my interest started waning after ~3 hours of gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game that takes place over 5 seasons of a reality show. The dialogue between the characters can get a little repetitive after a few seasons, but it steadily amps up in difficulty in regards to appeasing your audience. The good news is that remembering to buy furniture and buying the prompts will help you get passive audience happiness as you move around the house. Good game, fairly okay to 100%. If you finish A's story first, you can get both endings without having to replay the whole game from the beginning. If you do B's ending first, though, you'll have to start the whole game over for A's ending. Just something to remember if you're looking for both!

Luckily they included a casual mode for players like me who don't really enjoy a challenge in their games.The writing, despite being limited in dialogue, is all very funny and the hidden plotline seems intriguing, I'm sad that I have no interest in continuing the game for now since I am interested in seeing where the story goes.I wish I could give this game a neutral rating instead of positive or negative. _childDocuments_.review: I was VERY much looking forward to The Crush House being released - I loved the idea, the vibe, the gameplay concept, and I loved the studio's previous game too, and was excited to see what they would do with such a wildly different premise than their last game. And because of this I had very, very high expectations for this, and because of that was a bit scared that the game would not live up to these expectations, or not really be what I imagined it would be. And I can definetly say: not only did this game NOT disappoint, it was even better than I thought it would be.I need to preface this by saying that started the game, very shortly before midnight, just to see how it played and then maybe continue the next day, and was so engrossed that I played it until 5am in the morning, when I had completed the full story once. And I still wanted to keep playing.The Crush House works like this: You pick a cast for a season, you film them interacting or you film whatever your audience wants to see (some people dont actually care for the people, but for stuff like the drainage system in the villa, or fish or pretty plants in the garden and so on), and while you are not filming something, you send ads to get some money, and when a day is over, you might want to buy some upgrades to the house to force certain behaviors from the cast (want them to excercise to cater to the fitness freaks watching the show? then buy them more sports equipment). You need to get through a week, while audience requirements become harder to meet, and then you either succeed or fail at the season. And while you progress through a bunch of seasons, a narrative outside of the reality show starts to unravel, which gives the game a bit of a horror / mystery spin, without distracting from the glitzy, reality show side of the game. I don't want to spoil too much on that side, but it also adds a layer of depth to the game that I think is very appropriate for a game that makes expoiting people for views it's main mechanic. Visually, the game looks so good, the mechanic is super fun and innovative, the game is super well-polished, and the narrative The Crush House presents is really intriguing and there are so many tiny bits and pieces to it that are so enjoyable to see in the game. There are so many small features to this that all just work SO well together - the audience chat is a great feedback system on what to film without being too cryptic or too straighforward; the target audience's desires are very varied and make you try to come up with strategies on how to statisfy as many of them at once; tasks, that directly contradict what "fun TV" amounts to, which makes the days a lot more challenging; the layout of the mansion, which is super easy to learn and which you can do so much with and discover so much about; the game's character dynamics; the incredibly hard-hitting and profound moments that cut even deeper because of how shallow and glitzy the surface of the story is, and while not all the humor of the game landed with me, I did find the game incredibly funny and charming to engage with.I think there are some combinations of audiences you can get that are a bit annoying to statisfy (e.g. the "rich people" audience can be very annoying to please if you dont have a certain cast member in the show and haven't bought any "expensive" upgrades), and since some other audiences are super easy to please in turn, it can be frustrating to get a lot of target audiences that are very hard to please. Admittedly, this game is so specifically designed to include everything I personally latch onto in games, so maybe this is not the game for everyone, but this is totally your game if you have a morbid fascination with celebrity culture and reality TV, like narratives that are very casually queer-inclusive, and like a bit of a dystopian mystery, that still has a strong enough gameplay if you're not in it for the story. Also, I need to say that I loved that this game's easter eggs were all nods to small, mostly very unknown indie titles, instead of the same slog of pop-culture references that people usually use, which made recognizing the references absolutely insane. Seeing the other reviews - what surprised me was that a lot of people were annoyed at repeating dialogues and the main mechanic of filming the cast becoming repetitive after a while, because for me the game absolutely evolved after a season or so, when I stopped even really listening to what the cast was doing because as you continue to play the game, that becomes less and less the focus. I'm not saying people are wrong for that being their experience, but I don't really see the game to be about that at all, to be honest, so it makes me a bit sad that the game has so many negative reviews. I think if you imagined this game to be different than what it turns out to be that can be pretty disappointing too, but I personally really enjoyed playing it, and it took me 4 seasons to get through the story which I found to be a really good amount of playtime to not get tired of the gameplay. So like I said, I don't think this game is for everyone, but it sure is ABSOLUTELY made for me, so 10/10, one of the most fun games I played this year so far.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the concept of this game and was excited to try out the full version. It's quite a novel experience that satirises the Love Island-style TV shows with an underlying mystery/dark twist. You have to satisfy a large collection of audiences that want to see specific things each day, and this can be quite hard (but I actually found the middle part hardest, as by the end the larger audiences will feed off each other and you also have more useful props). You get to choose your own cast and they will interact in different ways. I think the game has a pretty cool and colourful visual style and a good soundtrack. The character designs are also very unique. Unfortunately, I just wish it was reflected more in their dialogue. After the first season, the whole process began to get old as I found cast members saying very similar lines and interacting in similar ways, despite me anticipating the difference. Don't get me wrong, they do have some original lines to themselves, but there's too much repetition in my opinion. Especially since the game literally requires you for any ending to go through it a certain number of times - it's not like I exhausted every possibility here. The thing that was motivating me to keep going through it was the aforementioned mystery, which I was really interested to find out more about as a big fan of story rich games. I won't give spoilers here but the ending I went through left me feeling like I was missing out on a big part of it. It's fast and there's a lot left unsaid. Also, the particular ending I found myself in, I was locked into that choice and it seemed my only option to explore other paths was to restart the entire game again. If I'm being really dumb and actually missing the next part or something I would love to know. But I had a quick look online and it seems others also feel this way. As it stands, it's a fun game but I wouldn't recommend it right now - but there's no reason this can't change.

_childDocuments_.review: in this game you play as a producer for a reality dating show. the idea sounds really fun and the art style matches the tone it was going for. The main issue i came a across was game play. game play basically consist of "record the actors and make sure you satisfy your viewers. if you don't then your show gets canceled ". It was fun in the beginning until it got a little complicated. the main issue i had was figuring out what viewers wanted. at first it was "Crush Fans" so naturally you just recorded the people talking. next was cinema buffs (or something like that). that took me awhile since it basically meant messing with the camera angle to satisfy them. i thought "i'll let it slide, seemed simple enough" and went on with the game. ill also add that you do get to choose the people that stay there so that was cool 👍. anyway, the other viewers request we're harder to figure out .If you don't know what the word "Voyeur" meant you were kind of on your own. if you did, you would have to figure out that you would have to film them from afar. Which i think defeats the whole purpose of recording your actors and hearing their tea and what not. Next i got was "landscape lovers". i literally just had to record random plants (kid you not). This is fine but i also had to record the actors from afar and for some reason NO ONE went into the garden. next i got "House Moms". still don't know what i had to do for this. What makes these worst is when you check the pad, they don't tell you what each one means or how to achieve them. also small bug, when you get into the thing the guest enter/leave the house from, you get stuck (this ones mostly for the devs). _childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the crap out of this. I beat the storyline in a weekend, which isn't so bad for the price point. The element that both defines and sometimes confounds this game is that you're supposed to focus less on filming the reality show and more on filming whatever the audience is interested in, with your success every day determined by how many audiences you kept happy. Which sometimes is normal things like the cast fighting or kissing, some are a little more specific because they just want to see feet or butts or men pumping iron, and other times you're literally filming a solid black painting so the motion sick audience members don't puke. If you fail, the show gets cancelled. Early on you have smaller groups of audiences and a little wiggle room to not please everyone, but this ramps up with each season and seasons are only a week long. At first its fun to see how many of these combos you can rack up at once as the game greatly increases your satisfaction points for each audience you can please per shot, but in the later stages of the game you're asked to please as many as 8 audiences and you're at the mercy of the RNG to hope there's enough crossover between them to actually achieve success. I ended up restarting a lot of days by season 4.Storywise, It might be better to call this a cross between a reality show and FNAF given the way it drip feeds story details to a random employee who has to keep the increasingly shady operation running and doesn't truly resolve all the mysteries, in a way to convince players to talk about the unresolved threads amongst each other and build lore. The cast members aren't deeply developed but the story is less about them and more about the increasingly disturbing world that you realize they inhabit. There's a couple of endings for the game that can't really be called a good or bad ending, just different endings that fill in different parts of the lore. In fact neither ending is truly conclusive, in the sort of way that DLC could build off of, but I wasn't upset. They made sense for the game and deepened the mystery. I'd say the biggest critique of the game is it can get repetitive but its not a super long game if you chasing the storyline so it didn't bother me as much because by the time I was getting weary of it I'd made it to the finale. If a DLC dropped with more options, yea, I'd pick it up pretty right away and dive into this world again wondering what else was humming beneath the surface. As it is, I may end up picking this up again and trying the hard mode or to complete the remaining character quests or even just to dig into the clues to the storyline with fresh eyes. But for the price point... its well polished, I only hit one progression bug that required me to reset a day, it oozes with style, and it kept me interested long enough to actually finish it which I am notoriously bad at! Just the kinda indie game I'm into.

_childDocuments_.review: My best friend and I were very excited for this one and booted it up to play on Discord together a little after launch. What we found was a really surprisingly disappointing mess of counter-intuitive writing and game mechanics.Every time the "Production Assistant", who is off site the whole time for some reason, nastily tells you what to do as "Producer", my blood boiled. The game has the roles incorrectly reversed, which is one of many ways it seems to not understand its subject matter or structure even a little bit.The mechanics are poorly explained and implemented. The game does not know what a good angle or shot actually looks like and will actively pressure you into making crazy unwatchable decisions in camerawork. Then it will reward them and punish most things that are actually way better in comparison. As someone who has done live film work professionally and *doesn't* actually expect this game to fully simulate that, it was still so frustratingly unfun for that core gameplay to feel so backwards.Another annoyance is that you, as the "producer" (really the production assistant) have to buy props for the set at INSANE prices ($800 for a plain watering can??) OUT OF YOUR OWN PAY. They didn't even bother writing the much more plausible scenario of the show getting a prop budget after each episode's ratings cashed in... You also have no door for your room, which irked me, and there is a weird mix of cool retro tech and lazy hologram pokeball things that really take away from the charm.I hope the devs continue to work on the game and fixing its issues because the premise is so interesting and unique. But as it is now, I unfortunately can't enjoy or recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a neat concept and the game is fun, however there are a few things that have put a damper on that fun for me. If I could leave a neutral review, or a 3/5 stars, I would. 1. Motion sickness, I can only really play for a few in game "days" before my head starts getting the best of me, even with the settings adjusted. If you have difficulty with motion sickness associated with FPS type games, this game might not be for you. Especially because some audiences require you to move the camera around quickly/zoom in-out/twist the camera in odd angles. 2. I love the concept as a whole, but it's frustrating that the camera isn't as sensitive to the scene you're shooting. For example, you might be trying to make the plant lover audience happy, so there's a plant in the video shot which should make them happy. However, sometimes it won't register or it will register for one +1 score, but then never again. I get that you have to change things up, but when you can only get +1 for certain things, it makes it hard to earn a happy audience. Which also means it's hard to maintain a "ON FIRE" shot, because sometimes the camera just randomly decides to no longer register that a certain item/effect/whatever is in the shot, like a plant/art/fire/water/etc. 3. Tailoring ads to your audience isn't well done. And honestly, I'm on the second season and I barely have free time to play ads. But you're suppose to be able to switch between ads based on what viewers you are catering to, but this is done by basically just switching between all the ads in a row that you've unlocked. Kinda tedious. Tailoring ads gets more money, and since that doesn't work effectively, and since there is little free time to have the camera off to roll ads in the first place, it's difficult to earn money in order to buy new props. Which means that most of the characters interact in a pretty similar way every day. **PS. I think there is a "free play" mode/difficulty in which the show can't get canceled and the focus is more on the story. I haven't tried this mode yet, but maybe that would be more fun since then there is less hassle about filming just right and earning money. Again, I haven't tried this mode yet, so idk exactly how different it is, but wanted to mention that it existed.

_childDocuments_.review: If an indie game has a seemingly happy, fun, and exciting veneer you know you're in for a twist: actually there's something really weird and disturbing going on.In The Crush House you're producing a 90's dating show where four singles get together and make friends — or enemies. Producing means you film the show trying to capture moments the audience wants to see and run ads whenever you can to gain funds to furnish the titular house further. A season lasts five days, each day giving you a chance to not only film the show but to complete quests the participants give you. Everything is pastel and everything is sort of a joke. That's how you know something dark is gonna go down.Under the hood The Crush House is a pretty systemic game. The audience reacts to things on screen and by showing a certain segment a thing they like you grow their level of satisfaction with the show. Satisfying three or more segments simultaneously sets the show on fire and the viewers start to feed on each other. Trying to please as many segments as possible at the same time and trying to find ways to abuse the system is a definite higlight of the game. Some people watching have funny specific needs such as the Butt Guys, Libertarians and Plumbers. Getting to frame someone's ass (Butt Guys) while they're next to a Tiki torch (Libertarians) and squeezing in a corner of the pool (Plumbers) was always gratifying.As fun as abusing the system was, I found myself pretty quickly trying to do things as efficiently as I could. I would quickly max out every audience segment's need (thus making sure the show doesn't get canceled) and then just run ads the rest of the day. This would net me enough money to always buy what I wanted. With the audience being random every day things never got stale and I always had to do a lot of thinking to find a way of pleasing everyone fast.About that dark twist, I think we've all been here before. The participants are actually clones and the show has been running in a loop since god knows how long. It's implied that after every season the clones get squashed into Crush Juice which is then consumed by the next season's singles. The player character is a clone too and your original (as the game calls the people who are cloned) is responsible for all the weird stuff. The game has two endings which seem to be almost the same one with a hint that this is not the last we hear of The Crush House.

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable game. Interesting characters, a fun premise, and a delightful twist (though, an obvious twist). The mechanic for the game itself is interesting as well, acting as a random generator for several minor AIs. It's fun to watch them scatter around the first couple of playthroughts, involving themselves in various relationships. A few negative aspects do tarnish the game: There's no real way to rewind or prevent progress, the game can get a bit stale after a few runs (though, that's partially the point), and the ending leaves a lot to be answered. My biggest critique would be to allow the producer to affect the goings on with the "stars" a bit more. It can get frustrating when you're stuck with a load of bad viewers and have to watch the shrubbery for five minutes. Regardless, I enjoyed my time with it.  A fun little puzzle, and a game I would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: So once you put together the design choices that went into Reigns, Nerial's really great series about keeping a bunch of progress bars balanced, you start to see the cracks in this  a *good way*.The trailer doesn't do it as much help explaining the game play as just experiencing it does. You don't control what happens, you *watch* what happens and try to line up the shots to include all the details you need. Suburban Moms watching? They love the contestant Emile. Movie Buffs? Dutch that camera angle. Libertarians? Yep, they watch too. And everyone's got different needs you can hit and MUST hit to fill up their progress bar each day. Don't hit the goals? Game over, do it again but with slightly altered audience. Or just change the difficulty and enjoy the ride.Now that the true nature is laid a bit more bare: this is a great game. A clever matrix of character interactions means that each cast set is guaranteed to behave in some unique ways with each other, and I wasn't able to predict who would go where, do what, talk to who, at all. It kept the experience fresh, you start to connect to certain characters episode after episode, season over season, and when it clicks it clicks hard. Failure just means trying again, not a big deal when the days aren't too long, and the overall flow of the game is pretty fun.That being said, I can already feel myself begging for more. An additional 3 contestants. Additional scenarios. A scenario EDITOR, UGH. Gimme the keys. This feels like it could expand out into something near endless with how the dialog system works with the audience system and filming. I really dig it, and I _don't_ particularly care for reality TV. This feels more like I am working to make the  show, rather than sit back and watch it (which you also do plenty of).Overall, a thumbs up for Nerial and Devolver here. Fun to play alone, or on stream with friends!

_childDocuments_.review: Truly unique gameplay with fun writing and tons of charm! If you love film/photography you will probably love this game. There are a few issues that will probably be ironed out in a few updates, but I'll throw them out here! Information Access- A few mechanics are not elaborated on much or at all- Like jumping. You can hold the jump button to charge a bigger jump and you will grab onto ledges and edges if you get close enough. This is really helpful in getting high-angle shots in more than two areas (and getting out of the pool). Audience retention is also something that wasn't really elaborated on- I was panicking when I couldn't please an audience that was impossible to please with my cast that season, but they left and got replaced with an audience that was much more manageable. The only COMPLAINT I have is the audience hints. Some of them are so incredibly vague and can only be guessed at, and if you do guess it... the game doesn't tell you the specifics. For example: It would be a nice reward to be able to review your audiences and see the portrait of their favorite character or the specifics of what kind of shot generally works with their requests after you complete them, or to be able to pay money to get another hint or example shot. Currently you are just given the hints on what each audience wants in a shot and how many times you've filmed each. Story- The game does NOT elaborate on one detail- it is VERY timed with a definite end.  to be specific. I wish there was an endless mode or that you could choose when to initiate the endgame just for a bit more time to try out certain combinations or interact with every character a bit more to make the endings hit that bit harder. It's long enough to meet everyone, but I don't know if it's long enough to know *everyone*.Repetition- If you play in one long burst, you will find that there is a decent amount of repetitions. The game is somewhat procedurally generated so arguments and relationships can occasionally be near identical, but most characters have unique interactions with most of the cast as far as I've seen. This can help keep gameplay reliable (if you need to film someone becoming enemies or friends, relationships very rarely stay stable for more than a day or two so you won't have to start a whole new season for one quest) but I could see it getting a bit stale after another play-through or two. This also makes any quest that doesn't rely on capturing relationship based very easy in comparison and anything relating to RNG sometimes a bit frustrating. . RNG can also just give you some losing days if you are playing above casual. I personally am worried about this the least as it's probably the first thing that would be added in an update. Overall I'm more than happy with what we got and I'm going to do another run or two to grab all the endings and learn a bit more about the cast members I only really saw once.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and interesting concept. I've heard some complain about the repeated text, however I feel like when you're working hard to get all the right camera angles for the audience, you end up not keeping up with the text and not seeing the full conversation until later (but perhaps that's just me). I do think some repeated dialog outside of the cast could be updated (Ex: The person who talks to you on the walkie talkie could say more than the same exact dialogue every time). I will say unfortunately I kept running into glitches and performance issues when playing. On the steam deck it works great but on my super nice computer, for some reason the performance is bad where it lags and skips frequently. Glitch wise, to avoid spoilers, I attempted to get a certain ending and the game just kept me in limbo the first time. The second attempt, it just didn't register my action and I had to start again. To be more specific: SPOILER  I'm hoping I'm not completely glitched out of finishing the game. TLDR, great concept, fun after a while but could use some spruced up dialogue and the glitches/performance needs to be fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: For the most part this game is pretty good. I enjoy repetitive gameplay so it worked well for me but I can see it getting a bit boring for others. I think the difficulty increase from week to week is well paced and I enjoyed the puzzle of figuring out what specific thing some of the audiences wanted to see. I do think that the audiences themselves aren't super well balanced, some of them are incredibly easy to please while others are near impossible without bending over backwards, so sometimes the randomly selected audiences you have for the day just leave you screwed. I did enjoy the underlying story, it added a great extra mystery to everything. Maybe I'm just stupid but I found it hard to follow at times. I don't think I really ever fully understood what they were talking about or what the *thing* actually was that was happening, I wish they'd been a little more clear. Also the very ending was a bit of a letdown, I feel like they set up some really cool concepts but didn't really finish them off well. Was a little disappointing.Overall though, most of the issues with this game can be fixed with small tweaks if the developers wanted to improve it so I would recommend it. A good game to get on sale maybe

_childDocuments_.review: Crush House was not the game I expected but I enjoyed it a lot anyway. While the character design is great, the focus of the game isn’t really on the characters but on the live-recording gameplay and the pleasing of the audience. I was a bit disapointed by the interactions/relations between the character which feel a bit messy and repetitive, but I was pleasantly surprised by how fun the gameplay is. Figuring out what each audience want is a nice puzzle and it created a lot of very silly situations that cracked me out. Also the art is gorgeous, but you’ve already noticed that.

_childDocuments_.review: The Crush House nails everything it's shown off: the believable-yet-satirical procedural conversations and subsequent relationships, the silly filming challenges which can be at times fairly difficult, and the task-oriented gameplay of combining a diverse cast of attention-seekers in order to illicit the widest variety of interactions from them. It's only unfortunate the game doesn't evolve much beyond those things.For my money, getting exactly what I expected was plenty and it all landed very well! Figuring out how to appease each audience, especially when opposing audiences like "wholesome" and "wine moms" would show up, was compelling from a social engineering meets framing puzzle perspective. Those challenges take up most of your brain after a couple seasons (when playing on Normal) 'cause you've just got a *lot* to do to hit your goals. Between trying to setup camera shots you get the bits of conversation coming through which highlight how bonkers exactly what you're filming (and why you're doing it from inside a well) is. All the characters are great and while they do seem to share dialogue along shared traits at time, I've many times seen a the same line result in different outcomes due to who was involved (or what came before it). So, I do very much recommend this game as I had an excellent time with it! But I think the idea is so incredibly strong and trashy reality dating TV is so well-known that the shortcomings in terms of scope are apparent especially if you're really into the premise. All that to say: temper your expectations and you'll have a lovely time breaking hearts at The Crush House~
_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.name: The Crush House

_childDocuments_.review: If Content Warning was set in the Sims...As someone who played through the game nearly twice now, I love it! I really enjoy the running around, trying to find the perfect shot and decoding what the audience wants to see, all while slowly unveiling the strange hidden meta! DO NOT go in expecting a visual novel or something like House Party, Crush House is more like if Content Warning was set in the sims. In a way it's almost rouge-lite, if that helps contextualise the gameplay. I got my enjoyment out of the management aspects, such as making sure there is the correct prop in each shot depending on the day's audience more than reading the character dialogue.Overall I think a lot of the negative reviews look like they came from people expecting a different game entirely. But to me, the game is well made and fun for what it is! I would recommend playing the Demo if you're on the fence and see if it's meant for you before buying!

detailed_description: Everyone in Dokapon Kingdom loves money. One day in this peaceful land, monsters suddenly appeared and began attacking nearby towns. The economy collapsed, and people were at their lowest. Taxes were no longer being paid, of course. So that's when the King took action! He decided to gather the bravest warriors to rescue these towns so he can get paid! In exchange, the one who collects the most shall be rewarded with the Princess' hand in marriage and the throne. And thus, an adventure for money begins, where absolutely anything goes! Key Features RPG & Board Game Lovers Unite... AGAIN! Originally released for the PlayStation®2 and the Nintendo Wii, the hybrid party board game is back! The game is simple: spin the roulette and defeat whoever stands your way! Connect With Your Best Frenemies Online Holding a grudge never felt so good! Players can now duke it out against their friends all over the world! 5 Game Modes & A Massive Game Board! Plot your revenge and choose from 5 different game modes: Normal, Story, Shopping Race, Kill Race, and Town Race. With a kingdom spanning seven continents, who knows what shenanigans you'll get into! Outwit Your Foes With 11 Possible Job Classes Wanna slash your way through the Dokapon Kingdom? Choose the Warrior! Interested in conjuring flashy spells? Pick the Magician! Choose from 11 job classes and earn experience points to level up your character! Purchase or even steal items and use them to your advantage!

_childDocuments_.review: Dokapon Kingdom is a fusion of classic JRPG, Mario party, and Monopoly. Rather than mini-games Dokapon focuses in on the sheer chaos and malice you can bring upon your friends by stealing their items, raining fireballs down on them from above, killing them and changing their name to Poopy McButtFace.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings out the demon in everyone. Your entire goal is to be a crab in a bucket, dragging everyone down to your level. Then, once you are at the top, you are like a Boomer in the housing market, kicking everyone down beneath you while you tell them it's their fault for being in poverty and referencing how you "picked yourself up by your bootstraps" despite the fact that you faced no economic pressures like your lessers. Just when you feel like you've been down on your luck for too long, a little demon comes and literally sits on your shoulders, telling you to dismantle the establishment board by board, leveling the playing field and draining the 1st placers of their 401ks. And to what end do we attack each other? For what cause are we pitted against our friends in order to rise to the top?This game is an allegory of real life after all. You must amass wealth and look better than your friends so that way you can be spared a singular scrap of coochie. Nothing gives a lady the ick more than showing any weakness, and Princess Penny will only accept the richest and most successful man in all the land.

_childDocuments_.review: Dokapon is peak, but this version is flawed.Instead of making a proper PC port they just three out the switch version on here and allowed you to remap the controller. All graphics still are Start, A and B buttons like on a controller, they dont bother replacing them with your keys. So you can forget comfortably playing this without a controller. You cant even use your keyboard to type, you need to navigate with the arrow keys and put in a letter with E. There is no borderless fullscreen option. 50€ might be an adaquate price for a game like this on the switch, but on PC this should be 30€ at an ABSOLUTE maximum.I really love the console versions of this game, I really do. But I can't in good conciousness recommend it in this state. I hope the developers fix this to let people on here enjoy this masterpiece without any flaws.If you still want to play this then go on, I'ts not worth it if your friends don't want to play this, and I doubt that you will ever find a random online lobby.
